It really is difficult for me to recommend or NOT recommend a game that is fun and great, if its story arcs are left unfinished after credits start rolling. Obviously there is going to be furure DLC incomming to keep the story going, however, this is a review of the game I bought, and is therefore not taking any DLC into consideration. THIS is what you get from buying the game:
- First things first: This game ends with almost every story line(main and side missions) unfinished! There are lose ends all over the place, so if you are expecting an all-around finished story of epic proportions, like Deus Ex and Human Revolution had, Mankind Divided is going to disappoint with leaving close to all of its story open. So if experiencing the story in its entirety is mandatory for you, be prepared to buying DLC in the future, because the game on its own does NOT deliver it. At all. Really. It just ends, with only a minor plot string resolved.
- One 'story' hub where side missions take place. It is split into two parts, and traveling in between those is always connected to a loading screen. The split is kind of annoying in times, because missions tend to make you go from one to another, but it's probably necessary from a developing point of view. Nothing too bad or really terrible - just a minor annoyance every now and then.
- Boss fight was really well done. Way more flexible than Human Revolution did it.(I only encountered one - if there are more, I managed to skip those by dialogue. Which would be a GOOD thing, since I like playing Deus Ex focused on stealth and social interaction)
- AI is nothing overwhelming. Be prepared to encounter shop owners that don't even care about you hacking into their computers or basement doors, when doing so right in front of their noses. No calling for help, no panic, no alarm, no attention whatsoever. Only guards and police care about that. But shop owners? Nope!
- Story might be left open ended, but I DO have to underline how well it is written. It kept me playing and entertained, so on those terms it keeps up with its predecessors.
- Game length is shorter than Deus Ex or Human Revolution. It is still ok for its price though!
- Sometimes the game crashed on dialogue sequences and I failed to figure out the reason(PC version). There are other people experiencing this, however they appear to be a minority. Also - while it WAS annoying - I still like the game a lot. It offers tons of weapons, alternative routes, explorative content, stealth passages. It felt exactly how a Deus Ex game is supposed to feel.
Would I buy the game again?
No - because I expected its plot to be told entirely, without leaving me hanging. I can still recommend it for those who don't care about that. Story is all I am not agreeing with. Everything else is fine! I will give a thumbs down however, because I would never support a game that is so obviously shoving DLC in my face. Here is what I would support: Release a finished story line, and add DLC focusing on side missions or about "what happens in between chapters" or "shortly after ending". Important part is: Make the main story line feel complete in itself.

I definitely recommend this game. Compared to Smash Bros, this game may not be the most similar, or the most interesting, or the most diverse alternative, but it is definitely the most fun.
The moves are tied to the weapon the player is currently wielding, which is obtained as an item pickup in-game. The "quick" (A) attacks of each weapon are the same for everyone, but the "heavy" (B) attacks are unique to each legend. If not wielding a weapon, you may fight unarmed or use other item pickups such as bombs.
Pros:
-Brawler (Smash Bros) Gameplay.
-Very accessible, you can just jump right in.
-Skill-based and fun (most of the time) gameplay.
-Each legend has 2 weapons, which means 2 movesets.
-30 legends as of Feb. 2017, each with their own signature moves.
-10 weapons as of Feb. 2017, each with their own movesets.
-New legend every 4-6 weeks, balance/skins every week.
-New weapon every 4-6 months, along with a new legend.
-Constant updates with a dev team that listens to the community.
-Free2Play and for once actually not Pay2Win. At all.
-There's a button that says "GG" into the chat at the score screen.
Cons:
-Can be frustrating sometimes, leading to a salty community.
-Only 10 weapons means only 10 movesets, aside from sigs.
-Gameplay can get a bit repetitive, best played in short bursts.
-Laggy depending on where you live.
(I live in NY, USA and very rarely have lag problems)
The game is F2P with a payment model similar to most MOBAs (heroes bought with either in-game gold or real money, skins and cosmetics bought with real money, weekly free hero rotation) so there's no reason not to give it a go and see for yourself. Even if you're not a fan of Smash Bros, give it a try and you may find you like it.

The artworks for that game are absolutely gorgeous, some of the most beautiful pictures I've had the pleasure to see in a videogame. Wouldn't be surprised that David Revoy was influenced by the works of Michi Himeno. Most of his stuff is in the screenshots of the store page. Out of all my Steam profile backgrounds, his geisha is probably my favorite. I didn't craft it, so I had to buy it. That's how much I like it.
Also, the music is pretty good. Uninspired, but good.
After the first couple of minutes though, the rest of the game is a real chore. First, there's the absolutely useless pseudo-city builder that forces you to go through bad animations of monuments in construction. Then there's the characters... Ah ah. Even if you don't know a thing about Japanese culture, it doesn't take long to realize this is all a big pile of cliché crap. They could have changed the setting to any other time period, any other part of the world, without needing to change much.
All of these things could be forgiven if the gameplay was any good. But it's also just as boring as the rest. It satisfies itself with copying the mechanics of a few other popular match-3 games, doesn't add anything new, the sprites are terrible (there's a reason most match-3 games use plain, simple and well differentiated graphics for their jewels/tiles: if they're readable, they don't get in the way of your actual matching prowesses), and there just isn't any feeling of 'power' when you match a large amount of tiles at the same time. Each puzzle is unrealistically hard in 'normal' mode, you'll need to play in relaxed mode, and even with this, it still takes 10 minutes or more to finish even the early puzzles... Not that they're hard: the game just expects you to play endlessly and enjoy it. On top of that flawed design, these phases are badly programmed (first time in years I've seen a jerky 2D rotation on my computer!), and overall the game probably has a budget close to zero... Heck they didn't even purchase a Unity3D license so you have to go through the default Unity launcher every time you run the game... That works for free games, not this.
I don't mind low budget. I REALLY don't. I mind the lack of care and passion. And those are crucial to the success of games, even those with such a small scope. Some games will add new ideas, others will bring a thoughtful implementation. There are just so many better similar match-3 games to play, I can't recommend this one. Off the top of my head, 7 Wonders II and Heroes of Hellas 2 & 3 are ten times better. Just check my review list if you're into those.

Tales of the Orient: The Rising Sun is a match 3 game with a little story and objectives. If you often play match 3 games, you might know that there are several types of match 3 games. This game actually has 3 types: swapping tiles (known as swap mode in the game), chaining tiles (chain mode), and popping tiles (pop mode). The great thing is, you can choose which type do you want to play and it won't affect the game at all.
There are 100 levels in total, although you can replay the levels after you completed all levels.
The graphics in this game are beautiful and they pictures the traditional japanese style very well.
I absolutely love the music. The music will reminds you about the traditional japanese music and it matches with the graphics.
The story in this game is quite simple. It's just about you who wants to rebuild your own country. After you complete a level, you will obtain some money to build buildings and sometimes a new objective which will ask you to build new buildings.
There are 2 difficulties in this game: Challenge and Relaxed. In challenge mode, you have to finish the game below the set amount of moves, while the relaxed mode will allow you to finish the game regardless of how many moves you made. Another great thing from this game is, you can switch between the modes whenever you want (even in game). The challenge mode is quite difficult and/or time wasting at later levels, and it's good that you are able to switch them.
There are 4 power-ups in the game, which can be unlocked after you build a certain building and can be activated after you match a certain tile in each level. Besides the power ups, you can rotate the board (either clockwise or counter clockwise) and manipulate the tile order as you wish. There is also a shuffle option which will be recharged in a few minutes which, of course, will shuffle all tiles in the board. The thing is, you can basically use shuffle to reorder and matching items in the game to use less moves in swap mode, making the challenge mode to be "wait for the shuffle" mode if you are quite unskilled/unlucky.
Pros:
- 2 changeable modes
- 3 choosable match 3 style game
- Powerups, rotatable board, and shuffle button to help you finish the level
Cons:
- Challenge mode at later levels can be quite long (because of waiting for the shuffle button)
It's a match 3 game with lots of helpful features. You also can choose which match 3 modes you want to play (swap, chain, or pop)

Infested Planet is a great singleplayer RTS where you control a handful of mercenaries and their toys to defeat
millions of aliens. Because of the big contrast in numbers from both sides, you have to outsmart the AI, use chokepoints and carefully plan out your route to conquest. This makes it a challenging game, which makes it very rewarding when clearing a level.
A great feature in Infested Planet is that you earn points from capturing enemy Hives, which you can spend on more toys for your guys. The best part is that you can redistribute your points at any time: this means that if a tactic is not working, you can fall back, reclaim everything, redistribute your points and try again.
The game has a 30 level campaign (17 story missions and 13 random missions); 5 weekly challenges at different difficulties, where you can compete with other people to get the fastest time; and a random map generator where you can change almost anything: from the number of Hives, the powerups (mutations) the enemy has, how much resources your team has, the difficulty and many more. This means you have endless fun despite being a singleplayer.

Infested planet is a nice twist to the RTS genre. This time around you get small squad of tough guys and need to fight thousands of insecoid aliens. The closest thing I can compare it to would be perhaps Terran vs Zerg in Starcraft, but taken to extreme.

The game mechanics are very well designed, missions are tough, especially later in the campaign, when aliens play all the tricks in their arsenal and you reallly need to adapt your strategy as the situations changes.  On the other hand you can make your life easier by playing some optional missions to earn cash. You can do it as many times as you want and then spend the cash on bonuses that will help you beat the campaign. An extra flamethrower or even additional rifle marine can be priceless. What is great about the game's design is that it allows you to recycle the resources you spent. This means you can try different things and if you make a mistake or circumstances changes in a way you couldn't possibly expect, you can still correct it. Well, you can at least try :-).
This is an indie game, done by a small team, so don't expect fancy graphics. What you'll see is clean & readable. For me that's perfectly fine.
The only real problem I have with this game is that it crashes to desktop on my Mac  from time to time. It doesn't make the game unplayable, but it's annoying.
If you like RTS-like games you should try Infested Planet.

A real-time tactics game where you control a small squad of marines and need to decimate a couple of thousand aliens.
The challenge comes in is that as you take over portions of the map, you gain resources to build more stuff, but the aliens gain "mutations" that give them extra powers and make it more challenging.  The end result is that the game starts easy and gets progressively more difficult as the game goes on.
The game is a tactics game, not a strategy game, so there's not much in the way of resource management or base building -- it's all about efficient usage of your few marines.  The game is also pause-able, and you can give orders while paused, so there's no requirement of fast reflexes or decision-making.
All in all, the game has a very satisfying level of difficulty, where it is hard enough to be a challenge without being unfair or impossible.  It also encourages experimentation with the various options, since any resources you spend on something will be refunded if you decide you no longer want it.
Each "mission" runs for 10-40 minutes or so, depending upon your aggressiveness and speed of play.  There's four tutorial missions, a campaign mode of ten pre-set missions, options for random missions of various difficulties, and a weekly challenge of four different missions with a leaderboard of who can do each one the fastest.
If you enjoy blowing up endless streams of aliens, or enjoy tactical squad-based combat, you will enjoy this game.

This game is a real treat for fans, but anyone expecting top-tier hack-and-slash action or deeply compelling original story or character content may be disappointed with the short, surface-level excursion provided by this game.
Early release price points and lack of content were also a bit of a sting, but when you consider that this started as a one-man fan project and then became Rooster Teeth's first official game, it's easier to look past these first-timer flaws.
And heck, as an obsessive fan of RWBY I will happily support the studio by purchasing and enjoying any and all current and future DLC.
Update: As the dust settles I can more candidly say that it lacks the substance you might assume there would be from an original storyline and original voice acting and so on. The DLC costumes are nice at times, at least until Pyrrha's split dress is flapping like a flag in the breeze of Grimm-slaying. Thank goodness for Monty's patented anti-upskirt technology, because even Jaune needs it here. All in all I would have liked to see a few things after the official release:
- More updates and fixes (still a number of bugs that require a restart - Phantom Grimmace anyone?)
- More/specific character interaction (rather than generic "you're the best teammate ever!" remarks - considering they had the original voice actors I find it strange that they don't specifically talk to each other in game)
- A revamped ranking system with tangible rewards (a badge next to your name is hardly worth resetting all your stats to grind all over again)
- PvP
- More characters (wishful thinking)
- More variation in battle types/terrain (put us in close quarters with an Alpha Beowolf, or more multi-layered levels like the underground bomb track where you can jump down to get Dust and so on)
TL;DR: A VERY short but moderately fun game for fans and the forgiving.

A pretty awesome, fast paced fighter in the style of the smash bro's series. I saw it at first as 'one of those smash bros clones' but to my joy, found it to be really well executed. and to top it off, the ranked community is usually insanely friendly. The devs also are involved and care about most of the players suggestions.
This game revolves around each character having similar movesets aside from signiture moves and stats, meaning some are better designed for speed and assault, where others may be insanely good at defending and edge guarding.
The game consists of many weapons that each have different movesets(they have the same moveset shared across characters when using light attacks) each character or "hero" has two that they can pick up from weapon pickups.
Some weapons include:
Hammer: High force and range, it's stuns last for quite a while too. Unsure about it's throwing capabilities but I think it has a lot of force if it hits
Sword: Light attacks create huge arcs and can be used quickly to punish players.
Spear: Can be thrown pretty well due to it's large hitbox and increased throw force, pretty versatile weapon that allows you to use moves that have quite a bit of priority if used right. Most hero's signatures with this involve dashing forward or spinning.
Gun: A weapon that has incredible range and a fair amount of damage, however the hitboxes do not protect the player against very close enemies. One strategy is to pivot around your enemy and pop shots at them.
Bow: They have a large amount of diagonal attacks and can combo pretty well, a large range and momentum gain too.
Rocket lance: amazing for defense. Mainly horizontal charge attacks. I don't know too much about it, rarely use it.
In short, I love this game. It's free, so theres no harm trying... Unless you have RSI.

This game is the sequel to Torchlight: one of the first RPGs I bought on Steam. Torchlight was a rather firm RPG, dungeon-crawler experience with a pretty yet cartoon-esque art-style. It was a decent game, however Torchlight II is much more than that.
When you first click that 'new game' button when you're in-game on Torchlight II you'll instantly notice one of the biggest differences this game has from the original. You make your OWN character rather than picking from one of three already made characters that you did in the original. However in this game, you pick from one of four classes: the Berserker, the Engineer, the Embermage or the Outlander before customizing them cosmetics-wise to your pleasure.
PS: There are still pets and you AREN'T merely limited to a dog or a cat. There are many other types of pets you can own in Torchlight II.
the Berserker plays as the melee-type DPS class, usually being the main source of melee damage. They tend to wield violent and threatening accoutrement. However, they might be rather brittle armour-wise.
the Engineer I would like to call the sword-and-shield-type Tank, who tanks most of the damage and wears the most reliable and elegant armour.
the Embermage is your obvious Mage. I don't know much about them, yet I guess that the Embermage plays as the Healer/Mage of the crew.
the Outlander is the ranged-type DPS (they also use a tad bit of magic) who tends to stay back from the action yet still deals a healthy amount of damage.
The other new big feature in Torchlight II that you may or may not notice is the fact that you can play the game alone or multiplayer, with up to six friends/strangers (LAN/system link or online).
Anyway, now lets talk about the actual gameplay.
Torchlight II plays extremely similar to the last game and keeps the rather easy difficulty (unless you bump the difficulty settings up to veteran or over, which you'll get the option to do once your character is created).
However, instead of progressing down 'dungeons' like in the original Torchlight, almost the whole game is played outside in a forest to a desert and occasionally a dungeon.
You could call Torchlight II very similar to Diablo, except a little bit more of a 'kids version' without the intrepid difficulty (again, unless you bump the difficulty up on purpose) amd the cartoony graphics which most computers could probably run.
The combat is rather basic, but as you get later into the game you'll unlock skills which will create more eventful scenarios for combat. You're given three skill trees depending on your class and when you level up you're given five attribute points to pump up either your characters Strength, Dexterity, Focus or Vitality.
When you level up, you're also able to upgrade/learn an additional skill on one of your skill trees. It's recommended to stick with one skill tree rather than building up all three, so browse for the skill tree you like the abilities of the most before randomly dedicating a skill point into an ability.
There are many bosses in Torchlight II, all are rather enjoyable and interesting to fight except perhaps a few.
The storyline of Torchlight II is rather enjoyable (yet predictable) but I wont spoil anything, in case you were worried. Talking about the storyline, the three playable characters from the original all make a rather large amd noticeable appearence in Torchlight II.
And finally, the music is pretty good, but it's not incredible. It's about a 5-7/10. (Keep in mind I can't remember it too well, but from what I remember that is what I think about it.)
Anyways, I recommend Torchlight II with a score of... 7/10 which is a great for me. There are little flaws with it, but it's very 'typical RPG'. It doesn't really dish out anything new. But if you're a fan of RPGs or have a few friends to play with, I 100% recommend this game! For 20$ (£15 or €20) (t's just about worth it for the price, especially if you're on a hunt for RPG games!
PS: Torchlight II has 100% mod support!

- Overall very good, the same as the last one, but still with some contrived design decisions.
The latest incarnation of Deus Ex is just like the previous games in the series, especially when compared to the last one.
It’s lost the annoying boss fights from the last game (except for the final mission) where the bosses were just not balanced. This game feels a lot better balanced and I never felt I was out-of-my-depth, apart from the final boss, but more of that later.
If you’ve played previous version then you will know what to expect with weapon upgrades, hacking and skill upgrades. It has the same game play approaches to stealthing or going full guns blazing.
I should say I played using stealth and did all the side missions (I think). This amounted to around 30 hours of actual gameplay. I think when adding in load times, pausing and reloading saved games ever time I died it ended up closer to 40 hours, but actual progress was around 30 hours.
I also played using a controller, which works well, so I can’t comment on how well the game plays using mouse and keyboard. You run at a decent pace, even though on occasions I did look for a sprint button.
I didn’t buy this with any pre-orders, nor did I use any of that nasty pay-to-win exploitative microtransaction nonsense. Which leads me to wonder why there are micro-transactions or those pre-order items. None of that seemed important to the game, so don’t let that stop you enjoying this game. The design hasn’t been compromised by the inclusion of said micro-transactions. The game seems well balanced that you don’t need to spend extra money to complete it, certainly not on normal difficulty. The inclusion of microtransactions says more about Square Enix/Eidos as a company rather than anything bad about this game.
All-in-all the game is good, ignore the haters that are down on this because of their pre-order woes. Don’t pre-order from Square Enix.
The extra Breach Mode is your typical free-to-play nonsense and has no place in a full AAA priced game, again this is Square Enix being the money grabbing gits they are. Also I haven't bothered with any of the triangle codes you can unlock and scan using your mobile phone. I suspect this is just a way for Square Enix to farm your personal data.
The story is pretty weak and doesn’t feel like it resolves anything. You would expect a lot more to happen in 30 hours of playtime. I got to the end of the game and it just felt like I had done one chapter of a book. Where is the rest of the story? If they keep the story plodding along at that pace and release a new game every 2 years the story might be concluded sometime in 2030.
Although I enjoyed the game there are some issues, which almost all come under the “We’ve made a load of very lazy design decision because we can’t think of anything new to do”.
As examples of this:
You can steal everything not nailed down. There is no concept of stealing an item like most RPG do these days. In one obvious case there was an NPC sitting at a table with a credit chip right in front of them and I just took it without any consequence. Really!
Most NPC stick to the spot and don’t move around. It really doesn’t make the world feel very alive.
Some systems that can be hacked feel like they are rigged to always be detected.  The detection percentage is ignored and always starts a trace, even if the percentage is as low as 15%. I tried multiple times and a scan was always triggered. The only way around it was to use a stealth program. That feels very fake and really doesn’t sit well. This could of course be caused by a bug and isn’t the intended way the game should work.
NPCs fires loads of bullets but only have 5 rounds left when you search their inventory. Also guards that like throwing grenades aren’t actually carrying any when you go to search them. That’s a very contrived way to balance a game and something I would expect from 10 years ago but surely we can move on from that and make things a little more realistic and try not break the immersion into the game by using such fake mechanics.
The final boss fight is just plain silly. All other characters are taken down by one tranquilizer dart but not the final boss. I put around 30 darts into the guy before I won. That was just stupid and breaks any suspension of disbelief I had. It never felt like his battery was ever running down and he able to use his augmentations without restriction. It totally breaks the rules of the game.
Also, alongside the final boss, droids will continuously spawn no matter how many of them you destroy. Normally using Smart vision you can see dormant droids sitting inside the walls waiting to be activated but not in the final area. They just appear and there seems to be no limit to them. Again this just breaks all the rules previously established in the game.
For example it would of better if the boss was the only other NPC to have the experimental titan shielding and tranq darts can get through it, thus making it not so easy to take him down with one shot. Also Emp should prevent the boss from using their Titan shielding. There should of been a better way to subdue the final boss that was telegraphed properly to the player, rather than break all the gameplay rules that had already been established. This just demonstrates the complete lack of thinking and laziness of the designers.
Overall a very good game, but it would of nice to see some new game mechanics that didn’t break the immersion into the game and dropped the old formulaic design tricks that most games have moved on from.

Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons is a game where you follow the story of two brothers mourning the loss of their mother and trying to save their ill father. The gameplay is very unique, using either side of the controller to control each brother, with plenty of puzzles to solve as you progress through the game.

Short and sweet, the kind of game I wish they'd make more of. Likely to be over in less than three hours, but without a moment of filler.
"Brothers" fits in the "Lost Vikings" tradition of puzzle games featuring multiple characters with unique powers: here, an older brother who is stronger, able to pull levers, carry heavy items and safely wield flaming torches; and a younger, who can fit through narrow gaps. The novelty is that both are controlled simultaneously, one with each stick (a controller is required for play), so puzzles are also games of coordination.
What makes it magical is its richly-realized -- and surprisingly, shockingly dark -- fantasy world and its painfully effective character development.
It's also a game worth playing as a masterclass in the use of game mechanisms for narrative impact. The very way you control the characters will influence how you feel about them.
It's one of the best games I've ever played, but not at all for reasons of its "gameplay" per se -- it's very short and very easy and it's better to think of it as a sort of interactive animated film. As that, though, it is superb.

This is a tough one to review. If you enjoyed the gameplay of Human Revolution, then this one has got the same gameplay but refined and expanded on. You can shoot or sneak or hack or whatever you want through the levels, which have also seen a huge improvement over Human Revolution.
But it's strange. After finishing this one, the first thing I thought was "wait, that's the end?". Many different plot threads are left dangling, and the ending of this one is clearly setting up for a sequel, if not many sequels. But the main PLOT of this one loses focus. You are given a somewhat cool villain, but he receives next to no buildup, and beyond ONE conversation with said villain, you never engage in a dialogue battle with him, you never learn the greater plan behind his actions. It's just left dangling. I read a review recently that perfectly summarised this - this game feels like the first episode of a potentially great TV show.
In saying all that, the side missions were cool, with some really interesting stories being told in them, and the gameplay of TACTICAL ESPIONAGE ACTION was great fun. Particularly challenging, but rewarding, is ninja-ing your way through every mission, without killing anybody.
The extra DLC crap surrounding the game is obviously ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
In summary - good story that loses steam (hurhur) and is left wide open (too open) for a sequel with an unsatisfactory end. Great (for the most part) side missions, and fun stealth/action gameplay. Dodgy publishers obviously trying to take a hot♥♥♥♥♥♥on an otherwise great game.

I'm a big fan of the previous game Human Revolution. I feel it came close to capturing the awesomeness of the original Deus Ex. This game I think I can say the same thing about, although it does most things better but a few others worse than Human Revolution.
The side missions are far superior for starters. Even better than the main story, with their only downside being that they are understandably short. The overall lore learning is still just as great. Dialogue is better I feel. Nearly all random npcs will have their own 2 unique lines of dialogue, in contrast to the previous games where said dialogue was often repeated among the random civs. There's also more named npcs you can have conversations with.
The overall gunplay is better. You can mod them as usual, but now some of the weapons have different ammo types. There are regular, EMP, and armor piercing. It doesn't make much of a difference in the long run, but variety is nice. There are a few less weapons, but it's not a huge deal, as long as the next game gives us more. You can also upgrade weapons, but with the exception of ammo capacity it didn't seem to make much difference.
Choices matter much more in this game. You will see more reactions to your choices from characters, including certain side missions being available based on your choices. The ending is also better because you get to see the consequences of a few of your choices, which is much better than Human Revolution's generic endings.
I like how energy is a single bar instead of multiple cells. It can regenerate the whole bar too, but as usual using certain augs drains the max value of the bar.
The new augments are really cool but they're also really overpowered. Especially the nanoblade. It 1 shots most enemies at a huge distance and is nearly silent. Get the explosive upgrade and it can 1 shot multiple enemies close together. Titan Shield is fun because it makes you nearly invincible. Icarus Dash is fun too.
From what little I've played Breach mode is pretty fun. You go on mini-missions in a VR type thing and earn credits and better gear. It's separate from the main game, but you can unlock Praxis Kits which can be redeemed on a single save file in the main game.
Jensen is apparently an alcoholic pill popper. Alcohol, pills, and hypostims are the only way to restore health. There's like 10 different kinds of alcohol but no food like candy bars. It's just funny.
Nothing against the characters, I just didn't find myself connecting with them like I did in Human Revolution. I liked interacting with Malik, Pritchard, and others. I didn't really care for anyone here. More opinion than anything really as the characters here were fine otherwise.
The one that will probably bother the most people is the fact that there's only 1 hub in the game, Prague. Human Revolution had 2. I think this game makes up for it because Prague is so HUGE. I spent about 15 hours exploring it and doing side missions before ever entering TF29 headquarters. Still, location variety would have been nice.
I'm not a fan of the fact that health will fully regenerate eventually. There's even augs you can get that make it regen faster and such.
People have claimed the game is short, taking 20 hours to do everything. I suppose that's true if you do almost no exploring and sprint from objective to objective. However, it took me a solid 45 hours to beat the game and I looked nearly everywhere and did all but 1 side mission.
People say the story is incomplete. While this is sorta true, it's not what you're probably thinking. What needs to get resolved is resolved (essentially you save the day). But the overall big shadowy bad guys who were behind it all are still out there, and that's what is implied the next game will be about; you going after the men in the shadows.
Yes there are microtransactions in a single player game. You can pay real money for Praxis Kits and credits. Yes these items are valid only for the one save file. But the cash shop is extremely easy to ignore and not in the least bit necessary for the game. When I beat the game I had used a ton of Praxis I earned and had 60,000 credits built up. You can also pay real money for these circuit things in Breach which lets you buy stuff. I don't know if you can unlock them yourself. I wish this game didn't have microtransactions, but it's not bad enough to say you'll never buy the game or give it a negative rating.
The game did have a rough launch, but it should come as no surprise to people when there's thousands of different system configuration combinations, but the devs continue to release patches. I personally had no issues. If you have issues when a brand new game launches, give the devs a week or two to fix things before you leave negative ratings.
If you liked Human Revolution you will most likely enjoy this game too. Don't let the haters turn you off, or the relatively low Steam review rating give you the mistaken impression this is a mediocre game because it's not. Those negative reviews were from people who had the misfortune to run into trouble when the game first launched, but most of the issues have been corrected while their negative reviews will always be there.
Hopefully we won't have to wait so long for the next game because I can't wait!

Trick and Treat isn't a remarkable visual novel by any means. The art looks low-budget, the music is pulled from royalty-free sources and the translation from Spanish to English is flawed in a few places. The story doesn't really offer anything stellar, and the game's length is about average compared to most other free-to-play visual novels. What keeps Trick and Treat from being absolute crap, however, is something less tangible: that doujin VN charm.
Yes, the art is low-budget, but it's got more heart than some of the other Ren'Py visual novels I've seen. Ashley's design is actually pretty cute despite the rough edges, and Lillian's design is also fairly nice-looking although a bit more generic. The interface seems like more effort went into it than was needed, although I can't say the same from the background graphics. There aren't any decent CGs to speak of either, but that doesn't bother me as much.
The story is an interesting beast, because it builds itself up to be an interesting horror story until it slowly turns into a typical rom-com situation. The plot itself seems to thin when it gets to this point, throwing away any sort of suspense in favor for something faster-paced and less thought-provoking. Not that that makes the story bad, just a little predictable. The choices seem to mimic the kinds of choices Fate/Stay Night often presented, where picking the wrong choice either quickly or subtly led you to a bad end. I do like the idea, but F/SN had the advantage of rewarding players who made the wrong choices, making the story more entertaining and telling of the protagonist's character, the world he inhabits and the people he encounters. There's not as much weight here, not because of the game's length but because the bad ends only serve as a means to get you closer to the true end, rather than an opportunity to challenge readers and reward them for their decisions. Oh, and there's a lot of spelling and grammar mistakes that could be fixed.
Despite all that, I did like this visual novel. I wouldn't place it on a pedestal like I did with Sepia Tears as a holy grail of doujin visual novels, but it's an interesting attempt at creating a visual novel with a decent story and charming characters. It just doesn't aim to be more than that. Pick it up if you're bored and have read through some of the other free-to-play visual novels on here. I recommend it. :)

Absolutely incredible experience and I highly recommend it. It reminds me a lot of the Team ICO games in terms of mood and of using gameplay to tell a story: this is a tale that wouldn’t have half the impact it does without being a videogame. Just, bring the tissues. Also like ICO and Shadow of the Colossus, this is a melancholy, sad tale. (And like them it’s short, but exactly how long it needs to be, I think.)
The controls are weird but once you get used to them they’re just fine. You use the two joysticks and outer shoulder buttons to control two boys who’ve set out on a quest to save their dying father, both at the same time. Big brother is stronger and faster, while little brother is smaller, weaker, and phobic of water after his mother’s recent drowning death.
Together, they use their different strengths to solve puzzles and help both each other and various NPCS out on their journey. Lots of very cool art design, well-done fantasy world in general. And the story is completely told with gestures and a Sims-like gibberish language (though the two brothers have distinguishable names).
Gosh, the ending though. It uses gameplay mechanics for incredible effect that I can’t talk about without spoiling, but that was an amazing moment and the game’s worth the price of admission for that alone.

Nowadays, there are two types of Match 3 games.
There's the mobile kind - extremely polished, shiny, free, greedy little critters that drain your wallet until you make it through the month on a diet of ramen and virtual currency.
And then there's the Steam Greenlight kind - so ugly only dev could love them, rough around the edges, rushed from start to finish, with weird quirky mechanics, but honest-to-gosh casual fun that doesn't ask for anything but your time.
There used to be the third kind - the Popcap level of eye-blinding polish and undilluted awe that brought us Bejewelled but it has become an extinct kind nowadays. It's either work hard and drive iPhone soccer moms poor, or be kind to the elderly women who vegetate on a PC.
This game, obviously, is of the second kind. I didn't enjoy the graphics, the UI is shoddy work with too much unskippable delays that do not belong there. However the game manages to stay easy and approachable despite adding more mechanics on top of Match 3 such as three match modes and rotation of game field.
I enjoyed the fact that you can endlessly shuffle the board rather than waste moves that do not achieve anything, but it felt too good to be true tactic, open for abuse. You can get away from even the toughest of levels without wasting your last precious moves, simply by waiting for the game to let you shuffle the field. I feel that this is due to developer not wanting to implement a complex move prediction algorithm that is mandatory in mobile games to ensure players aren't stuck with no moves. Still, I appreciate this feature since some of the alternative match modes are impossible to win on some fields unless you abuse Shuffle for hours.
I got this game for free, as part of a mass giveaway, but since you're probably looking at full price, I would still say it is enjoyable Match 3 game, especially if you'd rather play something on the lower spectrum of difficulty. But there are many better games of the genre especially on mobile.

I was pleasantly surprised by Tales of the Orient. The game is a simple get three or more in row type of puzzle game. With 3 different game modes, one where you simply click to "pop" the pieces that are next to each other, one where you "chain" pieces together by dragging a line through the pieces you want to remove, and the last most classic "swap" where you can swap two adjacent pieces to make pieces come together. There are also two main game modes "relaxing" and "challenge".
The boards are the same, but in challenge you get a set amout of moves to complete it, and in relaxing you can take all the time you need and click away at your own pace. There is a story in the game, but to be honest it's a hard genre to have a story in, and I doubt people but the game because they want a good story. The graphics are nice and pleasant to look at and colorful, bringing it to a nice game to look at and play. 7.8/10

This game is straight awesome.  Part Starcraft, part... well, Starcraft, but not the same.
It's got a TD feel to it, and you're always fighting Zerg-types, but there's enough variety in missions that it's not the same game over and over.  Further, there's weekly challenges with leaderboards, at varying difficulties.
You generally lose a mission when you've lost all your bases (which can be upgraded as you do missions and earn cash), though some are timed, with bonus time awarded for reaching objectives, and more cash earned for
more slaughter... and though thousands upon thousands of aliens die per mission, it's quick and easy to learn, with a good tutorial and good interface options between click/hotkey to make both options usable within a couple of missions.  Pay attention when Sarge tells you to get the shotguns, and use the hell out of them for the duration.
However, miniguns and flamers for win.
After you've played a few games you'll unlock new buildings/abilities/skills, which can be built/bought during missions, hence upgrades to your troops and bases.  You can also re-run missions to gain Steam achieves with the new technology (hence the TD feel).
Again: miniguns and flamers for win.
Most of the tough spots I've found so far have been such that I can park a couple of guys next to my bases, which, after you unlock bunkers, will keep them healed while they blaze away, while you figure out what to do next... and some of the scenarios are challenging enough to warrant a wider view of the map and observation of the flow of enemies.  Most non-starter scenarios have had bonus mission award (during-mission currency, used to buy upgrades for troops or buildings) options, so you have a choice sometimes between trying to zerg back at them for a fast win, or taking the long road and wading through thousands more bodies with heavier guns.
So like I said: miniguns and flamers for win... but officers help, too.
Fun game, for sure - good job, RocketBear!

Before I give my review, I just want to give my respect to the devs of Trick and Treat! You are awesome and I can't wait for your next project! Anywho, Trick and Treat is an interesting VN. It surprised me to put it bluntly with it's story and characters. It had, in my opinion, a very interesting story that hooked me to find out more and characters that I had formed close bonds with!
In a quick summary of the game's basic plot: You are Axel, a 17 year old highschool student who goes out on Halloween night with his two friends Alfred, and Steven to investigate a strange forest where people have mysteriously disappeared. It's from there that the game is a roller coaster ride of effective atmosphere, tension, and emotions. The music is great and add's to the scenes, the characters are memorable and are easy to get attached to, the story is interesting and emotional, and the overall vibe of the game is dark and lonely. Those last two of which perfectly sync with the themes of the game (Halloween and etc...).
Those are the good things but this game does have it's share of flaws. For one, the text is sometimes poorly written and grammatically incorrect at times. And sometimes there are plot points that aren't (or are poorly) explained and story moments in the game that make you go: "Wha? ....Huh what? I don't-I don't understand-". Other than those flaws, I absolutely loved this game and would definitely recommend to everyone. Please, show your support to the makers of this so they can continue to make amazing games!

While the other acclaimed games in the series were made as standalone projects, Mankind Divided is made to kick-start Deus Ex as a franchise. This has the unfortunate effect of making this game feel like you aren't doing anything nearly as significant as what you accomplish in Deus Ex or Human Revolution. The stakes are quite low, and even Jensen himself acknowledges in the ending that it was a small victory, and his biggest opponents are still out there.
That is just about the only large complaint that I have. Mankind Divided was an absolute blast to play. The new augmentations are a joy to use, and really make you feel like the jacked-up super soldier that Adam Jensen is. The level design is a big step up from Human Revolution, with the expansive, multi-leveled Utulek Complex being a highlight. There are plenty of side missions to undertake, and not a single one left me disinterested. There is only one hub world, Prague, this time around, but it is bigger than either Detroit or Lower Hengsha from HR, and filled with more discoveries to be made. Gone are the forced, outsourced boss fights from HR. There is a final boss, but even that can be bypassed in a way fans of the first game will be familiar with.
There are other reviewers here detracting the game for having microtransactions, but after playing the entire game without even redeeming the ones I'd received for free, I can tell you that it's a nonissue. You'll never feel like you're lacking in credits or praxis kits. In fact, by the end of the game, I had more of both than I knew what to do with.
In conclusion, I very much enjoyed my time with the game, and I'd definitely consider it a contender for game of the year.

tl;dr the story is great and fun to play but is hindered byu horrible performance on even up-to-date computers so don't expect perfection in terms of framerate or graphics.
FULL REVIEW:
The story is well written and interesting, that's the biggest advantage this game has. If you're a true Deus Ex fan you'll enjoy the subtle references to previous games and hints to the future of the story. Having logged over 120 hours in Human Revolution, Mankind Divided is an excellent narative sequal that should be played if you care about the lore of the universe and the lives of the characters.
My grief comes from the absolutely horrible PC combatability at the time of this review. In over 40 hours of play I was rarely clocking above 15fps, averaging about 7fps in a busy city. My PC isn't a 10 grand build but it is capable of maxing other fairly visually-intensive games like Dying Light or XCOM 2. The load times are also atrocious, with some quickloads taking over five minutes and some standard area-switching loads taking over twenty. Loads get faster if you're doing multiple in the same area but loads between areas gave me enough time to leave my computer and make a meal.
There are also a few issues I experienced with the control scheme, specifically that, after a quickload you have to press space. Space is the default jump button and after every quickload, Jensen (the main character you control) jumps. This can lead to you throwing youself into otherwise unaware enemies and I eventually just bound jump to "alt" to avoid it. Inconvenient, but effective.
I'm hoping that in the time after this review some patches will be released to boost PC performance, it has gotten better since release day, but I wouldn't bank on it too much.
The game is playable, and the more time you spend in one area the better your framerate will get, but I personally had a fairly stuttery experience. The fact that I'm still giving the game a positive review in light of this speaks to how much I did enjoy the game, even with all the technical issues.

Call of Juarez is a Western FPS, which you don't see too often. Unfortunately, it's a pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥ one.
Most of that is because of the gameplay. You alternate between playing Billy, a stupid and annoying Mexican kid, and Ray, who's essentially a religious, gunslinging version of Batman from The Dark Knight Returns. As Billy, you do stealth and Indiana Jones-style whip-assisted platforming, both of which are janky as ♥♥♥♥ and at times completely don't work. Sometimes I'd spend five minutes trying to get past one jump because of the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ rope physics, and the less said about the stealth, the better. Also, your health pool is a joke and literally anything can kill you. As Ray, you do shooting where the amount of damage it takes to kill specific enemies seems to be completely random and you have to reload every five seconds for far too long. Sometimes you're One-Hit McGee who can kill twelve enemies in a row before reloading, and other times one guy manages to eat five bullets and dodge seven more, making you reload both revolvers for what seems like a full minute before trying again while he and his friends take potshots at you. Eventually, cover becomes more common and you get less unusable guns, but it's still not a fun process. Things get bad enough near the end that every single enemy starts dropping a health potion when they die, which seems like the wrong way to go about fixing the issue. Still, it's better than ♥♥♥♥in' Billy.
But don't worry, there's a whole slew of other ♥♥♥♥♥♥ mechanics for both characters! Ray can kick down doors, which feels completely weightless and ineffectual and I think gets used all of twice. There's a weapon durability mechanic where a brand-new gun can break down to the point that it explodes in your hands over the course of a single level. There are dueling and fistfight minigames that you have to do occasionally, both of which ♥♥♥♥ing suck. You also ride barely-steerable horses sometimes. There's also some ♥♥♥♥ing ridiculous fall damage. Come to think of it, nothing except blindly firing a shotgun at an enemy feels good to do in this game.
To complement the travesty that is the basic gameplay, the story is mostly a slog. It's completely forgettable by itself, but it's mostly told by a metric ♥♥♥♥-ton of expository dialogue in lengthy cutscenes placed directly after save points, so if you die you get to watch them all over again.
To be fair, the game's not completely without its good points. You can see your whole body if you look down, which I always like. The sound design is generally good, and there are some impressively large environments and a few pretty good setpieces. The game is weirdly enamored with physically simulating everything that isn't nailed down, from dead snakes to your whip to your corpse when you die. This doesn't mean anything in gameplay terms, but it can be entertaining. That's about it for good stuff.
So yes, Call of Juarez is a piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥ It's unpleasant to play in every aspect, and any redeeming qualities it has are comparatively quite minor. I only really hated playing it several times throughout the whole thing, but the rest of the time I was filled with vague, omnipresent distaste. If you like it for some reason, great, but please don't go telling me about it.

Heroes and generals is a good example of a great concept that is sadly poorly made.
Like I say, the concept is great. Playing a war battle as tanker, pilot or soldiers where every players does its part to win the great war. Unfortunately the game takes this concept very loosely and there are too many flaws to make this game the ultimate success is needs to be.  The main problem lays with the developers itself. They don’t think things trough a lot when they implement a new feature or update their game. This is sometimes described as Retologic on the forums. A great example are there countless new render engine improvements they added that make the game more laggy and unplayable. Mostly these new render engines are removed in a few days or hours after release. Another example is when they give complete imbalanced weapons to each faction. For example the German paratroopers gets the powerful FG42 and the US gets a m1 carbine (the most useless weapon in the game). This leads to complete unbalanced representation and total  players numbers for each faction. This leads to battle where one team is outnumber and outgunned  and the other team have to wait all the time in line for their soldier for spawn  in battle.  Cheaters are not punished properly and retro’s  ‘anti-cheat’  is childishly simple that a average cheater can bypass it with one finger in his nose.
My last and greatest example that I can give is the Matchmaker in staged battles.  Although the games gives each faction the same amount of tanks and soldiers in there army pool the matchmaker does not take into account if  the players are able to spawn these weapons. This leads to battles where one side have snipers, aircraft, tanks and high ranker players and the other side is made out of poor newbies with only a simple rifle. This leads to a slaughter and makes it especially for new players a living hell where all they can do is spawn and die. I have played this game for hundreds of hours, I have been there where when the first beta was release years ago, but  the situation is not improving and I fear it never will be, not with these developers. This game needs a better team then Reto. They're not evil, they're just incompetent. Heroes and Generals is a great game concept that is poorly made.

They promote gameplay behaviours that players dont want to see, such as camping or "anti tank rambo" activity.
Until there is significant improvements and more developer-to-player interactions, I wouldnt recommend heroes and generals for any individual. The frustration that is expected to be dealt with simply isnt worth spending your time on.

I'm a big fan of this game, it's so good I just keep coming back to play again!
It's an action-packed top down RTS, with pause. The campaign doesn't get too weighed down with strategy and planning, instead focusing more on squad-based combat. Unlike other similar games, you won't spend the whole game waiting for building and research upgrade bars to finally reach 100% so that you can get on with the game. There are even inexpesive technologies that weaponise your bunkers, so you don't need to waste money on guards, or spend the whole game running back to re-capture defenseless capture points. That being said, there are certain times when strategy is necessary to win. You may need to think about how you put your group together, and which upgrades you give them to begin with, but after that it's just about blowing the hell outta alien scum!
You can purchase weapons and tech in whichever order you please, which gives you the option to prioritise upgrades to match your playstyle. You can even purchase single-mission bonuses such as an additional sniper at the start of the game. Levels give plenty of money to stay up-to-date with upgrades, but even if you're struggling earlier levels are usually quite effective to farm.
[ - ] Con's:
My biggest problem with this game was that I couldn't find any way to manually select a specific bunker for my troops to respawn at.
Admittedly, the graphics are a little lackluster.
Level design barely changes from start to finish
No difference in terrain. Eg. No "move slowly on this terrain" & no flanking bonus & no "less/more chance to hit" depending on whether you are on higher or lower ground.
Haven't played it very long, but this game is AWESOME!!! Great blend of action and RTS.

Infested Planet is a mix between StarCraft and Starship Troopers.
I will start with the negative points first:
The difficulty can be quite extreme in the later levels. Despite a very flexible gameplay system and some good level ideas or even some maps that are randomly generated, overall the game can end up feeling repetitive if played in long sessions. The art style goes from excellent to just ok.
Now for the rest. Infested Planet plays like a tactical game, or a light RTS (Real-time Strategy). The base construction is minimal, as there is no resource harvesting and there are no factories. The buildings just provide defense or a specific bonus. They are definitively not at the center of the game.
However the distribution of the bases are an important factor of the game. Each base is actually a capture point that can belong to either the player or the Aliens according to who takes it. In general, the player starts with one point and will have to battle through the map and capture each point.
Each Alien base produces a continuous swarm of creatures that attack the player's positions (and despite some minor pathfinding issues, the AI is not stupid and can change course to attack undefended point). The player then has to manage the defense against the flow of Aliens, and the offense to capture points. Capturing a point has two effects that allow the game its sense of progression: some building points are awarded to the player in order to upgrade their army, and the Aliens benefit from a new mutation (new enemy type, new defenses, new hives) that increases the difficulty. Towards the end of the map, the Aliens are very powerful but the player has a wide range of options to deal with them and adapt to the mutation.
Adaptation is an important word to describe this game. First, because there are a lot of options available to the player. Different kind of weapons for the Marines to equip (Minigun, Flamethrower), or different buildings (turrets, airstrike, bonuses for the Marines or buildings). And even if it is more gamey than realistic, at any given point it is possible to remove one of these options to retrieve back all the building points that it costs and change strategy on the fly. This is really GREAT and it allows to experiment without being stuck in a specific technological branch, and to react better to situations (however, some bonuses feel lackluster in comparison to others and thus the cost of entry is not worth investing). Since I am praising this gameplay idea, I also think that the UI (User Interface) and gameplay and level design are all based on the RTS formula but with some nice and subtle improvement touches.
An example would be the dreaded escort mission that plagues most RTS games. Except that here, if the escort dies, it just respawns and tries again. Thus the escort feels like an additional firepower help until the map is safe enough to navigate it, instead of being a burden!
What I like with this game is its adaptability, its polished touches that are delightful surprises, and its sense of progression and pace. Every little step won or lost to the Alien swarms can be felt by the player, and there are very tense moments. And then the overwhelming scary swarm can suddenly be overturned into a jubilating victory, until a new mutation tips the balance of power.
Really a unique and interesting game that shows that RTS games can offer more than we think if they are well thought-of and if the developers are not afraid to make changes in the classic formula.

For the sheer content, gameplay, and controls this game was amazing. If you liked Human Revolution, this game is like that game but improved in every respect that you wanted. Shave off maybe 10 hours for idling, and you'll see I've put in 40 hours into this game after completing ALL sidequests and doing a stealthy and non-lethal playthrough.  This is a very sidequest-heavy game: 2/3 of the content lies in the sidequests, and about 1/3 in the main story.
The microtransactions aren't anything to complain about- the game was quite easy on Normal to beat after leveling in side quests, so paying real money for Praxis kits wasn't necessary at all. Not to mention, I didn't even notice they were there, and they were never advertised at all! Far as microtransactions go, they were the best execution of the sort that I've ever seen.
I'm very, very skeptical about Square Enix forcing Eidos to cut out most of the main story from the game to sell more DLC.  Absolutely ♥♥♥♥ing shame on you, Square Enix, do you people not ruin enough games?  Eidos did an amazing job with this game overall and seemed to have made a visible effort to compensate for the lack of main story, by including some of the best-written sidequests I've ever seen in a game.
For about 40 hours of gameplay, I'd say that the $60 pricetag is fair.  This is overall an excellent game and a very worthy successor to Human Revolution.

After a long time I decided to give this game a try, that promotes itself with a very unique co-op gameplay with one controller. Being not that much of a fan of controller based games I was impressed how very well this game uses this advertised feature. After getting that small barrier (for me) out of the way, a very good story (for a 'puzzle platformer') presented in a graphical wonderful world awaited me.
The puzzles and platforming parts aren't hard at all, so it is possible to fluently play through this game without getting stuck. Every chapter holds some little secrets, so it encourages you to explore the small world a bit.
So if you are not afraid of multitask two players on one controller by yourself, then grab that game.

I completely ignored what the dev was trying to accomplish with the “single player co-op” mechanic of the game. I setup my 2nd controller to control the 2nd brother with a third party program and played the entire game with someone else in real two player co-op.
I thought it made a pretty good (real) co-op game and while I can appreciate what the dev was trying to accomplish, I think the game would benefit from adding a true two player co-op mode.
Most of the puzzles are fairly simple and the game often feels more like an interactive story rather than a game. It was still very much an enjoyable experience, despite it not being very difficult.
-Playtime-
The game takes about 4-5 hours to complete and I wouldn’t really consider it worth going though twice.
-Achievements-
Most of the achievements are for one-off activities that aren’t usually very intuitive. You will likely have to look up what to do for quite a few of them. Once you have completed the game however you can use the chapter select and get all of the achievements in less than an hour.
Recommend on sale.

The first installment of the Call of Juarez series that takes place in the Far West. There isn't a whole lot of games in this setting, especially on PC since we never got RDR, but luckily Call of Juarez is a pretty good series. The first one isn't as good as the sequels (except for The Cartel which is terrible and should be skipped) but is still pretty enjoyable.
You control two characters, Billy Candle and Reverend Ray both with entertwined storylines and slightly different gameplay. Billy has the stealth/platforming sections with a little shooting on the side, he has access to a bow which allows silent killings : it's pretty to fun to use as shooting an arrow slows down time so you can admire the ragdoll falling on the ground. Ray has a bulletproof vest, takes much more damage and can unholster weapons while shooting in bullet-time, however he can't climb and has no stealth sections. While the stealth sections aren't that compelling, except for one area of the game, you can still fall back on shooting everything when spotted which is a good thing. Other than that, the guns are what you'd except for a Western setting and most of them are fun to use. There's still a clunky feeling from the game which is understandable considering it's from 2006 and obviously didn't get a tremendous budget, it's an alright Far West shooter and will occupy you without problems for 6 hours.
Even though this one is the first in the series it's the last one chronogically, Bound in Blood being a prequel and Gunslinger's storyline having nothing to do with those two (we don't talk about The Cartel, the same way we don't talk about Devil May Cry 2 or Dragon Ball GT). I recommend getting this one on sale as it is still somewhat good, Bound in Blood is very good and is a must get especially if you enjoy the Far West setting, same thing for Gunslinger which is excellent and a nice note to end the series on.

Gameplay: 4/10 The gunplay is mediocre and the movement system and physics are bad.

Graphics: 7/10 Hold up decently 10 years later. Probably the best part of this game.
Performance: 5/10 The game runs decently on modern systems with settings maxxed. Significant stuttering when galloping through areas with dense foliage.

Story: 3/10 The events of the game don't particularly make sense. I was often confused or left saying "that's stupid".

Cat Goes Fishing is about the struggle of one cat and his quest to catch fish. As we start out the cat is just a simple prolitarean in a capitalist society. He sees the error of his society's ways and wants to rise up with his fellow workers against the oppressive corperate regeme he is living in. His father, who faithfully served for Whiskerslovakia as a boat millitarycat (also known as the navie) in the war against the hunter dogs, but was executed in the great fishpression of '92. After years of resenting his father, cat finally learned why his father was executed: "he was a scapegoat for it all" his revolutionary friend meowthew told him, and both of them should form a revolution against Whiskerslovakia.
At a rally that cat and meowthew organized, police turned on the demonstrators and stated executing people in the streets. Meowthew died in cat's arms and cat found himself alive, not as an act of mercy, but to bear the suffering of his now dead best friend. Cat went back to his normal life and did not engage in any revolutionary activity until as the sole survivor of the riots he was approached by Mr. Meowgi, an old friend of his father. This is the last connection he had with his family, as his mom had died after childbirth. Mr. Meowgi gives cat a fishing rod, and cat was finally ready to accept his quest.
Cat now knows he has has to leave. Our hero moves to the underground of the capital, Meowscow, and joins the underground resistance, leaving behind his girlfriend of five years, Sameowa. They were good together at first, but they had recently been going through trouble, and both were too busy to break things off. In the capital, his first assignment was to sabotauge regime fishing boats. Although a dangerous task, cat and his father before him were white cats, so they could easily blend in with the snow of Meowscow in Whiskerslovakia. Lapurrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrsha, a black cat, was also assigned to the mission, but she never made it to the boat. Instead, Lapurrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrsha was brutally beaten and captured. We can't be sure if she was captured for being a meowmber of the rebellion, or just for being black in an all white and calico society. This was the second time Cat saw the true face of his enemy. He successfully infultrated and sabotauged the boat, and soon forgot (three days max) Lapurrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrsha. After all, it's a cat kill cat world. Cat returns and recieves his sweet payment of catnip, and spends it on new armor for himself and an upgraded version of his fishing rod.
Cat had overcame his trials and was now ready to fully face his enemy. He leads a ride into the city to assassinate a senetor, Wood. Cat had found out that Senetor Wood was the one who captured Lapurrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrsha, and had eventually killed her. Cat was ready for his vengance. Cat had now reached the senetor, and was prepared for an epic fight. All of his platoon was killed except for him, who completed his mission, and returned with newfound condidence that he could now face his true enemy, the ultamate evil, President Raftdog, who is actually a cat and not my English professer. With his mind set and his heart pure, he entered the Impurrial Meowice. Cat was surprised about how little people were on guard at the meowice. It was empty. Raftdog was alone and it was time to strike and take vengence for all that him and his evil regime had done to cat. Raftdog told cat, "I know my time has come, but the Whiskerslovakian Empire will rise again!" With these last words, cat swung a swift stroak with his trusty rusty fishing rod, and ended Raftdog's life, or so it seems.
In the Meowice, cat finds Lapurrrrrrrrsha's lost collar, which was the key to her invunerability, and the whole reason why Lapurrrrrrrrrrrrrrrsha thought she could take the mission in the first place, unfortunately, the empire had found a way to bypass this invunerability, and captured Lapurrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrrsha. When cat returned, he was celebrated by all, and bestowed the highest honor by Mr. Meowgi.
In conclusion, I greatly enjoyed this anime, and can't wait for the second season to come out. This anime alone helped me achieve my doctoral degree, and was the topic of my thesis paper. I rate this anime 9.5/10 and hope that all of you reading this can experiene the greatness as I have.

Yes, I know, how can I spend 67 (omg) hours on a game I don't recommend afterall?
Steam's system is flawed, games and opinions are much more diverse than  YES  or NO. If there were other options, this game would get the "If there's nothing better" or "meh" rating, because it's just ... generic. It has a few strong points, and just as many weak ones, making it really hard to foresee if a random user would like it or not.
Start with the positives:
- The best one: you can choose your game: match 3, the classic swapper one. Pop, where you just have to click on groups of 3+ blocks to make them disappear, and for third, Chain - you need to draw a line between 3+ blocks to make them disappear.
- Power-ups: single block,  random 5 blocks, whole row, whole row + rank in a shape of a cross.
- If you can make at least 5 blocks disappear, you'll get a bomb with blows up the tile it's on + 2 in the four main directions.
- You can rotate the table
-Ability to randomize the table - timed, not charged.
- Pretty, colourful design.
- Lots of levels, if you enjoy the game. About 100 levels to build everything, and achievements for 200 played levels / 10 hours of gameplay.
Then the negatives:
- Totally unbalanced. In chain-only games, like 4 Elements, the longer the chain, the bigger the explosion. Here while the chain-mechanic has the potential of making much longer matches than the traditional swap, it's hard to pull of because you can touch one tile only once during drawing the chain, plus the game will reward the 6-7-8 block long chains with a simple bomb as well. Bomb will get placed where the chain ends, if it's long enough.  Pop mode makes this much, much-much easier - I think chain is the hardest mode because of the too many different colours present at the same time.
-Feature level bugs and annoying kinds of real bugs. Where you create a bomb you can detonate it in the air before it would fall, you can do this with any block matches as well.  You can rotate the table while creating the bomb making it fall "sideways". While the bomb's flames are present, the game treats the blocks as intact, so basically you can blow up a bomb, then make the soon-to-be-exploded blocks disappear in a match. But at least you can calculate with these, but I'm pretty sure it's not designed into the game as tutorial hasn't mention it at all.
Often (especially where creating bombs) blocks just spawn under the bomb, so it doesn't fall as deep as it should be, destroying tactics and plans.
- Challenge mode in my opinion is totally broken and borderline impossible. Levels are randomized, and challenges are based on the number of moves, not time. The table doesn't auto-shuffles where there are no matches, you need to do it manually. In challenge mode if you don't want to spend 3-4 moves for the *chance* of making a golden tile disappearing, you can try reshuffling.   Once in like every 3 minutes, making the game incredibly streched out and slow.
The powerups require like 50 blocks (14 3-block matches) to charge, making it usable like once on a level, if you're lucky. Another reason to call the game surprisingly slow.
And this is not a real negative, but it would be so much better if one could rotate the table with the arrow keys, like Clickr does, it would improve a lot on the fluidity of the gameplay.
Afterall, my problem with the game that is so average (and not a trustworthy kind of average game hence the constant glitches and bugs) that I can not recommend it - though if you want to play it, get it, preferably on a sale. It's not bad, it's not unplayeable, just ... there are better games out there in the match 3 genre.
( PS: an advice: Always escape to the menu and close the game - if you happen to alt-F4 while playing on a board to close the game,  your progress from that session gets deleted as I think there's still no autosave between the levels)

Tales of the Orient: The Rising Sun is a match three game that has two other types of matching modes built into the game. The game also has a story line, that is enjoyable to do as well. The main game is basically 100 levels and each level has a different board to play on. Instead of endless just matching pieces though, you are given goals to achieve to pass each level which keeps the game interesting as you go along. So checking your goals before you start is the best way to get going. What also makes the game more tactical in thinking is you can also turn the board to the left or right in 90 degree increments. There are four game tools that can be used as soon as they are "filled" up by matching certain pieces as you move along. One tool breaks one whole row or column that the tool is used in, one breaks a whole row and column. Making sure you know what fills each tool up can make or break you getting your board done to move on to the next level.
The story line consists of building up a village, each building you complete gives you extra moves to use when you want to. The games graphics are very beautiful and makes the game very relaxing to play. The graphics alone were a big reason I purchased the game. Getting all the achievements is not hard at all, so making 100% achievements is very do-able. This casual game gets a 7/10 from me.

It's a match-3 game clearly cribbing notes from Candy Crush, but it doesn't pester you for additional money past your purchase.  Plus, the art style isn't as annoyingly saccharine cutesy.
The game has a "challenge" mode where you are limited in moves like Candy Crush, but also a "relaxation" mode where you have infinite moves, just in case you're sick and don't want to think too hard, or you want to let your 4-year-old have a game without ever feeling frustrated.
In fact, the 4-year-old target audience seems like a good fit: You can rotate the board to change where the blocks fall, and you get infinite "shuffle"s to re-randomize the board.  You get overpowered special abilities that wipe out whole columns and rows of the board, and the recharging of those abilities carries over, meaning you can purposefully tank a level recharging your supermoves, then break them out at the start when you reset the level.  (Or just play relaxation mode where it's impossible to lose.)
There are three modes to choose from, with two of the three relying upon clicking already-existing matches, and the last being the "swap" mode that is familiar to most match-3 players.  The maps and number of moves are the same, and you give up automatic matches/chain matches when you play anything but swap, so there's zero reason to handicap yourself by using anything but swap.
You play as a... I don't know what you play as.  But apparently, someone burned down a village (although it's a pristine grassy field when you look at it,) and everyone says it's your responsibility to pay for rebuilding it.  Getting gold involves beating levels, so basically, you just play levels and then spend all your money on other people you are assured you are related to in some way.  There are only two characters, (the ones on the title menu,) and they only have two poses: normal, and blinking.  You'll get sick of seeing their stiff poses.
The village scenes are largely pointless.  You get a set amount of gold from each level you complete, and need to build 4 buildings to complete each set before you advance to the next set of buildings.  Since getting maximum gold is nearly always mandatory, it basically comes down to completing level 10 will let you complete set 1, and level 31 will let you complete set 2, etc.  Besides the first set, all the buildings give you are more "extra moves", which are basically what you pay money for in Candy Crush.  Since you get a set amount of money per level, it basically amounts to "click a button to build something every five levels, then go back to play more."
The story is paper-thin, it's about as relevant to Japanese history as a American Civil War chess set is relevant to the actual American Civil War, and the apparent priority you have in village building more than slightly absurd.  (You build a temple for geisha entertainers before you build a rice paddy, and sumo wrestler rings and zen gardens before you build a watch tower or garrison to prevent more raids.) The story involves a civil war, but fails to mention which civil war, which side you're on, or who was even fighting you.  You build a "Great Wall" to keep the invaders/rebels/whatever out that looks awfully Chinese for a Japanese story, etc.  It's clearly not meant for someone who cares at all about Japanese history.  (In fact, "Orient" is generally looked down upon by most Asians...)
In total, it's a match-3 game that isn't trying to rob you, and isn't all that frustrating.  Good for a break or giving to people who are definitely on the "casual" end of gaming.

If you want to play an older FPS, pick up something like Half Life instead.
