This game was pretty good. The story doesn't have as much of a WOW factor as HR or the original but it still makes for a plausible extension of the series' universe. The ending was a cliff hanger but I'll (personally) be fine with it as long as there's a sequel that addresses the meatier story elements Mankind Divided skimped out on. There's always been a heavy political and philosophical bent to deus ex games but to me the weakness in this games' story stems from it leaning too heavilly towards the political aspect vs the latter. Because of that it curtails around a lot of the fun, deep, larger than life concepts the game's universe is usually known for. In general I feel like the writers wanted to make this game more realistic than its predecessors but they may have gone overboard with this, causing the game to be more boring/predictable than it should have been.
The stealth element of this game was a lot of fun. It was smooth and full of options when it came to getting past enemies. The game could get laggy at times, usually when running through Prauge. The game actually crashed a couple times for me but for the most part it worked fine. In terms of the pay-for-praxis shenanigans I was indifferent to it, as it's definitely not required or even a largely noticeable part of the experience. Obviously though it's still something of a problem, I don't disagree with anyone there, but for anyone wondering how much this will affect your actual gaming experience...it probably won't at all.

I am amazed at the hate this game is getting. If you like near-future scifi, stealth action, and a dizzying array of choice in your adventuring, this game owns. There are so many ways to solve problems, the powers feel useful and fun, and the "talk fights" are better than ever. The game feels open and clever without being a total sandbox. The story is entertaining, not a masterpiece, but it's genre fiction and there are some shining moments.

Right when the game starts to pick up the pace and get good, it ends. The developer really needs to learn how to make better boss battles. The publishers needs to learn how not to scam people. If you're a Deus Ex fan, it's worth picking up on sale. If you're not, don't bother.

Just wanted to say that I really enjoyed this game. It says I only have 24 hours but I've played offline without internet connection.
The atmosphere of the game is fantastic, if you loved Human Revolution with its unique styles and influences based off of a gritty cyber-punk/Bladerunner-esque universe you should love the level designs. Prague, albeit small in the grand scheme of things, is fantastically detailed and there is a lot to keep you occupied in terms of quests. The characters and story are all A+, and in all honesty, my biggest disappointment is that the game felt short. This is probably because I've been waiting 5 years for a sequel. Enjoy it and savor it.
My biggest gripe is Square Enix' implimentation of Microtransactions in the main game. These are accessible via the "escape" menu and are pretty much paid cheat codes: ie, pay to purchase praxis kits, etc. I beat the game without even needing them, so you can easily ignore them.
However, there are a few game breaking bugs that are slowly being patched out. The explosion at the train station, the metro tunnel at m14, all caused issues for me and I had to wait for a patch before continuing to play. Other than that, I look forward to more Deus Ex in the future.

The plot was predictable and unsatisfying. We had a few sweet moments between the brothers, but nothing that made me care about them. Part of that was because they had a lot of near-death experiences together, but not any emotional connection. The ending was very drawn out due to the lack of emotional connection, and

The best feature the game had to offer was controlling both brothers at once. That was the highlight of the game, and it'd be cool to explore more games with similar controls.

After spending around 3,5 hours in this surprisingly beautiful and short monster hack and slash game which is based on the popular “anime” RWBY, its review time.
Gameplaywise is straight forward. You choose one of the 4 main protagonists from the show (Ruby, Weiss, Blake or Yang (which all have their unique skillset and playstyle)) You hack and slash your way through waves of enemies on different locations in different maps/levels. There are some variations here and there, but the core of the game is based around that good’ol hack and slash action.
The fighting mechanics are quite simple and you use you left and right mouse buttons to combo different attacks together to deal more damage to the enemy. There’s also room to mention that there is a skill tree and leveling, but you won’t really be spending too much time with it since its pretty washed out.
Can also mention that there are some multiplayer game modes except from the main campaign, but I did not really spend enough time with it to comment on it in this review.
p.s
Playing with friends is a hell of a lot of fun.
When it comes to the story its nothing you will really care about. Honestly, I was way too much into the hack and slash part to be able to really notice or care much for it. There are some, but it’s very bland and not interesting (in my honest opinion).
Graphics
Graphically the game looks surprisingly good! The art style combined with the shaders and lighting makes the game look gorgeous! And the animations fluidness makes this a game a good portion of eye candy to play though.
Music and sounds in this game are great. They are taken directly from the show itself and makes it really enjoyable to play though it when you are an already fan of RWBY. Nothing to complain about here!
All in all the game was a good. A little bit way to short and repetitive, but fun non-the less. I would gladly recommend this game to all RWBY fans out there, but would recommend people who have not watched the show or know anything about it to ether watch some gameplay footage or check out the show. You can find it on roosterteeth’s homepage, their YouTube channel or on Crunchyroll. (pssst. It’s really a great show so GO and Watch IT)
Oh yeah on a final note. The last boss in the game is ♥♥♥♥ing awesome and will took me and a friend around 30 minutes to down. #Goodluck

This is the first game in a really long time that I 100%'d. It took about 66 hours. I picked this game up on sale for $20, so for about 33 cents an hour, I'd say it was worth it. It made the online parts of this game really fun. The story does get old after the 12th time or so playing it (every rank resets EVERYTHING…) but you learn new things about each map every time. By the time you reach rank 10, you’ve probably learned all the spots you can break the invisible walls and you will be exploring the out-of-bounds area thoroughly. That there is truly fun end-game content (no seriously, you try playing "is this floor/mountain/building real" its intense!) The achievements in this game are hard (and slightly grindy), but not punishing. And that’s the important bit, I actually enjoyed the challenge of the achievements. I felt they were all fair and fun to get. Over all I love this game, and will continue to play it in the future.

The Sims 3 is a really awesome game. This is nearly an accepted fact, of course, because everyone loves The Sims. I'm sure that there are plent of other reviews that will tell you all about that, though. This review here is a cautionary tale, though most of you likely won't need it.
There are those of you, however, who won't consider ahead of time what a money-suck this game will end up being. Do not be ashamed to admit this, I myself have this problem.
You see, I'm a broke college student. Living off about $200 a month for food, I have a very bad habit of just not eating for days on end so that I can buy video games instead. The Sims 3 was the first game I bought on Steam. Prior to that, I was a dreaded Xbox gamer.
I bought the base game + pets for 29.99. Let's round that up to $30, remembering that I suck at math. That's our first number. 30.
I bought The Sims 3, rather than waiting just a few weeks for The Sims 4 to come out, because I have no impulse control whatsoever, and thought I'd save money by buying an older game. Perhaps I did initially save money. This, however, went down the toilet after six more DLCs, at 19.99 each. Round up to the nearest whole and our second through seventh numbers are each 20. For simplicity's sake, let's just multiply that out now to $120.
But wait, there's more (there always is): The Sims does this darling little thing where it shows you all of these awesome items and worlds and stuff that you can buy with points, or whatever they're called. I don't remember at this point. Now, I know that I spent at least $50 on these, not all at once, but over time. There was some cool stuff offered, and I like cool stuff.
If we add all of our lovely numbers together, we get $200, though without rounding, I suppose, it would be $199.93. This, however, is a very low guesstimate, due to the points I purchased. Keep in mind that The Sims 3 was not at all new by the time that I spent all this money.
This is entirely my own fault, of course. And I do take responsibility for it. However, with 7 total DLCs (world adventures and into the future likely causing the bulk of the issues), my game was unable to run after a while. It now crashes inenvitably after just ten minutes or so of play. These DLCs are HUGE, and to anyone who plans on buying them, it is important to remember that you really need to choose which ones you really want, they do put a strain on your system.
I actually bought the game thinking that it would be easy for my computer to run, since it was all sandboxy and such. I was dead wrong, and don't even know where I came up with that idea. Pretty much any other game will treat your computer with more kindness than this game will. At least in my experience.

This is one of the best match-3 games I have played, simply because of how customizable it is.
There are two game modes, challenge and relaxed. In relaxed mode you have unlimited moves to complete levels, whereas in challenge mode you are given a maximum move limit. Players can switch back and forth between these modes at any time.
At the start of each of the 100 levels, you are given an additional layer of customizability: choosing your preferred clear mechanic - swap, chain, or pop.
- Swap is the traditional Bejeweled-style gameplay, where you form rows or columns of 3-5 symbols by trading adjacent tiles. This is the only mode in which qualifying matches auto-clear from the board.
- Chain is similar to 4 Elements, where you click and snake your mouse through connecting matching tiles to form longer zigzagging matches.
- In pop style, you click on any grouping of 3 or more like tiles to clear it.
It is completely up to you how you want to play; you can stick with one style the whole time, or switch it up with each new puzzle. Certain levels are easier or harder depending on which option you choose, which means there are effectively 300 different levels in the game if you go back later and freeplay each level with each play style.
As you play, you gain currency that can be used to construct buildings, unlocking power-ups and extra moves. Moves gained this way go into a pool that you can draw from in 5-move increments in order to finish a level in challenge mode. This pool is finite, so any moves you use from it are permanently depleted. Additionally, there are only 16 purchasable upgrades, so use your moves wisely.
Over the course of the game, you will unlock four different power-ups that will help you overcome the various challenges presented in each puzzle. These power-ups have meters that refill as you clear specified tiles from the board, and any progress you have made toward replenishing these meters carries over between puzzles. You are also given a shuffle button that is on a timer, bombs that appear any time you clear 5 or more tiles simultaneously, and arrows that rotate the board, allowing you to refill blank tiles spaces or change the direction of how tiles will fall. None of these bonuses count against your move limit.
(I disagree with other reviews that imply you can keep rotating the board to solve levels. First of all, as previously mentioned, auto-clear only works in swap mode. Secondly, rotating the board can only clear tiles if you have open slots for new tiles to fall into, which isn't often. There are a handful of puzzles where rotation will help you form a few matches or save a few moves, but it will never complete the level for you, and usually the levels in question compensate by having lower total move limits.)
I felt the escalation of challenges was well-paced, and keeps the puzzles from feeling repetitive. There are a range of obstacles to overcome, from immovable frozen tiles to hidden bricked-over tiles, and the tutorial does a good job of introducing each new hurdle.
Once you work your way through the story, you enter freeplay mode, where you can go back and replay any level from the game. I had a small glitch with my game where the play button for freeplay was not initially available, and I had to exit the game and relaunch it for the button to appear. I had no further problems accessing freeplay after that.
I want to point out that the music for this game is absolutely fantastic. I can't remember the last time I enjoyed a soundtrack so much.
My only real complaint with this game is the story. It is a bad amalgamation of mostly-Japanese tropes and stereotypes, and really has nothing to do with the Edo period. I am fine with a game being set in an historical setting, as long as the developers do their research and make it at least plausibly accurate. They could have easily kept their theme and given it an educational bent, with references to a specific conflict or real historical figures; but as it is, it feels generic and slightly offensive. Even the voice acting felt forced. There is a difference between cultural appreciation and cultural appropriation, and even though the story didn't impact the gameplay in a significant way, it still made me shake my head.
Overall, this match-3 game is highly customizable, well-paced, has a wealth of replay value, and contains an awesome soundtrack, making it one of the top in the genre. Its only real downside is that it used a cultural setting as a cheap gimmick, rather than as a learning tool or a respectful homage. I would give it an 8.5/10

As a person who never got to play the Original GunZ, I was fortunate enough to enter this game with a sort of "free-slate" so to speak towards the massive dissapointment that most of the GunZ: The Duel players had.
However, because of this unbiased-ness I'm also able to clearly evaluate what's lacking, and in what areas. So here it goes:
I find that the tutorial to this game is clunky, for starters. They teach you basic manuevers (sure) and then don't bother to explain some of the more finer aspects of the game (like juggling, guard-breaks, parry's) and overall "Mobility" lessons that are quintessential to gameplay.
Right from the get-go you're confused though, as you're presented with three characters, with all their own different types of play styles.
A Sniper (Who most people go for stupidly, and I myself fell for this trap)
A Gunslinger (Balance between Offensive and Mobility)
A Shield-Trooper (Heavy-Offense, Super-Defense)
However, what it doesn't tell you is which one is geared towards beginners, and which one is geared towards advanced players. Take if from me when I say the Shield-Trooper is the best first choice, for both campaign and beginner's in general.
So now you're in the game, and you're excited. You load up a Co-Op game and figure: "Awesome! This is going to be so much fun."
Three minutes passes, and when you decided to stupidly try to go in for meelee kills, you were facerolled by enemies whose AI are set to "Easy Mode" And you're left scratching your head in mystery. "Whatever" you say, and use one of your tokens.
What you fail to realize is that your tokens are impermanent, and suddenly you find yourself penny pinching them for those last-minute saves. Meanwhile, your teamates (who are either higher skill cap and alive, or dead and furious at you, screaming for a "revive pls" every two seconds) are equally getting frustrated by the game, and with you and eventually quit.
Okay, so you figure that the campaign mode is merely bugged, and will get better with time, right?
No.
So you give up on Campaign and go to versus mode, where you're excited to play against other players. You begin searching for a match...and then you search some more....and then you search some more.....and then you search some more.... and then you search some more.... until -finally- you get into a match.
Oh how wondrous! You finally made it into a match, and you're fairly certain that you'll be ju~
-BOOM-
You. are. dead.
"WTF!?" you yell in annoyance, as you check what killed you. Turns out a guy whose ping is skyrocket, and is also the host, happens to be pretty much lag-owning everybody in the room. You suddenly find yourself unable to land clean hits, and you begin doing "Lag Compensation" shots.
You make last place, and throw your hands up in defeat.
Needless to say: I'm coming to this game as an old fan of S4 League, where I was God-Like in terms of skill. Coming here? Doesn't matter. I can't hit a target that literally phases through my bullets, or doesn't feel the effects until seconds later. Melee combat is a joke as well, and overall this game feels horribly clunky and bad.
There's a reason I uninstalled it.

I posted a sort of in joke for my reviews of DMC4&3, but I'm going to actual say things about Special Edition.
The Good: The game itself is DMC4 but better. Along with the three extra characters, some bugs have been fixed and the drop rate for Proud Souls and Red Orbs (Items used to enhance your characters) has been more than doubled from the original. And if you for some reason don't like the changes, you can enter a code that restores the balance of the original version, while still having access to the new characters and costumes.
All three of the new characters play far, -far- differently than Nero and Dante, and Vergil plays a bit differently than he did in DMC3, but not in a bad way - He has a few unique mechanics and far more options.
The graphics have been improved noticably, making the game look even better, which is a feat considering how well the original aged graphically.
The Bad: The enhanced graphics do terrible things to the framerate, or so everyone thinks - Framerate in general is a crapshoot, some people with PCs better than mine are getting worse FPS than I am, and a few with -worse- PCs are somehow getting better. Most people are blaming this on a few of the new graphical effects, which most people don't seem to like anyway.
It's not even that the framerate is -bad- as much as it is DMC4 was known for being absurdly optimized to the point where modern laptops with built in graphics chips could set all of the settings to max and still get 60+.  I can't claim to have a very good PC, but even I was getting 120+ FPS, and that's with a rather outdated, low-tier when it came out video card.
If you're already a fan of the series, and you don't have an XBOX ONE or PS4 to play this on, the PC version will work, it's still really fun even with the awkward performance. I should note that none of these issues seem to happen on the console version, and the game has been out for PC for less than 24 hours as of me writing this, so there's hope that Capcom will be able to patch these issues.

Guns are great, and destructible terrain is fun. Game-play rewards tactical thinking and choosing the correct weapon for the right situation. Game-play and gun-play are smooth, and graphics are pretty good for a game from 2001; I never had my immersion broken b/c of low-res textures. Level design never felt boring, though it was sometimes mildly confusing.
Some things are just outright frustrating, though. Maybe I've been spoiled by the recent generation of games that have direction finders and maps (though I didn't have a problem in Max Payne or Max Payne 2), but lack of directions and small switches to press to proceed can equal many minutes of running around aimlessly, looking for the way forward. Health is at a premium on any difficulty. Story is meh. Voice acting (except for Hendrix) is sub-par. Music is annoying and repetitive. The final levels felt tacked on, making the game too long - though, at 6 hours for a run-through, the game is actually anything but long.
And while I didn't have the bugs that other gamers have encountered (like the submarine exploding for no reason), I could only play an hour or so before the voices stopped sounding. I had to exit the game, and verify the file cache. There were usually 3 files that had to be re-acquired. Once done, the game proceeded normally - for another hour or so. Annoying, but not really game-breaking (I wasn't playing with any mods).
Worth a look for for any Red Faction fan, or someone who enjoys old-school shooters. But there will be no hand-holding. Or clues. Or detailed directions.
EDIT: Played with the Pure Faction mod installed, and the above problem with the voices disappeared.

TL;DR:
Clocked in 50~55 hours on first time non-lethal playthrough. Great time playing through, enjoyed the world building and gameplay. Am disappointed by the main story though.
Graphic:
Was streaming the playthrough so couldn't exactly max out the video quality but even at tweaked medium, the game looks gorgeous and I was still getting 60+ frames. At times I dipped to 40s, but those were brief stutter moments. Most of the time the game ran around 60 to 70fps. I will check back once DirectX12 goes live to see how much greater the world looks then. Utilization of props and layout makes places distinguisable (Red Light District, the slums, Church of the MachineGod, etc) even when they are in close proximity of one another.
Sound:
Same composer(s) as DE:HR and just as good. Due to the way physics works, you may hear audio looping endlessly when objects are colliding with one another. Might be my audio set up but I also hear crackling noises, very suttle though, whenever I use my vision augment (might just be the way it is). Audio queue for combat, alertness, and such are easily distinguishable.
Bugs:
Five patches in and I still have hacking computers lock up on me. Workaround is to escape out and quickly use it. Not much workaround when the hacking is glitched during the node capture phase. Glad the slow running on stairs was fixed, that one was very immersion breaking. There were bodies that spawned in inaccessible areas (elevator in ARC), most likely some error. Additionally, I was able to get the first cutscene with Marchenko multiple times (each time after the first, it will reset Golem City). Occasionally lack of memory messages and crash to desktop (running on an i7 950, 12GB of RAM, GTX 980) but those might be caused by system barely surpassing the minimum. Not sure if intended bug but some civilian panic will last indefinitely unless you move out of sight but still within their radius while others require you to leave the area completely.
Gameplay and Story:
Of the new augments, I only tried out the remote hacking and dash one. Remote opens up alternate paths to get to a spot but its most useful getting around laser armed explosives. I suppose I can also free up an emp pistol slot with the remote hack augment. The dash augment is something I suppliment the leg augment with, since the dash makes getting to just out of reach to jumping ledges easier. Do note the dash augment can break the level design of certain areas, since you can dash to the very top and glitch through the map and into specific rooms (useful I guess for the Church...). All the standard augs did the same as HR and are rather straight forward.
Shame there is only one true hub (separated into two parts) unlike other Deus Ex games with at least three hubs. Getting this out of the way, yes the game does feel like an incomplete story so maybe thats why there is only one hub. Despite it being one hub, it is the most detailed one I had the pleasure of exploring every nook and cranny of. You can do the main story and get a gist of the world's attitude between those that are augmented and those that are not. By exploring around, you suddenly get a deeper view of the way people are treated, their sacrifices that had to be made due to the incident at Panchea in the previous game, and you might run into a backstory involving Jensen. The last one was not touched on at all in the main story until the ending credit. The world building is phenomenal.
Side missions started off strong. The Neon sidequest...I feel as though whoever wrote that out was heavily inspired by itmejp's Rollplay show: Swan Song. The bank heist first time around almost reminded me of infiltrating Liberty Island in the first Deus Ex game. The two part detective case great from beginning to end. Heck its the only other true boss fight you get in the game aside from the ending. Doing favors wasn't too bad, the highlight was helping the Red Queen where you have to drag someone to a storage unit alive. The next interesting side mission was definitely the one where an AI contacts you. It will clear up more on the ending of DE:HR.
Main story started off interesting with the Dubai mission, then suddenly we were thrown off an international hunt into figuring out who did the bombing. THe former being more interesting to tackle and the latter is the excuse for keeping us in Prague. Finding evidence to the Prague train bombing from the locked down station did hint at some higher authority at play, but because of the brief snippet intro, we already know the Illuminati is manipluating everything. You'll eventually go to Golem City, and its a huge place, deserving to be a second hub area but its quite linear. In Golem City, you will find out who did the bombing at the train station you were at. You'll eventually run into the main antagonist of the game and then meet with Talos and things happens. You'll return back to Prague and see some slight changes. You'll meet someone in TF29 and turns out their interest in you is more than just for work once you dig around Prague. Nothing too interesting. You then run into evidence of who made the bomb. At the same time, you get note of significant evidence being removed from the bank. THe game actually locks you out of one once you have proceeded to a certain point on each mission. You can glitch through to do both... If you did not glitch through, someone will die in the story. The next part of the story bring you to a facility in the alps and lo and behold the antagonist makes it plain as daylight what his plans are. You'll find yourself out of the facility (really nothing special, you only learn the mercs there have similar augs as you were implanted with). Back in Prague the third time and it gets interesting as the whole city is now shoot on sight and hostile to you (well the police are). Can go around and see the changes in the organized crime family and finish up side missions but nothing too special here. Then you proceed to the last mission in London. Straightforward. It is once you reach Miller do you have a branching path again. You can do both. To get the best result, you need to get to the VIP first and fast. Yes there is a timer on this mission. To get an even better result, you needed to choose the bank mission prior as the bomb maker mission only extends the time you have at the last mission. The last boss fight...is a joke. As in, way too easy.
Other thoughts:
Didn't do breach mode yet (you get a snippet of it in the main game). Didn't do the extra story yet. Going to wait on those when its fully released.

This is a Real time strategy "Tower Defence" game.
You can play in fullscreen or windowed mode.
There are many different resolution sizes.
There is a music volume slidebar available.
There is a sound volume slidebar available.
Able to change the controls on your keyboard.
You are able to disable the screen shake.
Has skirmish mode, Story mode and DLC Campaign.
You will play with a set of marines to take over the enemy hives and elimating them one by one. There are literally SWARMS of enemies which will constantly attack you and you have to hold them off or engage them to stop the alien swarm coming out of the hives. You are able to upgrade your marines with better weapons, making defensive or offensive buildings or support upgrades. Hives will get stronger and they will gain upgrades and buffs whenever they are getting closer and closer to defeat. Aliens may change their attack pattern way and attack you from a different angle. Enemies could get like shields, Regeneration, stronger Aliens and alot more. This is randomized. Marines that dies while they are equipped with a different weapons, will not make them drop their weapon. The respawn timer depends on the equipped weapon marine.
Interesting story and has side missions.
Random maps and Enemy Buffs.
Defensive/offensive/support buildings.
Upgradeable marines with different weapons during ingame.
Could be repetitive but also addictive.
Upgradable/unlockable perks and buffs, Permanently and during ingame.
Interesting gameplay,
Decent music.
Easy controls.
Aliens will choose+Find an alternate path to attack and surprise you. Which will mean you have to keep your eyes and stay focused on all times. this is a really long review. So please, bare with me.
i got this game and it's terrible. But at the same time there is something intriguing about it that kept my playing until the Gryphon pseudo stealth part. Which was absolute nonsense. I am surprised people have good things to say about this game. but i have to say otherwise.
to start off i don't understand the comparison to half life at all. the only kind of resemblance it shares is that it takes place in a facility. Thats it. there is nothing that comes even close to half life . From the puzzles to the enemies or intriguing storyline. i think it's kind of insulting to compare this garbage to a classic first person shooter. call me neckbeard or an elitist for it but lets face it this game doesn't hold a candle to half life.
as far as story goes,you play as some guy, who has a name but i didn't bother to remember, going through this facility blasting♥♥♥♥♥♥on behalf of some rebellion and that's truly it. There is no other challenge other than maybe a stealth section or figuring out where the hell you are supposed to go. i made progress not because of interesting level design, but because out of pure accidental luck. there was so little variety in environment that i m surprised i got to where i am now. it's monotonous to say the least.
enemy variety is limited. they really aren't tactile enemies. their main tactics include and are limited to: running straight at you. standing in one place, shoot. cower or not even notice you until after you have taken out at least half a gang of mindless cronies. the only time they pose a threat is on higher difficulty settings. But that's purely artificial. You take more damage and they take more shots to kill. Also. there might be something wrong with hitboxes in this game. Since you can shoot an enemy at point blank with a shotgun and they will still take three shots to kill. And i'm not talking about the slightly armored ones i'm talking about the regular dummies that are supposed to be a threat.
the controls aren't exactly a benefactor. It feels so light and floaty. There is a lack of weight behind certain actions. Like reloading a gun, recoil or even things like jumping and character interaction. it feels hollow and it makes the game lacking in any sort of feeling.
the graphics are outdated to say the least. that's all there can be said about the graphics. But they aren't ashamed of the fact that a lot of elements were copy/pasted which lend to the games boring feel. You'll run into countless clones on both sides of the fight. and yeah, that's not to say Half life wasn't guilty of the same thing. But in that game there was creative level design that used the visual assets to good use. and also a plethora of enemies, characters and assets that kept the game from becoming a repetitive snoozefest. But this isn't supposed to be me talking about half life. I'm supposed to talk about this game. this game is so bad that i'm talking about other, more better games in this review. the character concepts in this game are as vanilla as bad guys can get. The only interesting thing i ran into was a ♥♥♥♥ing fish out of all things.
the sound design is awful. Voice acting is okay, but nothing outstanding or worthy of praise. Guns sound stupid or generic. The enemy punchlines are hilarious in the worst way. and the supporting cast of allies come across as whiny or ♥♥♥♥♥y. There is no reason to feel sympathetic towards the people telling you what to do or where to go. Because all they do is nag. i just wonder if they have enough cheese to go with all that whine. also everybody sounds the same. There is no variety in voice actors. you know what i mean with that.
Some shooters survive the test of time. Games like half life, halo, duke nukem, doom, wolfenstein, etc... are all games that till this day are still a blast to play through from beginning to end. Red faction is not one of those games. This game aged very poorly. And it's just sort of sad that people give it praise because of it's "revolutionary" engine or just for pure nostalgia's sake. But we're (mostly) grown ups here. And it's time to move on. If you still have red fever. Just play red faction guerrilla. Sure, it's not an FPS, more like a free roaming game in space. But that game is fun. Albeit not great. It's still a million fold better than this game. and even then. You are doing yourself a big disservice just getting his game for nostalgia. Spend that money on something better. Wether it be a classic or something new. But by all means. Let this game be forgotten. It's for the better.
short version: this game is a boring pile of garbage and you are better off paying 10 bucks on a better game.

DMC4: Special Edition is a fantastic game that only adds more to the already robust 2008 action game. The new characters all have brand new mechanics, and all play uniquely. The graphics have been touched up, and the combat has some minor rebalances, but the exploits that gave additional depth like Guard Flying and the Lucifer Exstacy glitch are still in.
Special Edition adds new costumes for Nero and Dante in addition to having 2 for all the new characters respectively.
My only gripe is that Capcom added DLC that, while cheap, has no reason for being, such as additional Souls and modes that can be unlocked, and only serves to let you skip content that is already not a hassle. Vergil's air trick being unlimited use seems kinda outlandish, too, but fun.
Overall, this game is a must-have for any action fans, and its combat is still the paragon of what an action game should be.
Motivation/10.

Between a crazy old preacher running around with bullet time at his disposal to rain down fiery retribution from God and a scared half to death thief who just keeps getting deeper about fifty miles the wrong way up sh*t creek, you met with a surprisingly decent first person shooter styled in the mid 19th century. You play as both these characters, one running from a mixture of crimes he did and didn't commit and a preacher who sees near nothing but evil in the world, their contrasting characters in what limited dialogue your given give an almost bleak tone to the lawless Western expanse of the United States. More so, this game manages to be driven by both fun arcade like gameplay with a strong though cliche narrative. Now though the game is very linear, the story and gameplay keep this game standing on it's own.
On the technical side, the game ran perfectly fine on Windows 10 OS 64 bit. Though I have seen others complaining the game can't run or has severe issues performing on both the Windows 8 and Windows 10 operating systems. So that is something to watch out for, I would simply recommend comparing PC specs to get a rough idea whether or not this game will be compatible for your system. But as said, I didn't have a single issue with this game running on it's highest specs at a 1600x900 resolution.
Pros:
-Fun arcade like gameplay
-Engaging narrative, though a bit cliche
-Bulletime
-Moderation between use of characters
Cons:
-Contrived platforming sections
-Too much bulletime
-Difficulty curve fluctuates back and forth a lot
Overall, this is a game worth playing. The graphics have aged okay though you can tell the gameplay was designed more for a controller than a keyboard and mouse, but for the most part the controls are fine. No spoilers, but I do recommend switching the sprint key for your horse from the caps lock button to shift, as that won't effect gameplay much if at all.

This game is something people wanted for years, but does it hold up? Well, the gameplay does, but I don't think the writing is any good.
Mankind divided is a very slick game in terms of its gameplay. As expected of a Deus Ex game, there's lots of freedom in terms of where you can go and how creative you can get in getting there. There's lots of augs to choose from, and once you have just a select few of them, playing the game really starts to feel like you're cheating; with just the aug that lets you see through walls and remote hacking, you become pretty overpowered in terms of your skillset, and that's not even to mention vision cones, brief invisibility to cameras and people, landing from any height, super high jumps, a blink dash like from dishonored, and even more. By the end of the game, I had about 10 praxis I hadn't even used yet because I felt like I already had more than enough. I'm not sure why they have microtransactions for it when it's absolutely everywhere, but at least they're very nonessential.
Yet despite all this, the game still ends up feeling fun to play. There's always new stuff to find and new ways to accomplish your goals. Often you'll reach your destination, only to find a vent you completely missed or electric breaker you could have used to kill someone or something along those lines.
There are glitches though, like how I never saw the alarm pop-up in my playthrough, but I didn't get the achievement for no alarms, which I painstakingly made sure I'd get (no failed hacks, no red text aside from a story part that as far as I know forces searching status). Other stuff I ran into was occasional crashes (every 8 hours or so I ran into one, maybe 3 total during the game) and bugs with the tesla system, where enemies would sometimes instantly turn hostile even when being shocked from an area not visible to them, which wouldn't happen if i did it again after loading from the exact same spot in the exact same way.
In terms of content, there's really a lot here. If you like exploring, you will spend hours and hours examining the environment for secrets and pickups. The world of the game is so dense and packed with stuff that I continually found myself surprised at just how much stuff there was everywhere, even in places you might not expect.
People will try and sell the game short and say it's a super short game, and that might be true, if you don't collect anything and just do the main story, but Human Revolution probably isn't that much longer if it is at all. Most of the game's content is in its sidequests, which probably outnumber the main quests 2:1, and overall the game offers quite a bit of playtime if you're willing to invest more in the side missions. A game is more than the sum of its hours, though, and I'd have honestly preferred if it were shorter but had a better story.
Regarding the story, there's a lot of weird stuff going on. The game is very obviously cut off so as to make room for the next game, but it's very jarring regardless of that. The game's central plot element is allegedly the augs vs naturals thing, and the illuminati working to make augs look bad. The first and most obvious problem is that the racism parallel doesn't make a lot of sense when augmented people are inherently more advantaged, and its effects are lessened because only very rarely do you actually experience what most of the other augmented people do, you just kind of experience it vicariously through other people, which kind of works, but it's so much less than it could have been. Yeah, you're insulted regularly and chastised if you ride the naturals train and they check your info if you use the naturals exit, but it never really stops you since you're an aug with special privileges that basically let you do the stuff normal people can, if with a bit of additional harassment.
Your interaction with the juggernaut collective is pretty much limited to Alex and Janus, and I feel like they should have been prominent in the story in the form of interacting with more people or places, especially given how big a role they play, even if they're saving part of that for the next game. The big reveal at the end that Jensen is actually doing what they wanted all along and looking for Janus is the most eye rolling plot development I could have imagined. It completely destroys the point of the entire game's developments in my opinion, which kind of annoyed me. And one huge point I was wondering was why the hell do you go back to your apartment to do stuff supposedly in private TWICE after your apartment gets broken into? Did it just not occur to Jensen or anyone involved that Picus could have put a bug in there, since they know where he is and could easily get there while he's gone? The plot of this game is basically a giant intro, and that's the main reason I didn't end up enjoying it much.
It's a good game barring the occasional bug, but don't play it for the story.

This is a great Deus Ex game. If you've been a fan of the series since DX1, then you'll like this. It's better than HR, and I loved HR. Prague is gorgeous, as everyone has already said. People have also been saying that Prague is the only place you play in. Prague is the central hub where most of the game takes place, yes. However, it's still "Deus Ex" in the sense that you are transported by chopper to areas outside Prague at certain points during the main storyline. So there is some variety; you're not in Prague the entire time. Eidos has taken the series back to its roots in terms of infiltration. Eidos has expanded on HR by really upping the amount of paths you can find to objectives. They also deserve kudos for blending these pathways into the environment in a seamless and logical way. If you want to go true non-lethal, you absolutely can. Hacking is exactly the same as HR (albeit with an updated 3/4-view interface), which is great because I loved how they did it in HR. Augs have been expanded on in a good way, and I'll just leave it at that. All in all, if you like Deus Ex games, you'll like this one. Especially if you like to explore. They did a good job.
Notes:
- No day/night cycle. Day to night is governed by main story advancement.
- The lip-syncing of conversations is poor, but it really didn't bother me after a while.

Of course people who make games want the description to be exciting and positive, but the description for this game has got to be from some other, more fun game that they forgot to make.  I picture a design meeting where they asked everyone to call out the first thing that came to mind when hearing the word "Japan".
"Sushi!"  yelled Bob from accounting.  "Samurai!" called out Jim, the janitor.  "Good, good, keep em coming." said Jane, as she jotted down the suggestions.  "Geisha!"  "Ninja stars!"  "Rice balls!"  Excitement filled the room as more and more wonderful ideas were called out.  Suddenly Albert the night watchman called out "Happy Ending!"  The room got quiet for a minute, then everyone started to cheer.  "We're totally putting that in there, or my name isn't Jane Doe!" said Jane Doe.
So yeah, it's about rather blandly generic, or possibly generically bland as you can get.  This game accurately depicts Japanese culture about as well as Taco Bell depicts Mexican cuisine.  Now, I must say that I'm a regular American, and I really don't care how they depict anybody, except maybe Americans.  Point is, the whole "Build an ancient Japanese village " and "Exciting adventure" thing isn't all that thrilling.
So how about the gameplay then?  Well, the next point in the description is "Rotate the board make the best matches."  At first rotating the board sounds pretty cool, until you realize that you can just keep rotating the board until you win, with the occasional match made by you to free up some space.  There are also your typical match-3 game powerups, charged by destroying gems.  Nothing revolutionary there, except maybe the bug that prevents you from clearing certain tiles.  Yes, I know they said they fixed it, and yes, it is still happening.
If you're a match-3 player, there are certainly other games out there better than this.  Heck, HuniePop is a far better match-3 game, albeit one attached to a whole other, less savory H game, which is not an inherently bad thing, but not for everyone.  Tales of the Orient is, despite the lovely description, rather bland.  Maybe it needs more MSG.

This is the Burger King of Match 3 games: you can have it your way.   There are 3 different ways to play:  Swap, Chain, or Pop.  Swap is the traditional match 3, as in Bejeweled, where you click on a tile, then click on a second tile to swap them and make a match.  Chain is like in Tidalis, where you use the mouse to create a path of the same type of tile and then clear them.  Pop is similar to Season Match, click on groups of 3 or more matching tiles to clear them.  Personally I prefer Swap.
There is also 2 different modes.  Challenge mode gives you a set number of moves to finish the level.  Casual gives you no limit.
The graphics are decent.  Nice backgrounds of Japanese scenery--both day and nighttime scenes.  Let's face it, you're probably not playing this game for the cutting edge graphics, so what do you expect?!
The background music get boring after awhile.  But again, are you really playing a puzzle game for great sound?  Sure it would be nice but it's not essential.
The story is bare bones, but they keep it interesting by having you purchase buildings for your village.  The buildings do not do anything, but it makes it seem like you are making progress rather than just playing for no reason.
I highly recommend this for match 3 lovers.  You can play whatever style you prefer.

I wanted to recommend it, but I COULDN'T.
The game is said to be set on Edo era in Japan, but It's so historically inaccurate and things are mixed up with Chinese. I don't think Geisha, Sumo and Samurai Temple being real. Having a Zen Garden too close to a Forge isn't very logical, either(As metalworking would make LOTS of sounds, and silence is important for Zen.). Childrens and buildings look too much chinese, and there are more things to complain, but I'll cut it for now.
Gameplay is bad, for a match-3.
- 100 levels. too much of them. And unlike gazillions of match-3s that are on steam, there is no minigame at all.
- Being able to rotate the board is an interesting take, but makes drops very unpredictable. I sometimes seen drops appearing from SIDES.
- On level 44, You're tasked to remove 10 Metal tiles(you have to remove twice to be able to reclaim the golden tile beneath it). But you only see TWO at start. so where are the other 8? THEY ARE SIMPLY INVISIBLE, because those invisible metal tiles are on normal tile.
- There is no freedom in order of buildings, because you get fixed amount of gold from clearing levels. Buildings after second tier(first tier give you powers) only give you "Extra Moves" for Challenge mode.
- I wouldn't recommend playing in any modes other than Relaxed Swap mode, because :

-- Pop-3 and Chain-3 doesn't have "combo effect" unlike Swap mode.
-- Also in Chain-3 mode, you can also chain wooden/stone blocks. Is it intended?
-- Shuffle recharges in time than moves, so you can eventually beat challenge mode with 0 moves, if you have patience for it.
-- And in Challenge mode, UI problem occurs when you finish a level with the last move.
- Achievements for playing 10 HOURS and 500 levels. seriously?
- While music is not bad, it doesn't sound too Oriental(or Japanese).

日本ネタのマッチ3だから薦めようと思ったけど、その気がおきなかった問題作。
江戸時代と書いてあるけど、全くそれっぽくない。Geisha Temple(芸者の寺？)やSumo Temple(スモウの寺？)なんて初めて聞くし、Forge(鍛冶場)のすぐ裏にZen Garden(庭園じゃなくて瞑想場?)があるのもおかしく思えたりする。他にも変なところはあるがここでは説明しきれない。

Although Match 3 games are relaxing, they quickly become dull because of their repetitiveness. That’s why when I started to play Tales of the Orient I expected to be bored after 30 minutes – 1 hour of gameplay. Instead of that I found myself playing it for hours straight, without needing a break.
What makes it so enjoyable then?
Maybe it’s the fact that the goals are so well set that they make you want to play “just one more level before I quit” – during each level you collect gold that you can use afterwards to buy buildings in order to restore a town damaged by the Civil war; it usually takes 4-5 levels to get enough money to build something, which is an easily achievable goal.
Or maybe it’s the flexibility that this game offers by providing 3 game styles:
– the classic Match 3 where you swap tiles to match 3 or more identical tiles,
– in which you click on a group of adiacent matching tiles and
– in which you have to drag a chain over a group of identical tiles. In addition to that you can choose to play in
or in
(limited number of moves).
Another thing that I liked about this game is the feature of rotating the board in either direction. This is useful in order to avoid empty tiles since they refill by turning the board; it also allows you to control the direction in which the tiles will fall after a successful match. In addition to that, there are of course power ups that you can use and that recharge over time and a shuffle option.
The nice graphics and relaxing ambient music make this game even more enjoyable. The tiles are colorful, which makes them easily distinguishable. In case you need to match a tile multiple times, the tile background indicates how many moves are left until it’s fully unlocked.

Disclaimer: this is the first “professional-like” review that I wrote. If you would like to, share me your opinions and criticism. There are some things that I have left out in the review based on the belief that they would spoil the players’ experience.
Set inside a Swedish fairy tale, the basic plot of the game focuses on two brothers set on journey to find medicine for their ill father. Throughout the journey, they will come across many obstacles and meet many new friends.
This was a pretty good story, I wouldn’t call it a great story, but it is good enough to keep you playing until the end.
The gameplay you’ll mostly experience is an adventure game with puzzle-platform elements. When progressing through the story and solving puzzles, you’ll notice that each brother has their own strengths and weaknesses. The big brother is quite strong and is able to lift up many things including his little brother. Though because of his big size, he isn’t able to squeeze through small spaces, where his little brother can. What both brothers
do is jump the same height. These are some of the characteristics that each brother have, gameplay-wise.
With the belief that this is an adventure game, this has pretty good exploration content. Basically, if you come across something that looks like you can interact with, you more than likely can. If you find an animal, pet it, you find a house with a door, knock on it, you see a bench, sit on it. What can make these interactions unique is that each brother can have different interactions with these NPCs or objects.
For voice acting, the majority of the voices are in Swedish and there are no options for subtitles. Though you don’t really need to know what the characters are saying, you get a pretty good idea of what they are talking about through hand gestures and how they interact with each other. The voices are able to be interpreted to determine the character’s emotions which helps set the mood for the scene.
For background noises, these both help create the atmosphere that you are in, as well as sometimes give you an idea of what to expect in an upcoming area.
For the OST, this as well helps out the atmosphere an area is trying to create. This also gives you the feeling of being in a Swedish fairy tale with the music tying into the setting.
Disclaimer #2: the majority of the game was played using an Xbox controller with some time on the keyboard. I have no experience using a Playstation controller.
The basic controls of the game are using the two joysticks to control each of the brothers (if you are using a keyboard, wasd controls the big brother, and the arrow keys control the little brother), the trigger buttons on either side for each brother to interact with the environment (space and right Ctrl) and the right and left bumpers to change the camera view (right and left shift).
The notice in the store page is there for a reason, if you have a controller to play with, use a controller. Even so, when controlling the brothers can get confusing at times. Other games played with a controller follow a pretty common mechanic, based off of those games, the controls for this game gives a new experience with how to use a controller. It’s pretty much like you are trying to play with two separate brains each focusing on one of the brothers. Even though this style of gameplay is uncommon, it may be easy to catch on with the controls, then again you may not.
It
possible to play on keyboard, but it is a lot easier to use a controller if you can. Controlling the big brother may seem natural. But controlling the little brother, along with controlling the other one, would be a little bit more difficult because your hand placement with the arrow keys along with right Ctrl is pretty weird. To guarantee progression in the game, it may be better moving one brother at a time, which would result in slower gameplay progression.
Let me start by saying that the graphics are AMAZING. It’s no high end visuals AAA games usually have but it has an amazing art style to give off a sense of appeal.
The world is extremely colorful and immersive. If you are a screenshot lover, expect to take lots of them since the game offers lots of picture perfect moments. Personally I have over 20 screenshots in this game, which is the most I’ve taken in any of the games I’ve owned. Even if you may have lots of screenshots in the game, you’ll have a lot more visual stunning experiences compared to how many pictures you may take.
For character design, they each have style and characteristics, though I wish there was a lot more details in their features. Though compared to how much detail is in the world, it’s understandable how much less features the characters have.
To sum it all up, this game has a good story, decent controls, and amazing graphics. I enjoyed myself with this game and you would too. A must buy, even for full price.

*Spoilers Ahead*
So, this game. I’m just going to break it down into sections.
Story: You and your brother? (I’m guessing, you look nothing alike) are on a mission to find a tree that has something that can save your Dad? (again, none of you look alike) from some mystery illness that the game never really explains. Honestly, I have no clue what was going on. The game was in some language other then English or some made up gibberish. I wouldn’t have a problem with this except there is no way of telling what they are saying since there isn’t any subtitles. So honestly, I’m still kind of confused about why trolls were helping us and why a lady turned into a spider and why we were doing anything in this game.
Controls: This game is played only with a controller. Sorry keyboard and mouse players. Luckily, I have a game pad that I could use. The controls were alright. You control the older brother with the left analog stick and the left bumper, and the younger brother with the right analog stick and the right bumper. The controls are made kind of clear in the beginning, but once you get to the epilogue, the game doesn’t help you at all. I had to look up what the ♥♥♥♥ to do because the game never explains it. Just as a heads up, the left bumper does things in the epilogue. FYI. Also, this game plays as a co-op on one controller. Have fun playing with friends because I found it difficult to control the brothers at the same time. Also, if one brother would get too far away, the other brother couldn’t advance until the one brother caught up to him. It was kind of ridiculous.
Puzzles: This game is just one huge puzzle. You can’t go 2 minutes without a puzzle. I found that fine. None of the puzzles were difficult though. All of them were easy to figure out, or you could stumble on what to do. It’s pretty simple.
Length: I beat this game in 3 hours. So, it’s pretty short. I found it isn’t worth the full price of the game for the content and the time it took to beat.
Achievements: There are no achievements based around the main story, it is all for side mission stuff. I highly recommend getting the “A Sad Tune” and “Windpipe” achievements, but other then that, it is not necessary.
Overall: Honestly, I didn’t really like this game. I was constantly confused about what was going on. There was really no context for anything. I understand that the developers probably wanted a game that didn’t have to rely on dialogue. This didn’t work in this game. Unlike in a game like Limbo, you couldn’t exactly understand the story without dialogue. Them just speaking their own language without subtitles was hard to understand. All I got was that a priest/doctor was helping our maybe Dad from whatever illness he had, and that my maybe brother and I had to find a tree that could help him, and somehow we helped other people on the way for no reason other then we needed to get passed them. And oh, the little brother sees his dead Mom. That’s fun. It would’ve been better if there was no dialogue, just maybe a little narration at the beginning to explain the situation of what’s going on and then have no dialogue after. Personally, I would’ve enjoyed the game way more if that was the case.
There’s also no hand holding. They just kind of throw you in with no explanation on how to do things, and they only mention the controls once.
I’ve definitely have played way better games. I’d wait until a sale to get this one if you’re going to get it. I played about $3 for this game. No way would I pay the full price. Honestly, it isn’t really worth it. If you want stunning graphics and to play for the soundtrack (which is pretty amazing), then fine, knock yourselves out. I wouldn’t play it for the story. The ending doesn’t exactly make sense. Like, I get why it happened, but I just found it unnecessary for the story and it wasn't satisfying.
Rating: 5/10

What an amazing game. Let's look at this one category by category:
This game has an especially interesting mechanic. Since the story revolves around two inseparable brothers, you get to play both of them. How? One stick controls one brother, the other one - the other. The gameplay is thus really interesting, especially since both characters often need to interact with the environment to progress. The puzzles are not too hard, so the gameplay is really enjoyable.
is not an AAA-game with phenomenal graphics, but nevertheless, the art-style and design are very satisfying. The world is breathtakingly beautiful, the characters are cute and everything looks just in place. The separate elements co-exist in a harmony that really builds up the whole world.
What is especially interesting about this game, is that there is no language. The characters speak in a fictional language, but still manage to get the point across. The soundtrack of this game is hauntigly beautiful, by the way. Goosebumps are guaranteed!
So, this is my favourite. As you can imagine, there will be spoilers (marked of course). The two brothers are out on a quest to find a remedy for their sick father. As they travel, they face threats that start out very banal and get progressively more dangerous. The whole game is based around the fear of death and losing someone. Coping is a big factor in this game. Around the end
the absence of language and character names in the game does not seem like a problem. Rather it seems to be the other way around - at times, the emotions are conveyed by undistinguishable sounds, rather than words and seem to carry more weight.
To sum this up, I have to say that this game is fantastic. The only minor quirks are that there are some little framedrops between cutscenes, but there is nothing that really disturbs the gameplay. This game is a complete 10/10 for me.

is a very short game about a typical hero rescuing his typical girlfriend/wife from a typical villain...who happens to be an alien race completely consisted of CommanderVideo.  How short is this game?  To be perfectly honest, less than half an hour.  It took me 24 minutes from start to finish.

So this is a great and bad game in several ways. If you have never played any version of Devil May Cry 4 then I highly recomend picking this one up.
So lets start off with the cons of Devil MayCry 4: Special Edition.
*New Cons*
-You have to play through the dreadful campain several times with the good modes only becoming playable after you have beaten it once or twice Legendary Dark Knight difficulty is an exception to this and THANK GOD because its an amazing gamemode.
-Level Progress does not transfer over to other characters you want to play. For instance, I can play Vergil all the way till level 12 and then deceide I want to play as Trish. I would have to start all over again on a new campain. It's a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥but its not the end of the world.
-The Special Edition looks better than the past version....but is incredibly more gpu intensive for whatever reason. I have not heard anyone complain about massive slowdowns or anything but instead people who would get 200fps on the old version no only average around 60~ or so. It looks slightly better but not enough to justify that level of intensity.
-Couple of new underwhelming cutscences for the new chracters that arent even worth mentioning.
*Old Cons*
-Story is pretty lame even for a Devil May Cry tittle
-Level Design loops back around....litterally
-Same repetive music track over and over and over and......
-Bosses really arent that incredibly well designed
*New Pros*
-ERMAHGAWD the new characters are amazing. The quality control of these playably characters are incredible. Each of them are absurdly unique with there own little niche and advantages.
-Great Skins are great. Some are underwhelming and there arent that many but they look great and show up in cutscenes as well.
-Legendary Dark Knight mode is just everything you want from the game. Hard as♥♥♥♥♥♥and enough punching bags that you dont get bored.
-After you unlock Bloody Palace you can play all the chracters anytime you want which reduces a lot of complaints about the story.
*Old Pros*
-Game looks pretty decent even by todays standards.
-Cutscences are interesting.
-Nero is a great addition to the party which gives us a nice break from Dante's charming but over powered ego.
-Great combat and leveling up mechanics. Essentially dont get hit. Button mashing might work sometimes on the regular enemies but button mash on bosses and you're gonner.
-Great varients of difficulty.
Overall Devil May Cry 4 is a great game that you may place once and enjoy it; or play it again because you have completly fallen in love with the game.

I've been a fan of the series since buying the first one when it came out many years ago.
And I can safely say this is a great Deus Ex game. It took me a total of 37 hours to finish my first (pacifist) run through, and I missed a few side quests along the way. Add to that the around 2 hours the Jensen Story “DLC” lasted me and the fact I haven’t even touched Breach yet, you are looking at a solid 40+ hours of gameplay if you take your time and explore.
I had 0 issues with the way the game ran on my system and had 0 crashes, 0 bugs and 0 glitches during my entire time of play.
As far as graphic settings go, this game is IMO the new Crysis in how it can bring mighty new systems to their knees (and consequently send the owners of said machines to the forums to complain about it) but with a bit of common sense you can set it to run well and look great with the huge amount of settings that Nixxes gives you to tweak. (I posted two screenshots in regards to my in game fps in my steam profile).
The game is slightly above average in regards to the clichéd main story line. Where it truly shines are the great side quest missions, and the vast amount of story related information spread on computers and pdas found everywhere across the game’s world. It also pays to stop and listen to the NPCs talking; I learned a lot of things about the world around Jensen by doing so.
As far as the micro-transaction controversy goes, I didn’t need them and I wasn’t prompted to use them and if it wasn’t due to the nerd-rage flowing through the internet in regards to them, I wouldn’t even have known about them.  I’m not a fan of micro-transactions, but I know they are the future; all the yelling isn’t going to change that fact.
Two things keep me from giving this game a higher score on my personal 1 to 10 chart.
1) All of the preorder bonuses should be there for every new play through. Period.
2) The Jensen Story “DLC” is painfully obviously ripped out of the original game, and the way it ended makes me sure that the rest of the coming DLC is probably going to be the same way.
So to wrap this up, I give it a solid 8/10 and highly recommend it to anyone who likes stealth/combat rpgs.

Call of Juarez tells a cohesive narrative of two brothers who set out to avenge the murderous of their mother. The twists and turns are pretty unpredictable, and it wraps up quite nicely as a wholesome western story. They even did a great job basing the story from the points of views as the brothers – one in a traditional shoot-em-up cowboy style, while the other is more cunning in terms of clunky 2008 stealth mechanics and tedious obstacle mantling.
However, I cannot recommend this game from a gameplay perspective. The whole game offers more of the same in terms of repetitive environments, and an overall lack of diversity in terms of combat. Weapons all felt the same with little variation, and enemies were too predictable. This could have been made up for if environments had engaging obstacles to surpass or they peppered more of the story into these levels, but a lack of either made it feel as if the levels were dragging on. Stealth elements were unbearable - you crouched in bushes to hope no one saw you, and the second they turned their back you were allowed to run full force in the opposite direction. But if they were facing your direction, you could be spotted even at a hundred metres away.
While many games can come out alright if the story can surpass the gameplay, but even then there still needs to be a baseline level of interesting stuff to do to make it worth sticking around for. As a result, I just didn't feel that in my playthrough of the first Call of Juarez.

This is an excellent but short FPS along the lines of Half Life, but in a faithful western setting.
While old, it has aged well and runs completely bug free in 4K under Windows 10.   Numerous graphics settings round out the PC-first ethic of the developers.
Gameplay is novel, with two protagonists (each level has you controlling one of the two), each with different strengths and weaknesses.  While this could have just been a gimmick it was implemented in such a way that you can enjoy the strengths of each character without being frustrated by their limits.
Great level design gives you multiple paths to achieve the same outcome, and excellent re-use of assets stretches the game out from the (admittedly short) 15 hours it took me to finish.
A few small gripes - the "quickdraw" duel mechanic is janky and annoying.   Some of the puzzles are obtuse.  The game is dated (but has aged well).    These aren't showstoppers, however.

Call of D̶u̶t̶y̶  Juarez is a m̶i̶l̶i̶t̶a̶r̶y̶  western themed first-person shooter. The levels are pretty linear and slow-motion is used constantly.
Real talk tho, this game is good.
The story covers most of the usual western fare; Horseback chases, a train scene, a lone badass laying waste to the population of an entire town, everything is covered fairly well. The voice acting and writing is nicely done, though the written text can get a bit sloppy, such as the unforgivable "of" in the place of "have".
An interesting thing to note is that the game doesn't let the player abuse corpses and innocents, sometimes punishing the behavior with a game over. This can get annoying during particularly intense battles. If I accidentally click on a corpse, I'll be prevented from shooting for a second while the character I'm playing as tells me that he won't do it, and sometimes that moment is enough to let something kill me, but that's the thing; From a story perspective, it makes sense. Both of the playable characters have established personalities, and neither of them is a heartless enough ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to disregard their morals, even when it may be convenient.
However, it sometimes gets unrealistic. For example, during the carriage chase, when other horseback riders appear, the only real option is to shoot the riders, and not the horses. I've emptied guns into those animals, but the game doesn't let them die because the developers have made it clear that this is not how the game is meant to be played. The flipside of this is that they can be used as instant barricades to take cover behind, and I did this several times when playing on the hard difficulty.
The best examples, I feel, are the stealth sections as Billy. For most of them, you are not allowed to kill the people you are trying to avoid, essentially making it forced stealth, because they also happen to be innocent, and the entire first half of the game is Billy fleeing from a false murder accusation. However, there's one part, where he has just escaped from town, and the people he has to avoid are criminals. THEN, he has other options.
This game excels at depth of gunplay, and it does so without feeling insulting or overpowering to the player. There is no lock-on, unlike in many other games of the genre. Slow motion is used, sure, but only when it makes sense, such as duels, or to give the player a small advantage in combat. Multitasking is rewarded immensely via the full akimbo shooting. The weapons are all unique, and each has its own practical application; I found myself voluntarily using every type of weapon the game provided to staisfy certain combat situations. However, because the guns degrade and eventually break from continuous use, the player will sometimes have to make use of unpreferable alternatives just to survive. It's all enough to keep the shootouts tense, and that's what really matters. That's when the game is at its best, when the player is ducking in and out of cover with extremely responsive controls to fend off hordes of enemies.
My biggest problem with the game is that it just feels lacking. It's difficult to put into words, because pretty much everything it does, it does well, but it never feels like it goes quite as far as it could. The levels often contain wide stretches of traversable land, but the objectives are fairly linear, so while it is possible to explore much of what there is to see, there is usually no reason to do so apart from (maybe) collecting some pickups. I had to play through it several times before I felt satisfied.
The multiplayer is also pretty dead nowadays. There aren't many populated servers, and most of the ones I found had pretty high ping. If you're getting this game, you're going to be sticking mainly to the single player, so thank heavens it's breddy gud.

If you're reading this, there's a very good chance that you've heard about The Sims. It's been difficult to escape the popular franchise's web, what with two full games and a seemingly endless stream of expansions. The first thing you may be asking, then, is whether The Sims 3 is worth playing, or if it's just more of the same. Well, it most certainly is worth it, and yes, in some ways it is more of the same. But in this case, that's a very good thing. For anyone who's played The Sims or its first sequel, this familiarity will let them ease into it, feeling like a welcomed guest rather than an outsider. But this doesn't make The Sims 3 a simple rehash of what's come before. Instead, returning elements have been energized and extended by a number of terrific improvements, such as expanded customization tools, additional tools for interaction with other sims (and other players), and more tangible goals and rewards. Most importantly, the free-to-explore town makes you feel like part of an entire virtual society--a feature approximated but never fully realized in the previous games. By blending together the old and the new, developer Maxis has created the best, most charming game yet in the series.
So what is it that makes The Sims 3 even more addictive than its predecessors? It's partially due to the deft handling of rewards; it doles out new social options, new aspirations, and the possibility of better furniture and wood flooring at a slow but even pace, which keeps you tied to your computer for hours at a time. It offers the element of surprise, showing off its abundant charms through funny social interactions that make you want to be part of the improved virtual community. Although it could have offered even more right out of the box, there's still an awful lot of content here, and it's bound to put a smile on almost anyone's face.

Charming visuals and audio
Good balance of sandbox play and specific goals
Loads of content to keep you busy for months

First off. My original negative review, is somehow missing, and I didn't delete it. So I'm writing this.
The Early Access version of the game, made big promises, such as 4 campaigns, more then 4 playable characters, and horde mode. Of these, Horde mode is the only one to have happened. As somewhere between the original promise and the JNPR dlc update, they decided to make JNPR paid dlc.
At the end of Early Access most of the community wasn't happy with the state of the game. After launch, that didn't change. There's several reasons for this, but I'll explain why I wasn't happy.
The finished campaign we got took only about 2 and a half hours to beat. Very short. And what next? Nothing. That was it, there was nothing else to do in the game. Except repeating it over and over, to level up your characters, reset them, and level them again for hunter rank. A meaingless addition that meant nothing, because doing it, gave you nothing.
A short game that got more expensive as it got to release, for such little value. I got my value, in the first EA build, before the mechanics and such were changed with cobmat update, but since that original build is lost forever, I guess it's meaningless to keep talking about. But I want to mention it because. The early build is where I had the most fun. Easily while the combat wasn't as depthful, the enemies were fun to kill. More spawned, and they didn't have their silly counters that spammed right through your attacks to hurt you in the middle of a combo.
That brings me to my second reason for hating RT games. With the JNPR dlc, much the community really liked the new team's design choices. Bringing fun and new playstyles to the game. I don't know personally, as I refuse to give RT my money. Because of what they did after this positive feedback.
The devs said flat out, they WOULD NOT revisit team RWBY to bring them up to JNPR's new standard, because it would take time and effort. Now, making a game is hard, yes? Anyone can agree. But the dev's have done nothing but ignore the community, and refuse to act like a game developer. Developing a game means support after launch, including fixing base game problems, such as the complaints of the original team vs JNPR.
RT Games works on a measurement of time vs money. RT as a content producer is very corporate in this. With videos, it makes sense. A finished video is finished and out the door. But a game is a living breathing thing. It needs more development time after launch.
With such short content, and only promises that imply it will be paid dlc IF it does come. I cannot recommend this game.

Brother - A tale of Two Sons is both a well written story and well thought puzzles! You learn pretty much all of the control mechanics within the first 10 minutes but it's the clever way in which the game implements them that keeps you thinking throught the 5-10 hour campaign. The game starts off very much as a light hearted fairy tale, albeit with a sad back story. Yet half way through it shift's very much from a pleasant, whimsical fairy tale and follows the path more akin towards Brothers Grim. This sombre tone compliments the soundtrack beautifully, which overall is really quite enchanting. The puzzles themself never feel overly taxing which allows the story to flow nicely. As for the controls they can be a little tricky to start with even for the most ambidextrous of people. Big brother is controled with the left analog stick whilst little brother is the right. The respective back buttons are used to control the brothers action and the trigger buttons rotate the camera angle. The end result is a game that allows you to experience a really moving story and also lets you attempt puzzles that will still give a sense of saticfaction when you complete them. Worth looking at if you have an interest in puzzle games :)

A great little game with a very engaging story, original gameplay and a unique way of controlling the main protagonists, the two brothers. I played this on my Nvidia SHIELD TV using the SHIELD controller and it played great. The controls are intuitive and feel really responsive. I have read that the game can also be played with mouse and keyboard but a controller is really recommended if you want the best experience.
I was surprised at how engaging the story was without any sort of real dialogue or narrative. The journey is quite emotional and the music and especially the sound design add a lot to the overall atmosphere of the game. Though it's only 3 hours long, the length of the game feels about right.
It's also a very nice looking game with beautiful rendered backgrounds and fluid animations. The locations you visit are very diverse and the game never feels dull or repetitive because of this. All in all this is a game that everyone should give a try. It's a great testament of what a small group of talented designers can do. Be sure to pick it up, it's well worth it.
