When the original Deus Ex was released in 2000, it was unlike many games of its time. It aimed to provide the player with obstacles that could be overcome in different ways, depending on the player's preference. The concept wasn't new - System Shock already struck a similar chord. However, Deus Ex was among the first games to take this concept to a dynamic, urban cyberpunk environment that acknowledged player choices. It featured elements of role playing games, first person shooters and stealth games, and despite each individual element not living up to the quality of a proper entry in each genre, Deus Ex combined them into one tight package on a scale that hadn't been done before.
While sales weren't overhelming, Deus Ex left a bit of a mark on the industry. At the time of release, it was showered with praise by publications and players alike for its open-ended level design and the story involving possibly every popular conspiracy theory conceived in the last decades. To this very day, Deus Ex has a dedicated following and continues to top "Best Games of All Time" lists.
Big shoes to fill, but developer Eidos Montreal lived up to the challenge with their 2011 prequel Deus Ex: Human Revolution. It proved not only that you can make a game like Deus Ex with current industry conventions, but also that there's still a crowd for it. A crowd large and loud enough to warrant another game.
So here we go again. Deus Ex: Mankind Divided improves on the core elements that make the series interesting. The player has the opportunity to tackle missions in even more ways fitting his individual playstyle, whether he prefers to sneak, shoot or talk his way to success, provided he invested in the right augmentations. This is what makes those games so addicting: Even if there's an initial setback, you never really hit a wall since there's always a vent shaft you can crawl into, a computer you can hack, a hidden passage you can enter, a guard you can persuade in one way or another or an augmentation you can use - all you need to do is keep looking. Meanwhile, well-placed guards and security measures ensure there's tension of getting caught. In fact, the game does a great job of conveying that you're playing a teched up secret agent rummaging through things where he shouldn't. When everything else fails, the player can always shoot his way through, which thankfully feels as satisfying as never before in a Deus Ex game.
Apart from the obvious paths, Mankind Divided offers more surprises than Human Reovlution did in terms of level design and options. And those options are equally viable, too. Where Human Revolution kind of threaded you into going the stealthy hacker route due to it netting the most experience points and providing rather scarce ammunition for lethal weapons, that favoritism is gone in Mankind Divided. Also, player choices get acknowledged more often or influence the game in some way. For instance, going on a killing spree in the previous area might anger a non-player character and make him unsusceptible to getting talked down. Additionally, at several points the game will ask you to make a binary choice, which may change aspects about an upcoming mission.
Visually, Mankind Divided is an absolute delight. Eidos Montreal continues to present designs that look contemporary yet futuristic with a bit of Starbucks latte extravagance thrown in for the mix, although that aspect isn't as strong as in Human Revolution. Prague is an unusual choice as a backdrop for a cyberpunk game. Especially the daylight segments evoke flashbacks to Half-Life 2's City 17 - an Eastern European city where sci-fi elements fester out of the architecture. But during nighttime, Prague is just as capable as a stage for a cyberpunk game. The environments are cluttered with items, which properly gives the impression of them being inhabited. However, obsessive compulsive types might experience that as a negative since the clutter hides useful items on more than one occasion. Environments are important for storytelling as well because they contain a lot of background information, which is the best way to do story in a video game: It doesn't bother you if you don't care, but it's readily available if you do. Plus, the player can explore it at his own pace without having to take a break from the actual game.
Regarding the story itself: Since Mankind Divided progresses further in the timeline, references to the first Deus Ex get more frequent and prominent characters from the original make an appearance in person. The actual plot is a rather standard affair and serves mostly as a vehicle to flesh out the big, overarching conspiracy leading to the events of the first game. The problem with the story is that people know what's coming and all the prequels do is prep work. Because of that, focusing on Adam Jensen was probably a smart move since his role is undefined by the games set later in the timeline. The characters can be a bit bland at times, but they are usually well-rounded enough to be liked or disliked, although the chemistry was better between Human Revolution's cast.
There has been a bit of moaning regarding the ending. It's not that it's bad, sudden or incomplete and more that it leaves you with little progress. The conflict introduced in the first moments of the game is resolved, but the answers ultimately point towards the same organization that has been pulling the strings in the shadows the entire time anyway. In most other games, this would be the moment where the story really kicks off. Instead, Mankind Divided rolls the credits. Considering the game was planned with sequels in mind, it's a more of a Fellowship of the Ring situation. Here's hoping we won't have to wait another five years.
If you enjoyed Human Revolution for its gameplay, getting Mankind Divided is a no-brainer as it improves on every single gameplay-related aspect: Environments are bigger, more detailed and missions offer far more options to be completed, all while more of your choices will get acknowledged in some way. Fans of the original game will enjoy the stronger ties to the first Deus Ex, but be ultimately let down by the story. For cyberpunk junkies, this is a more than adequate fix.

After a marathon of nearly 30 hours I finished Deus Ex: Mankind Divided. I did my best to poke around the cities and find out secrets but I couldn't find all of them in just one playthrough.
Mankind Divided features more alert enemies and a smarter AI compared to its predecesors. The graphics and enviroments are gorgeous and the effects are amazing. I spent an hour walking around Prague just to get a look at the city.
Skills-wise the game features new augmentations that allow you to either mow down enemies or be even stealthier. For me the game is at its best played through a tactical-stealth type. It would be too easy to simply turn invulnerable and go out guns blazing all of the sudden.
The one thing that irks me is that the main story is too short. It should be around 20-25 hours of gameplay. A one day game marathon if you get hooked into it and don't stop playing. There were the ocasional bugs that didn't affect me as much as they should have, such as repetitive dialogue from characters that were saying something else via the info-link, or characters that I couldn't save coming back from exile or prison. I wanted to experience a longer story line, for some reason I feel like it took me longer to wrap up Human Revolution than Mankind Divited. There are still story and plot holes that need filling and I wish the story was longer.
I still enjoyed the game and I appreciate the effort Edios Montreal put in the game. Hopefuly there will be more DLC's to further flesh out the story content of the game.

When I was younger everyone I knew was a huge fan of 'Half Life', myself included. And 'Red Faction' was a pretty popular game upon it's release, but for the most part nobody really cared about it all that much after that. Which makes sense I suppose, I mean, 'Half Life' had the mod 'Counter-Strike' and it's revolutionary multiplayer, and 'Red Faction' had the gimmick of being able to destroy everything in your path, which was actually a pretty big deal back then if I remember correctly.
But still, 'Half Life' was the game everyone cared about, the game everybody played; so it's safe to say that 'Red Faction' was swept under the rug for the majority of kids growing up in the 90's. Which isn't all that surprising actually, games were much more hit or miss back in those days, so when people found something that was great, they stuck to it and played it til they could no longer. To say it best, 'Red Faction' was the Utah Jazz to 'Half Life's' Chicago Bulls. Yeah, let's see how many of you get that reference.
However, after coming back to this game after almost two decades, and having never beaten it until just recently, I can honestly say that 'Red Faction' is just as good as 'Half Life', if not better. You would think that such an early game with the premise for total destruction would be mediocre at best, but the developers nailed it the first time around. Combine that with combat that's just as fun as any other first person shooter on the market today, controls that feel natural from the get-go, and the ability to drive vehicles much like in the 'Halo' games, and you've got yourself one hell of a timeless shooter.

My first experience with the Red Faction series was Red Faction Guerilla, so I've only gotten around to playing this game recently despite its age.
This game is basically a standard corridor shooter with a few twists, mainly in the form of the Geo-Mod engine and vehicle sections. The Geo-Mod engine lets you blast holes through most walls/floors/ceilings/terrain, which is pretty amazing for a game from 2001 and it's very unfortunate that most modern shooters still don't let you do that.
The single player campaign is solid, with a good story and some interesting vehicle/stealth sections mixed in. There's a nice variety of weapons as well. Unfortunately, the game is still very much a product of its time and the game is a very linear, twitch shooter. There's a few sections with multiple paths and places where you can use the Geo-Mod engine to create an alternate path, but these are sadly underutilized. There's also a major difficulty spike about 3/4 the way through the game and the AI has some issues as well and can be quite annoying at times. Still, it doesn't have any major shortcomings compared to other shooters and is worth playing through once, especially if you're a fan of the newer games and want some more of the backstory. The story is good, but the game is a bit short and ends rather abruptly.
Multiplayer is where this game really shines. The Geo-Mod engine provides lots of tactical opportunities that are lacking even in modern shooters.
Audio is good, with well-done voiceovers for the campaign, unfortunately the graphics have not aged well and the game requires a 3rd party patch (PureFaction) to fix some issues with running on modern machines.
Overall, a fun game and definitely a classic.

The Sims 3 can take awhile to get the hang of it if it's your first time playing a Sims game. But there should be no problem learning since there are tutorials you can view for pretty much everything in the game. Anyways, The Sims 3 is a life simulator and open world sandbox that lets you do whatever you want and play how you like. First thing to do is start creating your Sim. There are tons of different customization options for them from the type of clothes they wear, accessories, facial features, the way their body is shaped, etc. You can also download additional clothes  and accessories from the Sims store and even user created content! You can give them traits which make up their personality, make additional Sims and choose how they are related to each other, name them, then move them on into the world to start living life. There is no story mode but you can choose a "lifetime wish" which is exactly as it sounds. As you play, you can work on fulfilling your Sim's wish and in reward, you get lifetime points that you can spend towards special things that can make your Sim's life easier. ...Or you can ignore that and do whatever you feel like if you want! Your Sim could get a job and work to pay bills for the house or you can be completely irresponsible and go dumpster diving if you like.
Your Sim can interact with other Sims as well and get to know them. You have several conversation options such as chat, gossip, insult, compliment, etc. You could become friends, enemies, or even lovers! The game will let you have romantic relationships with a Sim regardless of their gender. So they can be gay or straight. Your choice.
Now the next thing to know is that your Sims have "needs" which are an important part in the gameplay. The needs are represented by bars and they change color depending on how your Sim is doing. Your Sims have needs such as hunger, bladder, energy, social, hygiene, and fun. You have to pay attention to these because they will affect what happens in the game. Like if you ignore your Sim's hunger needs, they'll die. Or if you don't bath them, your Sim will stink and be embarrassed around others. Your Sims can also automatically control themselves and they will do things such as get something to eat or hop in the shower if their needs become too low. But keep in mind that this does not always work because they may wait until a certain need becomes incredibly low to fix it and it's good to always check them every now and then to make sure they're not too busy talking to someone for several hours rather than eating!
Now, the lifestyle you want for your Sim is entirely up to you. You could work your way up and become rich, get as many friends as possible and become popular, romance up several people and have several girl/boyfriends, or just maybe take a walk in the park. Haha. That being said, I totally recommend this game and there is plenty to do and many ways to live your life however you want. And there are also many expansion packs that completely change the world and add lots of new content onto the already lot there is. I've easily spent over 50 hours and that's only in the base game with my first Sim family. Totally worth it!

RWBY: Grimm Eclipse is simply not a fun game. However that's not quite the biggest problem I have with this title. Like a number of modern games we've seen, RWBY is yet another result of a developer , Rooster Teeth Games, falling into the bad habit of not only being an early access game, but the final product being rushed out to consumers with almost little to no care.

The gameplay structure is mostly basic. You go through each level with a linear path beating up hordes of mostly grimm. Occasionally there are certain points where you have to defend a post, but the AI do little damage to the post that this particular part of the game is pointless and mostly feels like patting. Along with the small handful of moveset for each character, you can do ultimate attacks and even trigger a 2-man team attack. However the team attack feels random and to pull them off you have to meet specific requirements. The idea behind it sounds good on paper, but in practice its feels like a convulted mess. The whole gameplay really just comes down to a boring button masher will little substance.

The levels themselves look decent enough, but are mostly empty and feel hollow. The levels seems to only serve the purpose of hiding relics you can collect throughout the game that give you experience points. Leveling works somewhat like a MOBA game. Each level you gain, you get a point. Those points can be used to gives characters new abilities and alter their moves. You can use up all your points ( which you can get up to 10 points max) or get the points you used back to change different abilities  so there's some room for variety.

As for content, there's little to go on. Aside from the 2-3 hour campaign mode there's hardly any replay value to be had. Even if playing through the same levels with each member of Team RWBY, there just isnt enough to keep players coming back. There is an online co-op mode, but even with that players may not get a whole lot out of this game. There's just too little to do and see for a $25 title that was suppose to evolve out of its early access stage.

The bottom line is that RWBY: Grimm Eclipse is not a completed game among other things. I wouldnt even recommend this game to fans of the series given what little effort went into this title. From the way Rooster Teeth has handled RWBY, despite it being a small scale title, they were looking for a quick cash cow they could milk off of.

A lot of RTS games tend to be all-or-nothing, in that once one side starts winning, they keep winning. This can often lead to situations where the game is over ten to twenty minutes before you finish it. Not so in Infested Planet.
Even as you capure Control Points, gaining more resources to bring more upgrades and units to bare on your foe, they similarly mutuate and upgrade, developing new abilities that often force you to reassess the stratagy you're using. On more than one occasion I have been sweeping across a map, when suddenly I realized I had pressed too hard too fast, and the combination of mutations the enemy had developed threatened to undo me!
Even later in the campaign, when mission paramiters diverge from the standard "Kill all aliens" model, things stayed interesting and tense. The game really captures the feel of an endless horde barreling down on a few desparate defenders.
The fact that you can always pause the action to assign move or build orders makes micromanagement possible for those who like it, while the more macro-focused can experiment with a plethora of functional build combinations between upgrading your own troops, building defensive emplacements, or contstructing buildings that enable global upgrades to your entire side. The game is great for casual dips once you've completed the campaign - I usually play a quick game or two every day as a break between other things.

In Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons, you go along with two brothers on a journey to get some important medicine for their deadly wound father. It's necessary to play with a controller, because you have to move both brothers at the same time.
That can sometimes be very frustrating, but the great story, the beautiful sad soundtrack and the lovely graphics really make up for it.
This unique game has a gorgeous world with many beautiful details. The graphics are very cute, mostly the expressions of both brothers are quite realistic.  It is shown a really strong bond between Naia, the older brother and Naiee, the younger one. Both of them have simple, but striking personalities, for example Naiee is usually some kind of animal-loving jester, but he shows a deep traumatic fear towards water.
The uncommon music fits perfectly into all six landscape you will explore.
Another great point which I only recognize in this game is the language. You know exactly, how the characters feel and what they are trying to say, but you aren't able to understand the language itself, because it's only a fantasy language.

Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons is a true marriage of gameplay and narrative. It will make you laugh and it will definitely make you cry at the end.  This game is a real must-have for all lonely and depressive people out there, for all of you who don't have much faith in their own abilities, for all of you who want to see how strong love and friendship can be, for all of you who maybe fear the future.

Mount & Blade is a timeless classic.
I remember first playing the original Mount & Blade, before the "Warband" revamp, and being completely blown away by how simple, yet fun the core idea of the game was. Ride around, recruit some soldiers. Feed them, train them, take them with you on your conquests. Serve a king, be a king, be a lawless man. Burn a village, or get gifted a village and build it up. Buy some armor and a sword, or maybe a bow and a horse. Wars start and end, kingdoms grow in size or dwindle. War parties form and march to the enemy's land without you doing anything. It's a really simple, but living and constantly evolving world in which you are, for the most part, just another guy dying in a terrible war.
Given the sandbox aspect of the game, you can play it for as long as your imagination allows. It may be that, after playing for 100 hours, you're still not satisfied. And if you are, there are mods that will give you another hundred hours or so of play time. Gameplay is smooth, swordplay feels unlike anything else I've played before it. In fact, I would argue that it spawned a whole different way of doing combat in action games. You can swing your sword in different positions and the enemy will try to block or parry the blow. If you swinged the right way, your blow will go through their defences and harm them. It's amazing. And I can't even begin to describe what that kind of action does for Multiplayer. Once you learn to use your weapons, you really feel like you're matering the art of combat. It's not just progress through level-ups and stats, although you have that too. The soundtrack is great, too.
Now, don't be fooled. It's an indie game, made by TaleWorlds, a turkish video-company not really known for anything else. And those turks sure know how to leave bugs behind in their games. Mount & Blade can be a buggy mess. And it can feel unfinished and unpolished at many, many places. After all these years, however, I could even ague that those bugs and unpolished edges are what made the game great. As it usually is with ♥♥♥♥♥♥, bugged sandbox messes of games, the community fills in the voids and mod everything they can. What we can't mod, we joke about. Either way, there's something good to be taken from every ♥♥♥♥♥♥ thing in Warband.
It's timeless, it ages like fine wine, and it will make you scream and laugh as you cut down your enemies on a huge 200 vs 200 battle in an open field. It will also make you curse your enemies when you're backed into a corner and try to defend your sieged castle against armies ten times the size of yours.
There is no game that gives you an experience like this one. Mount & Blade is a game category of its own.

I have mixed feelings about this game/kids story.  It was definitely worth it for free, but I would have been disappointed if it was more than $1.  I gave it a thumbs up because it is free.
What I liked about it was the cute story and innocent childlike graphics.  However, I wish they would improve the speed of play.  The speed is almost unbearably slow.  By way of background, it is not really a game or a movie.  It is a kid's “choose your own” story with very few story choices.  The frustrating part is that the single lines become visible in a slow fade with only one sentence at a time.  I spent half an hour “playing”, or more aptly reading, what I would have preferred to read in just over five minutes - and I am not a fast reader.  The game becomes a game of clicking as fast as you can to get the damn text to display quick enough to read before your conscious drifts off to sleep.
I think the game/story would be drastically improved with a  mechanism that allowed the reader to view and read whole paragraphs or pages.  One complete storyline takes just under 30 minutes (clicking at inhuman speeds) and allows for about 3 choices.  There is an option to play the other story lines (and you can fast forward through what you already read).  However, I did not have the patience to do so.
All in all, it is slow and a bit boring, but the cute, innocent childlike graphics and story are nostalgic enough to remind one of childhood daydreams.  I think the reading/story level might be good for a ten year old, but I don’t think most ten year olds would have the patience for it.
I wanted to like this book, but I can only give it only about 3.5 out of 10 stars - worthwhile for a free book, but not for much money.  If they can fix the speed issue, then I would raise my opinion dramatically.  I hope the author will accept my apologies for being so critical.

First review of a game ever. Square Enix what were you thinking? You wasted my money! I will never buy a pre order ever again. Ths should have been HR 2.0. The game is getting a lot of unfair thumbs down because of Square Enix policies, but I gave a thumbs up to Eidos for developing a great game and to Nixxes for quickly patching most of the bugs that plagued the first release. I also give a thumbs down to Square Enix, though. Yes, the microtransactions doesn't affect the single player, but to me it looks like they forced Eidos to create Breach mode for the solely purpose of selling IAP. That developing times could have been used for the story mode instead.
I still didn't finished the game, but I played it for 25 hours (non violent run) and I'm enjoying it a lot. Yes, the story is less epic than in HR but playing a Deus Ex with today's graphics and the extra augs compensate for that. The art direction is awesome as always. If you are the kind of gamer that every once in a while stops to admire the art in the game you won't be disappointed. I love the attention to detail. You can explore every item in the inventory and the level of detail it's amazing. It's totally useless but it shows the game was made with love.
I like that the game is much more stealth friendly. For example, most weapons have no lethal ammo and some of the new augs makes stealth game a breeze (remote hacking is great). In the other way, violent gameplay it's also much improved. Guns feels a lot better than in HR and like with stealth gameplay, some new augs makes violent gameplay more interesting. Gun modding on the go it's also a great feature.
On the downside I wish they added another hub, but at least you revisit Prague at nightime and Golem, while not a hub, it's quite big. I spent around 4 hours there. Also, as many reviewers stated, facial details are quite inconsistent and many times animations are awkward and exagerated.
My recommendation, explore the hubs, talk to everyone, but before leaving an area check online where you can find sidequests, because some of them are quite hidden, some are more interesting than the main story. While I'm ok with non handholding I think that there should be some icons to indicate where you can get the sidequests. It's a shame so many people is going to miss these great stories.
To sum it up, if you liked Human Revolution you're going to enjoy this game. It's more of the same but improved in many areas.

Holodrive is an early access fast paced multiplayer platform shooter up. Developed by BitCake Studios and released on the 25th of March (24th in America) 2016. This is the first game from BitCake and boy is it an interesting one. But interesting, is the only thing I can say about it.
When I started up Holodrive for the first time, I was greeted by an excellent tutorial that taught me what to do, shoot bad guys, defend object, win game. But I couldn’t help but notice that something was missing. The music was dull, mainly for the fact that there wasn’t any music. This made the tutorial boring quicker than it should have. But I was blessed with some generic dubstep music, better than silence, but it won’t be in my Spotify playlist anytime soon. The first thing I noticed was the option to buy micro transactions for keys to open a box full of goodies. The goodies contain anything from cosmetic skins (which I’m okay with) to weapons that can give you an advantage. It wasn’t clear if I could unlock items by just playing the game, but I did get a few cosmetics during my time.
But how was my time? My time was occupied by either finding someone to shoot or actually shooting. When I was looking for games to join I’d either be put into a lobby instantly with a few players or I’d be in a lobby by myself. Sometimes I’d have to wait a few minutes for a lobby to be found, and when a lobby was found, it was just 1 other player. This is a disappointment, because when I was in having a battle, the maps felt like all routes were meant to be clogged with players trying to get into the objective with non-stop action. But sadly it feels empty with only 2 players on each team and there are a few silent moments when playing, forcing my-self to stop going to the objective to spend time looking for an enemy was not fun. But when I did find a player to kill, it was extremely satisfying to hear the ding when your little foe was killed. To kill your foe’s, you pick up rocket launchers, sniper rifles, hyper sub machine guns, shot guns, all the fun jazz. They all feel different and have their advantages and disadvantages. The only problem is the weapon selection system, when you have all the weapons in the game (you lose them on death and you have to find them in the map) you can pick them by using the scroll wheel or by pressing 1 – 7 on the keyboard. You’d think if I picked up my sniper rifle it would be 2 if it was my second weapon. But no, it’s 7. Weapons have their own hot key no matter what order you pick it up in, this is annoying because I think that “oh, I just picked up a shotgun, 2 right?” nope, 5! When you complete a game you’re spawned into an arena where you can shoot the losing team with weapons and its incredibly fun while all of your stats appear on screen, this reminds me when I win games in Team Fortress 2, but on a platform. If you’re the MVP of the game you have a golden star above your head for bragging rights which makes you a target in the scoreboard area.
But shooting is only half the fun, the maps. I have mixed feelings about the maps. One is very tight and action compact with bullets flying everywhere and is very streamline and intense, the other gave me a headache with different colors and I was hitting every wall, meaning I was being slowed down + it was cramped and it just generally annoyed me. What also annoyed me was that there was no music in the game other than the main menu. Something rapid and fast paced like Hotline Miami would make things a lot more fun as I “get into the jam”. When there were more than 2 people on the screen, the action heats up. Quick. Rockets flying across my screen, bullets in one direction while shells in the other, the objective just in my reach, but I didn’t feel a sense of rush, I feel that the game should be a bit faster paced and more explosions and sparks need to be on screen to make the intensity scale to be turned up to 11. But right now it feels like a 7. Until you pick up a power up. These can double your speed, make you invisible, deal 2x damage, drop a trap power up, its excellent! These really kick things up a dial when in a hot zone.
The sound in this game (other than the music) is fantastic! When on the death screen overlooking the map, if you spawn in the left the spawn in sound plays in the left ear, which is good when you’re trying to see where you’re spawning in. It’s just a shame that I’m deaf in my left ear. Oh the wonders of surround sound, you’re all so lucky with your two ear hearing. The sounds of the weapons blasting off is satisfying, especially when I’ve got the sniper rifle fully charged, I feel like I’m about to shoot the words most powerful sniper, and when fully charged, if you hit someone it’s an instant kill, same with a rocket if it hits you. And ‘you’ will be hitting characters that instantly remind me of sack boy from the PlayStation exclusive Little Big Planet, just a whole lot less character. My lil’ minion bores me, generic futuristic sack bags. He, or she, or it… alien? Does the same animation in the main menu, poking… its tongue out while pretending its hands are guns. You can change the appearance by unlocking cosmetic items after leveling up or buying boxes to open. HoloDrive runs well, as my frame rate never dipped on the highest settings with a GTX 960, i7 4770, 16gb.
Holodrive is a game that I don’t see myself returning to… often. I found it fun to play a quick game while trying to kill time, its shooting mechanics made it fun and the momentum you can get from running down a slope makes things interesting and the power ups remind me of the fun days of Mario kart! but with a lack of music, non-consistent map design, it makes it hard for me to return to it, when I have other games to play.
SCORE: 6.8/10 (68)
PROS
•	Fun shooting mechanics
•	Power ups
•	Leveling system
CONS:
•	Lack of music
•	Non consistent level design

Well, damn. This is really, really enjoyable, especially for a Special Edition/remastering of a game. In all honesty, I'm enjoying this much more than I enjoyed Devil May Cry 3 Special Edition. Improved graphics, 3 new characters (which aren't just carbon copies of other characters, by the way [aside from a couple of recycled moves, but they fit in perfectly with each character's moveset, Vergil has a move from DMC3 that Dante uses!]), and a couple of new cutscenes. Vergil is absolutely overpowered, but he's fun as hell to play as (while still being a little bit broken). Worth the 25 dollars. Seriously, if you're thinking of getting DMC4, spend the extra five bucks and go with the Special Edition. You won't regret it.
However, this game isn't really optimized for lower-end graphics cards (unlike DMC4, which can pretty much run on a toaster), so you might have some issues getting 60fps if your card isn;t that great. I used to be able to run DMC4 at nearly 900fps. Now I'm barely passing 180. Not much of an issue if your card is good, but you might want to make sure your card is good enough to run this game decently.

THIS REVIEW MAY CONTAIN SPOILERS
tl;dr - It's great, go play it.
First off, let me just say a massive congrats to the Elements team. They really pulled it off with a short, concise but still compelling experience.
And when I say short, I truly do mean short, with a runtime of around half a hour. 45 minutes if you're a bit thick and get stuck on one of the puzzles like me.
You don't really get too much time to properly learn the story, understand who you are or why you are there. - I missed half the 'journals' that you can pick up, which might have shed a bit more light on the story. -
Now, for the technical side. The little additions to the Source engine - the bloom, the subtle filter on the screen - really does add to the atmosphere.
The AI is nothing short of astounding. In the dark, turrets won't shoot you and zombies won't see you. If you go out of sight for long enough, Striders and Combine troops alike will lose sight of you.
All of this was (mostly) made by one man. I look forward to see what he does in the future, as this was nothing short of astounding.

The Good:

Typical flash game fare.  Do the thing, unlock things that make it easier to do the thing, do the thing more.  Unfortunately, it suffers from unfocused game design, and leads to a lot of frustration.
There are four different sizes of fish, each having a minimum size of bait required to catch them -- but ALL fish go after and try to steal ALL bait, not just bait their own ranking.  The only way to get this bait is by catching a fish of one rank, and throwing it back in to get bait of the next rank.  Lastly, any time you're pulling a fish in, any larger fish it passes will nibble on it, damaging your catch and lowering its value (and making it not count towards quests - though it can still be bait).  This bait system works against itself in the worst, least productive way.
So let's say you catch a small fish.  You throw it back in as Medium Bait, and start trauling for bigger -- oops, no, another small fish ate it.  You start pulling in your new small fish, and the medium fish you were trying to catch darts in and eats half of it before you can get it back on board.  So you throw it back as medium bait, and try again.  Three attempts later, you finally catch your first medium fish.  You throw it back as Large bait, aiming to hook a big one -- oops, no, the cheapest variety of small fish just ate your bait, and then got eaten to the bones by a medium fish again.  And you have a quest to catch three large fish, and the game will not progress until you manage.
Unfortunately this ruins it as a casual experience, adding difficulty via grinding.  I'm holding out hope for an eventual upgrade that will make it go away, but it's not in sight yet.  I'll change the review if I find it.  Example upgrades that could turn it around if they exist :
- the ability to buy bait of the desired size
- permanent upgrade that raises the minimum rank of your bait
- permanent upgrade that makes fish on your line immune to being nibbled on on the way back
- making fish stop stealing bait too low rank for them
- making fish stop biting bait too high rank for them
..but really, it would be better if one of those things were available from the start.

I have enjoyed playing Holodrive in it's first form "Project Tilt" for a long time and seeing it as a fully fledged game on Steam makes me very happy. Though there are some bugs and crashes the game is very enjoyable and I recommend it to everyone. There is 1 problem that kind of bugs me. The game crashes every time I go into multiplayer and this gets kind of annoying. I am aware that it is an early access game and it's still under development but this needs to be fixed.

If you caught my Holodrive video last week you already know I really like this game, I think it’s one of the few games we see these days that’s still just about having fun instead of trying to force some longwinded story down our throats. That’s not to say narrative should always take a backseat in games, not at all but not every game. Holodrive has no complex story or hour long tutorial, Holodrive just throws you in with simple and easy to learn controls and says shoot the other guys. It’s a refreshing change of pace.
Holodrive keeps it simple putting you on a 2D plain in what I can only describe as a platform death match, as you traverse the level jumping and using your jetpack to reach higher levels you can pick up more and more weird and wonderful weapons. These include sniper rifles, phasor beams, rocket launchers and even assault rifles, these all have their advantages and disadvantages such as the sniper rifle stopping your jetpack from powering up when in use. As you progress you’ll also unlock variations of these weapons that can be setup in your load out, these also have their own stats.
You also unlock outfits as you play, letting you customize your little robot/avatar which is pretty much the main goal in Holodrive. Holodrive doesn’t really give players advantages as they level, even the alternate weapons don’t offer advantage just work in different ways so you can find what suits you the most. I can see this turning some players off as they like to gain an edge, but I favour this more balanced approach.
There are a plethora of levels and ways to play available to the player, team Deathmatch, standard Deathmatch, a capture the flag style game and the list goes on. But this is where I begin to have an issue, the game explains very little about what you are meant to be doing and while I value the hands of approach Holodrive takes it wouldn’t hurt to have some info instead of being left to work it out yourself.
But this unfortunately is where my review takes a turn for the worse, you see while I love the game and hugely enjoy playing it. There are some glaring issue to contend with, like the micro-transactions. Now I’m fine with micro-transactions in a free to play game, but currently Holodrive is £6.99 on steam while it’s in early access. When it’s officially realised it will be free, but if you want to get in early you’ll have to pay. I’m not sure Holodrive need to be early access and I don’t think it’s right to charge your earliest supporters for something you’re going to give to everyone for free eventually. Add to this the game is peppered with “Buy credits!” adverts and it leave a little bit of a sour taste in the mouth. I think BitCake are walking a very thin line with this way of developing and I could see it causing issues later on in the games life.
Outside of this the biggest issue that might be implemented in time is the lack of any way to setup your own matches, invite friends or have any control what so ever. I’m reluctant to critic this as it may well be coming, but it is missed and I look forward to its implementation.
I like Holodrive, I really do. It’s a game full of fun and enjoyment, but a game isn’t just successful on its gameplay alone. It takes clever marketing and friends wanting to play with each other, this is an area Holodrive suffers in greatly and I’m unsure of its future because of this. I personally can’t recommend it for these reasons as knowing it will become free at some point I’d have to say wait.

NOTE: This will be a lengthy review for anyone wondering if they should buy this game.
If you want a short answer: This game is addicting, and my friends thought I was dead for a week.
TorchLight 2 is a dungeon crawler, hack-and-slashgame. This means most of your gameplay/time will be consumed looking for loot. You will also spend a lot of time building your character with every level up. If you wish to skip to a section, go right ahead.
Story: There is a story? I didn't even notice I was following a story in this game. The story is practically non-existant. The only time I noticed it was when the game was changing acts. If story is what you love about games, look somewhere else. While it didn't have a story, I found myself pulled towards the game and continued playing for hours.
Graphics: I love the art style of this game. Its colorful, bright, and enjoyable. Compared to Diablo 3 and Path of Exiles, I prefer these graphics. But that is my personal opinion.
Characters: There are 4 classes to choose from. Outlander (ranged), Embermage (magic), Berserker (melee), and Engineer (melee? its the only class I have yet to play). But lets not forget that this game allows mods, and there are some pretty good character mods out there. In terms of how you build your character, its really up to you. Its not as expansive as Path of Exhile's skill tree, but it will keep you interested enough to try more combinations. The max level cap is 100, and there is a "fame" system that caps out at 33. Giving you 133 (end game) skill points to use. The leveling up is well balanced, I don't think I didn't go into a dungeon and come out the same level (or at least not close to leveling).
Pets: Free pets from the get-go! It does not depend on which animal you choose, they all do the same thing. So don't feel too conflicted when choosing an animal, its purely for looks. But the feature that all the pets have are: They fight for you. Playing solo (like I do), this is handy. The pet's level grows along side you, and can learn any spell you want to teach it. (I teach my pet summoning skills so that I have an army, and don't have to waste Manna). The pet can also return to town at any time to sell loot and buy potions. This means you will rarely have to return to town until you are done with a certain quest.
Loot: Tons of it, very balanced when it comes to finding stuff (I have yet to get repeated rare items). Every item feels like a choice. Do you ditch the armor that boosts a stat for the armor that grants you better elemental protection?
GamePlay: This is what makes the game. The gameplay is smooth and addicting, and well-done. The game is all about the gameplay. (Though to some it may get repetitive). You attack by clicking a target, simple enough. You use a set skill by right clicking. Simple. Now throw in about 50 enemies, a giant boss, and tons of gold dropping every where and you have a good game.
Diablo 3, Path of Exiles, and TorchLight 3. I have played all three by now. I played about 80 minutes of PoE, and 1h of Diablo 3. I grew bored of both quickly. For some reason, this game kept me hooked for quite a while. I enjoyed every second of it (except ya know... dying...). So is this game worth $20 bucks? To some (like me), its worth more. However if you aren't sure if this game is your cup-of-tea, then I suggest waiting for a sale. Either way, its a game worth the experience.

Concept: 10 / 10
AI / controls: 6.5 / 10
Mission design: 0 / 10
The core mechanics of this game are good.  The early stages are fun, and the shop system makes you want to keep coming back.  The targeting AI for your marines is meh, but not bad enough to ruin the game.  The first half of the story missions are of acceptable quality.
The second half of the game is a complete mess.  Later missions contain game-ending events, and unless you take an extremely specific set of precautions, you're dead.  The only way to beat some of these stages is to play them over and over until you learn the stage in advance, and specifically play to avoid the pitfalls you know are coming.
The ambush mission is a great example.  You simply spawn at the top of the map, and alien hives randomly appear around you.  You have two directions to go, but one (securing the top of the map) isn't the "correct" way, and you'll die every time if you go there.  If you try to defend your starting point (an extremely logical move), you will die because alien hives appear under you for the rest of the stage until you die.  The "correct" answer to the stage is to fall back and let the aliens destroy everything as you retreat.  If you attempt any other strategy, you'll die.  There is no indication that this is the correct answer.  And that's what makes it so infuriating.
If the level design wasn't so tremendously bad in the last half of the game, I could recommend.  Right now though it's just a $15 pile of frustration that will last you about 20 hours, tops.

Original review follows:
-----
I liked infested planet.  I bought the game on a bit of a whim when it was on sale, and it had been sitting in my gift inventory.  All I really knew about it was that you ordered people around and they shot aliens.  Which sounds like a hell of a lot of fun, really.
And it is.
The basic premise of the levels is that you start with a single capture point, and you must destroy the alien hives which sit atop their own capture points, until you control the map.  With each point you capture you get more resources (called Build Points) and the alien army 'mutates' and creates an additional complication that you must overcome.
The game plays at a great pace.  It's always tense, and yet, when you take a step back, the gameplay actually evolves slowly.  You'll often find yourself wondering if you really need to drop a turret to cover an alien attack, or if you could just spare a single marine and spend the resources for the turret elsewhere, and all the while the lines of battle are being pushed and pulled.  It's a great feeling.
And those choices.  Those options!  There are so many different things you can do.  There are three main 'classes' of upgrades you can spend points on: weapons for your soldiers, localised power buildings like turrets or healing crates, or global upgrades that can do all manner of things from giving your soldiers grenades to having reinforcements dropped in by helicopter mid-fight.  The best thing of all?  They're practically all valid courses of play.  Everything feels balanced and nice.
I mean look; there's a building that summons robotic clones of your soldiers when they die that fight on for a while.  This means that yes: suicide missions are possible.  And sometimes they are even optimum.  If you -need- to capture that next point before the next attack wave comes in, and you don't have enough points for something to siege with, then an all out infantry rush might just do the trick.
Then there's the opponent.  The alien swarm controlled by the AI.  Here's another thing that's been done really well.  While I was playing I got the distinct impression that behind the alien swarm was another player.  Or at least another thing playing its own game.  It had different rules to me, but it had to abide by them nonetheless.  Each mutation the aliens choose have a profound impact on your play and options.  You might be happily shotgunning the swarm one moment, but with the next capture suddenly the alien has consolidated its power into pseudo-human guardians, and you need to swap out your cheep shotguns for expensive sniper rifles.  At higher difficulties the AI even counter-picks you.  For example, if you invest in a lot of personnel upgrades, the aliens will send clones of them. The game doesn't look the prettiest, and the sounds are okay, but what it does well is the gameplay, and it does that amazingly.

So, I thought this would be a smash clone, or at least something based off of smash from just looking at the trailer. I expected some sort of intricate combo game and interesting play styles for each character. Coming from the competitive scene of Melee I am always open to cool new fighting games with this sort of knockback system and when my friend recommended this to me I was genuinely excited. I opened the game, set up my controls to be like that of a Smash game, and then hopped into some practice. Immediately I realized that the comboing system is land a hit, and mash A in the opponent's direction. I thought maybe I was just bad so I hopped on to ranked mode and tried to see if anyone else was good. I pick a character at random and the match begins, and I with a gleamor of hope in my eye I start trying to imitate a dash dance and establish a neutral game.
The opponent doesn't really care and rushes towards me and mashes A, initating a dash attack. He hits me up and I expect a follow up, but no he just jumps and I dodge away. Shortly after a sword falls down from the heavens and he picks it up, sadly it wasn't sword that he picked up but a pair of guns. This is when I realized this game is actually garbage. At this point I had very little idea how to respond to this and was killed pretty quickly by the equivalent of a spike/dair. The range was absolutely mental and his movement options seemed to increase. He'd just jump above me and do some weird aerial that covered everything under him, after a bit I got used to dodging this but still this game just lacked anything special. For the next few minutes I just snuck in a few hits and tried to get some items, and when his health bar or whatever it is turned red I started going for a kill move. He doesn't really care as he just runs away and throws item for me and I do the same, this goes on for about 4 minutes and I'm bored out of my mind. Each match takes way too long with only 3 stocks on the board.
I kill him once with a lucky aerial, he kills me with a bomb, I throw at him what I can only tell to be a mine and he explodes. We're now down to our last stock both coming down from our spawn platforms, I get the nearby item which turns out to be a polearm and I do a dash attack into him, hit him up, and he's off stage. While he tries to recover I do a spike and he dies. I win the match with no sense of satisfaction and I feel like I wasted a large sum of my time just running around the stage chasing this guy. I can only imagine that this isn't the end of the depth of the game, so I hop into a few more matches and everyone shares this play style. Run around and grab items, try to sneak in some dumb hit or throw it at you, and then get a kill by using the generically named: "Strong Attack." I don't blame anyone, because there isn't a better way to play this game.
Like I said there isn't really any combo game aside from maybe one hit after a dash attack. The stages lack character and for the most part are just open arenas, the music isn't memorable but the sound design is OKAY at best. The controller support is very lacking as it often won't dodge or do an aerial in the direction you are holding, and as far as I can tell doesn't know you are holding a direction except by moving in that direction. Making aerials and air dodges way more counter intuitive than need be. My other two matches weren't much fun and I feel like I gave this game a sincere attempt and it just didn't have much to offer. For a quick play, in a really casual match it may be ok. But at a competitive stand point, or even as a fighting game this game just isn't that. Being unable to string hits together and the very surface level gameplay when not just punching your opponent make this game extremely linear even when I feel they were trying to reproduce the winning formula that the Smash franchise discovered.
In conclusion, I have to say this game is extremely underwhelming; very basic, and just boring in general. Matches are drawn out without any real approach option and recoveries are insane, being able to come back  from ANY horizontal distances and almost any vertical distances with most characters and especially some items. I cannot stress how much I dislike this game and the cheesy attributes of it. It's very campy and the game play is extremely slow. I practiced for a large part while Steam was in offline mode, and it didn't seem to record my game time, but it was closer to 60-70 minutes, and that still isn't a very big window but I don't think I can get anymore from this game. I give this a 2/10 and recommend staying away from it unless you don't already have any "fighting" (AND I USE THAT TERM EXTREMELY LOOSELY) games in your library.

I have not written many reviews because most games I play don't compel me too, but Brawlhalla...that's another story. Brawlhalla is probably the best alternative to Smash Bros., and actually feels preferable in some ways to it. The movement and fluidity of the game outshine Smash Bros.
I found out about Brawlhalla from some friends who were playing it while they were streaming. Curious, I downloaded it and joined their game without knowing what I was getting into. My Smash Bros. skills from over the years kicked in, and I won my first match. I was hooked to a game that hit me with nostalgia and new content at the same time. I learned to love and hate certain characters(♥♥♥♥ you Bodvar :D) just like I did from Smash Bros. It then hit me that this game is free, and that cosmetics are the only microtransactions in the game. After playing this game with friends for only 2 hours, I feel compelled to give Blue Mammoth Games my money for producing such a great free game. I look forward to my next trip to Walgreens to pick up groceries and Steam cards so I can purchase the All Legends Pack, and maybe even some Mammoth Coins!
All in all, Brawlhalla is a very complete game that I believe could compete against legendary titles like Smash Bros. Brawlhalla is very deserving of a 10/10, a rating I seldom give due to my cynical view on a lot of games. Brawlhalla's simplicity and great design make it fun for all.

Why wouldn't I reccomend this game?
While I do understand that the game is in beta, and a lot of these issues could be resolved, here is why I wouldn't reccomend the game. Usually, no, always, when I played a game in beta, the company would always be super communicative with the players. This is a must, because if you want a game to get better, especially in the beta phase, you need to communicate, you need to mold the game to what the MAJORITY of the players want. CSGO has a nice system of letting you know whether or not your reports led to a ban on someone, this would be a great addition to this game in particular because honestly, sometimes you wouldn't know whether or not you just saw hacks or you just saw a glitch. speaking of which, THE GLITCHES MAN.... Half of your signatures will go right through people im so serious. Another sad thing this game follows is the 'Release character OP' gimmick. Where when they release a new character, that character is close to impossible to beat. I still didn't express why I wouldn't reccomend the game though, here goes the MAIN REASON WHY
This game does not follow the simple rule that all games of this type HAS to follow. Smash bros understood this rule and is why the game is so succesfull. The simple rule goes like this, The larger the hitbox - The less damage, The smaller the hitbox - The more damage. You have people like hattori and queen nai with OBNOXIOUS hitboxes, WITH IMMENSE DAMAGE, and as an added bonus, queen nai just happens to have one of the highest armor values in the game. Without this rule, complaints of balance will never cease to exist. Smash bros implemented this rule perfectly. Think about it, you use megaman, you'll have large hitboxes, but the damage is minimal (Which is a good thing) and you can use someone like Link, with smaller hitboxes but way more damage if you land it. Honestly this game is headed in a good direction, there are just small things that I KNOW they can fix before the official release. Hopefully they can succesfully implement the simple rule, for a greater and more enjoyable game.

Torchlight II is a sequel to a classic hack'n'slash game developed by Runic Games. If you have played the original Torchlight, you know what to expect. For those of you who have not, the game is all about exploring, slaying, looting, and levelling.
The story is pretty straight-forward: the world is threatened by the Alchemist and, oddly enough, the world needs a hero. You are the aforementioned saviour of the land of Torchlight. Quests require you to go to a certain location, get rid of monsters, grab a certain item, etc. A tried and true formula. The setting is an uncommon mix of medieval-influenced fantasy world (magic and melee weapons) and steampunk (firearms). Like in the original, a player can choose a pet to travel along. What also makes the game stand out is marvellous graphics which does not seem to age. It also has low system requirements.
There are four classes in this game: Embermage, Berserker, Outlander, and Engineer. They are not as conventional as they are in the original (the classic trinity: warrior, sorcerer, and rogue) and may take a while to get used to. For instance, Berserker is great at dual-wielding, but, unlike melee-focused classes in most games, has low health. Nevertheless, they are well-designed and support a variety of playstyles. Interestingly enough, every class can learn up to four spells, so should anyone fancy, they can summon skeletons, cast fireballs, etc. while playing as any class. Some skills are clearly better than others, but I believe that most builds are viable. Speaking of variety, there are tons of mods available online, including Steam Workshop.
The only downsides are that the game is repetitive and steals time like nobody's business. But that is to be expected, right?
To conclude, Torchlight II is a worthy sequel with lots of replay value. If you have played the original Torchlight or you just like eviscerating thousands of monsters, I strongly recommend getting this game. Don't forget to bring your friends along!

So much for mostly positive reviews. All I'm seeing is negative ones mostly but you know what, I agree. I mean I love the concept of third-person shooters, it's just that there are some things this game has that other games don't and one of them is 'mouse sensitivity'. What on earth is mouse sensitivity??? I have never heard of a feature like this and it's like why is this even a thing???!??!!? And also, is it normal for a ping to stay at 999 throughout?
Also, another thing I'd like to add is playing in a server with teams. It's fun and all but it's really overwhelming. You're put in a team against other players, only there is no distinction between them telling you who is with who except for RED letters telling you that's your opponent. They've basically got you rowing up a creek without a paddle here. I haven't played on the other servers yet since I'm still new to the controls. Also, you gotta make sure you have enough gold in order to get another character. 10,000 gold. Can you believe it?? I don't think I can make it to that much without wanting to spend it on other things.
The only good thing I'll say is that the tutorials are helpful, it's good that they've got you focusing on the objective at hand even if it is just cakewalk. I'm not sure how to rate this game, to be honest with you. Do I recommend this game? Yes, yes I do. I'm pretty sure you won't lag as bad as I am if you're using a desktop more than a laptop if you ask me. I'd still play this, though. I might have missed a few good points, but I'm sure all the other comments will have you covered.

Hacking

Updates/support
This game hardly updates, when it does it's mostly a balance patch, and personally I don't mind, balance patches I think, are a good thing, the prollem is they do it wrong.
Also, the focus of this game has changed region several times, first in closed beta for korea(totally different game then), then kill it off and bring a new beta to EU(resembling what we have today), then bring the Open beta to the US on Steam, then pull it off steam in EU and sell it to Aeria games which doesn't seem to care about the game in the end as it somehow died there and is now back up in steam in EU I think? I don't even know, AND NOW IT'S IN MALAYSIA!
Cash Items
While I would prefer cash items to not exist, and I personally don't think the Tesla system is bad in the sense of earning a weapon, it makes it a real hard sell for people wiling to put money in the game, you're paying, to get a chance at getting a  weapon. Netcode

Hands down, this is one of the best RTS games I've ever played. What makes it different from the rest of the genre? Well, for every alien base you capture, you get points that can be spent on units and buldings - but you can also sell what you have and re-distribute your points when needed (units respawn after a little while when they die).

Simply fall back, rethink your strategy and redistribute your points if necessary. You can also browse the map and give commands while the game is paused, removing the need for super-reflexes and making it easier to deploy your tactics, however detailed they might be. The graphics and explosions are also very satisfying - you really feel you crush these nasty critters :)
All in all, a very rewarding game that doesn't require full-time dedication to get into, while continuing to provide an enjoyable experience even after the 100th game. I find myself going back to this once in a while for a game or two.

I honestly wanted to love this game. I really did. I mean I can't remember the last time I saw a WWII free-to-play game that promised this much other than maybe War Thunder. You could pick your nation and decide to be a paratrooper, tanker, pilot, sniper, a run-of-the-mill infantryman, or a commander. The game's FPS and strategy mix seemed great on the outside but the latter was a little lacking in my opinion. This game's maps get repetitive--and I mean VERY repetitive. You'll be playing on the same map match after match and while the game remedies this by changing up the attack points and angles, the maps never feel different than one another and battles quite honestly became a little mundane. ANother thing I could never stand about this game (but is expected for a free-to-play) is that a total newbie could theoretically unlock the best weapons in the game (unarguably the German MG42 once upgraded) by spending some cash. This game's progression is mind-numbingly slow. Not even kidding. Weapons and vehicles will cost anywhere from 50,000 to about 350,000. Tank crews (which I think are the coolest solider type) will set you back a cool 100,000 credits and a general will cost a incredible 1.9 million credits. And, while you can convert existing soldiers to specialized tasks for less money, you will be grinding for weeks trying to get a German tanker with the Tiger II since you'll earn 12,000 credits on a great 45 minute match (not counting ammo, repairs and weapon maintenance, which'll bring you down to around 8,000). Now, I don't blame the devs for making the grind long and hard-- afterall, they made this game to make some money, and I get that free-to-play games all need to have a slight "pay-to-win" aspect to drive up their profits. In Heroes and Generals however, this system is kicked into hyperdrive for the reasons I mentioned above. It will take you an incredible amount of time to get a soldier with vehicles, weapons, planes, tanks, or modifications that'll make you competitive against the 100's of players who have either spent money or played for 30000000 hours... not the funnest thing to have to deal with. Another thing is cheaters.... man. I don't think this has gotten any better recently, but when I actively played 2-3 months ago, it was BAD. The game's reporting system is very unyieldy and almost discourages you from reporting people... You'll need the guy's name, the "barcode" of the game you were both in, the time at which he cheated and what he did. There was even a guy who STREAMED himself going 150-10 with hacks and was KNOWN by the entire community in my area as a blatant cheater that had been reported numerous times (I know because entire teams would do it all at once...). I sincerely hope they change this game for the better because the first few hours with a new powerful gun or tank that I had spent a week to unlock were incredibly rewarding, but the rest is a terrible grindfest. I've seen the game is planning to add more maps, planes, weapons, and new features ( like medkits). Hopefully those aren't stuck behind a pay wall forever. I can't wait to come back in a few months and see what's new with this title because a lot of things look promising. But, at the time of this review, I cannot recommend this game to anyone who loves WWII vehicles like I do. If you're set on being a pilot or tanker, try War Thunder, even though that game has its own share of problems.

you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

Rockstar themselves seem to treat Grand Theft Auto V and Grand Theft Auto Online as separate games, despite being inextricably linked to each other. As such, I'm going to treat them as two separate games for review purposes.
Grand Theft Auto V is a very solid game. It's that GTA formula we're all familiar with, 'shoot guys and drive cars and shoot guys while driving cars'. The gunplay is engaging and doesn't feel arbitrary, the driving combines a realistic sort of physics with the arcade-y driving of a pre-GTA IV era, a world that stays true to Rockstar's attention to detail, missions are fun and interesting with only a couple exceptions, the heists are engaging and encourage multiple playthroughs to experience the alternate routes, characters that are interesting and interact in interesting ways (or they're funny, at least), it's got it all, basically. The PC version is essentially the definitive version, especially with a robust modding scene, it's an extremely good game that I would personally recommend to just about anyone who's got even a passing interest in video games as a whole.
Grand Theft Auto Online... not so much. The same mechanics are there, for the most part, but the core focus shifts towards an interminable grind. The player is going to spend a lot of time grinding for the next vehicle or business that they're going to practically need in a public session, unless they purchase one of the Shark currency cards. The problem with these currency cards is that they are valued extremely poorly since many things in Online are going to be out of the price range of the $50 cards, with a few even out of range of the $100 card (a yacht will run most of the $100 card and leave little room for upgrades). Combine that with a community that's rife with hackers/cheaters/modders (whatever you call them, they're basically just 'guy with mod menu and a scripthook that runs in Online') and Rockstar's bizarrely opaque banning practices (if someone else runs a mod menu, and drops cheatmoney on you, it's possible you'll be banned, this rule seeming to change with every update), and you've got a recipe for disaster. Online is (evidently) more fun if you're in it for the PvP aspect, but I can't attest to this personally.
Basically, if you want a solid single-player experience, this game can't be beat. If you want an online experience that lets you simulate the dreary grind of a 9-5 job, GTA Online is the game for you.

RWBY: Grimm Eclipse is a game very much based on that of a game like Dynasty Warriors. A nice, casual hack-n'-slash game style that is very much fitting with the World of Remnant, however I feel this game does not fit the quality of the show itself.
For one, the game's art style, and the character models.
They do not seem to be very close to the character style that was set in for volumes 1 - 3. There was a point before its "official release", where they had used the same poser models for all four characters, and it was fine then. Why they changed it at all, I'm not sure.
Two, I'd like to talk about the changing of the combat system.
At the start, it was pretty shaky; not alot of variety, and characters usually had broken animations, or had no animation to stop shooting, so they could just shoot all they wanted, with an unlimited distance (i.e Blake). This allowed people to get an unlimited amount of combo for their counter, and gain their Ultimate bar without having to get up close and personal. I know this wasn't the case with Yang, but it was DEFINITELY the case with Blake. Nonetheless, I welcome the changes set in place with the combat style. It makes it to where you have to put in more 'work', yes, but you also can no longer abuse something that can be seen as... broken.
Character progression & "character achievements"
Before the 'official' release of the game, Character progression was locked to the campaign you were currently playing, and would reset if you completed the campaign to play another. It would NEVER save, for the small fact that if you rejoined a game, you had the choice to spec your character again. Not a good system. The character achievements, making it grindy to get the better types of your specific character's moveset? Not a very good system, either. That is the same with how the progression system goes now.. for the small fact that; your character progression saves through the entire game, and if you wanted to respec your character, you had to max the entire character's TEAM in order to respec it. This throws the concept of "trying out something new" to the wind, i.e playing the same character with a different style. That, and if you want to respec when you don't like playing other characters - too bad! You won't be able to respec them at ALL if you don't play the others and go up a Hunter/Huntress rank.
The story is very.. arbitrary, but I won't go into that right now.
The game just feels vastly incomplete, and I've seen alot of complaints about the final boss. The day I got it at Christmas, it was just fine and dandy; for a while, anyway. My friends and I got very quickly bored with the game, and soon dropped it, along with the problems it gave us; graphical crashes, and disconnects at the riverbed.
TL;DR
The game genre is a good mix with the show, but the way this game was executed makes it feel incomplete, and the art style makes it look and feel inaccurate to the show.
Would I reccomend this? No, I wouldn't, because it simply feels incomplete. You're paying money for a game that says it's "released Officially", but is no more, and feels no more complete than it was when I got it in early release over Christmas.

The long-awaited sequel to Human Revolution has its issues, but no matter how hard Square Enix might have wanted to butcher this game, chopping off its limbs and selling them as DLC, Eidos Montréal actually managed to release one of the most brilliant experiences of 2016, a game that not only improves on many aspects of its predecessors, but also offers one of the most satisfying stealth experiences in recent history, thanks to an absolutely masterful level design.
Let's start with the bad parts :
- Yes, the ending is abrupt and the story could have benefitted from a few more hours and levels. It's far from being ME3 levels of bad tho, it just leaves you wanting more because the experience up to that point was pretty great.
- Yes, optimization could be better, as the game running with all options maxed out brought my i7-6700k and GTX 1080 combo to its knees, but turning down a few options, mostly the MSAA, will give you a smooth 60fps, and the game has many options to customize your experience.
- And yes, there are microtransactions in a AAA game at launch. While they are totally unintrusive in the main story (thank god !), and your opinion on them might vary, you should not pass up on this game because of the inclusion of microtransactions. Make your voice heard on the internet, but stay respectful, all Square Enix wants is your money, they didn't kill your mom (yet).
Now, on with the good stuff :
- The art direction and overall atmosphere of the game are simply superb. It's not a technical marvel (tho it does look pretty good, especially with some effects turned on/maxed out), but it will definitely stand the test of time thanks to its beautiful world and excellent character design, not to mention the many options available to customize your graphical experience.
- The level design deserves every single word of praise it gets, because it is simply out of this world. Where Human Revolution gave you two or three ways to traverse a level and deal with a situation, Mankind Divided gives you twice as many, and it feels super rewarding to explore every level and hub area to find every nook and cranny the developers hid in the world.
- The music is once again composed by Michael McCann and is just as good as it was in Human Revolution. Special shoutout to the TF29 HQ theme, the intro theme and the credit song which are all really beautiful.
- The sidequests ! They are many of them, and they're just as fun as they were in Human Revolution. Usually well written with fun side characters, they flesh out the world in a more robust way than the main story, and help the world feel more believable. You'd be missing out on some quality content if you avoided them.
- The gameplay is a step up from Human Revolution, and the new augmentations are a delight to use, whether you're hacking a laser grid from afar, dashing from cover to cover using the Icarus Dash, or becoming a literal walking tank with the Titan Shield. Sneaking your way through the game is just as satisfying as it was before, and I for sure am going to go after that Foxiest of the Hounds achievement.
There are many more things to say, good or bad, but I think I covered the most important aspects of the game in this review. Deus Ex Mankind Divided is worth it, it is SO worth it. Do not pass this up, it's a great game, one that actually deserves a purchase for the main story alone. The support from the devs has been excellent since release, with three patches fixing major and minor issues in only one week, allowing many who were getting crashes on the 14th mission to finally complete the game. I am one of these people, and I am grateful for the time I got to spend with this game. I hope you'll love it too.
