Let me straight with you.
This game is old. It feels old. But there are some shining moments that made it worth the few bucks I played it. The slow motion effect for shotting and the bow and arrow mechanics are pretty cool.
Worth a playthrough (if you don't mind old games) on sale.
But a recommendation? Probably not...

First of, yes, this game is old, and it sometimes shows. Especially finetuning the game to get it work on modern machines under Windows 7, 8 or 10... You might get the game running, and then you notice, the sound isn't online... next you notice there are graphical glitches. Thank god there are workarounds for this, and if you have some skill in research you will find them quick.
The story is good with two protagonists, who are antagonistic. They are old school antiheroes of the italian western style. It's a love/hate thing in this game. Sympathies are misplaced though because both protagonists are more or less... well let's just say they are both not the kind of neighbor anyone wants to have close by. One is a scoundrel and loafer, while the other is a bigot and former gunslinger turned priest. This should be enough about the two protagonists. The story that unfolds during the game is nice though, but you have to kill a lot of people in either forms, they are different in style and in motive. Both are driven by revenge.
I played the game when it came out back then, it was fun to play. Now there is of course the feeling of a rerun. Which might scratch a bit on the patina of the game.
There is a lot to like about this game, first, the characters are developing during the game. You will see a story and misunderstanding that only unfolds during the run of the game. It is a FPS game, yes, but also it is an adventure.
To modern standards this game is a bit dated, it shows in several ways, smudgy textures, not so well in supporting higher resolutions, and then there is the trouble with soundsystems and startup. But with a big "But!", this game is fun once you get it started. It reminds a lot on the time when the game was first introduced. Which has been ten years ago.
If you like hardcore FPS with some puzzles and twists, some agility parcours and a good backgroundstory, then this game is cut out for you. Besides it's inexpensive and offers a lot for that.
On my personal score this game has on a scale between 1 and 15 a rock solid 9 Points. Which would be a C+ or 3+ if put into notes. It's not the perfect experience from back then, but it still has a lot of charm. Even though it's technically far behind, you still can play it and have fun with the game.

If I were to some this game up in a sentence:  Frustrating but rewarding.  That's the feeling that permeates my experience playing.  Some controls and features have a tendency to cause a lot frustrated cursing.  But after those moments are eventually conquered, a rush of excitement is usually the reward.  From riding in mine carts to burning down brothels, this game succeeds more often than not in making the player feel like they playing an action packed western movie.
Pros:
-Pretty solid visuals that hold up fairly well considering the games age.
-Music that won't be making Ennio Morricone jealous any day soon, but certainly fits the mood.
-Great voice acting from Marc Alaimo as Father Ray.
-Father Ray.  Pretty much the main reason I keep playing.  A psychotic priest that quotes bible passages while shooting hombres.
-Quick, exciting gunfights filled with tension as well as adrenaline.
-A pretty good learning curve.  It takes a while to get used to, but it doesn't through you into situations that you don't feel entirely unprepared for.
-Pretty entertaining story.  But I'm mostly in it just to shoot people.
Cons:
-Billy Candle.  A bland, whiny little waste of code that exists to drive the plot forward and introduce new game mechanics that usually don't involve shooting bandits in the nuts.
-The whip mechanics.  Trying for an Indiana Jones vibe.  Doesn't quite stick the landing.  Literally.  I can not tell you how many times I've died because I didn't swing far enough to make the ledge, or fell to my death because the whip didn't actually grab the branch.  Probably the most frustrating aspect of gameplay.
-Kind of glitchy.  This might due to the games age.  I don't mind glitches normally, usually find them pretty funny.  But there have been some occasions where I died because I fell through the ground, or enemies literally materialized into existance right in front of me.  Not game breaking, but a bit annoying.
-Tries too many gameplay styles.  I think this is a syptom of the games time.  At the beginning of the 7th generation of consoles, developers crammed all sorts of differing play styles into their games hoping to impress consumers with variety.  This leads to games sometimes feeling more like glorified tech demos than straight Action/Shooter/Platformer/ect. Again, not the end of the world, but hurts the final product.
-Father Ray is pretty much only half the game.  The other half is stealthy, whip-swingy douchbag Billy Candle.  Missed opportunity.
All in all.  A fun western shoot'em up that loses it's way a bit under the weight of it's own ambition.  Totally reccommended for fans of the genre, so long as they're willing to put up with some of the games idiosynchrasies.

Cat Goes Fishing. Cat catches fish. Game gives quests. Difficulty increases. Game is Zen.

Unsurprisingly you are a cat and you are fishing: you'll start from the bank and slowly buy upgrades, new poles and even boats with the money you get from selling fish you catch.
Cat Goes Fishing is a pretty charming game with a cute premise, decent gameplay and a good amount of stuff to do: sadly it can get repetitive fast and its progression is a tad too slow.
-while very simple the graphics sport a charming art style
-good amount of different fish to catch
-quite many upgrades, things to buy and hats providing bonuses to be fished out of the water
-two different game modes, one being more laid back while the other features a breakable line
-simple music gets repetitive quite fast
-quests can't be abandoned, thus if you get one requiring a fish you can't/ aren't able to catch you're going to get stuck for a possibly long time
-gameplay can get frustrating, even with upgrades having to cast in the right place, wiggling your lure between useless fish, hoping the right one will be hooked and that no other fish will take a bite while you reel it in can be challenging: having to do so several times and failing will teste your nerves and ruin the relaxing atmosphere the game wants to create
-unlocks eventually get too pricey, requiring lots of grinding
-no way to save and exchange hats, you can only equip one and have to sell those you don't wish to keep
-some things aren't explained, for example what the different fishing pole stats actually do
Cat Goes Fishing is a decent game overall, I had fun for a few hours trying to catch fish, getting a nice hat, unlocking stuff and then trying to get a shark eat my bait: it's charming, has novelty value and can easily make you go "just one more fish before I quit".
Sadly all this eventually grinds to a halt when you realize that the high end upgrades are very pricey, we're talking about a range from 250k to 320k when many big fishes can be sold for 7k: add to this the fact that you'll often have to also buy one time bonuses (rockets to go deeper, bombs to scare away the first fish that bites etc) not to mention having to rebuy upgrades for each new pole and you'll see how this can eventually get tiring.
I was a bit torn overall but ultimately decided for a thumbs up due to the fact I had some decent fun with it and the game will do the same for you  for at least a few hours provided you don't mind its shortcomings, just don't be surprised when it loses its charm: if you're interested I'd get it on sale.

Blew a hole in the wall only to find a giant robot of death on the other side. Blew a hole in the floor to escape and fell into lava. Lots of explosions, lots of bad guys, and a hell of a story buried in this gem. If you plan on or have played the more recent installments in the franchise, you owe it to yourself to experience where it all began. Rid Mars of Ultor Corporation and usher in a new era of peace. Just don't blow up the bridge you need to cross before crossing it.
Lots of Mars rocks.

So let’s jump right into it. Red Faction is a first person shooter that was released in 2001 for the PC and PS2. It eventually found its way to other platforms including Mac and the Ngage (of all things).
Here’s the plot…which was obviously inspired by Total Recall. The year is 2075. The Ultor Corporation is running a mining operation on Mars. The living conditions for miners suck at best and other miners are getting taken out by an incurable disease known simply as “The Plague”. You follow Parker a miner drawn in by Ultor’s promises of a new life as a miner. Parker finds himself at the forefront of a revolution.
So what can I say here; the story is actually quite good. The game itself is actually quite long; so there was several times that the story was what kept me from getting bored and quitting. The story is compelling there’s enough twists to keep things interesting….well until the very end at least. I found the ending to be a bit disappointing. But overall I dig it and for that I’m giving it an B.
Red Faction is an older game. I mean it was originally released in 2001. I have to remind myself of that quite a bit because in my opinion the look has not aged well. The graphics have a jagged style typical of the time. I remember back when I first played it the games look was amazing. Things have changed. The game as it stands is displayed in a 4:3 format, but there’s a way around that. There is a community made patch called Pure Faction. Installing the patch opens up higher resolutions. And interesting thing to note is that playing this older title on newer hardware seems to have issues. I’m not sure if this is a problem with the game itself or with Pure Faction, but I encountered at least one glitch. In the sub bay before the underwater lab when you attempt to launch the sub; the sub just explodes. Why does this happen? Well it’s all about frame rates apparently if the games framerate goes above 200 frames per second the game glitches out causing the sub to explode. Fortunately with the help of Pure Faction you can counter act this issue. All you have to do is use Pure Faction to adjust the frames per second. I’ve left a link to the moment I figured it out in the playthrough.  While it’s true that the graphics haven’t exactly aged well I certainly wouldn’t toss them into the junk pile. So…B
The Cinematics in the game do their job. They convey the story during the in-between-bits. The game used in-game graphics rather than pre-rendered cutscenes. I usually like it when games do this. The game also throws on these little communication cinematics (Hendrix talking to you, or Eos bossing you around). I find these to be nice touches, and it certainly helps keep the story moving. Interestingly enough the cutscenes are probably the times that I noticed the age of the graphics the most. Jagged character models and choppy frame rate are typical of what you’ll run into. It’s entirely possible that some of the choppy framerates were because of the screen capture software. The cinematics aren’t bad…but they certainly aren’t great, and tossing in a lackluster ending….meh C it is.
The audio in the game is good but nothing to write home about. The only reason I say that is because there was nothing sound effects wise that ever really stuck out to me. Everything was pretty much what I would expect from a game of this type. As for the voice acting….well I’ve definitely heard better. The delivery seems off for me; all of the dialogue seems forced and unnatural. Once again…C
The soundtrack….holy crap the soundtrack…it’s cinematic…it’s huge…it’s well orchestrated. It’s awesome. The unfortunate fact is during the playthrough I muted all of the music. I had to. That is the nature of the Tubes. Just take my word for it….fantastic soundtrack. So the Music is an A all the way.
Controls are typical for FPSs. Keyboard and mouse all the way. This is where the age old argument continues. Keyboard/Mouse vs gamepad. Console gamer vs elite PC Master race. I’ll say this I have both the PC and PS2 version. And I have to say the PC control scheme is much more ideal. Honestly I get quite frustrated playing this with the pad. But that’s just me and that’s a personal preference; I’ve always preferred playing FPS titles on a PC with a mouse and keyboard. That being said there are ways to use a controller with the PC release of Red Faction, but I haven’t explored it. Using classic and what I feel the most ideal control scheme for a PC….that deserves an A.
All right let’s hit the gameplay. Overall you’re looking at some pretty standard point shoot bang bang action. However, the Geo Mod engine does add another layer of gameplay dynamic. The Geo Mod engine allows the user to modify the level. You can blast your own tunnels circumvent doors by going through walls….the world is your oyster.  When I first found this game way back when; I fell absolutely in love with the Geo Mod engine. I was obsessed with burrowing my own tunnels. But here’s the deal with Geo Mod it starts out really cool….and YES I will readily admit that it is a very cool idea…the thing is you end up using it less and less. To be entirely honest I barely used it after the first few stages. To kind of go with Geo Mod the game has included some pretty nice weapons…a healthy chunk of them are explosive in nature…that brings us to the fun of sticking mines to your enemies….good times….good good times. There are some other great weapons…sniper rifles, precision rifles…heck even the pistol is great. I have to recommend that you stick with the precision weapons. Like the precision rifle, sniper rifle or the rail driver….if you’re feeling crazy go with a rocket launcher. I had a tendency to steer clear of automatic weapons because the shot grouping for all of the automatic weapons is ridiculous. It’s nearly impossible to hit a target without using dang near all of your ammunition. My personal favorite weapon would have to be the Rail Driver. You see the Rail Driver allows you to 1. See through walls 2. Fire through said walls to take out enemies. The Rail Driver is even strong enough to take out hover crafts….I guess that’s what they are. Heck I even shot one through a wall without seeing it….probably one of the coolest accidental shots I’ve ever done. So, gameplay is pretty standard, Geo Mod is awesome but it wears thin…and the weapons are great (with the exception of the automatic weapons). Gameplay is good just not great…B
The final thing I wanted to discuss is the multiplayer mode. When I first got this game I think I ended up playing multiplayer mode more than the solo campaign. Playing it today really takes me back to the Good Ole Days of multiplayer gaming. No voice chat….it’s like heaven. The game is pretty old but I was pleasantly surprised to find that there is still a bit of a community playing the game. It’s funny because you’ll run into a lot of the same players quite a bit. As best I can tell there are still folks creating custom maps. This is pretty impressive in my opinion. It bears mentioning that it’s really in multiplayer mode that Geo Mod shines bright. In the course of a match a map will start out pristine and end up completely trashed. Sometimes it’s by design there will be hidden paths and powerups that are only accessible by blowing holes through stuff. So much fun. Multiplayer mode is awesome well worth playing… A
So let’s look at the report card. After looking at the arbitrary grades I gave the aspects I’ve discussed and assigning them a numeric value….and then calculating an average. Red Faction gets an overall B. Red Faction isn’t the greatest game in the world, but it has some nice aspects. Gameplay is solid, the soundtrack is excellent, and the multiplayer mode is still a boat load of fun. Overall it gets my recommendation.

Lots of potential, but so far they're kinda blowing it. Early access review, so take it with a grain of salt- but long story short, I don't have much hope for the long term success of this game.
The devs claim it's not a pay-to-win game, but that's not actually true. In Holodrive, you earn an in-game currency called "bits" that you can use to purchase additional items to customize your bot. You earn bits by playing the game, getting XP and leveling up. You can also earn bits by doing daily missions, things like that. You use the bits to buy item blind-packs called holopacks, and in each one is an item that you can equip on your bot. I know what you're saying- "oh no, in game currency!". Hang on- that's not the real problem.. in-game currency by itself does not make a game pay-to-win.
Part of the problem is that some of these items skew the balance of the game in a PROFOUND way. IE) there's a rocket launcher that fires through walls, rapid fire machine gun that ricochets off of everything, flamethrower that does an obscene amount of damage over time, etc. Oh, and by the way most of these upgraded weapons do a LOT more damage than their non-powered counterparts. That said, that by itself isn't the root of the problem. Players need to be rewarded for their hard work, right? Giving super experienced players uberpowerful weapons is kind of lame if you're trying to sustain a community of new players, but fundamentally I get it.
The real problem is that you can buy bits using real money. Yes, microtransactions. Everybody's favorite feature. This means that you can spend a wad of cash to essentially buy the items you want- and dominate everyone else with overpowered weapons. THAT is why Holodrive is pay-to-win by even the most forgiving definition. If these items were 100% cosmetic I would have no problem with microtransactions- but they're not.
With that out of the way lets talk about the problems with the actual game:
First, they drop you in without explaining ANYTHING. The tutorial tells you things you should already know if you have a steam acount and a pulse. "Hey, heres how you shoot. Here's WASD movement. Here's how you tie your shoes". I hate tutorials like this because somebody spent real time working on it, and it's a joke- nobody has ever jumped into a platformer and said "Hrm i wonder how you jump?". Instead, tell us about the teleporters! I had over an hour of in-game time before I knew WTF they were or how they worked- i just kept getting randomly teleported to other places and had no clue why. Or how about explain wtf the powerups are or when/why they might be useful? Experimentation is great, but when I'm getting analy penetrated by a guy with glowing armor and a rocket launcher that phases through solid walls it's kinda hard, yeah? The "Collector" game mode has great potential but so many people don't know how to play it because the only time you ever see instructions are on a loading screen, and even then they're super vague. What are the red walls? Sometimes they turn green and you can go through? Under what conditions do they turn green? Is it a timer? did somebody press a button? Information like this is ridiculously easy to communicate to the player, so it's frustrating to run into issues like this.
The UI is a complete mess- finding things on the main menu is a challenge, as the sections of the menu sometimes don't make any sense. For example- the area where you equip items you've unlocked is called "album". I could think of 100 different words that would better describe that section of the menu- here's an easy one "ITEMS", or "INVENTORY".
The in-game HUD isn't much better. You get helpful arrows showing the direction of other players on the screen if they're within range, but information that is immediately useful (such as which powerup you're carrying) is pushed to the margins of the screen, forcing you to take your eyes off the action.
I played most of my time using mouse and keyboard, but also tried out gamepad so I could do a thorough review- gamepad support is barely there. I mean, you can use a gamepad and the game will work- but good luck figuring out which buttons to press, because all of the on-screen instructions will remain keyboard commands. Cycling weapons on the gamepad is a nightmare.. using bumpers to cycle through weapons? C'mon, it's 2016- use a weapon wheel.. infinitely faster and actually possible to utilize muscle memory rather than tap-tap-tapping while you stare at the tiny icons under your character hoping you picked the right one.
I've got other gripes with this game, but I'm going to stop here because I'm ready to be done with this game in every sense of the word.

Summary
Infested Planet is a top down strategy shooter where you control a squad of mercenaries on an alien world fighting against swarms of aliens. The team can be boosted with different weapons, health or speed. But the aliens also evolve different abilities to combat you. In the campaign, these mutations are rolled out in specific stages. The game also offers a skirmish mode where the mutations of the aliens are random.
Review
The campaign component of Infested Planet is quick and offers a good way to introduce the player to the various aspects of the games enemies and mechanics. A lot of the missions are varied enough, with standard kill everything type scenarios through to last stands. The game tends to flow at the pace set by the player - that is, if the player is quite aggressive and pushes hard, the aliens evolve faster and the game requires faster adaptation by the player. Conversely, the player can actually take the game at a slower pace, and the aliens won't evolve as fast.
The pace is measured by how many alien hives the player destroys. With each hive taken down, the aliens evolve a new ability. If the player is gung ho and smashes through hives quickly, the game will adapt just as fast. This can leave the player somewhat on the backfoot strategically, as the tactics employed up to that point may no longer apply with the newly mutated aliens.
Overall, the game is quite fun. The variety of alien abilities provides significant challenges, while the upgrades to the player squad also allows for fairly deep strategies. Throw in the quick fire nature of the game, and you get a surprisingly fast and easy to grasp strategy game with a solid amount of punch.
My only criticism is that, for me the game seemed to have an uneven difficulty curve. Some missions were dead easy, while others felt like repeatedly smashing your face into a meat grinder - relentless and painful, but over too fast for you to react. This may be a side effect of my skills in strategy games, but it might be something to consider if you prefer your games to be a little more lenient.

This is genreally a positive review BUT only if the game is on sale because it does have significant flaws. I got about 4 fairly enjoyable hours out of it but I think I'm done. Reminded me of my experience with Defense Grid where it was enjoyable for a bit until you find out that it forces you to only use one weapon.
So this game is pretty much a realtime strategy version of top down shooter games like Crimsonland or the classic Smash TV. There are alien hives spawning endless waves of enemies and your marines have to mow them down, eventually gaining enough ground to take out a hive which will respawn unless you capture the point. Aliens can recapture points for the hive to respawn. You get more money for each point you capture, BUT the aliens also get tougher and receive some kind of upgrade (the crimsonland monsters get perks!). Buy enough stuff to capture all the points before the alien numbers and upgrades overwhelm you.
What I like is that there's no mechanics of lost resources. You can sell or unequip anything at any time for a full refund. Destroyed buildings refund their full cost. Killed marines respawn for free. You're free to change up your entire strategy at any time.
SO HOW IS THIS NOT THE BEST THING EVER?
The unit selection is sluggish. You can drag to select fine but that's about it. Selecting individual marines is way harder than it should be. You cannot double click to select all marines of the same type.
They needed a better visual design. It's too hard to tell marines apart. Shotgun marines have an angular helmet. Officers have a slightly shorter gun (not a problem since they're useless and you'll never buy them). Snipers have a slightly longer gun. Notifications will pop up about new alien mutations and the text box will take up the entire top half of the screen, effectively blinding you for 5 seconds every time it happens. The amount of alien upgrade icons gets very cluttered and they eventually start poking out too far to obscure visibility.
There are about 20 different upgrades, marine types, and buildings, but you'll only use 4 of them and you'll be buying the same two first thing every single map. This is mostly due to the prices being out of whack. You can give one marine a shotgun for 4 points, or for 6 points you can construct a building that gives all marines an overpowered grenade launcher (can fire 360 degrees on the move) in addition to their main gun. For 7 points you can construct a building that gives you a delayed air strike every minute, OR for one point less just give your all your marines the overpowered grenade launchers for the same amount of firepower every five seconds. 7 points and you can place one turret to guard one capture area, OR for 7 points you can construct a building that gives all your capture areas a free turret, armor, and a healing aura. For 5 points you can construct a building that respawns all dead marines back into the fight instead of back at base, OR for 5 points you can build a portable heal bot that makes it impossible to die in the first place. 6 points gets you one officer who triples your damage for five seconds after killing a hive (useless). 8 points gets you a sniper who is only good against turrets. 7 points for a flamethrower that is only good against short ranged weak enemies. 4 points for a shotgun that is only a moderate upgrade over the standard rifle. OR 14 points for a minigunner who clears out swaths of enemies at any range, obliterates turrets and buildings, and has a shield which makes him virtually immortal. It's like they just picked random numbers for the cost of upgrades because they're totally disconnected from how effective they are.
Every single map it's grenade building, capture point turret building, portable heal bot, then keep buying minigunners until you win. Maybe one fast moving flamethrower to respond to distant hotspots. That's it. Keep winning.
The other major thing that drags it down it the accursed random number generator. The aliens get a random upgrade for every capture area or two you take. Some of the upgrades are MUCH deadlier than others. The counterattack upgrade gives aliens a super speed boost every time you cap a point, overrunning everything you have unless you're prepared with a bunch of♥♥♥♥♥♥ If the aliens get that upgrade early then you might as well restart the level. A lot of the upgrades just further reinforce "grenades + healing minigunners" as the mandatory strategy because eventually all aliens and turrets will come with shields that only grenades and miniguns can punch through in reasonable time. Snipers are only good for one-shotting turrets at long range but the turret shield upgrade make them useless and another upgrade gives turrets a longer range than snipers. And so on and so on for everything in your arsenal except grenades and healing miniguns.
Provides a couple hours of amusement. Campaign takes too long to unlock more than just shotguns.
Either buy it on sale for an afternoon distraction or skip it.
EDIT: For proof that spamming mini guns is the most effective, but boring strategy, check out my rank on the leaderboard. I tried the weekly challenge and got #9 in the entire world on my very first attempt, without bothering to pause for maximum micromanagement effeciency. I simply ordered my guys to walk up the every hive with concentrated fire, and (after the grenade and robotics buildings) did nothing with my money but upgrade everyone to mini gunners when possible. If I had used the pause feature I probbaly could have micromanaged to split up for fastre completion and cracked the top 5. It's just a shame the game forces you to use the same straight forward strategy over and over again. It would be great if you had to constantly reconfigure your forces to respond to mutation threats, like different mutations required different setups to counter. But no the answer is miniguns every single time because no other weapon can break through the shielding mutations and no other marine can tank the increased damage.

Torchlight II is overall a great game especially to its predecessor! Torchlight II improves in all most every way compared to Torchlight II, below I will state the new things compared to Torchlight I. I don't see anything bad about Torchlight II's sequel, there is also new co-op mode and lots of workshop support if you are interested in modding, and the game is fairly affordable, and offers hours upon hours of fun and has a lot of replayability.
-------------
Graphics: This game doesn't have the best graphics, but the art style is great and it all fits and plays together really well, I actually like the graphics for this game, plus it's optimized pretty well so you can play on low-end machines just fine.
-------------
Gameplay: This game is mostly a hack N slash but as you progress through the game you can get a variety of skills that can mix up the gameplay and certain classes are capable of summoning such as the engineer (Peronsally my favorite), and you also have tons of quests, a pet which I'll get to later, and the maps are wide and have many things to explroe from.
-------------
Maps: Especially compared to Torchlight I there is a lot more exploration and variety in the new maps, plus Torchlight II there is a lot more outside maps so that makes it more unique, and there is some graphical improvements as well and more environment interactives and events that take place, and all of the maps are completely different.
-------------
Looting: Most of these types of games looting and grinding can get boring, but Torchlight II offers a ton of loot especially from tough enemies and just overall everthing, and you'll constantly be switching stuff in your inventory to improve your character or to get stat boosts. Not only that certain loot have gem slots so you can change if they have fire resistance or more damage or whatever, there is a lot of customization.
-------------
The Pet: This is one of the best features of the game, your pet not only assists you in combat it has a variety of other things it can do. It can go and sell things for you, you can request it to buy things for you, and you can also level it up by your side and also you can feed it fish to transform it into terrifying beats or other monsters, you can also add tags and collars to your pet to give it boosts and change how powerful it is. You can also add spell scrolls so your pet can casts spells such as fireball which comes later in the game.
-------------
Skill trees/Customizatoin: When you first come into the game you can customize your character and it is quite decent, there are 4 different classes ALL different and unique, and there is a huge amount of pets and you can customize them, all characters/pet combos are unique in hundreds of ways. To the skill tress, there are a huge amount of skills and buffs you can unlock and each skill/buff can be upgraded 15 times (Each 5 increasing a tier and there are 3 tiers in each skill with certain buffs as you go up tiers), so there is a ton to do.
-------------
Boss fights/Enemies: Overall the AI in this game is very well-done and higher difficulties the AI will get progressively harder and also the story gets harder as you go along, enemies will try to use their environment against you and also use their allies to their advantage, usually ranged staying in back and melee and heavies coming to attack you, and some enemies may run in fear. Boss fights are very unique and intense, featuring a lot of different tactis you can use against their weaknesses, and all bosses have many unique abilities and are just all different in general.
-------------
Modding: Even though I mostly play the vanilla game the workshop offers great content so make sure to check it out.
-------------
Overall Torchlight II is a great game and I completely recommend it, I would give it a 9/10, especially if you like hack N slash and games kinda like diablo and RPG games, even if you don't like story you will still enjoy Torchlight. Plus it's cheap and great reviews. Make sure to try the demo if you are unsure or want to know what the game is like, but the actual game is way better than the demo.

Warhammer 40K: Deathwatch is a turn-based tactical combat where you lead a kill team of 5 space marines against an Tyranid invasion force against all sorts of Tyranid creatures, from gaunts to hive guards, from pyrovores to hive tyrants. There are 36 missions and replayable in 3 different difficulty levels. And while the adaption is faithful, ultimately the game failed to satisfy the fun factor, and it became a grind to collect all the space marines and gear for achievements, and the horrible performance for a turn-based game is inexcuable.
I won't bother to describe the mechanics in detail. Basically, you take 5 space marines into combat to achieve certain objectives, like pass through certain square(s) on the map, reach exit zone, kill certain enemy, survive X turns, and so on. When you win a mission, you get a "card" and requisition points depending on your difficulty level (20, 30, and 40 respectively). First time you win a mission on a particular difficulty level, you get a "pack" of 3 cards. You can buy a pack of cards if you have 100 requsition points. The cards can be weapons, wargear, or additional marines. All items are available in four "tiers", normal, mastercrafted, rare, legendary. The higher tiered versions have more capabilities. The idea obviously is to field a team of Tier IV marines with Tier IV gear and weapons. You can 'sell' duplicate marines and weapons you don't need back for 6 and 4 requisition points respectively (and maybe buy more card packs).
The actual combat is like XCOM-lite, with very simple rules on line of sight... unit in front will BLOCK unit in the back from view. (So if you kill one, there may be another behind it!) and aiming around corner can be a little problematic. You have both melee and ranged weapons, as well as variety of heavy weapons, from missile launchers to plasma guns.
It is very obvious that the game is a mobile port, as the interface is HUGE, and lack of filtering and sorting in the "inventory" screen and space marine "barracks" screen shows the game was meant to be on a touchscreen. Finding duplicates of items is annoying, and when you are expected to collect dozens of marines (each faction has 2-3 for each tier, and this "enhanced edition" added more than a dozen from the other chapters of WH40K like Imperials Fist, Black Templar, and so on, rather than just the "big 3", i.e. Space Wolves, Ultramarines, and Blood Angels. But the additional marines are only Tier I and II, so they are just for collection's sake. To win the game you still need the Tier III and Tier IV stuff.
Another thing you'd notice is the game's performance is ATROCIOUS. My machine is a bit out of date, but it plays XCOM and many other games just fine. And this ia turn-based game, right? Yet loading a level takes 10-20 seconds, same with exiting a level, sometimes animation makes me wonder if I'm watching a flip-book slide show, even with performance level turned all the way down to LOW everything. Even the background music started to hiccup after a while. This game was not optimized AT ALL.
Which brings us to the gameplay problem. The game wants you to take your time to plan your moves... By making an interesting mechanic... A typical mission generates maybe 2K to 3K of XP per character, but when you go to level 30, each level costs like... 17000 XP, and it steadily goes up from there. And if you should happen to get one of your marines KILLED on a mission, that marine's XP will be RESET to ZERO.  All those XPs you saved for leveling up? Poof. Sayonara. It's not permadeath, but it's very close.
And the XP for the tougher levels are not commensurate to the risk taken. I can play the normal level with my leveled up marines and it'd be a cake walk, even against the tough bosses. If I take them to play the tougher level, I risk losing 3-7 mission's worth of XP, for a pack of cards (once) and slightly higher requisition points. It's not a fair trade. There really is no reason to play the tougher levels until I grind through the lower levels, over and over, until I top out my marines to best my odds, and that's just... boring grinding. Remember, there are only 36 missions (9x4).
In fact, there are a few missions where there are certain places I can just sit there to farm XP, if I have the patience to do so!
Overall, even at the low price, WH40K Deathwatch just turned out to be a BORING GRIND after a while. There is not enough reward to justify risking my characters to play at higher difficulty levels other than a few more marines and gear that are NOT useful to the game. I can't recommend this game, unless you really really love WH40K.

First, I got this game 90% off and it's full of bugs. The little dialogue they have to add character to your space marines is broken (My Ultramarine Champion only prompts Blood Angels Assault interactions with my Ultramarines Tactical marines). Your achievements will not unlock at least half of the time. Abilities and actions are sometimes skipped except for their cost (like overwatch), and the controls are not great.
I am a really big fan of warhammer 40k and turn based tactical games like Xcom and Massive Chalice. Units and weapons included in this game give a great spread of space marine chapters and their wargear. As a tactical game, this comes up short against those two, but there is a lot this game does well. You can order multiple units to move at the same time, which is efficient. Shooting orders must be fully resolved before you can issue a new one, so you don't waste actions shooting at dead enemies (however see above). Overwatch uses a 90% arc that cleary shows you target squares, and is very dynamic (again, however see above). Your characters gain abilities separately from leveling. Instead, you choose to spend experience on either leveling up their stats or adding abilities (I like it).
I think most people will not feel like playing through this game three times to beat it 100%, but they will still get about 20 hours of gameplay. Some people will hate the booster packs. They are the core mechanic for acquiring wargear and expanding your roster, but for less than $5, it's worth picking up.

For me, this is so far the best game in the series (with all the respect to the original game, it's gameplay is just too obsolete these days, and the stealth gameplay is just really not that fun in the original).
* Incredible atmosphere - The art direction, the music, the amount of attention to details in the environment - Top notch
* Great level design - Numerous multiple paths and secrets around every corner, and the sheer scale of the places you visit are just amazingly done
* Side missions - Unlike the previous game where side missions were very few and short, this one boasts quite a few side missions that have multiple phases and outcomes, as well as they are really fleshed out and relevant to the core story of the game - You will not find simple "fetch quests" here, but complete investigations and narrative
* Really good UI - Usually not something you think about, but everything flows and feels so natural, while giving lots of customization options
* Graphics - Looks pretty damn amazing, the sheer amount of details you can see in one scene is mind boggling
* Main story - While the story itself is very detailed and fleshed out, it ends in a rather lackluster way, leaving quite a few story threads unresolved (obviously leading to a future story continuation) - It's not bad, and definitely not short, but the ending leaves a bad taste in the mouth.
* Minor issues - There are some really minor issues, such as bad lip syncing and a couple of bugs here and there, though Eidos seem to be releasing patches pretty fast to solve the troublesome things.
Overall, I loved the game, and plan on replaying it over and over in different ways - I can't wait for the continuation of the story as well!

The only reason I'm writing this review is because the amount of negative ones (and their reasoning) is ridiculous. Yes, the fact that microtransactions exist in this game is lame, but it never forces you to purchase them. And you don't have to. We can only hope that SE and Eidos will learn their lesson. I must say that it borrows many things from the original Deus Ex (2000), after Human Revolution the series are finally going in the right direction. When you'll first enter the TF29 office (which is ran by.. guess who? Manderley!), when you hear the Hong Kong music from the original Deus Ex, when you see young Bob Page - all these little things just make you drown in nostalgia. The world design is amazing, it's noticeable that artists had a lot of fun this time to make it feel alive, to immerse the player. Many people say that the game is unoptimized and I am shocked that I am able to run this game on Ultras with no fps drops (mind you, I don't have 1080 GTX). Am I just lucky?
Gameplay wise it feels like a much better version of Human Revolution. Same thing about the artistic choices. I am glad they got rid of the yellow filter and decided to fill this game with more classic cyberpunk color moods, sometimes it once again feels like an original DE with updated graphics. Overall the game feels like an improvement compared to the Human Revolution, because it finally starts to emulate a prequel to Deus Ex that we all love.

for all its faults, bugs and the two sadder 'one off' DLCs - this is STILL A GREAT GAME with a decent storyline
(although to fully appreciate it - does help if you played DX:HR and the original Deus Ex, because why not - theres alot of tie ins, hints to the story)
the game is a visually stunning cyberpunk masterpiece - with crazy amounts of depth and detail im still discovering as I play through - example: snooping through peoples houses, safes, emails and seeing how all their interpersonel communications tie into the story - and get more intel then what the cutscenes simply show you.
**NOTE: PLAY THE SIDE MISSIONS!!!, i can see how some of its shine can be lost if you strictly play just the main storyline - the game is actaully very side mission heavy, and some side missions can span longer than some main missions - they extended the context of what is going on and further flesh out the world --> or you can listen to A.H's complain about the game being bad and later admit they only played the main mission, because thats how call of duty taught them to play a game...
some people might be harshly critique the conclusion - but I for one can't wait to see how the next installments/DLCs turn out.

A simple, but entertaining time killer. Cat Goes Fishing is a fishing simulator from Cat5Games. Let’s get rocking.
The Good
Cat Goes Fishing gets everything just about perfect. The controls are as simple as they come and you won’t even need a tutorial to figure them out. If you did, you’d probably be some sort of mollusk…and not one of the smart ones.
There is a delightful plethora of fish for you to catch. The small fries can be caught without any special baiting, but, the further up the scale you move, the bigger the bait you’re going to need to attract your Moby♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s interest.
There are several items for you to purchase that will aid you in your fishing endeavors. You can get new rods (and upgrades for each of them), you can buy boats to take you out further onto the lake, you can get a sonar to show you where fish are in the lake, and much more.
The boats were especially useful. Some fish only appear further out in the lake and, so, would be unreachable without a boat of some kind. The boat also lets you store a finite amount of fish so that you can sell them when you get back to shore.
CGF offers the player “quests” to complete. This results in the player gaining experience and working towards a level up to unlock more gear, but it also fights back at the repetitiveness of the game itself. When you’re given a goal to work towards, you don’t get bored quite as much.
The Bad
Inevitably, CGF does become repetitive. There’s only so much digital fishing one can do before they get tired of it.
The Meh
CGF also has hats for you to find in the depths and equip your character with. The hats are absurdly hard to find and you rarely come across one at a moment when you could actually try and snag it with your hook.
Verdict: Yea
Cat Goes Fishing is fun, but it’s more of a novelty game for killing time. If you see it go on sale, by all means, buy it. It’s worth of few bucks. You can find it in the Steam Store. As always, thanks for reading.

Call of Juarez, formerly known as The Lawman is an western first-person shooter developed by Techland and published by Ubisoft in 2006-2007.
In Call of Juarez you play two sides of the coin, on one side you play as Billy Candle and on the other as Reverend Ray. Billy Candle is an half-white, half-Mexican in search for the legendary lost gold of Juarez, a treasure hidden somewhere inside this city. When Billy is not capable of finding this treasure, he decides to go home to pay a visit to his mother and stepfather at the farm. On arrival, Billy is confronted with the death of his parents, murdered. The other character, Reverend Ray is Billy's step uncle and preacher. Ray is an reformed revolver hero who is dedicated to spreading the tales of The Lord, but when he hears about the commotion at the farm of his brother, he is going to pay a visit as well and sees Billy being panicked and Billy runs away from the dead bodies. Ray thinks Billy is responsible and promises Revenge and start hunting down Billy as long as he can.
During the storyline, the game switches from character now and then. The game knows several features such as akimbo (wearing double weapons), sneaking, climbing by rope, revolver duels and bullet-time where you have to time and mark your shots at your enemies in order to finish them off quickly in the end. You also have to deal with several types of enemies like bandits, Apache Indians, Mexicans and several landlords.
I really like this game because of the western atmosphere, the smooth switch between characters that initiate a story cliffhanger at the end of each chapter, the wild gunpowder action, voice acting, traveling by foot or horse and the vast landscapes from the rocky mountains, lurid towns and barren tundras filled with various wild animals.
I highly recommend this game to people who like western first-person shooters with a very good storyline and large areas, certainly when the game is on sale!

Channeling a little Starship Troopers with a sprinkle of Cannon Fodder, Infested Planet is a very specialized kind of real-time strategy game. What it lacks in production values it makes up for with inventive gameplay that centers around “stemming the tide”. As you progress through the silly B-grade plot of the campaign - which harkens back to 90s video game storytelling - you face off against alien hives that spawn infinite enemies. Hundreds of alien grubs are constantly flowing towards your bases and marines. It’s a bit like a puzzle game, figuring out which marines to use for defense, where to place turrets, and which hives to take out first.
When you destroy a hive, it becomes an additional base for your side and you gain “BP”, points added to a pool you draw from when building facilities, calling in more marines, or changing marines into different classes like Flamethrower or Sniper. You can undo your choices at any time to get the points back, and fluidly adapting to the situation becomes required. When you take a hive, the remaining hives on the map get a random mutation that can drastically alter the situation. Even if you fail a mission, you earn some money which can be used to unlock permanent upgrades or temporary boosts for the next mission.
I think they could have fond a way to keep mods in single player and keep OpenIV team alive!

Several years ago I played a cool game called Attack of the Paper Zombies. It was a free strategy game I'd read about somewhere online, where you play a small band of marines tasked with wiping out alien zombie "hives" (control points), but with each additional point taken, the hives mutate various (random) abilities that increase the challenge of further progress. Apparently, this game was popular enough that the developer decided to quit his day job and focus on further developing and polishing his game for commercial release. Infested Planet is that game.
I won't go to in depth about the game itself (special thanks to filly73 for seeing it on my Steam wishlist and gifting it to me), and while I didn't really notice that much "different" about the new game (other then the changed art style, better graphics, background story, and such), when I went back and played the original again, I realized that a very significant change had been made, that significantly increase what I found the most enjoyable about Infested Planet—basically, the removal of any penalty for changing your strategy…
Basically, every time you capture an additional control points, you gain additional "research points" with which to either increase the number of "mercenaries" you control, upgrade those mercenaries with a variety of weapons, or build offensive/defensive structures such as automated gun turrets, or unlock various effects to support your control point–capturing efforts. While many of these features are nearly unchanged from the original Attack of the Paper Zombies, the significant change is that in Infested Planet, there is no cost to "recycling" any of these upgrades. Spent 4 Research Points on a gun turret, or on a flame thrower for one of you mercenaries? Recycle it, and get back all 4 points to put towards some other upgrade, whereas in the original game, you'd only get back 2 points. In my opinion, this change not only made the game more "fun" (you can experiment with different strategies without incurring any penalty), but also allowed opened up the option for employing strategies that DEPENDED on repeatedly changing your arsenal, something that would have resulted in attrition in the original.
TL;DR: A fun strategy game that allows a great deal of variety in how its challenges may be approached.

This one had most of the problems of typical visual novels. As a genre they could be much improved by:
1. Logical connection between choices and outcome
2. Something more than a superficial concept on which to build a story
3. Plot, characterization, emotion, conflict, good writing...visual doesn't make it a novel. If I want a pictue book, I'll read Goodnight, Moon.
4. At least make the reader care about the characters -- much can be forgiven if the characters aren't cardboard
5. Avoid silly dialogue and response - in this one, the most common words were idiot and angry.
You get what you pay for ... except when you don't. The ratings on visual novels are much less reliable than the ratings on games.

This is the first game that I bought and played on steam.
Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons is a marvel of storytelling and clever gameplay and a must buy for players who enjoy such.
The first thing that I should say is that unlike what the notice says on the store page, this game does not require a controller to play.
Gameplay and story:
During the game you control these two characters with the arrow and wasd keys as the camera adjusts itself to the area that you are playing. The game itself is relatively simple and linear, requiring the player to overcome easy obstacles in the way of the protagonists' journey to save their ill uncle. In the course of their quest, they assist others in need and grow closer as brothers. It is slightly challenging to get ahold of controlling the brothers simultaneously at the start of the game but becomes much more fluid and easy as you progress through the levels even with a keyboard. Complement to the controls, the challenges along the way begin to require more ingenuity as you learn to control the brothers.
Graphics:
The areas themselves are beautifully designed and the game pauses every once in a while to allow you to enjoy it. From climbing crumbling ruins to scaling massive caves the game uses every area to show you just how beautiful and well crafted it is.
Sound:
There is no major dialogue so to speak but everything in the game is clear without it using too many words. What the lack of dialogue gives way to is a wonderful soundtrack that captures the emotional range of the story in ways that dialogue would never have. As the game becomes darker the longer you play, the sounds and music mature likewise.
Overall:
On the front, Brothers may look like a simple, light hearted puzzle adventure for a casual player. Playing it, I've come to appreciate the subtle and fine ways that this game was made elevating it in quality above many of the other games that I play. The story and gameplay are simple, the music complements the graphics excellently, and the entire experience is an emotional journey as two brothers enter dark and dangerous worlds to save their family.
I cannot recommend this game enough and constantly badger anyone who would listen. It is a quick (approx 6 hr) playthrough and the ending left me sobbing. I have to say, this is a different caliber of gaming. I've never experienced anything like it

This is a great game for WH40k fans (my 30 hours into it can attest to that), but by no means is it a perfect game (if you want to play it you have to be patient):
:
- Impressive detail and variety in the unit models (seriously the space marine models look awesome)
- Large weapon variety true to WH40k lore (weapons also look fantastic)
- Great enemy variety that keeps the game interesting until the end of the campaign
- Solid selection of skills between characters that allow for nice tactical depth and replayability
- Nice mission variety so it doesn't get boring
- Basically XCOM set in Warhammer 40k (to me it is much more fun than Space Hulk or Regicide, but that's a personal opinion)
- Entertaining banter and dialogue between kill team members during missions
- Ability to rename individual battle-brothers
:
- A ton of technical issues (game freezing, corrupt save files, crashes, extremely slow loading times, etc)
- Extremely slow loading times (in the beginning I thought the game had frozen, but it turns out it's just slow as #*$%)
- Simplistic animations
- Limited visual effects
- Absence of certain hover over tooltips that force you to memorize skill effects (on account of it being an IOS port)
- Clunky inventory management
- Pretty grindy due to the RNG loot system and experience gaining rates
- Lines of sight are not very clear in the game (although you start getting the "feel" of it after some trial and error)
- Broken achievements
:
- Backup your save file (located at: C:\Users\als48\AppData\Local\DeathwatchGame\Saved ) - trust me it will save you a lot of frustration and anger because the game often corrupts the save file when it crashes.
- The loading times take an eternity, so use that time to do something else. It might seem the game is frozen, but 2-3min loading times are a consistent problem in Deathwatch.
- I play the game with everything on low (textures on Max) and that has ensured only occasional framerate drops (usually at the beginning of a mission and only 1 CTD ever), so it might be a good idea.
That's it. If you are a patient person who wants to play a fun XCOM style game set in the WH40k universe this is the game for you (preferrably if you can buy it at a discount).

Rockstar themselves seem to treat Grand Theft Auto V and Grand Theft Auto Online as separate games, despite being inextricably linked to each other. As such, I'm going to treat them as two separate games for review purposes.
Grand Theft Auto V is a very solid game. It's that GTA formula we're all familiar with, 'shoot guys and drive cars and shoot guys while driving cars'. The gunplay is engaging and doesn't feel arbitrary, the driving combines a realistic sort of physics with the arcade-y driving of a pre-GTA IV era, a world that stays true to Rockstar's attention to detail, missions are fun and interesting with only a couple exceptions, the heists are engaging and encourage multiple playthroughs to experience the alternate routes, characters that are interesting and interact in interesting ways (or they're funny, at least), it's got it all, basically. The PC version is essentially the definitive version, especially with a robust modding scene, it's an extremely good game that I would personally recommend to just about anyone who's got even a passing interest in video games as a whole.
Grand Theft Auto Online... not so much. The same mechanics are there, for the most part, but the core focus shifts towards an interminable grind. The player is going to spend a lot of time grinding for the next vehicle or business that they're going to practically need in a public session, unless they purchase one of the Shark currency cards. The problem with these currency cards is that they are valued extremely poorly since many things in Online are going to be out of the price range of the $50 cards, with a few even out of range of the $100 card (a yacht will run most of the $100 card and leave little room for upgrades). Combine that with a community that's rife with hackers/cheaters/modders (whatever you call them, they're basically just 'guy with mod menu and a scripthook that runs in Online') and Rockstar's bizarrely opaque banning practices (if someone else runs a mod menu, and drops cheatmoney on you, it's possible you'll be banned, this rule seeming to change with every update), and you've got a recipe for disaster. Online is (evidently) more fun if you're in it for the PvP aspect, but I can't attest to this personally.
Basically, if you want a solid single-player experience, this game can't be beat. If you want an online experience that lets you simulate the dreary grind of a 9-5 job, GTA Online is the game for you.

The Internet was♥♥♥♥♥♥back then in Australia as most people were limited to dial up. I imagine that some of you would have no idea how some games worked back then given the speed limitations. But we managed and we enjoyed what we had. LAN parties were much more popular then if you had a set up supporting one. Thankfully friends would occasionally bring their rigs and we’d party on for hours playing the best games of that era. But it’s long ago. We’ve all grown up in the intervening years and most of us, including myself, don’t live anywhere close to the same area. Thankfully high speed Internet makes playing games such as Holodrive not only possible but a reality.
And the reality of playing Holodrive struck me within my very first matches.  Although Holodrive has its own concepts that make it a unique game I couldn’t help the fact that I was reminiscing a time that I thought was lost. It wasn’t the same friends that I had come to know and love – and love to kill when playing – but it didn’t need to be. I had forgotten just how fun a game such as this could be. I had played a number of online games in the years since my arena shooter days but for the most part they were of the MMRPG games such as EverQuest, World of Warcraft, etc.  It’s safe to say that Holodrive is an ode to some of the best gaming experiences of my life and for that I am quite grateful.
The game itself is extremely fun. The action is fast and furious. You’ll die – unless you’re insanely talented – and just as quickly you’ll be killing the ever loving♥♥♥♥♥♥out of your enemies. I won my first game in deathmatch mode but before the final scores flashed up on the screen when the game had finished I was certain that I had gotten my♥♥♥♥♥kicked and I’d have been more than happy with a mid table finish. Color me shocked when I saw the final score. It’s that type of game at the early levels. I can’t write about the advanced levels because I haven’t played the game long enough to experience the ‘end game’ but if all you are after is some casual fun and you love multiplayer shooters then there’s no reason for you not to pick this game up.
I don’t generally like games that get given away on FAILMID (that’s not where I got my copy from, I got it from the developer directly as per usual) because they’re given away in such mass quantity and is a sign of a troubled game or product but I have to say that this time it is precisely why that site exists. It got players enmasse playing their game very quickly and helped them develop a community. I have yet to speak to anyone before, during or following a game but the games that I played have been filled with more players than bots and this is a great sign for the game.
I’ve treasured my short experience thus far with Holodrive and thoroughly recommend it. I can’t wait to play more. My name in game is Steamified so if you see me please say hello.

A fun, casual game. It reminds me a lot of a title I used to play called The Showdown Effect. Basically, it's a 2D arena-style shooter.
You have a target reticle that guides where your bullets go, but, unlike The Showdown Effect, your bullets are projectiles that hit everything in front of and behind the reticle, instead of only what is underneath. This makes aiming in this game extremely easy for anyone to pick up.
The game, though, is extremely casual and battles can be largely determined by the items a player holds. If you get into a duel with a player who has the "Disarm" powerup, for example, he can literally knock the gun out of your hands from half a screen away for 5 seconds. In a game where it only takes 2 seconds to kill someone, this is a death sentence. Other powerups such as an invicible force-field, 2x damage (which, combined with the already low TTK can kill enemies in a second) are not much better for creating fair fights.
As a future free-to-play game, though, I wont hesitate to recommend this to anyone interested in playing a casual, fun, 2D shooter.

Was too young really to play this around the time it came out, so the nostalgia factor is missing. But honestly a very mediocre game.
Positives
-Gun Variety
-Weapons and explosions sound good.
-Geomod Engine
-Vehicle controls top notch
-Soundtrack pretty good
Negatives
-Story extremely dry, especially towards the end with new main characters being introduced more than halfway through the game.  The main character is completely unlikeable and the other characters who I assume you are meant to care about are very 2D with almost no personality. The guards all have some hatred towards miners for a reason that is never explained. You are reminded of this with them saying 'Miner scum!' every 5 seconds. There is no incentive to go anywhere and it feels like the reasons to go from one place to the next are just made up on the spot.
-Voice acting and cutscenes are alright at the best of times and ususally cringe inducing.
-Graphics are bad even for a game that came out in 2001.
-Landscape is boring and levels are often the same corridors/red caves OVER AND OVER. There is almost no variety in the level design and the levels are often stuck together very badly e.g. when you are in a mining/disposal area and you take a 5 second pipe journey to the science labs.
-Enemies are overpowered for the majority of the game (when playing on normal) mainly the railgun guys who ONE SHOT you whenever you turn a corner, forcing you to save the game before almost every corner at the end of the game.
-Geomod Engine used about 5 times throughout the game in very scripted formats.
-Online seems impossible to use for a new player as the servers all say that my level is not high enough when I try to join. It doesnt even display what level I am.
-Endgame was awful with a recycled boss fight and a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ timed puzzle as the last thing you do. One of the most unsatisfying endgames ever.
-So much more to say e.g stealth missions, useless companions, npc glitches, those aliens in the caves that were almost impossible to hit, things like monitors which seemed like they were going to be useful but didnt get used at all properly.
In conclusion this game seems very dated and a lot of the game seems rushed and copied from half life. Just buy half life instead.

Basic facts: A western story-focussed FPS game with two stories running side by side, crossing over and twisting around together. About 8 hours worth of gameplay, with many interesting and innovative features, including some way ahead of their time.
CoJ is a rather good game as games go. The story covers Reverend Ray on one side, and Billy Candle on the other. Ray's gameplay in rather combat heavy, with lots of gunplay. Billy's story is more stealth focussed, with a bullwhip for mobility and a bow for stealth/long range combat. If the game had an unremarkable story, its gameplay would earn it a decent enough review.
But the story is where this game stands out. Without revealing anything or putting up any spoilers, it features two awesome characters who you genuinely begin to feel for at various points in the story. The first 2 thirds of the story set what would appear to be a set in stone atmosphere, but this changes in dramatic fashion. One of few games which would make a good movie.
Well worth playing for anybody who appreciates a fantastic story. If you just want a western shoot 'em up, Dead Man's Hand is a better alternative of similar age.

This game has been one of the most pleasant surprises this year for me. I love "marines vs aliens" games, and I found out about this game accidentally. In the beginning I was dubious to buy it because of the below-average graphics. In the end, I decided to go ahead thanks to other gamers' reviews, some specialized magazine impressions and that it was on sale for half the price. And what a good decision it was, as Infested Planet is a joy to play. So far I am about 10 hours played, and still having a blast just like the first time.
Let me speak a bit of what this game is about: It is a blend of RTS and Tower-defense genres, though instead of TD's typical waves you have to face a constant stream of dozens of thousands aliens. The key in this game is to control the huge constant flow of enemies with a handful of marines, with the help of quite different loadouts (sniper guns, shotguns, flamethrowers...) and the support of several buildings that add various passive buffs (like health regeneration, grenades for your marines, so on) and active abilities (aerial support, different turrets deployments...).
In order to win, you have to conquer all aliens' nests, which act like some kind of hardpoint bases. Once you destroy one nest, and conquer it, you build one of your bases on top of it. This act gives you points that you can invest on upgrading your marine's arsenal, build support facilities or deploy turrets/mines. These variation lets you try very different tactics and approaches. However, the aliens also gain "evolution" perks when they loose one nest, making them tougher to win. These perks vary from match to match (like the map, which is randomized), but include faster creatures, more range for their turrets, improved poisons and so on.
The difficulty is challenging but fair, and the first campaign's missions make it easier for you to catch the ropes of the game.
There are a few game modes. The first one is the campaign, where you advance by winning somewhat-varied scenarios. While you advance, you will find side-missions which are randomized but belong to three different modes: "Domination", where you have to overcome all nests against difficult odds, "Survival", where you have to survive for a period of time, and "Go-Go faster" where you have a limited time to capture the next nest.
In spite of the campaign looking short so far (I think I will beat it in about 15 hours), there is a lot of replayability, thanks to the different game modes, and weekly challenges where you can compare your performance against other players.
In summary: If you can forget about the graphics, and like "marines vs. aliens" games, you will find in this game a precious little gem that can keep you entertained for 20 hours or more. Recommended!!!!

This is an excellent tower defense style game that offers a few fun and challenging twists. Most notably, the endless swarms of alien bugs that try to swarm you all over the play area. The swarms may be periodic, specialized and may vary their attack patterns as the games progress. With your mobile marine squards, you must battle the swarms and take care of threats as they arrise. Flexibilty is the key to playing the game as the swarms don't attack just one location and you only have so many resources at your disposal for dealing with them like setting up stationary guns and equiping your marines with the right weapons. This makes the game very challenging and quite fun. I recommend it to anyone who is a fan of the tower defense genre.

Well, obviously... Deathwatch is an iOS game ported to PC. "Enhanced" means just better looking (still far from PC standards). So, don't except any high concept... it's a simple turn-based game. If you need comparison - XCOM, but faaaaar more basic. Is it any good? Well, it's decent.
This is a grindfest. Missions give you XP, you unlock new "cards" - marines, new gear. You'll be encouraged to reply every mission to farm more items or better squadmates. I've managed to reach almost 70% of the game without any farming, but ... i got to a point where my best marines were slaughtered like sheep. So, farming XP and better gear was a necessity. In the iOS version you could buy equipement packs for real money - here you need to replay most lucrative missions to the point of complete boredom. Tactics, planning - not really important here.
So, waste of time? Well, i know that some people enjoy that kind of gameplay. Collecting "cards", filling that equipement checklists, getting all the possible Space Marines. I'm not really into that. If you're searching for a deep, tactical expierence, check elsewhere.
Still, i'm giving it a thumbs up. It's a competent little game, just not for me.

Deathwatch is the kind of turn-based strategy game you can just pick up and play. While bigger games often have too much overhead (i.e. you have to spend hours on character creation, learning complex game mechanics and the meta game) this one is reduced to the fun parts but still adds a bit of variety with loot drops, different classes and (straight forward) character development.
It's also an example of a mobile port done right IMHO: it looks great, works well with mouse and keyboard, there are no microtransactions and it doesn't have artificial difficulty barriers that are intended to force you to grind or pay.

+ An absolute plethora of equipment and marines, A huge choice in how to equip your squad and a vast amount of Space Marines to unlock and choose from

Cons

All in all I would highly recommend this game on sale, and if its not, wait till it is because spending the full amount on this game is not reasonable.

First off, I just want to congratulate the creators of this game for having motivated me to write this, my very first game review. To be honest, I am practically new to Steam and even more so to Visual Novels; this being my first. That said, I am happy I chose this game to introduce me into the magic of VN's. Now, I am hooked.
As for my experience with the game, I really want to say that although I noticed a little more than a few mistakes in translation, as well as slight phrase/word repetition dulling the involvement of the story, the game is a master piece. The music and sound effects are so adequate and so soothing, they succeed in making you feel the emotions trying to be conveyed throughout the story. The visuals, charming and gentle, perform an excellent job at helping tell the story; only obscured in excellence by their repeated and prolonged use as well as the absence of some in critical moments. Lastly, as short as it may be, this game is worth one's time. I truly enjoyed this game and I will certainly recommend it. I honestly hope it grows enough in popularity to make it into a bigger story, either anime or sequel adapted for it contains a huge potential. Aside from this, I don't believe a game of this quality deserves to be a freebie, but it being so allowed me into this genre and for that I'm grateful. If you liked the game, don't forget to show your appreciation by donating what you believe is right on [ eidolon stigma trick and treat ].
10/10

Trine 2 is a gorgeous problem-solving game that I missed out on for way too long.  It has challenges requiring the use of multiple characters that will remind any SNES fan of The Lost Vikings, but with graphics to match the modern day.  Interestingly, most problems have multiple solutions, even allowing you to use just 1 of the 3 characters to get through whole stages.  On top of that, it has a very forgiving default difficulty in case you're more interested in the puzzles than the adventure game aspects.  By and large, a relaxing game, well worth the time and price.

Holodrive, previously known as Project Tilt, was released for Steam in early 2016, by Brazillian studio BitCake Studio. Described by the creators as "Mario Kart meets Quake, in 2d", this game is a 2d run-and-gun set in an arena where players can run, fly and shoot their enemies into mixed nuts and bolts. Imagine Metal Slug, Contra, Shoot Many Robots or even Thing Thing. Now place that gameplay in a 2d arena with other players, and weapons and powerups to freely pick up and replenish as long as you stay alive. Now add a community with in-game purchases for cosmetics and different gun loadouts. Then make each player's character a robotic dummy which can be dressed up as yo please. Now you have Holodrive in a nutshell, and it's great.

I'll open by getting this out of the way, I haven't played The Cartel. Reviews were negative and the whole first person,GTA knockoff thing didn't appeal to me. I've only played this, Bound in Blood, and Gunslinger. So, on to this game.
I think this is the best, and worst game in the Call of Juarez series. First, the good stuff. With the exception of the stiff facial animation, the graphics are kinda neat for a 2007 game (obviously aside from Crysis). The foliage actually looks better than most games I've played, and the screen space sun rays make for some cool lighting. The shadows are actually higher resolution than the sequels. But the thing that most impressed me, regarding the visuals, was the dust effect from bullet impacts. In other games, you shoot a tree, the ground, whatever, and the bullet kicks up a small cloud of dust. Call of Juarez goes one step further. If you fire a bullet, an arrow, or even use Billy's whip on one of those dust clouds, it will spread out and away from the projectile. I love the dynamic effect this has on shootouts.
How's the gameplay? Pretty good, when you're in combat. As Ray McCall you can dual wield pistols and occasionally activate a sort of bullet-time for a few seconds. As Billy, the game enters slow-mo every time you aim your bow. Levels tend to be fairly wide open with plenty of space to move around. But there was one thing I could not stand, the duals, which, like the sequels, were a real pain. Overall, the combat is fun, though difficult. However, this game isn't all fighting. It also has stealth and platforming sections, but these were worse than the duals. Enemies seemed to spot me no matter what I did. And there's nothing more infuriating in this game than thinking you've just escaped, and a sharp sound indicates you were caught, triggering an instant fail state. If you manage to get past the stealth sections without rage quitting, then the platforming level might just do you in. Jumping gaps feels awkward, and while using your whip to swing on branches SOUNDS cool, it's almost impossible to accurately determine where you'll land. I lost count of the number of times I fell to my death because of the clumsy first-person platforming.
The story is alright, better than Gunslinger, but worse than Bound in Blood.
I recommend this game IF you can get past the frustrating platforming and stealth levels, and have fun with the combat and visuals.

Mankind Divided is a cyberpunk-themed role-playing stealth game and a direct sequel to Deus Ex: Human Revolution.
You play as Adam Jensen, an augmented Interpol agent working with a special Interpol unit to capture a terrorist group of augmented humans. He is also secretly working for the Juggernaut Collective, a hacker group out to stop the Illuminati.
You are a double agent.
The main story is about 10h long. It did take me 38h to finish the game but just because I tried to do every single side-quest and explore everything.
You can approach each situation the way YOU prefer. You can use combat, stealth, hacking or...talking.
The game itself is presented with a first-person perspective, with a third-person cover system.
If you prefer combat over sneaking then you're in luck because you have a pretty wide arsenal of "tools". You can do lethal and none-lethal melee takedowns, unlock augments that can kill an entire groups of enemies. You can also loot, buy and upgrade weapons. There are assault rifles, shotguns, sniper rifles, pistols, different grenades and more. All firearms are customisable.
If you prefer stealth then well, you're also in luck. You can sneak around in ventilation shafts, look for alternative routes and use cloaking augmentations that let you go unnoticed for a certain period of time. You can also hack doors, cameras, turrets and drones.
You can also persuade people into doing what you want. For that you need common sense and a social augmentation. The game uses a conversation wheel similar to Mass Effect. I think it's pretty self explanatory.
Contrary to the popular belief Mankind Divided is quite well optimised. It can give you some trouble with all maxed out 4K resolution but other than that it runs just fine. It's totally playable even on the weaker systems and that's a blessing.
I encountered only one bug in my entire playthrough. A gamebreaking bug tho. I couldn't use the metro during Mission 14 or the game would crash. This was kind of a big deal.
However the bug has been fixed so it shouldn't concern you anymore.
