As everyone knows, whoever plays this game is OBVIOUSLY a RWBY fan, but if you're not, try out the show! Volume 1-3 are currently available to watch on YouTube with a price of a subscribe. ;3 Volume 4 is currently ongoing on RoosterTeeth First⭐️, that's a paid subscription (free episodes on YouTube after a week airing too).
Now time to go on about the game:
Pros
- Fast paced action play
- Easy controls for new players and surprisingly challenging in higher difficulties
- Art designs are exactly the same from the show
- Everything is easily understood within 5 mins of the game (if you're a experienced gamer, which I'm sure you are)
- Challenges that are actually CHALLENGING (depending on your standards, I felt it was fairly normal)
- Horde Mode is quite fun with solo and with other players
- Spicy quotes from characters
- OST that cut into instrumental and slightly different for the game
- Story that isn't a part of the show
Cons
- Somewhat overpriced for small content (There are cheaper games with more content than this game, surprising ain't it?)
- Story seems too plain, short and washed out with little immersion
- Skill system seems too short and simple (some free games provide better skill system with more details and a deeper understanding for use in offense, defense, support and such, which aren't all pay to get either with micro transactions )
- Lag spikes when near trees with lots of particles like in the map "End of The Line" and with enemies more than 12 will kill your frame rate no matter on Potato graphics or Ultra (my PC is mid-end, so no hardware problems here)
- Not enough bosses and way too many wave survival areas (maybe some rescue scenarios be fun too, adds more challenging stuff)
- Enemies are of little variety (meaning there isn't much variety of Grimm and other enemies)
- Cutscenes were... Unique! Yea that's the word
- Not enough spicy quotes from characters
- Speed run challenges or ranking for that be cool since its kind of an arcade like game
- Fun's too brief, way too brief. 10-20 mins = entire game even on Legendary on SOLO (can't play eclipse because I'm a ♥♥♥♥♥)
- DLC characters could have a separate mission but didn't (don't just give us characters, give us a separate story too! Price don't matter too much but CONTENT! RoosterTeeth, you guys should know this better than most people!)
- ULTRA settings isn't as "ultra" as you think :P
Reviewer's note: Honestly, I love this game and it could go better than it is now. We do have millions of fans of RWBY, and I mean millions. Shouldn't it's own game receive just as much love? We know we ask a lot, but if you can MAKE IT! WE BUY IT! I mean some of us spend like 60-80 dollars for games almost almost every 3-4 weeks you know? Some even more!
P.S: RoosterTeeth Games, if you're reading this review, love the game, love the art, love almost everything. But do me one thing! JUST ONE! LAG FIX PLEASE! PLEASE! PLEASE! Ok thanks bye! *Waving*

Portal 2 - The Final Hours is a book, not a game. However, that doesn't mean it's not worth looking into! This only really has value if you've played Portal 2, and especially if you liked it...and especially if you're interested in how it was made/behind-the-scenes info, and ESPECIALLY if you're into game game-making process in general. It has a lot of neat little tidbits to learn that really makes you appreciate Portal 2, an already stellar game just to play, even more.
It's not walls of text, but instead has plenty of pictures and little sidenotes. And, of course, little interactive bits where you can click on things or slide the mouse. But really you're getting this to read. This isn't a long "book;" I finished it in a few hours in one sitting. Though that's probably a good thing, as it still had a lot to read about and kept me engaged the whole time.
This is more or less a guaranteed recommendation if it looks interesting at all to you. I'd probably wait for a sale even at its low price if you're fine with waiting, but $2 for some neat knowledge is a fair trade to me!

I have pretty much found this game by mistake. It was listed on flash sale, briefly checked what's the game about and it was marines vs hordes of aliens in a rather simplistic top down view. But don't let the looks fool you. The game is really fun, has lots of depth and tactics. And who doesn't want to decimate thousands of aliens. It's a proper Serious Sam inspired 2D shooter with a very interesting approach to strategy gameplay.
And now that i've played several skirmish battles and also progressed deeply into the campaign i must say it's a pretty damn good game. I've played many strategy games and none has pressured the player so much to continue and fight off aliens as this one does. For example in C&C qames i usually use the steamroller tactics. First you fortify your base, gather enough resources, make huge army and steamroll over enemy. Here, while you sometimes can do that, killing the wrong hive can re-route enemies differently to parts you thought were secure without turrets or marines and it can flip the entire fate of the battle. Limited resources also mean you have to use them carefully to build turrets, upgrade soldiers and buy new abilities and also pressures you to kill more hives to progress and gain more resources.
If you love strategy games and you want to kill seemingly unlimited swarms of aliens, this is the game you want. It's unique, original, runs well even on older computers, yet it actually looks pretty nice (not that you have time to admire anything else but massive swarms of aliens :D ). And the reason why we play games, it's good old fun. Highly recommended!

The game is quite big considering its genre in terms of exploring and variety of side quests which are all unique and well done.
Level design is great, never have I played a stealthy game with such great focus on verticality. There are 'necessary' augmentations and others that are 'optional' (like usual), however you'll usually find at least one use for the less required ones more than often.
Haven't gotten that far into the story yet, I've only finished 2 story missions and I'm already 28 hours in - you decide how big this game is.
Enough of the good, I'll focus on the bad here:
1. It's terribly optimized. It requires a ridiculous machine to run well on max settings, which doesn't sound that bad, considering we're talking about max settings, but that leads to my second point:
2. It doesn't look good.. It's just not impressive in terms of graphics, but is extremely hungry for resources, which isn't acceptable, not to mention the stutters and other random bullsh*t happening, like graphical glitches, sound freezes etc. I'd rather have DX:HR level graphics but no stutters and smooth gameplay instead of this crap, it seems that it runs the same both on lower and higher settings on my rig (excluding resolution).
3. Launch was awful, majority of people (including me) would crash after the tutorial mission which is just disgusting, not sure how the game was even released like that. Crashes are still common even now (over a week after release)
4. Microtransactions, yes, on a singleplayer game.
5. Loading times.. Loading times are a-f*cking-trocious, loading screens sometimes take longer than 5 minutes, that exceeds even heavily modded Skyrim/F4's, Witcher 3 etc. loading times, not sure how they managed to do that. Even when it's on a SSD it takes about 2 minutes for it to load.
6. Random glitches, including important things like Achievements not registering, people seem to not get Foxiest of the Hounds etc. for no apparent reason. (still no counter for alarms/kills, really)
Recommended if you enjoy either Stealth games or cyberpunk/sci-fi story ridden games (both would be perfect).

Deus Ex Mankind Divided continues on from the story of Deus Ex Human Revolution, personally one of my favortie games of all time
The gameplay is really solid, they've refined the gameplay, and made non-lethal less of a hassle this time around. The levels are solidly constructed, with multiple paths; some I found as I was leaving the mission area. The perk/auguments tree is still good, and the addition of these new augments are very satisfying
Stealth and Loud are viable options, and the game gives you the tools to do both, including the auguments. I personally went non-lethal stealth, as leaving the enemies alive felt more rewarding, even though it was more risky than just killing them. New auguments such as the TESLA launcher were great for stealth, but there is a bug where the stunned enemies become hostile for a second; which may trigger other enemies. [WILL CHANGE IF FIXED]. I personally haven't done loud, but Stealth is a little broken if you have the right upgrades and enough fuel. Glass-Cloaking can be especially helpful/broken during areas with large amounts of enemies and traps. The fact that glass-cloaking allows you to go through lasers without triggering alarms is a little over-powered, but you can also use EMP Rounds and Remote Hacking to get them anyways
Prague was more fun to explore than Hengsha and Detriot from the last game. It's vast map size and one location allowed the developers to add so many little details that really improve the atmosphere, like little sticky notes; or emails that can contain codes for locks. Hacking was very satisfying, multi-tools were good if you didnt have time to hack, or just couldnt afford to get caught. The Side Quests definetly give more hours of enjoyment, and the little stories they give are great; my favorite one being the one about helping an underground rebel group get dirt on a large company, and expose it to the world. The game doesn't have an barriers to access an area, aside from the story locked ones; and can make some areas later in the game quite trivial if you did get the right items. Also I heard Eidos will be patching in new Side Quests, so I have hopes for it.
My one complaint is the weapon variety. All the interseting weapons from Human Revolution, such as the Laser Gun, Plasma Gun, and Heavy Rifle; gone. The ammo variety can pose some problems. The Unqiue weapons in the game don't allow you to put Mods on them, and only can use ONE type of ammo, usually the ones that can't be used in combat much. Like the EMP rounds, they become useless after you Remote Hacking, or get skilled with the Glass-Cloaking.
The Story takes place two years after Human Revolution, with Adam Jensen joining the hacker collective group mentioned in The Missing Link. He also joins up with Interpol, in a new Task force called TaskForce 29. The story is about Adam investigating a bombing, but that bombing is inter connected with a mysterious group, The Illuminati; which is more than a cutaway joke like in Human Revolution. Theres a subplot about the sociopolitcal environment of Augs vs. Naturals. It gets a bit too liberal for my tastes, with all it's BlackLivesMatter and Muslim allegories; but to some, it may be a good thing. It also gets a little less into your face later in the game, as you have to deal with Augmented terrorists.
A big problem I had with the story was the ending was so abrupt. I got to the boss, and thought to myself, "HOPEFULLY THIS IS THE FIRST OF MANY". The fight wasnt even hard, I stun gunned him once and pressed Q, knocking the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of him. I immidately get the "Finish Deus Ex: Mankind divided on any difficulty" achievement. It really bothered me, considering all the combat upgrades this game gives you, assumably for taking on hard enemies. Hopefully we get DLC similar to Human Revolution's "The Missing Link"
I personally enjoyed the ♥♥♥♥ out of this game. People are saying, "oh it's too quick!" That's only if you run through it. I did 90% of the side quests, and investigated all the maps (except for one). If you take your time with it, you'll get the most out of it. As of 8/30/16, I haven't been able to play Breach, but once I do; I'll update this review.
8/31/16: I've played Breach
Breach is an Arcade version of Deus Ex, pretty much; little bit sized chunks using the mechanics of the main game, designed to be speedrun.
There's a persistent inventory thing (you do your loadout before attempting the missions) and the rewards feel pretty good. Guns and special ammo and stuff is in RNG style booster packs, but the game gives you enough credits via rewards to keep you stocked up.
Unlike the main game, which emphasizes "invent a solution" Breach plays in a faster, more deliberate way, often straight up saying "this mission must be completed with perfect stealth" or "this is a boss mission, no you can no do a stealth takedown" etc. and expecting you to grab whatever you have from your bank to meet the mission on its terms.
Narratively, its a lot like how the story is presented on other "hacker sims" You do a bunch of acessing nodes in order to uncover evidence, which you then present to a series of contacts that you talk to through the same IM interface the game uses for the IM conversations in the main game. You may also be supporting off screen ground military ops in addition to your detective work. Complete a quest, you get some really nice items and a full on Eliza Cassan news report about the real in-world fallout from your investigations.
All in all it does a good job of saying "hey, how about some Deus Ex VR speedrun missions?" and finding a semi-plausible way to work them in to the universe.
If you like hacking sims like hacknet or uplink, you'll like this mode too.
It has the microtransactions, but they're positioned like the ones for the main game. The game isn't really designed around them, but you can spend money on them if you want to be OP I guess.
As long as you don't care horribly much about global leaderboards and just wanna have speedrun competitions with your friends, or just play it like an odd deus ex spinoff game once and come back when they add more quests, it's not going to bother holding your wallet hostage.
And on the issue of microtransactions: Who cares? I got everything I needed 18 hours in, and the bonus points I got, I bought the unnesscary auguments which I didn't use, save for trying once. It's a non-problem and its only there to serve the lazy whales who don't want to explore and want to beat the game "easily".
I give this game an 7.5/10, you could probably buy this during a sale, it's worth every cent.

Yes, yes... This is a good game... I've yet to complete the game but I'll add more comments when I do. There are so many similarities to Diablo but so many other interesting things as well. I've listed them down in the PROS and CONS.
TL2 is slightly below Diablo in terms of content quantity... 4 levels are really, really fast to finish.... But for the price, it was worth it.... I am also very annoyed with the creation of another Runic account to link to my Steam account. I would like to be able to transfer my game to another Steam account not the one I bought it with.
Another pet peeve (which can't be helped) is the feeling of repetition deeper into TL2. You can see copies of Ratlings, skeletons and Brutes appearing over and over again. They just come back with a different name and different skin.
$4.00 SGD
PROS
1. Great map design
Quests and story rolled into one. Not all the quests are in the town, some are hidden away in the map, so it makes you want to explore. However, the downside is that you might miss some of these quests as you don't know where they are. E.g. Zephari Envoy
2. Secrets
There are lots of interesting secret areas. One memorable one was "It puts the lotion in the bucket" (obvious reference to Silence of the Lambs). I shouldn't spoil how to do it but let's just say it will be interesting to find the lotion.
3. Skill trees
I like the way you can upgrade your skills and that there are so many skills to work with, per character. Each skill is tiered into T1, T2, T3 with a special upgrade at each tier. There are a lot of way to play your character.
4. Semi-Live NPCs
The NPCs give you information on current events which are related to your quests and they don't function purely as lamp posts. I think they could have made it better by making the NPCs come alive even more though.
5. Train Travel
Although a cut-scene, it was cool. I was hoping to interact with the train though. I think that it would be better if we could go onto the train and do stuff on it.
6. Interaction
Quite a few items but not everything. You can break urns, rocks, explosives and barrels but those are a given. Lighting the braziers to provide light was most innovative. I think having levers or switchs that moved big bridges would be quite cool.
7. Knocking creatures off
There are some ways to knock off tiny land creatures, off the terrain and into a pit. Very cool, much better than an invisible ring. Of course, you can be knocked off as well.
8. Pack mule / Pet
I love my pet and the ability to sell items without going back to town.
9. Spider Mines
I can't believe there are spider mines that seek out enemies.
10. Alternate weapons
Press W. Switch from range to melee. Great move. Change playstyle instantly. *Star star*
11. NPC hunting
You can get more NPCs to help out in the town if you go out of your way to do side quests. Again, a potential pitfall as you might miss them totally, but it's okay. The similarity to Suikoden's hero collection is great.
CONS
1. Bugs
Can't pick up items that fall onto ledges
Can't shoot creatures who are no more than a few feet above or below you.
2. Murder Hobo
Almost everything is still mass murder. Kill, kill, kill, kill and more killing for any quest. I'm a mass murderer in this game. I've yet to come across a quest without premeditated murder.
3. Stupid things
You are face-to-face with an enemy. However, you can't reach him because of a crack that runs through the floor, dividing you and the enemy. Most ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. I think a jump would be great.
4. Runic Account creation
Most annoying. I have to create another account just to play online. <------ This here pisses me off.
5. Spell keys
1,2,3,4 are easy to reach. 5,6,7,8,9,0 extremely hard. Would have been better with 1234QWER.
6. Repetition
Ratlings, goo, skeletons repeated. Just with a different colour palette and skin.
7. Fame
What does this do?
8. Content
Only 4 levels. I breezed through them. It didn't feel like there was enough interesting stuff. Just lots of similar level bashing.
NEUTRAL
1. Trash drops
I am not so certain about trash drops that just keep on generating a lot of junk for me to sell. Perhaps, something else can be done about trash drops?
SUGGESTIONS
I saw ladders in the game. Could Runic code an interaction with ladders?

: Himeko’s Epilogue is recommended for fans of Narcissu 1 and 2, and non-fans may feel unsatisfied with the content they get (about 1 hour of reading) for the price they pay.
As the title says, this is an epilogue for Himeko, who is a main character in Narcissu 2. As such, it is strongly recommended that you finish Narcissu 2 before starting Himeko’s Epilogue. The epilogue is short as you may expect, with about 1 hour of reading, and it takes Himeko’s story from Narcissu 2 to the very end. That’s not to say that the ending in Narcissu 2 is unfinished. The ending of Narcissu 2 satisfactorily closes the story of Himeko and Setsumi, so reading Himeko’s Epilogue is not strictly necessary to understanding the story.
Himeko’s Epilogue focuses on the friendship between Himeko and Yuka. Without spoiling any events, you could say that Himeko’s Epilogue is a story about two friends supporting each other to get through the difficulties they are facing. Yuka is a minor character in Narcissu 2, and her character develops a little in the short amount of time covered in Himeko’s Epilogue.
There are two options for going through Himeko’s Epilogue – Normal and Classic Mode. The only difference between the two modes is the artwork used for the background. The artwork in Normal will show character’s faces, whereas Classic will not, and the artwork in Normal is larger.
The chronological order of the stories is: Narcissu 2 -> Himeko’s Epilogue -> Narcissu 1
Setsumi is a main character in Narcissu 2, and Narcissu 2 is a prequel to her story in Narcissu 1. Narcissu 2 explains some of the actions that Setsumi takes in Narcissu 1, so if you can’t stand seeing characters doing things for seemingly unexplainable reasons then you may like to read Narcissu 1 last. Otherwise, you can read Narcissu 2 after Narcissu 1 and have several moments of “Ah, so that’s why!”

You can get the full series (this game, Bound in Blood, and Call of Juarez: Gunslinger) for $35 even without a sale, which is completely worth it, but if you want to wait for a sale it'll be a steal.

If you liked Half-Life, GET THIS GAME.  (IT'S FREE!)  You will feel like you're Gordon all over again.  The interface is the same, the baddies are (mostly) the same, the plot (as you piece it together) is good enough that you don't mind what isn't there.  You're not here for a plot anyway - you want to shoot things, solve a few puzzles, and get lost in the Half-Life universe.  Oh, will you ever.
And as a bonus, you get a new gun that makes its first appearance in a "Half-Life" type game:  A rocket "anti-grav" gun that you can use to "rocket jump" to dizzying heights or across gaping chasms.  And soon after you get the gun, there's a scene where you need to use it to clear two waves of zombie-type baddies.  You will have a BLAST doing it.
You don't know how you got where you are,  you don't know what you're supposed to do, and you sure as heck don't know what's around that next bend in the pipe.  But you don't care, because the only alternative is to sit and do nothing, and you're not here for that.  As you first wake up, you hear a voice saying, "The right man in the wrong place can make a big difference."  That's you, buddy.  Go forth and wreak havoc - FOR FREE!
No add-on purchases, no annoying ads.  FREE.
Did I say it was free?  The only reason I clicked the "Yes, I recommend this game" button is because there was no "I ABSOLUTELY FREAKIN' RECOMMEND THIS GAME" button.

Deus Ex Mankind Divided continues on from the story of Deus Ex Human Revolution, personally one of my favortie games of all time
The gameplay is really solid, they've refined the gameplay, and made non-lethal less of a hassle this time around. The levels are solidly constructed, with multiple paths; some I found as I was leaving the mission area. The perk/auguments tree is still good, and the addition of these new augments are very satisfying
Stealth and Loud are viable options, and the game gives you the tools to do both, including the auguments. I personally went non-lethal stealth, as leaving the enemies alive felt more rewarding, even though it was more risky than just killing them. New auguments such as the TESLA launcher were great for stealth, but there is a bug where the stunned enemies become hostile for a second; which may trigger other enemies. [WILL CHANGE IF FIXED]. I personally haven't done loud, but Stealth is a little broken if you have the right upgrades and enough fuel. Glass-Cloaking can be especially helpful/broken during areas with large amounts of enemies and traps. The fact that glass-cloaking allows you to go through lasers without triggering alarms is a little over-powered, but you can also use EMP Rounds and Remote Hacking to get them anyways
Prague was more fun to explore than Hengsha and Detriot from the last game. It's vast map size and one location allowed the developers to add so many little details that really improve the atmosphere, like little sticky notes; or emails that can contain codes for locks. Hacking was very satisfying, multi-tools were good if you didnt have time to hack, or just couldnt afford to get caught. The Side Quests definetly give more hours of enjoyment, and the little stories they give are great; my favorite one being the one about helping an underground rebel group get dirt on a large company, and expose it to the world. The game doesn't have an barriers to access an area, aside from the story locked ones; and can make some areas later in the game quite trivial if you did get the right items. Also I heard Eidos will be patching in new Side Quests, so I have hopes for it.
My one complaint is the weapon variety. All the interseting weapons from Human Revolution, such as the Laser Gun, Plasma Gun, and Heavy Rifle; gone. The ammo variety can pose some problems. The Unqiue weapons in the game don't allow you to put Mods on them, and only can use ONE type of ammo, usually the ones that can't be used in combat much. Like the EMP rounds, they become useless after you Remote Hacking, or get skilled with the Glass-Cloaking.
The Story takes place two years after Human Revolution, with Adam Jensen joining the hacker collective group mentioned in The Missing Link. He also joins up with Interpol, in a new Task force called TaskForce 29. The story is about Adam investigating a bombing, but that bombing is inter connected with a mysterious group, The Illuminati; which is more than a cutaway joke like in Human Revolution. Theres a subplot about the sociopolitcal environment of Augs vs. Naturals. It gets a bit too liberal for my tastes, with all it's BlackLivesMatter and Muslim allegories; but to some, it may be a good thing. It also gets a little less into your face later in the game, as you have to deal with Augmented terrorists.
A big problem I had with the story was the ending was so abrupt. I got to the boss, and thought to myself, "HOPEFULLY THIS IS THE FIRST OF MANY". The fight wasnt even hard, I stun gunned him once and pressed Q, knocking the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of him. I immidately get the "Finish Deus Ex: Mankind divided on any difficulty" achievement. It really bothered me, considering all the combat upgrades this game gives you, assumably for taking on hard enemies. Hopefully we get DLC similar to Human Revolution's "The Missing Link"
I personally enjoyed the ♥♥♥♥ out of this game. People are saying, "oh it's too quick!" That's only if you run through it. I did 90% of the side quests, and investigated all the maps (except for one). If you take your time with it, you'll get the most out of it. As of 8/30/16, I haven't been able to play Breach, but once I do; I'll update this review.
8/31/16: I've played Breach
Breach is an Arcade version of Deus Ex, pretty much; little bit sized chunks using the mechanics of the main game, designed to be speedrun.
There's a persistent inventory thing (you do your loadout before attempting the missions) and the rewards feel pretty good. Guns and special ammo and stuff is in RNG style booster packs, but the game gives you enough credits via rewards to keep you stocked up.
Unlike the main game, which emphasizes "invent a solution" Breach plays in a faster, more deliberate way, often straight up saying "this mission must be completed with perfect stealth" or "this is a boss mission, no you can no do a stealth takedown" etc. and expecting you to grab whatever you have from your bank to meet the mission on its terms.
Narratively, its a lot like how the story is presented on other "hacker sims" You do a bunch of acessing nodes in order to uncover evidence, which you then present to a series of contacts that you talk to through the same IM interface the game uses for the IM conversations in the main game. You may also be supporting off screen ground military ops in addition to your detective work. Complete a quest, you get some really nice items and a full on Eliza Cassan news report about the real in-world fallout from your investigations.
All in all it does a good job of saying "hey, how about some Deus Ex VR speedrun missions?" and finding a semi-plausible way to work them in to the universe.
If you like hacking sims like hacknet or uplink, you'll like this mode too.
It has the microtransactions, but they're positioned like the ones for the main game. The game isn't really designed around them, but you can spend money on them if you want to be OP I guess.
As long as you don't care horribly much about global leaderboards and just wanna have speedrun competitions with your friends, or just play it like an odd deus ex spinoff game once and come back when they add more quests, it's not going to bother holding your wallet hostage.
And on the issue of microtransactions: Who cares? I got everything I needed 18 hours in, and the bonus points I got, I bought the unnesscary auguments which I didn't use, save for trying once. It's a non-problem and its only there to serve the lazy whales who don't want to explore and want to beat the game "easily".
I give this game an 7.5/10, you could probably buy this during a sale, it's worth every cent.

Now specifics...
+
In addition to great graphics (when they work, see below) the game has incredible art design. When I first walked through Prague I found myself staring at the police uniforms and marvelling at the level of detail they put into the design without going overboard (very easy to do in a futuristic/cyberpunk style) and the same goes for just about everything in Mankind Divided, not to mention how many times in a dialogue sequence would I say "F&#@, Jensen looks cool!"
+
These different approaches add greatly to the replay value as you can do each misison with a totally different style.
+
+
The takedowns from Human Revolution are back in similar style, still freezing time while you stab your enemies in the neck, although this time around they feel a bit more snappy and while they still seem to jump to different poses than what they were before, it happens far less often in Mankind Divided (more situational animations.)
The best part: a small but vastly improving change is that if you are snapped into cover and you perform a takedown, enemies will be pulled in towards you before taking them down. For example: if you are crouched behind a desk and an enemy walks by, Jensen will pull him over to his side of the desk and give him a quick jab to the face, making hiding bodies much easier and adding a more fluid feel to the whole procedure.
+
+
While not without it's faults (below), the game does a good enough job during your first playthrough of making you a little bit suspicious of everyone and wondering who's behind what.

How they managed to take one of the best-performing ports of last-gen and turn it into this, I'll never understand.
If you rely on integrated graphics like I do, this game is simply unplayable because of the constant slowdown. Mind you, I've clocked nearly 100 hours in the vanilla version between an old laptop and an off-the-shelf desktop, and I've never had a problem getting it to run at 60 fps. I don't see how the additions in this version warrant such a performance drop.
If you have decent specs then it might work just fine, and I would highly recommend this title to anyone who missed out on the original DMC4 if only to experience the base content.  But understand that this version's performance is completely unacceptable.
That said, even the content they added is somewhat unpolished. You'll still be playing through the same levels from the vanilla version. You can even see in the official previews that the new characters were implemented with a complete lack of effort beyond their gameplay. Notice how each time an enemy mob is activated, there's a short cutscene where the camera pans around a bunch of static character models. Where in Dante/Nero scenarios the enemies might at least have some spawning animations, with the new characters it looks like the scene was hastily thrown together in the engine as if it was an alpha build.

Pretty simple, casual 2D fishing simulator. Visuals are nice, animations are fine, and music is okay to listen to for a while (then press M to turn it off). Upgrades come in pretty quickly at first, then mid-game there is a lot of unrewarded gold grind while you save for better rods + upgrades, boats, and other upgrades. Quests are decent gold but you can easily get stuck on a quest if you haven't gotten the proper rod/upgrades yet. Also, fish take time to respawn so you may have to wait for the fish you want (or get a boat to increase your fishing range). At end-game once you can grind the shark/maw/anglerfish, gold comes in quickly enough to upgrade everything you want and more.
Fishing is pretty straightforward: catch a small fish to catch a medium fish to catch a large/huge fish while avoiding fish you don't want to catch. I upgraded reel speed and lure sink speed to better avoid fish I didn't want to take. The Bait Guard and Crankbait upgrades are really useful, but are also very expensive to grind. Minimap and radar upgrades are nice for avoiding unwanted fish, though you can throw your line beyond the radar (which might be fixed in the beta). Radar is also useful for finding where the Maw/Anglerfish spawn and where you can cast to avoid the most fish on the way down.
Pretty fun for a 2D fishing simulator, though I would've liked more special fish like the shark. The shark takes your live fish and drags your line further away, effectively extending your rod's reach further than you normally could go. It's pretty fun to use when you're starting out with mediocre rods and no boat, but I don't think there's any more sharks further out so everything beyond the initial screen is just simple fishing.

Up to now I've only played two games in Call of Juarez series: this one and Call of Juarez the Cartel. I'll be honest and I know this is going to be a controversial statement: at first, I enjoyed the Cartel much more than this one. Idk, this one just seemed a little too old school and somewhat archaic for me to get into it. On top of that, the action I experienced (the first two stages) wasn't really all that engaging, unlike the Cartel where (despite that game's lacking polish) I was engaged from the very first level due to the fast-paced combat. Having finished The Cartel, I decided to give this game a second chance and... wow.  How wrong I was to put this one down so quickly. I got past the second level and carried on through the game, marvelling at how much fun it is and how solid it is in execution.
While Call of Juarez the Cartel features nothing more than endless firefights with mindless explosive combat and a terrible story filled with unlikeable characters (kinda like a playable Michael Bay movie), this one features a really engaging storyline along with two types of gameplay: stealth and gunfighting. You play as two characters: Reverend Ray and Billy. Billy's the one you start out with and he's all about the stealth. Unfortunately, it's not that good a first impression. Billy's gameplay is typically slower and less exciting than Ray's, focusing first person platforming and stealth. The mechanics  for his gameplay take a little training to get used to, but once you do, it's a lot of fun to play. Still, it's nowhere near as fun as Ray's segments, which are straight up "kill-everyone-in-sight" actioners that leave you breathless by the end. Ray's stages aren't exactly as fast-paced and explosive as the gunfights featured in The Cartel, but that in no way means they're any less good. In fact, they're prpbably better due to one reason: a little something I like to call "Gun-Punch". The shooting in this game, despite featuring mediocre animations for both shooting and reloading, feels very punchy and satisfying. Whenever you shoot an enemy, it feels like the bullets are really punching through the enemy's body and leaving him in pieces (not literally, there's no gore here).
The controls, while a little outdated, get the job done and eventually start feeling natural. The graphics are outdated as well, but that doesn't mean they're exactly unattractive. The environments and gun textures are both gorgeous for their time. Unfortunately, the same can't be said for the character models (which lack detail) or the aniamtions for pretty much everything from jumping, to shooting and reloading your guns. Fortunately, these problems don't detract from the game's enjoyment factor or playability. WHat might detract from the playability though is that the game has some slightly poor optimization. I have a mid-range laptop with an nvidia gt640 card and, while I can run the game on max settings, it sometimes drops from 60 fps all the way into the low 30's. Keep in mind I can play games like far cry 3 at very high settins with an average framerate of 60-40 fps so a framerate like this on a game this dated-looking isn't really my system's fault. Still, even in the low 30's the game feels smooth enough so it's not really a problem. To sum up:
Pros:
Viscerally satisfying, punchy combat (not including some flat-feeling hand to hand combat sections).
Some gorgeous environments and good-looking weapons.
Engaging story driven by two very likeable and interesting characters.
Stealth segments are capable of providing a good sense of tension.
Absolutely nails that Wild West atmosphere.
Atmospheric soundtrack.
Cons:
Ugly character models and animations.
Stealth segments take a little getting used to.
Controls are very different from modern first person shooters and might trouble some players.
Lacking optimization in the framerate department.
Bottom line: For such a dated game, Call of Juarez is a ton of fun packing one of the most interesting storylines I've ever come across. The flaws are a little annoying at times, but they certainly don't break the game. If you consider yourself a fan of the Wild West and are jonesing for solid shooter set in that scenario, don't hesitate to pick this one up. For 10 bucks, it's a steal.

All in all, Call of Juarez is a great game that blends elements of old and new FPS together in an intriguing way. Combined with an awesome story and voice-acting worthy of any good western film or novel, the game is more than worth the cost. It takes a little getting used to but if you keep at it, you won't be disappointed.
The game regularly shifts between two characters, which is very cool from a story perspective, as you see how two people sharing the same story can have very different perspectives. However, the two characters are mechanically different, which can be a pain as one gets used to the play style of one, only to be thrown back into the other guy and having to adjust abruptly.
Billy plays fast and light, and integrates some modern ideas of platforming such as grabbing ledges and using a whip to swing across gaps or climb up to higher places. The whip requires precise placement to work correctly and the timing of jumps and swings can be tricky to learn, but it beats having to stack boxes to get over a two-foot fence any day. Save often though!
Reverend Ray is a very different play. He can only do classic hop-style platforming, which means even the simplest fence can require piling of crates to surmount, a distracting thing to do in the middle of a wild shoot-out.  However, he is a great gun handler and even wears a breastplate that blocks a lot of otherwise painful shots. However, this is essential as Ray is not very fast and fighting from cover is not the easiest thing to do. However, there are few things more evocative than to walk through a town full of bad guys, shooting them down while listening to some of the best voice-acting I've ever heard in a game. Fear the wrath of Ray!
Shooting is very much a mix of old and new. The basic shooting is very old-school with lightning reloads, no ironsights, and most guns need multiple hits to kill even basic baddies. But there are more sophisticated shooting modes such as dueling mode and quick-shooting which wouldn't be at all out of place in the latest games today.
One thing that must be addressed because some gamers really get hung up about these things: there is culturally-insensitive content in this game including casual racism, sexual violence, and religious extremism. This is a spaghetti western in game form, not a documentary trying to encapsulate the truth about people in the Old West. Movie stereotypes and cliches are in full force here. Mexicans are portrayed as brutish and dishonest; Christians, both Catholic and Protestant, are intolerant and cruel hypocrites; and aboriginal Americans are either wizened animists or blood-thirsty savages. There is also plenty of bad language, much of it sexually explicit. This game is not remotely as extreme as many, but it earns its M-rating nonetheless, so parents be advised.
All that said, enjoy this first of a great franchise, one of the best western FPS ever made, and a delight.

If this game caught your eye, it's probably because of a certain Nintendo franchise. No, there's no shame in being one of those people, and yes, it'll probably satisfy that itch.
Brawlhalla is a fighting game, although you probably know that already. The combat is fast-paced, the movesets are varied (for most of the game), and it's easy enough to pick up and play. (A friend of mine was able to beat me after only a few matches.)
The distinguishing characteristic for Brawlhalla as opposed to, say, your favorite Smash game is that everyone starts out with the same, somewhat limited moveset. The focus of the game is weapons - which vary movesets completely and completely change a character's dynamic. Each character has two weapons to keep variety. The weapons feel effectively balaned, although a few characters have somewhat powerful moves. (A good example of that is Cassidy's hammer, down-strong.) The other items are only usable with no weapon, which gives unarmed combat efficient as well.
The other aspects apart from the fights themselves are bare-bones. There's a training mode where you can use any character (as oppposed to the ones in the weekly rotation), a "tournament" mode, and a shop. The shop carries mostly cosmetic items, with permanent unlocks for the characters also available (which unlocks use outside of the rotation). Only the fighters and some color schemes (unlocked after playing a certain fighter a lot) are available with the regular currency - the others require Mammoth Coins, which translates into real money. A pack of all the characters at once is also avialable - which also contains unrelased fighters.
The game is still in beta, so there are a few things that aren't finished. However, what is here is superb. I  highly reccommend it for fans of Smash, or imitations thereof. ...Now that I think of it, this game is very Smash-like, but I thoroughy enjoyed it nonetheless.

- Short -
I would rank this game in my top 5 favorite games of all time. The blend of grand strategy, open world, massive battles, RPG, Trade Sim, and empire building is truley unique and ever since the original Mount and Blade came out I have been dying for any game to come remotely close to the level of what this game provides.
- Recommend Mod -
Battle Sizer - This game is old, and as such, battles in this game were originally scaled to be smaller with reinforcement waves, with battle sizer you can make each wave larger. My computer when this first came out could barely handle 100 soldier on the field, now if you have a decent comp, it can easily handle about 800 which makes it even better.
- The Long -
Hello peasant, do you someday dream of going from a lowly trader to king and ruler of a kingdom? Perhaps a userper who decides to overthrow a king, or maybe a bandit who wishes to plunder the villages and countryside? In this game you get to do that, your character starts with the background of your choosing, there is no direction and your decisions actually do affect the world and not just some cutscene that doesn't really matter.
You get to experience battles from small skirmishes to literally thousands of warriors on blood battle fields. You can conquer castles and cities, pillage, start wars, usurp kings, create your own kingdom, trade with cities and villages, upgrade those cities and villages, upgrade your companions with armor and weapons, even join a tournament and joust.
If you are a fan of medieval times and rpg games, I doubt you would ever be dissapointed in this game. That being said, this game is older, with graphics that by modern standards are atrocious (they honestly weren't that good from the start)., but in a way that is a plus, as if the graphics were excellent, you wouldn't be able to handle battles that were as enormous as this game provides.
While the game provides a lot of different things for you to do, most are not extremely dynamic or complex, the game more provides a well-rounded medieval experience, while you can train and upgrade your units after recruiting them, you won't be able to have a tremendous amount of control of them on the battlefield, you can tell them positions, hold fire, attack and retreat, but the rest is up to them. As well in towns, most upgrades are very simple.
Pros & Cons
Pro -
Excellent replayability
Large scale first person battles
Open world freedom
One of the best player progression systems I have ever seen in a game
Despite the age of the game, the workshop community is still active and updating mods
Cons -
Bad Graphics - But as said, this can be a plus as it allows enormous battles with little lag
One of the worst player appearance customization screens I have ever come across (would you like to look ugly, uglier, or hideous? Good thing there are plenty of helmets to hide faces in this game)

Before early gameplay leaks and reveals it was my intention to only experience the gameplay myself, and I failed on that front. Because of previews my expectations were extraordinarily low. Vergil looked overpowered and simple to play in every regard while Lady and Trish both looked to be only moderate potential at best with loose options and pure fundamentals respectively. As soon as I started playing, thankfully, my preconceptions were crushed.
Vergil:
The very first thing I discovered starting with Vergil is that you have to commit to your attacks more than you would expect because jumping out of them requires much greater timing. This is good. Overall, Vergil is much, MUCH stiffer than his 3SE counterpart and demands you adopt an entirely new, more conservative playstyle than you'd be used to in any previous game except maybe DMC1. Trick's invincibility frames have been shortened considerably so it's no longer the easy perfect dodge button and because you trick to enemies by shooting a summoned sword, tricking too often is more likely to get you hit because you're more likely to hit a nearby enemy with a projectile than one outside of the range of the attack you intend to dodge. On the opposite side of this, many of your lengthier moves can be canceled by tricking so it balances out in speed. Potentially, 4SE's Vergil is much stronger than 3's, but at a base level he's much harder to play that well without spamming.
Lady:
Heavily recommended that shooting/charging your gun be put on something other than the face button, I suggest swapping Square/X and R2/Right Trigger. It's also the configuration I use for Dante (With Sword switch put on Left Trigger instead). With this setup you're able to attack and charge your guns simultaneously to keep combat more active. Lady is very heavy damage with a bit of the same conservative, defensive playstyle. Meaning several of her moves aren't easily cancelled. Her equivalent to Devil Trigger allows you to break any of these animations, but doesn't function like a Devil Trigger. Instead, you get a large window of invulnerability along with a circle of grenades that does damage on par with DT Explosion from 3, draining the enitre meter in the same fashion. Her playstyle makes up for this and a lack of melee combat by being very mobile depending on what you're shooting with. Handguns charge for brust and delayed damage like Nero's Blue Rose and the second most mobile gun provided you compensate for recovery animations and end your rapid pressing early. Shotgun charged behaves like Coyote-A; Gunstinger is a great move that even hits if you end up on the opposite side of your enemy and allows for some close dodges. Kalina Ann seems to be the weakest of the bunch in terms of potential combos but grapple does its job and its moves are high damage. It's even more important to know your enemies as Lady than Vergil.
Trish:
My prediction turned out to be correct about Trish, in that she's moderate potential with heavy and exaggerated fundamentals. From the perspective of someone who loves the franchise and picks apart every little detail, she's boring. That said, Trish is by far the best thing for beginners in this game and people need to be able to play her through the entire story without switching. Trish's weapons are the tried and true "Sword and Fist" combination all the way from DMC1. Unlike DMC1, or even other characters in this game, she has both simultaneously on two different face buttons. Fists function similarly to how they always have and Sparda brings along one of the major teachers of juggling: Round Trip. While Sparda is active away from you, your fists' directional input attacks are altered and its combos extended, allowing for overall fantastic crowd control. I can't stress enough how good this character is for people too stubborn to play the first game, despite it being the hardest and most complete in the franchise.

Infested Planet is a hectic horde RTS title that matches a handful of marines with thousands of bugs and mutated nasties, overwhelming battles will remind you of Starship Troopers' scenes where death and retreat are inescapable.
All missions start with one or more base and a team of marines, with slightly varying goals in the campaign, which ultimately require the capture of all remaining bases and/or destruction of all alien hives. Variety is lacking, but the constant tide of aliens vs your rag-tag team of marines will keep you on the edge, inching slowly towards full domination.
Sound and music are serviceable, graphics are bright and clean, albeit a bit too monotone and can make spotting your troops a bit of a challenge (especially with some overhanging cliffs textures). There is enough structures and technology to keep you engaged in random missions and skirmishes, but not enough depth of strategy to warrant investing more than a few hours after finishing the main campaign.
Good fun for tough RTS fans but implementing multiplayer with a hive faction DLC would make this a solid title! 3.5/5

it is one of the gems from the past. the story is a blast and the general game mechanics are pretty neat to think of when the game was made. the game takes place back in the wild west of texas in 1884 as a youngster call'd Billy Candle.
the story is pretty straight forward and easy to grasp. Billy was the "trouble maker" and everyone in the town hated his guts. the only one who liked you in the home town was your ma, and a girl at the brothel named Suzy. after everyone giving Billy the hardest of time, he ran away to look for the Gold of Juarez. some time later he returns empty handed, and the town is still on his neck.
im gonna skip the rest for now to get onto the gameplay, you get 2 pistol sloths, this is pretty cool as you can dual wield identical guns or diffrent guns. some might be rusty and break after a few barrels, some might be ready to break. you get a sloth for ranged and shotgun on the share. its a small variety, but enough to get you trough thte game without losing intrest. there are more sloths, but they are specific for each char.
with that said, you play between 2 characters: Billy and Ray. Ray being the brother of you stepdad, being a priest. while Billy is the acrobat, Ray is heavy and have a chance of dodging bullets thanks to his chainmail armor. but this takes away his ability to climb. Ray can use dynamite whenever he finds it and got a bible he will always carry around. Billy on the other hand.. personally i never found dynamite as billy.. but he gets to use a bow which is the most usefull weapon you get. there are plenty of ammo, and i always had above 50 bullets, but when aiming with the bow, you enter slowmo, making it easy to hit moving targets, but you gotta aim infront of the run motion, or else you'll just hit the air behind him.
another good thing about controlling billy is the stealth mechanics, it doesnt work too good on its own, but during stealth chapters, its pretty fun. you get prectiaclly invisible in bushes and the AI dont know you'r whereabouts unless they've seen you hide.
here is the downside, tought.. sometimes during cutscene, if you see the screen sorta shake, get ready to load back, cause you'll either fall trough the map, or levitate up, just to fall to your death. its a problem i had a few times, mostly as Ray, but just stand on solid ground before entering the cutscene and try from diffrent angles and you'll bne fine.
another bad thing that is more major to the game is the Whip mechanic. as billy, you get the whip that will help you around, over clifs, scaling mountains and some other places.. but its so inacurate that it was a pain to use instead of fun. the whip is so short that its barely usefull, and you gotta stand on the edge of the cliff to use it, risking falling down. and you can even use it on the thinest of branch.. it is usefull as a melee tough, as you might not wanna waste bullets on the wildlife or close up enemies.
aiming from a distance with the guns need some work, and you're practically a sitting duck if you try. unless you got a rifle. you collect health from bottle of alcohol(?) and depending on the difficulity you choose, it gives a fair amount of health.. i usually play on the hardest difficulity to get the challange and put the game to the challange, but i barely could stand the 2nd chapter, because the aiming and the cutscene went against me. it got too frustrating, so i finishd the game on easy. its hard enought to fight against the game mechanics of the first stages. but it either smoothes out the futher you play, or you simply get used to it
there is a dual system that is alil funny and alil wierd. when you are challanged, you push your mouse up to draw your gun. you dodge bullets in slowmo while aiming for the kill.. nothing to say about it. its fun and difficult, but not because of the game mechanics, its because you gotta do serval things at the same time. aim for a lethal shot on the enemy, watch out for bullets, dodge bullets. even if it is slowmo, bullets travels fast, so you gotta keep up.
i give alot of these verdicts, and i cant really tell why, but i enjoyd the game enough to give it a 7/10. its clunky and got some stupid things, yeah, sure. but that didnt really take away from the whole experience. Call of Juarez is a game serie i could get addicted to if it wasnt for the lack of games and replayability. atleast this is a game you might just wanna play trough once or twice. the others however... i will cover that on those games ;P

I really wanted to like this one because I loved the sequel (Bound in Blood), which I played first.
Overall, the production values were great. Voice acting, art style, story, etc. Switching between characters on both sides of the fence also made for interesting gamplay styles and narrative.
However, some of the gameplay mechanics are very flawed. Random difficulty spikes and changes in mechanics like fist fighting weren't really fun. There are some stretches of the game where you have to go a long time without heath pickups, and whether you take damage or not is dependent on a random dice roll of whether or not enemies hit your armor or head.
The maps are generally linear but whenever new path ways open up, it's not always evident where you are supposed to backtrack to find a new path. This leads to a lot of wandering around, and if you are in a sequence where you have a time limit, finding out where you need to go may lead to failure. There are also stuck in geometry problems if you wander off the the path.
It was probably great at the time it was new but it  seems like the game didn't age very well by today's standards. By the end it felt like a boring (but very difficult) slog.
I'm still glad I got to get closure on this story, but if you are interested in a western themed shooter, play the sequel Bound in Blood first, and then decide whether you want to play this one to get the full story. The sequel is actually a prequel story-wise, so you don't really lose anything by playing them out of order, in my opinion. Playing this one really made me appreciate the sequel. The devs learned many lessons and improved upon pretty much every gameplay aspect.

If I have to describe what I feel about this game, I would say:
It's like having your favorite dish served to you, but the waitor tells you that they are out of fork, knife, spoon and chopsticks, so you have to use your hands.
In detail:
The two biggest selling points of this game compared to a classic dynasty warriors game are, first, that this game merges the combat system of dynasty warriors and "a little bit" of strategy aspect of "Romance of the three kingdoms" game. While in battle, you fight just like in any other dynasty warriors game, and while outside of battle, you can take care of politics and economical matter, recruiting officers, planning next battle, changing equipments and so on. Instead of following a storyline of one faction at a time, the game mode always involve the entire land.
Second, you can create your own custom character and make him/her part of three kingdoms lore and create different course of history. You can basically puzzle together your ultimate warriors, with different musou attacks from different playable officers, your own choice of EX-weapon. And when you are ingame, you can choose to serve a lord of your choice, transfer between factions, or become a independent vegabond army or even raise banner and declare independency. Taking random quests (mini battles, guard/escort, assassination, infiltration etc.) that will either raise or lower your reputation and raise friendship with the client, even join invasion/defense battles and help shift the course of history. Recruit officers to your faction, become sworn siblings, maybe even find a partner and have a son or daughter, who will also be randomly generated officer and eventually joins your force.
For me, the battles are more fun than those from a classic dynasty warriors game. If you are in charge, for example being the leader of a raiding party, or a ruler and invading a territory with your army, you can give very specific order to every officer on the battlefield, to capture or defend a base, to escort someone, or to do whatever they see fit.
Every map has a network of bases. You have to establish a chain of captured base all the way to the enemy's main camp in order to lure out the enemy commander and to win the battle by either defeating the commander or capture the main camp, no more "charge straight to the end boss and finish this level" way to win a battle, you will have to fight your way there. Various siege weapons and tactical manuvers can be summoned/executed by strategy spells (called "stratagem" ingame) will help you capture/defend bases.
The battle isn't necessarily lost if you run out of your HP. If you brought sufficient amount of soldiers with you, the number will go down but you will respawn, same goes for every other officer. One is only truly defeated in the battle if the soldier count is exhausted. Same for capturing and defending a base. Every base has durability, and it can be reduced by defeating soldiers/officers and destroying defense towers in there. Once the durability reaches zero, the attacking side will capture the base. So, coordinating you officers can be very beneficial (if you are in charge of course). When facing huge invading army, you can order your officers to defend certain chokepoints, buying you enough time to pick off enemy officers, and before they respawn, you can order your army to advance and capture some bases and resume defense once the enemy officers have respawned, just one of many possible tactics.
I often find myself going over very high KO count, sometimes over 2000, which is something i rarely do in a classic dynasty warriors game. In this game, you will be so busy focusing on capturing and defending bases, you will reach a high KO count without even noticing it.
A few things I'm not happy with:
1) No weapon customization
Every weapon you get in the game is pre-set. No randomness at all. Every level 4 dragon spear you get in the game will all have the exact same attribute and attribute level. I don't know why they would do that, removing the freedom of players to decide by themselves what kind of attribute they want their weapon to have. Some weapons are given pretty decent combination of attribute, some aren't so lucky, and there's nothing a player can do to fix it if he wishes to modify it.
2) "Pretty much everything you do, will cost you one round."
Sometimes, you want to dismiss officers from your faction, and maybe promote and recruit some other officers. By romance of the three kingdoms standard, all these can be done in one round, but each action will cost you some action points, but they tend to be sufficient. In this game however, you would need at least 3 rounds to get all those things done. To earn 800 gold, to gain 800 materials, to scout an officer and fail, all these would cost you one round. Each round is one month, failure at scouting an officer means you haven't achieved anything in a month. In the meantime, neighboring faction might attack you. Your kingdom consists of more than just you alone, you have plenty capable officers under your command and yet you can't defend multiple territories in one round. If you have two territories under attack at same time, you can only defend one, the other one will suffer damage and you might have to spend another round just doing repair.
3) Time limit
It's said that it is game over no matter what when a game reaches year 50. That's 6000 rounds. What's the point? Why not just let us play as long as we like and let us decide when it is time to end it and start a new game?
4) The whole bonus point thing
For every battle, you earn bonus points. And they are mainly for unlocking features at the begin of a game mode. You can spend bonus points in Option to unlock those preset weapons, but in order to have them showing up in a new game, you will have to spend another 4000 bonus points to enable that feature. And that everytime you start a new game. And to unlock items, strategems will also cost additional 4000 bonus points each.
"Oh wait this is not what I wanted to do, I better start a new game... Oh wait, I haven't grinded 4000 bonus points yet, I need to have my weapons/items/etc. ..."
But in the end, still a pretty enjoyable game, but fixing some of the problems mentioned above could greatly improve the experience.

My review of Red Faction,
At the start of the game you have the option to do a tutorial to learn all the controls, and I have to say it was one of the best tutorials I have ever played through. The game gives a fair amount of background to the setting, you play as Parker a miner on the planet Mars and a member of the Red Faction, a rebal group. From what the game tells you the conditons of the mines are horrible and everone is worked to death and the guards don't give a rats♥♥♥♥♥ there is also a plague going around in the mine that is killings hundreds of miners. The goal of the game is to overthrow the Ultor. I played through the entire game in about 3 hours and 15 minutes, so yes this is a very short game. I can not stress enough this game is short but very hard, It's been a long time since I have considered a game to be "hard"  but this game delivers! There are really only a few things I didn't like about the game the main thing was the MASSIVE difficulty curve about half way through the game, your just running around with your handgun and assult rifle killing guards easy as pie, then all of a sudden a new enemy type is brought up called "Mercenaries" a LOT of them carry a gun most of us know as a Gauss Rifle which will kill you in one hit no matter what, oh also the enemys can shot it through objects. The final thing I don't like is that it lacks in originality, IMO, if you have played Half-Life a game that came out around 3 years before Red Faction you will notice a unsettling amount of similarities, the game feels the same to play, the textures are similar the doctors have the exact same animation when healing you. THE MOST IMPORTANT THING IS that none of that bad stuff matters, it doesn't take away from the game at all, like I said before the game is very short but it is a fair story that for once makes sense. I had a large amount of fun playing this game and I recomend it to anyone who likes a FPS with a good challenge.
My final rating of the game is a 88/100

Warhammer 40K: Deathwatch is a cautionary tale of why we, as gamers, can't have nice things.  Created by the now-good-as-defunct Rodeo games, Deathwatch initially appeared on iOS first and served as one of the greatest turn based strategies on that platform.  Similar to a simpler, stripped-down XCOM, Deathwatch still showed a surprising amount of depth for an iOS game, coupled with attractive Unreal Engine 4 graphics.  It's strength was firmly rooted in its staggering array of reliquary items, space marine variations drawing from various chapters and its surprisingly deep tactical gameplay.
Spacemarines and reliquary items come in four tiers, with Tier IV items being of the legendary variety.  A truly impressive variety and attention to detail is lavished upon the space marines and all the weapons all have unique traits and identities.  Space marines  can gain levels and can spend XP to obtain chapter-specific traits and abilities.  Each marine can also hold various reliquary items that may boost or augment his abilities.
Selecting the correct five-man squad that will complete over 40 missions is up to you.  The tactics you employ and the speed at with which you also progress are also up you.  Obviously, some load outs are more effective than others.  A team of high level devastators with Tier-IV plasma cannons will obliterate most targets quickly.  A balanced team with strong-melee powerfist front-liners will make short work of most groups.
The story isn't epic but it is satisfactory and once you can complete the campaign, you can reattempt it in two sequentially higher difficulty levels.  Obviously the allure of the game is to obtain all the space marines and gear so that you can customize your squad to represent your notion of what a multi-chapter Deathwatch team should look like.  With that goal, the game succeeds marvelously.
However, the game has painful flaws that will dissuade any but the most hardened and ardent WH40K fans.  For starters, the game lacks any depth outside the combat zone and you don't have access to base-building.  The enemies amount to horde waves of Tyranids.  The game would have benefited tremendously from other enemy races, like Chaos, Orks, Eldar, Tau or Necrons.  Even the offering of such content via DLC would have been welcome.
And yet, despite the game's overall good quality on iOS, it sold in middling numbers and Rodeo was unable to continue developing new enemies, maps, coop, multiplayer and other promised content.  In short, the developer's funds dried up.  The lack of monetary support also undermined its ability to develop the Steam version, leading to crushing bugs that affect visibility, lack of tooltips, bad achievement glitches and even crashes.
The added chapters on the Steam platform version are poor shadows of the original three and almost no new weapons or items were added.  Consequently, the iOS version is a far better value.  Finally, because the iOS version had IPA to purchase packs to accelerate the unlocking of rare marines and items, the grind was limited.  The Steam version has no access to such a storefront and, consequently, only requisition can be used to purchase packs and items.  That results in an impossible level of grind that diminishes the game's fun dramatically.  Luckily I was able to grab my iOS save game which had 250 hours on it and port it into Steam so that I could slingshot my development without grinding all over again.
It's a shame that Rodeo wasn't able to complete its vision for its game.  The game lacks a ton of content and features that would elevate it to an extremely competent and fun TBS experience.  As it stands, the game is a great foray into strategy-based gameplay for avid WH40K fans.  When juvenile and simplistic games like PokemonGo rack up 45 million downloads while complex, rich games like this one wither on the iOS vine, ... that, is why we can't have nice things.
A worthy pickup for WH40K fans. 7.5/10.
Not so much for anyone else 5.5/10.

By video games standard, this is an old game.  However, the atmosphere, the voice acting, the action, the gameplay and the storyline all come together to make a great western.  Techland, creators of Dead Island and the Call of Juarez series, offer a wonderful graphical experience.  There are some little issues here and there with the game.  I had my share or horseriding issues, or the strange sneaking ability that doesn't always work. I completed the game a week ago, so while my memories of this game are still fresh I'll write a review.
What I gotta say first, I love western games and overall I liked Call of Juarez. This game is pretty old now and there are some problems with this game, but I still liked it very much and I recommend it to everybody who likes western theme.
First, let's talk about the good things. What I especially liked is the atmosphere, soundtrack and the story (except for this terrible final ending scene). You know, there are some games that keeps you interested in the story from the beginning and till the end. Call of Juarez is one of those.
About the gameplay - we have 2 playable characters with different playstyles. When you play Reverend Ray its your classical FPS, where you shoot your enemies using rifles, shotguns, dual pistols and stylish slowmotion ability. When you play as Billy Candle, prepare for some stealth and lasso swinging (both are extremely unpolished, but you will get used to them after some time). Actually Billy's missions can be frustrating at first, but when you get used to them, they will not be a problem.
Unfortunately there are plenty of bugs in the game, I've had some funny ones with people stuck in the walls etc. Weapon variety is not impressive either. But anyway, the game is decent, and you should try it.
VERDICT: There are some problems, unpolished stuff and bugs in the game, but captivating story, decent soundtrack, "dark atmpsphere" and Reverend Ray, who is a total badass makes this game worthy of your attention. I honestly didn't like it at first, but the more I played, the more interested I was. If you don't like western setting, maybe you won't like it. But if you do, this is a must.
My personal rating for the game is 7.5/10

Dynasty Warriors 8: Empires is not an easy game to defend. Jim Sterling has decried the game as “a contemptuously assembled recycling project”, citing that it does not really offer anything new to non-players of the series, and copies too much from past games in the Dynasty Warriors series, both in normal, and Empires forms. I acknowledge all this. But, I feel that I have to defend this game for the 2017 Steam Awards. And, in order to defend this game, I have to talk about another game.
I am a huge fan of the “Romance of the Three Kingdoms”. The Chinese classical novel, written during the Ming Dynasty, retells a medieval romance set in the waning days of the Han Dynasty, and the resultant three kingdoms that spun from it, until the eventual reunification of China under the banner of the Jin Dynasty. Befitting such a romance, that is, “a medieval tale based on legend, chivalric love and adventure” according to Webster, the novel tells of the exploits of the Kingdoms of Shu Han, Dong Wu and Cao Wei, as their respective leaders fought for the title of Emperor of CHina. The novel has inspired East Asian culture greatly, to the extent that the Japanese have various anime, games, and manga, based off this one novel. Shin Sangokumusou, aka Dynasty Warriors, is one such series, but there are many others. And I shall detail one of them here: Sangoksuhi Taisen. Or, roughly translated, the War of the Three Kingdoms.
Sega’s Sangokushi Taisen was an arcade game. But it was more than that: it was a real-time strategy game. Yes, like Warcraft and Command & Conquer, that kind of RTS. And, to top it all off, it was a card game. The game could only be played on specialized machines at arcades through East Asia: I had the benefit of being able to play the game in Singapore, up until its demise in 2015. Gameplay can be summarized in the following manner: each arcade machine, along with a screen, had a board which simulated the battlefield on the screen. The players cards simulated a general, and with it, the generals respective troops. Each card had distinctive art of a specific genera: Sega hired a lot of artists for this game. As the player moved his card on the board, the machine detected these movements, allowing the player to fight against the opponent, which could be an AI or, as it was a competitive game, various players throughout East Asia. For the decade that the game existed, it was a memorable time: it was one of the more popular draws to what was the dying industry of arcades, and, there was a certain thrill to amassing a card collection after completing a game, and receiving a free card.
But all things do not last. The game came out in 2005, had three versions, lasted for a decade, and, in 2015, ended. Recently, Sega has been attempting to revive the game with Version 4, but, all the art and distinctive style that the first versions had are gone. The first three versions of Sangokushi Taisen ada my favorite design of Sun Shang Xiang, designed by 獅子猿, aka Shishizaru, as well as a very unique take on Cao Cao and the like. The game also featured distinctive designs for as many of the personages of the Three Kingdoms as possible - there was even a card for Sun Jian’s wife, Lady Wu. All gone.
And that is where Dynasty Warriors 8: Empires comes in. Yes, it is a rehash of every other DW game, and Empires game, before it. But it is also the only game of its type on Steam: the other preceding Dynasty Warriors games, and Empires games, are not available. I would consider 7 to have the best story, and, from my understanding, 5 had the best Empires game, but both are not on Steam, nor on PC. While RotK XI is considered to be the best three kingdoms simulation by Koei, that is also not available on Steam and, being an old game, may not optimized for new systems. This leaves us with DW8:E. And what can DW8: E offer? Well there are other games that do wargames better of course: Sega does publish the Total War series by Creative Assembly. One can get a better Hack & Slash game from Nioh, Dark Souls, Fate/Extella or even (and especially)“normal” Dynasty Warriors 8.A nd one can recreate the Three Kingdoms setting in many, any games, as a mod. But thats not why one picks up DW8:E. One picks up DW8:E, because one is already three kingdoms fan, and, wants a game that is tailor-made for this purpose.
And it is with this in mind that the game starts to shine a bit more: the game presents the Three Kingdoms, and its characters, as a playground for the San Guo buff to try out. There is the option to swap out certain officers in the game, with characters the player has created: which means theoretically swap out the DW Lu Bu, for the Lu Bu from the Ravages of Time, Or even the Ikkitousen Ryofu, if one fancies that. For me, I finally have the option to preserve the memory of Sangokushi Taisen by attempting to replicate the unique designs of the three kingdoms personnages in the cards in-game. Of course, it is not for everyone, and the system does have notable flaws: Koei did make this game with console players in mind first, and typing descriptions, and info, for certain characters is a hassle when only a controller can be used to pick letters. But that aside, there is a chance, a chance to relive Sangokushi Taisen in some way, and that is through this game. I still pride on the remaining card collection I have.
I do wish that Sega would bring back classic Sangokushi Taisen, perhaps even expose it to the rest of the world. But for now, reliving a fantasy in DW8;E suffices.

I'm sorry to say this glorified PDF file is of little interest to anyone looking to get a look at the creative process behind Portal 2. In fact, the whole thing feels like an incredibly convoluted internet ad. There is a 'Buy Portal 2' button constantly present on all pages, right next to the permanently visible link to the author's website. One page early on in this document has as many as 7 'Buy on iTunes' icons, as well as the text 'Song previews provided courtesy of iTunes'. After the splash screen, four pages of marketing material for the author, Portal 2 and Valve follows, only then to land on the document contents screen. Sometimes you'll come across videos that are available in the document, but then there are also YouTube links to Valve and Portal related videos. And guess what? not all of them are available anymore - they're set to private viewing only.
Although it's mildly interesting to read about the varied backgrounds of some of the creators, and to get a glimpse at internal Valve projects, there is really nothing you can get out of this thing that you can't get out of the Portal's and Portal 2's excellent commentary modes. I sincerely think that this would have been better off as a free PDF download. But hey, it's only 2 euros, so if you feel like reading an extended internet article at the price of a full magasine, go ahead.
