I was fortunate to not have any technical problems with the game. My review is only related to the gameplay. I love the series and I had very high expectations coming into this release. I'm happy to say that Mankind Divided didn't disappoint. I'll admit that in some ways the devs played it safe here, It's everything you loved about Human Revolution but prettier. You can make an argument for more innovation but I think that's nitpicking. What we got was a refinement of a game which most of us loved. This game is very polished and a satisfying iteration in the franchise. Is it GOTY? I'm not sure, but if you have any interest in the franchise or in stealth action games in general you really can't go wrong with Mankind Divided.

I can see a lot of people leaving a bad review - in essence - because of the business policy of the publisher, ie DLC and microtransactions. This is like panning the Mona Lisa because you think the Louvre tickets cost too much... Another criticism is length but if you explore and do side quests and play non violently, you should get 30 hours of fantastic entertainment.
As a game, if you liked DX:HR chances are you'll love what's going on here. Fantastic level design, multiple paths, great atmosphere. Pacing is a little off as you are left to wander round Prague shops for 5 hours at the start with little in the way of core gameplay. My biggest gripe was that they replaced the excellent transhumanism, have/have nots divide and media manipulation themes of DX:HR with a simple 'racism sux' one. Also too many rat runs lead no-where and some controls are clunky/slow. Other than that, it's a brilliant game.

A few steps forward (gameplay, sidequests), a few steps backwards (main quest/story, performance issues). DX1 is still king.
In-game store is scummy but inconsequential.

Gameplay: An improvement, every issue I had with HR has pretty much been fixed and the game really makes you feel like some badass spy tom cruise mission impossible kinda dude. The new augs are fairly useless besides the remote hacking which is a lifesaver and the tesla which is borderline brokenly overpowered. The controls need some work and I encountered some issues in the last level where menus kept opening while trying to drag bodies around. But overall id give gameplay a really solid 8.5/10
Graphics: the game is really good looking but am I the only one who found the sharpness filter that is on by default to be horribly annoying? 8/10
Acting: average but every time I hear Adam Jensen speak it makes me laugh and I consider it a good thing 7/10
Performance: Ran just fine on my gtx 970, very high present and only had a few framerate drops. 8/10
Story: It just ends. The game builds up 20 hours of sidequests and sideplots and all sorts of conspiracies and it ends with you fighting a augmented tank dude and then saving a few people from drinking posion and then promptly ends. HR had a bad ending as well but at least it was a self contained story and felt like a real ending, this feels like the end of the first chapter. It is blatantly obvious that there was MUCH more to this game at one point but it was cut out so they can pump out sequels in the future. This ruins the game for me and I cannot recomend it because of this. 3/10

I just finished the game for the first time, and I wanted to let everyone know what they are getting into.
Firstly, if you can speand $60 on a game like No Man's Sky, then you should easily and happily spend $60 on this game. Its 60x better than that game.
Graphically, I mean people are complaining about it not running optimally, yes you have to tune the graphic settings a bit, you can't just put in all on ultra. But if you're like me, I like to tune my settings anyways. The results is a beautifully designed world that runs at about 60-70 fps on my R9 390X. Make no mistake this game looks gorgeous.
The World Design is great, when you first open the door of your apartment you are greeted with a world that is alive and buzzing with activity. You can listen in on conversations, read newspaper articles and just break into peoples computers to learn more about the world around you and what exactly happened after Human Revolution. And wait till you get to TF29 Headquarters, it is single handedly the best example of what I'd think an Intelligence Headquarters would look like. I was in awe. Then my eyes glimmered as I realized I'm about to violate all these peoples private property. (By the way I played the game for about 10 hours just exploring and learning about the world, before I did my first Story Mission. Hello Skyrim?"
Secondly, the complaints that the story was short or that it ended suddenly, are those complaints valid? Yes. Does that shortcoming take away from the $60 sales price. Definitely no. To be honest, I didn't have the biggest problem with it. This story is a setup for the finale which is the next game. There are many loose ends, if you want an example, think Metal Gear Solid 5: Phantom Pain. You know how random that story ended? This is kinda like that. But both games are still great games. But at least Deus Ex is going to have a sequel, unlike MGS5. I want to assure you that even tho the story does seem a bit short. It is still a good solid story with setup to our next game. And the replayability will give you many more hours.
Lastly, Replayability. Its in spades. There are so many ways to complete missions and I haven't even finished exploring the city and I've played for like 50 hours. I'm about to go play a non lethal playthrough and use augments and guns I never got to use in my first one. Im, going to finish missions a different way and try not to slaughter every single person that was rude to me on the street. Ahhh, my self restraint is going to be tested.
Anyways, I know this is a really hasty review, I can probably go into much more detail. but thats the gist of it. It's a great game guys. I'm not even going to say whether it's worth the money. This is a must buy and a must play.

If you like the free game "attack of the paper zombies"
you'll love Infested Planet (IP).
I think of IP as a roguelite RTS. You control a small set of soldiers, vie for control points with an AI alien swarm enemy, get awarded resource points, spend then on your soliders, or use them to build base defences or support for your team. If you dont like how youve spent your resource points you can refund them instantly for full value (which means you can try multiple tactics without penalty - I think this is better than what I recall in AOTPZ). As you capture more contorl points and push back the aliens the remaining ones get random upgrades which dynamically makes them harder to fight, meaning you might need ot change your (previously) winning tactics - its a great mechanic.
Its expertly put together, featuring a campaign (with fixed maps) and two different types of randomly generated skirmishes with varying difficulty.  Controls, graphics, animations, etc are all great.
My only criticism is the wording of the "single mission use" unlocks - these actually appear to unlock a "single upgrade" for use on any mission - making them much more valable than what I understood them to be (I thought it was use it and then lose it). As it was, I played through the game without them, which was much harder than it would have been with them.

Think of this as a simpler version of Starcraft, minus the Protoss. There's no versus mode, but the game captures well the feeling of fighting thousands of alien creatures with just a small team of marines, akin to Starship Troopers.
Getting through the campaign is easy enough, but the game lives on it's randomly generated maps, which provide the bulk of the replayability. It's up to you whether you want to dump a lot of time into this game. At $15, the average person will get at least 20 hours out of the experience, which is a decent value. I myself got tired of it at the 30 hour mark.
Overall, the game has high replayability but doesn't possess a lot of depth. It is genuinely fun though, like taking your favorite game from the arcade home with you until you get sick of Pac-Man and stop playing.

I've been playing this game since a very early beta and have watched it change and become the glorious game it is today. Everytime I play I get a new mix of mutations and have to change my strategy on the fly. Love the feeling when a hive is taken down and I start to make some headway.
Lot's of strategic planning is required and each new situation throws up tons of options. The latest patches have introduced weekly challenge maps with three levels of difficulty so we can all compete on a global leaderboard.
It would be cool if we could share maps from the skirmish mode with other players and compare scores, maybe a feature for the future.
All I can say is if you like strategy and rts games that give you time to think and don't rely on twitch reflexes give the game a go I'm sure you'll have a blast and find a new gaming addiction.

Due to Steams refund policy, my time in game has been short. But, after nearly an hour of gameplay, I feel very confident stating what I found were immediately obvious pluses and minuses.
Plus:
Its Warhammer. If you're a huge fan of the Warhammer Genre I'd pick the game up and just give it a test run for an hour. You'll know long before you're in danger of passing the critical 2 hour mark for a refund whether or not the game is for you. (in my case being a big fan didn't help at all)
Minuses:
The Camera Angle is worse than poor, and unlike other Warhammer 40K games, swiveling and panning the camera does nothing to help.
Even after 25 minutes, I was struck by how repetitive and boring the gameplay was. You literally crawl half your alotted AP steps each turn, just to ensure "Overwatch" is available each turn. Cover an angle, shoot interlopers, rinse, repeat.
ZZZZZzzzzzzzzz. I pushed forward for another 25-30 minutes past this point just to try and be fair. But it was a struggle.
Leveling your Marines is super, super, anti-climatic. I mean, who cared? I didn't. (And the benefits upon leveling were so mundane, and with no obvious in match effect)
Graphics, are very standard and not impressive at all. I have a high end gaming rig that runs titles like Metal Gear: TTP, Witch Hunter, H1Z1, Heroes & Generals, Dying Light, and every other demanding title without a hiccup. So the blah pixels were all the games fault.
I feel bad writing such a negative review, as I am a big fan of the Warhammer 40K, and warhammer gaming pantheon.
This title, just wasn't worth the time or money to me. (MAybe you'd feel differently)
In fact, writing this review was more rewarding than the 50 plus minutes I spent in game.
So, Be like Manning, and Pass!!!

The game has fine art assets but seriously lacks in features. This was a mobile game and it shows. The fact that this costs over 20€ is absurd. Only get this if you're a die hard 40k fan boy/girl. It's really a shame because this game has a good vibe. The devs clearly know their lore and are enthusiastic about the universe. If only this was made with a bigger team and a bigger budget.
The Good:
- Nice art. The planets look and feel different. The space marines look bad♥♥♥♥♥
- Functional turn-based combat. It's really basic, but works fine.
- All weapon classes are significantly different and have synergies with individual space marines.
- The chapters look and feel different. Sometimes they even banther with each other during a mission. You get different results depending who you have with you. Rank also matters.
The Bad:
- XP system is flawed. You can basically farm experience on many maps. Enemies spawn endlesly and can be killed before they do any damage. Without farming, progress is really slow. Also Marines come in 4 ranks. Higher ranked marines are just plain better than your lower ones. But you need to level them up from the beginning if you want them to shine. This pretty much mean you need to grind xp if you want to upgrade your squad. You get 1 random marine in a card pack. More on this subject on the looting topic below.
- No sound options. DansGame
- Game breaking bugs on launch.
- Loot system is really bad. This was originally a mobile game with microtransactions. You bought packs that gave loot with real money. This game has those packs as well, but you get them by completing a set of missions. The packs and mission rewards are random so you can get the same♥♥♥♥♥♥over and over. That means you have to grind if you want the good stuff. You can also buy those packs with an in-game currency, but the economy for that is horrible as well.
- Animations are really slow and cannot be skipped. This applies to cut-scenes as well. Enemy animations can be made to go faster, but your's can't. This will get frustrating later in the game.

pick a character whose a free officer (or betray your characters current lord) build up your forces, recruit plenty of officers (your going to need them) and raise your flag! if you succeed in taking the territory you rose up in, your faction is established, you can issue commands, assign different ranks to your officers (prefects (essentially dukes or barrons) first marshal, no idea what they do haha, and strategist, again no idea what that does) but that can be kinda hard to do, so if you want, you can join one of the existing factions if your not a member already, do good and you will rise through the ranks and become a prefect yourself, and your lord gives you your own province to manage, do even better and you can become his strategist (im saying his, as all the leaders are male realy) or first marshal, giving you more power then before (like being able to organise attacking provinces yourself) have fun out there! oh and two things, your going to find the keyboard controls a little bit.....weird, like really weird, its WASD to move, but JKLI to move the camera and GH to attack.....yeah and you cant command your forces with "defend" or "attack" orders during battle and it may be a little hard to figure out how to activate the card abilities. so maybe bring a controller if you have one, i personally have a ps3 controller, its very comfortable and easy to control the game with

Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons is a very linear, story based game. it follows the journey of two young brothers on a quest to save their father. With little to know intro to the game, you're thrown right into it with just the briefest of tutorials.
Your father has fallen ill to an unknown virus, and the only thing that can save him is water from an ancient tree (a slight cliche but I can over look it). The doctor who is taking care of your father sends you away to find the water, and there your journey begins.
You must journey through woods, mines, castles, battlefields, and icey waters. This quest takes you through all of these different environments but at the same time makes it all flow seemlessly and beautifuly. The animation and artwork in this game makes it by far one of my favorite games to date. With a cutesy (but just realistic enough) design style, this game comes across just realistic enough to keep you immersed, even with the fantasy involved.

$0 - stand alone mod
I'm a huge fan of Source powered titles — even more so of mods going "pro". Transmissions: Element 120 is yet another title like that of Black Mesa (without the cost).
I've played most of the Source Engine Mods out there, and this title is certainly one of the best, if not the best of them all. Still using the older Orange Box engine (in reality it's the 2013 build of it), the game plays almost the same as any of the HL2 games do.
This title certainly isn't just a rebrand of the same game with new maps. It comes with new maps for sure, but with new game mechanics, this title shows off its very well done level design without relying on just what Valve came up with.
For sure I was stuck a few times, but that really goes to show that it has Valve's philosophies embedded into the title.
If the game was about four times as long in length, I would have certainly dropped $5-$10 dollars on it. Whether or not this title will be expanded is up in the air, but I would certainly look forward to seeing more of the same good solid level design and game mechanics.

There isn't a particular storyline tied to this mod, though there is some background information regarding the events that occured in the places the player goes through.

Please note: I am playing this game with an Xbox One controller, which is what I *highly* recommend you do as well.
This iteration of Deus Ex is no buggier than Skyrim was (after a couple weeks of patches I'd even say it's significantly less buggy than Skyrim was), and people still enjoyed the hell out of Skyrim. Save early, save often, use simple troubleshooting to get past the crash or two that you might run into. God forbid you lose ten minutes of progress. Past that, the issues have not been showstoppers for me.
I am truly enjoying the game overall. I expected it to be a stealthy/hacky RPG shooter, and that's exactly what I am getting out of it. Is Jensen the most dynamic character in all of video game history? Absolutely not. Still doesn't ruin it for me. I just pretend he is being played by Keanu Reeves with a cold.
Breaking into servers and the other stealthy aspects of the game are right up my alley. I typically try to avoid conflict at all cost during the game, and it almost always pays off by opening up new ways to fulfill the objective. There's also a very tense air to the game, and you never know when someone is going to get in your face or start shooting.
And the graphics.... oh, the graphics. So beautiful. I can't help but take screenshots of certain areas/missions, and Prague has a completely different personality at nighttime than it does during the day. I turned off MSAA and played with a few settings, had to turn a couple things down a bit, but the results are smooth and immersive. Face models aren't the best in the world, but you can tell a *lot* of love went into designing all of the outfits, weapons, storefronts, buildings, etc.
I would recommend this game. 8.5/10
This game is fantastic. I feel compelled to explore everything and do not want to put it down.

I know there's the whole upset regarding the in game store with one time use only single player mode items and I fully understand those gripes. Personally I disagree with that tactic as well however besides that the game itself has thus far proven to be excellent imo.
I'm playing it with everything on high save for the fact that MXAA is off and Anisotrophic Filtering kept to a minimum. It runs between 50-60 fps for me on average.
What I admire most about the game however is its sheer attention to detail. Prague is loaded with things to see, explore and discover. From notes to newspapers to emails and other sights everything feels densely packed but not too overwhelming. Places feel like they're actually lived in with clutter and items strewn about in a believable way. Random adventures in any apartment room will yield a different 'personality' that clicks with that of its occupant if you read their emails. Some are unkept, others are neat but have items scattered here and there to make it clear someone lives a busy life there. They're filled with random notes, graffitti, writing and stuff that just sucks you into the game's world.
The music as well also sets the mood with its gritty futuristic feel.
That said, if you liked Human Revolution the gameplay in this one has been improved whether you choose to sneak, go in with combat or something in between.
I recommend a buy.

Micro transactions have a bad stigma and this game sure does not help. We all know the storys, but unlike other micro transactions you CAN play the game without it and you CAN shrug it off like I did and accept that Eidos Montreal made an amazing game, but Square Enix ♥♥♥♥ed it up.
Really great game, fantastically made (in some aspects,) but the game-breaking save bug left me a little salty.

Built by Warren Spector and Ion Storm, Deus Ex was 2000’s most innovative and award-winning documentary. Its augmented vision of a dystopian corporate future rife with civil disorder and terror attacks and people wearing sunglasses at night has proven prescient. Taking on the trenchcoat of J.C. Denton, a bionic anti-terrorism agent, players found themselves at the clockwork heart of a global conspiracy, making decisions from how to bypass a locked door to deciding the course of civilization. Now, sixteen years after it redefined the RPG, critics are divided. Does the latest entry in the Deus Ex series smash the state of mediocre modern games, or is it A BOMB?
Mankind Divided is the direct sequel to 2011’s Deus Ex: Human Revolution. The story takes place two years after the events of Human Revolution but offers a twelve-minute video recap for those who didn’t play the previous title. Players reprise the role of Adam Jensen, the quadriplegic cop who doesn’t play by the rules and never asked for this, armed with an array of cybernetic enhancements called augmentations that replaced his limbs after a workplace accident.
The gameplay draws heavy inspiration from Crysis, Metal Gear Solid, and Splinter Cell. It supports lethal and nonlethal playstyles. You can be a ghost, blinking from cover to cover as you taze unassuming police officers or you can reinforce your chassis with additional armor, mod your weapon of choice, and be a lone gunman. Additionally, there is a skill tree that allows players to choose between augs like faster hacking, the ability to punch through walls, heat vision, Watch Dogs-style remote hacking, more batteries, and improved social skills to help you talk to grils. There is also a crafting system that allows you to further customize your gear. All of these playstyles are mostly balanced, though a fully-upgraded cloaking system can trivialize some of the game’s infiltration missions. Thankfully Eidos Montreal mostly eliminated boss fights so it’s possible to complete the game regardless of your stats.
Mankind Divided’s writing is competent but uninspired. It creates a compelling setting, vivid characters, and parallels to real events; however, for the most part, it fails to capitalize on them. On the other hand, Mankind Divided sets up some electrifying connections to the original that I won’t spoil here. The masterful world-building makes the adequate plot look dull in comparison. Still, aside from an abrupt, though enjoyable, third act, the story kept me invested for the 25 hours I spent playing the main game, side content, and the Desperate Measures mission that suits obviously cut out for DLC.
Speaking of DLC, there are microtransactions that allow players to purchase PRAXIS upgrade kits and credits in addition to single-use preorder bonuses. People who are cyber-punked into purchasing these are just sabotaging the delicate balance that Eidos Montreal worked so hard to create. You can almost see the cigar-smoke billowing through the boardroom meeting where the publisher held the devs at gunpoint and forced them to program an in-game shop. What a shame.
I never once noticed or cared about these microtransactions. Simply exploring Prague, sadly the game’s only hub, and completing side missions will give you more credits than you can spend and enough upgrade points to achieve about 70% of the upgrades, the rest saved for a subsequent playthrough or New Game Plus. Reviewers are right to chastise this idiotic monetization scheme, but technically the fault lies with the publishers, not the developers, and I am choosing to review the game, not the lemonade stand that Square Enix built outside.
Speaking of technical problems, I experienced about four crashes and one game-breaking cutscene bug in my 25 hours. To be safe, you will need redundant saves. I did not have any performance issues aside from the melee system leaving corpses clipping through desk chairs and stuck through walls. Speaking of melee, the takedown and cover buttons are the same, and pressing spacebar to continue after a loading screen makes you jump and alerts guards to your presence. Those control issues are stupid but might be mitigated by using a controller. Also, the lip syncing is abysmal, but I’m choosing to believe that it was purposely evoking nostalgia for the first game.
Graphically, the game is stunning. Like Human Revolution, the art design is unparalleled. From anti-aug propaganda posters in the red light district to neuropozyne addicts huddling in the slums of Golem City, not even the rebreather augmentation will save you from Mankind Divided’s atmosphere. One of the best moments in the game is a scene where Adam walks through an abandoned train station and stares at his augmented arm. Everything feels real.
The gorgeous visuals combined with Michael McCann’s soundtrack and solid voice performances by Elias Toufexis and the rest of the cast make this one of the most immersive games ever. The secret is that Deus Ex games were never really about choice. That’s why the sequels never took your previous actions into account. Nobody cares if you entered 0451 in the keypad, walked through the air vent, or took the stairs. Decisions rarely had a real effect on the plot aside from some flavor text. It was about immersion, the suspension of disbelief. The graphics, the sound design, the writing all welded together to make you, the player, believe you were a cybernetically enhanced super-soldier whose choices could change the course of human history. That’s why the games worked. That’s why Deus Ex is the best series of all time.
I give Deus Ex: Mankind Divided a 9 out of 10.

A fun game with infinite replayability.
Each map is randomly generated (with the exception of the campaign missions) with a starting point for your marines and however many alien hives you need to stomp into muck. As you go through a mission you need to decide how to invest your resources on the fly. You can upgrade your soldiers with different weapon classes such as flame throwers, shotguns, snipers, or a towable med station; or you build structures that enhance your soldiers with regenerating health and grenades for crowd control (which do come in handy). Another way is to leapfrog with self-building siege cannons and turrets, great for decimating hives that are close together.
It is important to plan how you want to tackle each map. After defeating a hive, the aliens will mutate and gain an upgrade of their own. This may range from a spore minefield to acid howitzers to heavily armoured defenders coming at you in droves.
Outside of the campaign (where you purchase upgrades between missions,) the custom mission options are pretty thorough. You can pick what kind of map, how many resources you start with, the number of hives and their potential, and more. This is great for testing out different strategies or throwing difficulty to the wind and crushing the enemy under your cannonfire and airstrikes.

What a ride it's been! After 101 hours, I've gotten all 61 achievements. I'm sure it could be done faster, but I decided to do everything in the game that didn't even include achievements simply because I liked it so much!
Kingdoms of Amalur is a open(ish) world, 3rd person roleplaying game where you play as a fateless hero who has resurrected from the dead with the help from a gnomish invention called the well of souls. You are quickly thrown into the action and for the most of the game, you try to figure out who you were before you died while also helping in the war against the armies of the fae king Gadflow.
I will be making some comparisons to the game Skyrim in this review, as they are very similar games. And since Skyrim is such a well known game, most people reading this will have an idea what i'm talking about.
+PROS+
+The absolute biggest compliment to this game is the combat. It's extremely smooth and responsive. It is in my opinion the strong foundation of the game. It does however have one flaw that I will mention in the CONS section.
+ While having lockpicking that's the exact same as in Skyrim, they also have the addition of dispelling. Which is a small minigame where you need to click at the correct time on runes while you are on a timer. This is far more difficult and dangerous than a lock. If you fail to dispell an item, it will explode and either curse you or deal alot of damage to you.
+ Every zone has lorestones. Lorestones are blue stones who tell a small story when you interact with them. They can be rhymes, stories of the zone, some lore about the world or information about people. If you find and interact with all the lorestones in an area, you get a permanent buff. Like extra health, mana, goldfind etc.
+ The three skilltrees you can choose from are rogue, warrior and mage. But you can also split your skill points into several trees. And for a small fee, you can reset your skillpoints to go a completely different route if you want to switch it up.
+ The game looks very beautiful visually.
+ Some really awesome cinematics.
+ You can earn several properties who has a shared storage box.
+ Many cutscenes where your character is present. Making it feel like you are actually part of the big story.
+ The music in this game is great, but there aren't that many tracks.
+ All quests are voicelined.
+ Several factions you can ally yourself with and do quite long questchains for.
+ Interesting story with equally interesting characters.
+ TONS of sidequests which will send you all over the world.
+ Cheap DLCs although in my opinion, only one of them is good.
+ Many different enemies who you should approach differently.
-CONS-
- As mentioned, the combat in the game has one giant flaw. Stagger.
See, when you attack an enemy, you set up an attack chain. The last attack of your attack chain will stagger the enemy, meaning it will get stunned, knocked down or disoriented for a few seconds. While they are staggered, you are free to keep attacking them without them being able to do anything in return, and your new stagger attack will hit them before they break out of their original stagger. This means the enemy can be permanently stunned while you hammer away at it.
This goes both ways though. Whenever you take damage, be it from a spell or sword, your spellcasting will be interupted and you will take half a second to recover. This may not sound like much, but if you are fighting 4-5 enemies and they attack you at different times, it might result in you being stunned the whole fight. I mostly found this as an issue on hard difficulty though.
- The carryweight system. If you are anything like me who likes to pick up anything you see, you are gonna hate this.
In Skyrim, you have a set amounts of weight you can carry, and items are weighted accordingly, like a piece of paper will be weightless, a bearhide will weigh 2 and a greatsword will weigh maybe 18. In Kingdoms of amalur however,  everything weighs the same, and you have an item cap instead. You can purchase bagspace in every major city, up to a total of 120.
- Some quests doesn't make sense at all. As an example, person A wanted me to kill person B. I went to person B and he told me that if I went back and killed person A instead, he would double my payment. Being a rogue, I figured I'd take him up on his offer and then stab him in the back as soon as he turned around. So I accepted, waited for him to turn around, backstabbed and killed him. The quest was then counted as FAILED. I went back to person A, but he had nothing to say to me anymore. So the questing system can be a bit black and white, and not very flexible.
- The world itself is very instanced. It is PACKED with invisible walls around edges and your character cannot jump. So it doesn't feel very smooth when you move around in the world.
- There were a few bugs with the music sometimes. Especially in the city Mel Senshir.
- The further you get in the game, there are less and less sidequests and interesting things in the world.
- The only DLC worth purchasing is Teeth of Naros. The others are empty and bad in my opinion.
The game is made by 38 Studios and Big Huge Games. Sadly, this was the only game 38 Studios created before they went bankrupt, so there will never be a sequel.
If you like RPGs like Skyrim, then give this game a chance. If my CONS has made you doubt the game, get it on sale. It usually has a 75% discount during summer and winter sales. Although it has problems, it's an extremely solid game.

This game was suprisingly deep. I'm not ashamed to admit that I had very low expectations of this game when I first read its description. I have been very pleasently suprised. The central plot was a little hard to understand, but once I finished a couple of ending it became alot more clear. The graphics were nice if a little outdated by today's standards, although I felt this helped the overall feel of the novel. The music was okay but I found it to be a bit repetative at times and it didn't always help better the atmosphere of the story. The only real complaint I have might come from me being inexpirienced with visual novels, but I didn't appreciate having to complete every other ending to open the final ending's option, which to do you had to go back to the first story choice to follow up the tree. In all honesty this is a rather small nitpick but for some reason it bothered me that I had to go back to find this route. I understand that the way its setup requires you to go back so as to not upset the true ending of the story, though it bothers me.
TL;DR Trick and Treat has a decent plot, good but somewhat dated art style, and music that becomes somewhat repetative but is still enjoyable to a point.
Final score: 8/10

I personally would like to start off that I'm a big fan of Rwby and with all honesty I did enjoy the game. However, there is some things I'm really concerned and annoyed about this game. Rwby: Grimm Eclipse is basically a hack and slash game where you can play with others and achieve certain goals. However, as I spent some good amount of time in this game. The game lacks in many aspect of a way that can entertain gamers like us. The story line is interesting but as the game progresses it becomes really repetitive and the grinding just to get ranks in the game is absolute madness. The game is boring after a while but it can still be amusing when playing with friends. However, I'm really hoping the creators are still making progress of ways how they can improve the game. If not then I'm really disappointed that they called this as a final product. So would I recmmend this game? Yes if your a huge fan of Rwby, but sadly I would not recommend this game. If the creators decides to respect gamers wishes and develops more on the game then I would reconsider of recommending this game. Yet, as of now I'm sorry to say its disappointing.
Honestly, the game is liked just because it's RWBY. It's simple at best and doesn't have that much to offer but I didn't regret getting it.

So, I personally like this game even with all the hate its getting and its understandable. The campaign is relatively short with difficulty only really arising in the final boss fight where the mutant deathstalker can one shot you if you aren't careful and if you ramp the difficulty up pretty high. It's a pretty decent story as long as you know the characters. I would not recommend this game if you if you have just stumbled upon this game without prior knowledge of the show. Its fairly incomplete but I would definitely recommend getting the dlc for the 5 extra bucks. Its just a small increase but definitely makes the game more enjoyable due to the dlc characters being more fluid than the original 4. When it comes to controls, the game is much easier with a controller due to being able to combo easier. It makes it easier to use to few frames to counter enemy attacks which is basically the only way to survive when being swarmed. There are some exploits I've been able to use in the system such as constantly countering as Blake when there are a horde of beowolves in order to just evade all damage. Its a pretty mediocre game for fans with pretty good multiplayer if you have friends (which you don't) but it probably should be priced lower even with more progress being made on the game. I feel the price point is a little high but it's worth it for some pretty decent fun for fans of the franchise.

I had high hopes for this game (like most of the people in this reviews section) and i have to agree the game really hasnt added much at all that would warrant such a high price.
In short, save for the amount of beautiful maps the game has to offer, this game feels more like a flash game you could find on Newgrounds. Four characters with a limited variety of attacks that have gone almost untouched since the earlier stages before release, barely any combat depth, not much enemy variation and a short campaign - I feel like this sentence can be used to describe a handful of Newgrounds flash games.
I personally have no problem with paid DLC but when the base game is lacking this much and is priced that high for what it offers, this really seems like - and I rarely use terms like this - cash grab.
I'd only recommend this game if you have plenty of friends that are die hard RWBY fans ready to play the sort of repetitive content over and over again whilst cycling through the same four base game characters that don't reflect what the About section defines as "intense combat action".
As a final note, I bought this game back when the price was much lower and I still feel I wasted my money sadly. Anyway cheers for Volume 4.

Where on earth do I begin with this one. Right. Okay, what is it? It's not a traditional strategy game in the usual senses of the word. It's not an RTS in so much as that the forces are hideously asymetric, and it's not Turn Based either. I would call this a "Swarm control" game, where the concept is that you have a small number of deployable troops, as well as static defences, and from this you have to construct a working strategy that funnels a much larger force into killzones and crossfires.
Combat works on scales that you don't generally get to think about in such games, your 4-7 little poxy marines will end up riddling thousands, yes, thousands of enemy aliens with holes over the space of one mission, and quickly you stop viewing the enemy as a mass of individuals, but as mentioned - a swarm, one to be controlled, funnelled, and pushed back.
When you finally "click" with the concept, and you start figuring out how to approach the swarms and manage them, the game suddenly starts falling into place, systems and mechanics which were until then entirely unmanagable become second nature and intuitive, and you quickly fall into the habit of securing outposts, setting up turret crossfires, assessing where you can do the most damage, how to maximise your soldiers efficiency. You stop thinking in individual terms and if anything, approach the mission almost in a "grand strategy" way of things. That's the beauty of infested planet.
Graphics and sound are decent, it's an indie effort, and the graphics achieve what they set out to do (you won't get confused and lose track of what's going on, be thankful), ditto for the sound, the plot too, again, servicable, but the gameplay clicks, it takes a while to get over the learning curve, because the game is so radically different from what most people will be used to, but the investment eventually does pay off. The experience is very much unlike anything else around, and is definitely worth checking out if you fancy a change of pace from normal RTS experiences.

The overall story is pretty simple. It's your basic FPS with a variety of weapons killing the same guards over and over as you try to escape Mars from the oppressive mining organization Ultor. Later, you realize Ultor has been experimenting on the miners for some undisclosed reason. Must be a new evil pasttime. As soon as you dispatch the evil cyborg scientist, who evidently is also a magic user somehow, you continue your quest. However, then you have mercenaries drop in on you, along with their ruthless commander, who ALSO has unexplained magic powers.
Graphics seem like they belong in the old Quake games, characters forgetable, and the voice acting is laughable. Gameplay is as simple as it gets; go from point A to point B while shooting down anyone and anything within sight. I do applaud the little bits that break the linear paths. Every so often, there's an alternate path in which you can traverse, and end up completely skipping a wave of enemies you'd normally face if you went the obvious route.
The biggest problem I had was the enemy AI. At the beginning, the evil guards are laughable, the way they seem to dance all over the place and shout at you in a very cartoonish manner. "Miner scum!" "Where do you think YOU'RE going, miner trash?". For those who enjoy sneaking behind a group of enemies and catching them unawares will be repeatedly disappointed, as the enemy seems to have eyes in the back of their head. And as soon as ONE guard notices you, everyone and their mother unloades on you. It gets even more difficult in the second half of the game when the guards take many more shots (and multiple headshots) to kill, and your still as weak as ever. These armored up baddies also can blast you with one-shot killing rail guns, which they tend to fire just as soon as you pass around the corner. Sometimes, they don't even have to see you; their rail gun shots go through walls. Many rage moments were had.
This game has so many glitches in it that I could go on and on about all of which that I've encountered...but I think you get the overall message.
Don't. Just don't.

I enjoyed the game overall but certain story elements are very irritating.
I liked the previous game, Deus Ex: HR enough to play through 3 times so I was really looking forward to this one. The beginning was fantastic. You jump right in with all your augs active so it feels like the last game segwayed right into this one. My immediate fear was that game developers are created in read-only mode, in that they follow game design formulas like zombies so I knew I should enjoy that first chapter while it lasted because those pre-activated augs were going to go bye-bye very quickly. I was right.
So the formula is that you activate augmentations as you gain XP. Not unexpected but it was still a bummer. My first complaint of the game is that Praxis kits come way too slowly. The fun of the game is using cool abilities. Gaining the abilities is a means to an end but the developers emphasized that aspect way too much. When I got to the end of the game, it was a total surprise because I hadn't activated most of the new augs.
The surprise had to do with mission management. I know it had to be a really difficult job, setting up the mission flow but sometimes side missions just expire without warning. I see no reason for that. Why cancel a side mission when you travel? No police detective ever comes home from vacation to find all his cases have been "canceled." It's ridiculous.
GAME UI HAS BIG PROBLEMS:
This is a definite problem in implementation. I saw someone suggest that they introduced bugs in PC play by placing more emphasis on console play. This may or may not be true but one thing for sure, the game UI sucks. You open some containers and extract items by pressing "E" and other containers you can press "E" until your finger falls off and you will get NOTHING because THIS particular container says to press "Enter" for some strange reason. From start to finish, this is something I COULD NOT GET USED TO.
Also when you make some changes like switching key bindings with "B" or "V" it will freeze action until your selection is made. Other adjustments happen while the game is live so you be getting shot by someone while hacking for example. Keeping the game world live while hacking is realistic but what's not is when you need to break off, some actions you can break with the Escape key "Esc," some you break off with "X" or by clicking "disconnect" or "Exit" on-screen. There should be ONE KEY that breaks off ANY activity. Sometimes I'm getting shot and pressing ESC brings up the menu to Save/Load game and when you press Esc to leave that screen then you're getting shot again. That's terrible.
Also sometimes you can jump high enough to reach the 2nd floor walkway of a building and then if you walk a few feet the opposite direction you can only jump half as high as before. Some ledges you can jump onto and others you plunge to your death. For example you start the game with Icarus Landing activated so you can jump down 10 stories to attack someone on the ground. Then the next chapter that power is taken away so MY FIRST TOTALLY IDIOTIC DEATH was falling into a sewer because I missed the ladder. A bit ridiculous to jump down 10 stories then a few minutes later to die by missing a ladder and falling 10 feet.
Conclusion:
I wish they accomodated more gameplay styles. I don't like bosses that are impossible to beat without hiding. Sure make the game challenging but Jensen's augs are supposed to be "military grade" but he can't activate them for long at all. Enemies can stay cloaked forever and use armor augmentations a lot longer than Jensen. This story element is so inconsistent with the world design that it detracts from the story-telling because it's a constant irritant. A really clever coder should be able to think of a way to make a game challenging without letting the bad guys cheat constantly. Like Call of Duty which has very realistic mission-ends without impossible-to-kill bosses. It's much more creative and proves that a big guy who takes a million hits is not the only way to end a game.

Long term fan of the series perspective:
I would say this is a marked improvement over Human Revolution, however some sacrifices do seem to have been made.  Three steps forward, one step back.
In terms of the gameplay, there are some significant improvements from HR, for example: You now get exp for opening things with the codes, not as much as hacking it, and no hacking bonuses, but it does feel more balanced.  I think the augs are better, in general here as well.
I didn't spend a lot of time with the new augs, but the Tesla aug which lets you stun 4 enemies at once was extremely useful.  Remote hacking is kind of meh, but does add a new wrinkle to stealth sections, and open up a few new paths.
Graphics are good, framerate held steady for me, a balmy 40-50 on my 970 at 2560 * 1440.  A far cry from pushing my 144hz monitor, but it's playable, and upon a new GPU upgrade, I'm sure it will be even better.
I experienced a few crashes, the only truly frustrating one was in the intro sequence, causing me to have to replay the whole last section of the dubai mission, this has been patched already however.  I expect stability to improve.  That said, save often.
Some have criticized the main story here, I actually disagree with that assessment, the main story here felt stronger than Human Revolution's.  There's a lot more of interest here, and you can really start to see the plot threads that lead to the world of DX1.  You can tell a lot of time was spent on the side quest design, some of them are somewhat annoying in making you shlep to the other end of prague, but by and large they are a new high watermark in quest design, almost reaching the heights of the witcher 3.
Perhaps most interestingly is the social narrative weaved into the story.  I think this is as close as many people will get to experiencing life as a disadvantaged class or minority.  Some say it was handeled too heavy handedly here, I disagree.  I think after so many games like bioshock infinite which pretend to say something but ultimately say nothing, by contrast, the social commentary here feels fresh and substantive.  Gaming hasn't seen many high profile games willing to take on this issue.
The bizzare choice for the single save purchase DLC stuff is admittedly pretty terrible, but it seems to be by and large an idiot trap, you in no way need any of it to succeed and excel in the game.  Doesn't justify its existence, but it doesn't materially detract from the game.
I have not experimented with breach or the provided 'jensen's story' yet, but I am hopeful there will be significant post-release content, hopefully story related content.  There is roughly 30 hours of content if you make a point to complete all side quests, and do not skip dialogue excessivly.
Overall, for fans of the series, I would rate this a must buy, even at $60.
For those unfamiliar with the series, or less into it, I would rate the game at a $35-40 price point, which I'm sure will happen at some point before the end of 2016.

TBS Warhammer 40K period. it`s a mobile port, but a rather good one at that; Unreal 4 not only generates alot of nice visuals when it comes to enviroments, but more importantly the Marines look detailed and polished...just like their minature counterparts; that said since it`s a mobile port the game runs on pretty much anything.
i haven`t encountered any bug whatsover, some people do report 1 particular bug concerning the ai`s turn-end;
the turnbased strategy component of the game is very(!) solid: special abilities, overwatch, lots of different playing weapons and marines are all around; missions vary from defense tasks to search`n destroy and escape-scenarios (there`s a total of 40missions currently in the game, with 3 difficulties).
but the meat of the game is the collectors aspect:
each Marine, each type of gear, weapons, etc. is represented as a card; you gain 1 card after each mission, a booster-pack (3 cards) after each chapter-end and you can buy a booster via some ingame currency (you can also sell cards to earn said currency aswell).
marine`s earn exp, which let`s you upgrade their base stats (accuracity, health, crit) and unlock new passive or active abilities (aswell as utility-item-slots), each Space Marine Chapter, type and rank provides different stats, skills, etc. and as such the game is very motivating; collect em all and level/gear em all.
items vary in quality aswell and come in tiers, each tier providing new boni and better stats;
since you can always replay every campaign mission (in whatever difficulty you want after you beat the campaign once)
grinding and collecting is very comfortable.
the story is pretty much nonexisting..or a side show; you will get voiced mission-instructions and your marines sometimes start typical Warhammer 40K esque conversation; the core of the game is collecting and ofcourse the battles themselves.
it`s a very enjoyable little game, offers quite some good feelings for 40K fans and is a rather good mobile port.
hopefuly it will get expanded on, adons, or a sequel; the potential this game shows screams for more 40K TBS content ;)

I was so torn between giving this game a thumbs up or not. But in the end, I have to say no, because of the lack of a cohesive story. Although, I must say its 90% price is worth buying just for the incredible artwork. Full price: sorry, no.
Unlike what the store page says, you do
need a controller to play, but I would recommend it to facilitate the use of cranks and the “interact” button paired with movement that are used throughout the game.
Using the controls is, at first, clunky and awkward, as you move two characters sometimes simultaneously (Big Brother becomes your left hand and Little your right). I never got completely used to it, as the camera angles like to switch at undesired times, throwing off the directions.
This control system of a “single player co-op” isn’t common, but also not entirely unique. I was reminded of an old flash game I played called “Fireboy and Watergirl” that required you to control one character with the WASD keys and the other with the arrow keys to solve cooperative puzzles. Or other games like “Trine” or “Goodbye Deponia,” where you have three characters you must switch between to solve puzzles. (Granted these two are not direct comparisons.) I cannot ding a game for having the same controls, as another game (that would be ridiculous), it’s simply a small point I wanted to make.
Brothers has three main elements: Atmosphere, story, and (simple) puzzles that drive the game. First, I’ll address the puzzles.
As you would think, each brother has their own set of traits. Big Brother is stronger and taller and Little Brother is nimbler and, well, shorter. These traits are exploited on elements that could be counted with one hand. (You see a fence, use Little Brother. See a tall ledge: use Big Brother to boost Little Brother.) Use these simple rules to pull lever A to get to lever B. Meh.
Alright, so Brothers is not for puzzle aficionados, and just gives the player some much needed time in the lovely landscape. Let’s move onto the story.
The story is incredibly linear and offers no playback value. Leaving players with roughly three hours of content. I think I can sum this sub section up in one sentence: potential wasted.
Why is this? Let me start by saying that perhaps I’m so hard on the story aspect because I wanted so badly for
to enhance and back up the beautiful artwork.
The story was strung together by good
, but no good transitions. I felt like I was playing a truncated, bulleted
of an epic journey: being jerked around from point to point with little to no context of why. I repeatedly had “Wait what?” moments as new elements such as trolls, giants, and gryphons were introduced and I was just supposed to lay down and take it as commonplace that these creatures were bound to appear and react as they did.
I found myself asking over and over, where’s the
? I want the
. There’s no context to the story. (Aside from the flimsy, dad’s dying we need to go help him.) Without the background, I absolutely could not make myself invested in the story, no matter how hard I tried. (Believe me, I wanted to.)
Where’s my
? Where’s the scenes to tell us why we’re going on a perilous journey to save dear ol’ dad? Or why the brothers have such a strong bond? (Aside from the common knowledge brothers do)
Where’s my
? The game gives us wonderful scenes that have so much
to tell us another story within this story. To give us the
behind the creatures we meet. To tell us the
of how the events we stumble upon came to be.
I would’ve been happy with just a few pictures as cut scenes at least trying to explain the scenery. All of this would only serve to enhance the amazing locations the game places us in. For a story-driven game, the lack of context and cohesion is unacceptable.
When I ended the game, all I could say was “What a cop out.” When such a tragic ending as this happens, I want to see a
behind it. Does it further the story? Does it add to character development? Etc.
I saw no purpose but to rip out our hearts and saw aggressively at the strings with no subtly or nuance. And it didn’t even do that, because I wasn’t
in the characters, all because the lack of character development and background I had previously stated. I hate to sound heartless, but this tragic twist ending of a trump card didn’t do anything for me.
The end also falls into that Lord of the Rings question of “Why didn’t they just fly there in the first place, god damn it?!” It felt like a hasty wrap up that tried to sew all of the locations together with a “travel home” montage, which could have been used to, perhaps, flesh out Little Brother’s character or something more constructive.
Finally, we come to the atmosphere. This is a very big pro in my books, so I’ll make it short, since the story is what I wanted to discuss the most.

I love cat

is a casual, cat-induced, 2-D fishing ‘simulator.’ The goal here is to use an array of tools, including rods, boats, even bombs in conjunction with upgrades to complete a host of quests.
The casting mechanics are fairly straightforward, as there are only three buttons you’re likely to ever use. Click for casting/reeling & A/D for movement. There is no tutorial as of the writing of this review, but getting the general sense on how to start casting to maximum effect is quite simple. There isn’t any Menu either.
While, the casting & movement mechanics couldn’t get any simpler, there is some depth on how you choose to complete the quests. There are many different types of effects you can apply to your rod to target or dissuade various types of fish or to augment other elements. There are also tools both temporary & permanent that will come in handy.
As you catch fish & complete quests, you will level & accrue currency. As you level, the quests get progressively more difficult. However, from my experience, there does appear to be a degree of randomness with respect to the quest system; old quests will pop up time & again. The quests will progressively get more & more grindy. Completing them will require you to farm currency for pro-longed periods of time, before you can purchase the necessary items & upgrades to complete them.
Yes,
does have an array of hats. They are obtained by catching them so keep an eye out. The sad part is that you can’t collect them. You can only wear one hat at a time. Each hat provides a useful boost. Be wary of accidentally selling a hat, as it is easy to do.
There is an in-game catalog giving various details on the different types of fish, so it may yield some assistance in catching your desired fish.
The artwork is exactly as shown in the screenshots. The background scenery is under-utilized & quite bland. The sound is one uninspiring track looped continuously. Luckily, it can be muted with the ‘M’ key.
In conclusion, I wouldn’t label
as a fishing simulator. I wouldn’t recommend it to those who love fishing & desire that experience, albeit through the eyes of a cat. Rather,
is a game you pop in when you have a few minutes to kill, just for the posterity of seeing a cat catch some fish, while wearing a snazzy hat.

Oh, immortal GunZ, how we missed you! Wait, you changed... WHAT HAPPENED TO YOU?
After long years waiting, we finally have the second iteration of "GunZ: The Duel" on our hands, and it's bitter sweet. On one hand, it bring us that K-Style, fast-paced pump action that we all knew and loved and the ever so memorable maps! But there are too many "deviations" from the original that keep this game on its predecessor's shadow: gone is the free-reign customization you had with your character, opting now to offer you only classes with very limited customizable options.
The addition of special moves, like a Hurricane Kick and a Deathslash are cool concepts on paper, but take A LOT out of the skill based game that was GunZ. Who likes to be one-shot with an uninterruptible special move from behind? Only with Headshots, the most sublime art in GunZ, do I condone one-hit deaths.
AND DON'T GET ME STARTED ON MATCHMAKING! WHAT MATCHMAKING?
"Are you new to the game? Are you an old veteran of the original game, but have already forgot how to play the game? Here, go play with level 20 characters that kill you with three hits from a sword-cancel Butterfly and reload shot."
All in all, it's a great game. If it was a totally new experience, or If you never had the luck to touch the original GunZ, I would recommend this game. But with the memory of the original still imprinted in my mind, I find it lackluster, and do not recommend it for the OG GunZ player.

I loved this game in the early 90s and I'm glad to say it holds up really well.
Secret Agent is a basic puzzle/platformer that's all-around really solid. Your moveset is limited: You can run at one speed, jump, and shoot. Despite these limitations, the controls are very responsive and your protagonist is pretty easy to control. You can stop on a dime, even in mid-air. Your jump is also always the same height so you learn pretty quickly to recognize out-of reach ledges and collectibles.
What really makes Secret Agent shine is its great design. The level design gets deviously trickier as you progress, pushing your mastery of the simple controls to its limits. The point in every level is the same: To escape by finding and blowing up an exit. To do that you'll usually need to find some dynamite, collect keys to unlock color-coded doors, find a floppy disk and use it in a PC to deactivate laser fields, and sometimes find glasses that make new platforms visible. Besides that, many levels have optional objectives to net you more points. The letters S, P and Y offer 100 points each, and en extra 10,000 points if you collect them in order. There are out-of-the-way satellite dishes you can destroy for 5K. There are hidden money bags you can trigger by jumping in certain areas. You get a 25K bonus for beating the level without getting hit. All of this adds a surprising amount of depth to the game. You can play it like an arcade twitch game and just try to find the quickest path to the exit, or you can try to maximize your score by thoroughly exploring the level and seeking out all its secrets. Should you risk taking a hit and missing out on the 25K bonus in order to backtrack to a satellite dish? Shoulld you use 5 bullets on a relatively easy-to-avoid enemy or save the bullets for a future stage where you might need them more?
The graphics, though incredibly basic by today's standards, are absolutely packed with charm and awesome details. The background elements include a security cabinet with an animated view of a camera looking down a hallway, armories stacked with crates and various (decorative) weaponry, and even lived-in touches like pool tables and steaming coffee cups. The brick wall tilesets include convincing shadows when a ceiling light shines down on a floating platform. Everything looks very clean and recognizable and is pleasing to the eye. The sounds are sparse and, though limited to PC speaker, are still quite charming.
It's certainly possible that my nostalgia for this game has influenced how I currently see it, but I think Secret Agent is a gem of a game. The level design is fantastic and filled with optional challenges. The controls are solid and responsive. The graphics  are delightful. Recommended.

Time to get to one more childhood classic of mine: "Secret Agent" by Apogee.
It's a 2D platformer starring an agent à la James Bond (more like Daniel Craig actually which would be anachronistic) who has to master each level by collecting certain items, opening gates and doors, shooting bad guys and finding the exit. So a real deep story is not present, it's very basic. It's not even like you can drive awesome cars or have some stealth action or hot loving. You know, like your next door agent.
Nevertheless, it is quite a fun game but also a challenging one. The challenge is that you can die pretty quickly and you need to memorize and learn in order to pass certain dangers properly or to avoid mistakes that can mess up your progress.
You choose levels à la "Commander Keen" by looking at maps and enter accessable levels you can find.
You can save and load your game but just by typing numbers (goes like "Save your game by pressing a number between 0-9"). Just keep that in mind if you're used to clearly visible safe spots (as all of us) or if you share "Secret Agent" with other players.
The gameplay is not flawless (it's especially not always easy to control your character when it comes to landing jumps precisely) but in general it's okay and easy to learn.
The graphics are not bad for the time period it was made in but unfortunately it uses a whole lot of grey, so it gets kind of dull here and there. So it's not one of my favourites when it comes to graphics in classic platformers/Apogee games.
When it comes to music: There is none. There's only sound and it's also rather minimal and hardly heard. Mostly you will heart bullets or rays being shot, sound cues that tell you when an important event has happened and your own jumping sounds.
One word about the villains because they are a lot of fun compared to other elements in this game: Have fun checking them out because there's quite a variety of them. From robots of various kinds and Terminator-like dudes to rolling ray guns on the ceiling.
So, "Secret Agent" is surely something to try out for classic platformer enthusiasts. But others might find little attraction in it because of the dull and dated graphic and sound design or the same tasks you have to solve in every level while performing trial & error lots of times.

This is one of those great platform classics from the beggining of the 90's. It might not have been as popular as Duke Nukem, but it still has a charm of its own. This title doesn't really have a complex plot. You're just some secret agent who's trying to stop the evil plans of this criminal organization. I don't think that's something bad though, I mean, when the plot is something as cheesy as that, the last thing that I could possibly care about is the story. As for the levels, there're 3 different episodes available and you can pretty much navigate throughout the island and choose wherever you want to go, kinda like Megaman style, but fancier (or more bureaucratic) in a sense of word. That said, compared with some other games from nowadays, Secret Agent doesn't really have some smooth graphics, cool sound effects and not even a proper soundtrack. Either way, the most important factor is still there, which are the gameplay and the fun factor. The controls are very responsive and they're also compatible with a X-Box controller, which makes everything much interesting for someone like me, who as a kid, only had the first episode available (shareware), and also had to play the game on a keyboard. Since the game is old, it still relies on that points score system, which nowadays it's somewhat irrelevant. I mean, even if there's the internet available for you to compete with the whole world, there's always a funny guy to mess things up with an exploit or something. The only bad thing about this Steam version, is that you have to download nearly 1gb to play something that could easily fit in a floppy disk... Well, and the price too, come on, have mercy! That really makes no sense whatsoever. Well, that's pretty much it, I hope that you may enjoy this game as much as I do, even though it may seem so outdated, it's still quite fun and challenging in my modest opinion.

Me and a friend both purchased Trine 2 yesterday on impulse because it looked good, it has co-op and well, that 3,39€ price tag is so damn tempting. We played for a couple hours and it was very enjoyable. In the game you play 3 characters, a wizard, a knight and a thief. Each one of them have some abilities that help you in both combat and puzzle solving and their own skill trees. The puzzles are clever and require a bit of thinking to solve. The game gives you the option to allow it to give you hints for the puzzles after a set amount of time you're stuck, making sure that all players will be able to pass them, without having to resort to walkthroughs, and get on with the storyline.
Combat on the other hand is rather easy(maybe even too easy), especially in multiplayer. I encountered a boss fight once and even that one was too easy when using the thief's frost arrow and hook.
I would definitely recommend this game and so far I believe it's worth its full price as well. The puzzles are great, combat is ok and the story telling and nice graphics give you the sense of being in a fairytale world.

So let me say, this game sat in my library for years. One day I saw an article that tied my favorite author to the game, R.A. Salvatore. He is one of fantasy writings greatest authors, and my personal favorite. When I realized he was a signficant creator in the lore of the game, I finally dove in and started playing. Now let me also say, there was some significant legal/funding issues that gives this game a bad wrap, the game itself so far does not seem to be influenced by these outside issues. In the first 10 hours I have completed several quest areas and the characters all have fantastic voice acting with rich-warm tones. The environment and the music create a whimsical, mysterious fantasy world feel. You really feel like your in this big adventure with the way you are pulled in. The game feels a little too easy early on as melee focused character, so I recommend any skyrim/rpg veterans to crank the difficulty up to hard out the gate.
The combat system feels very rewarding with honestly, little effort beyond remembering to frequently dodge, I haven't faced any terribly difficult combat encounters yet. The moves themselves as well as the flow are very satisfying for all the abilities, and I really like the character leveling system.
Overall my only gripes with the game in my first 10 hours are the difficulty doesn't punish mistakes in combat enough, and the camera angle is annoying, but I've gotten used to it. If you like an RPG adventure with a fast paced combat system and a beautiful immersive world, I'd give this game a shot, truly a hidden gem.

Pros:

Extreme Example: "Oh god they killed X" -> X -> "X is my best friend I loved him, we have to find his murderer, but who could it be?" -> murderer ->  "Someone killed my best friend, that makes him a murderer!" ->friend -> "My best friend was murdered, oh god, we have to find out who murdered my best friend!"

Don't get me wrong: this game has issues (Not dealbreaking, but important nonetheless): You can't team up with people that's not the same class as you, so if you made a Recon and your friend drives a tank you can't even get in the same games (The game just won't let you). Machineguns are ridiculously overpowered: they shoot far, they are very precise and have gigantic clips so if you are pitted against a soldier with a MG you will die every time unless you snipe him or empty a clip on his back. The grenade hitbox works like♥♥♥♥♥♥(A grenade may explode next to you and deal no damage, or explode in a house 10 meters away and kill you.
Having said that, this game is FUN (specially if you play with a/some friend/s). It has a tactical feeling not even Battlefield 2 can provide. Sure, your team may never even speak to you, but it's still exciting to be defending a building with some teammates in every floor, or surrounding the enemy in a jeep hoping none of them panzerfausts you. The game is definately not P2W, but some of the weapons you can get are just broken (refer to the MG rant above). Being an infantry man is fun, but classes are also cool, dropping behind enemy lines with your parachute and stealth-capturing an objective, or shooting down a plane, or preventing infantry from reaching cover with your tank. Every class has its place and if you have skill, you can reach high even if your equipment leaves a lot to be desired. And the fact that everything is just so freaking expensive makes getting it a bit more special. Camouflage is rare, so camouflaged soldiers stand out. Getting the money to buy a new class makes you feel proud, and being able to buy a new weapon is an accomplishment on itself.
At the very beginning, the game may seem unbalanced and like a grind, but give it a chance.

I was a massive fan of the original Torchlight, and thought that this one would have big shoes to fill if it was to be a worthy successor.  The TL;DR version is that it's a quality game... with a couple of caveats.
It's a bit more messy. Torchlight saw you carrying a few quests, and it was fairly straightforward how you were going to complete them.  This game - even though there are GPS points on the minimap - frequently left me wondering why I'd not got a 'quest completed' message... because I'd missed some tiny passageway which opened up into a boss fight.  This meant there was a lot of going back over old territory, which I just find a bit frustrating.
Other than that - if you liked Torchlight, or if you like any sort of Diablo-esque game - you'll find TL2 a worthy addition to your collection.   I wouldn't call it deep, and it's certainly quite linear... but then so are almost all of the games of this type.
Graphically nice. Rather cartoony. Crappy cut-scenes. Excellent voice acting (though not much of it) and nice crisp controls... and clever pets that you can send off to do errands.  The game is frequently frantic, rather engaging, and in short, very nice.
It's basically smash if you wanted to kill yourself after playing it. All in all I give it a 10/10

The "About This Game" section tells you that this game has engaging missions and storytelling, but that is false. I bought this game in Early Access and enjoyed it for some time. RWBY: Grimm Eclipse is by far not the worst game I have played, but it is not one that I can recommend to my friends.
The "story" is bland and boring, while the missions are repetitive and dull. I could not bring myself to continue playing without having something else to do in the background to take my mind off of what little content the game had. The game tells me that it takes elements from Dynasty Warriors and Left 4 Dead, but only the flaws seem to be present.
If these were the only problems with the game, I would still probably be playing it, but they are not. The enemies are as terribly fleshed out as most other hack and slash games, but they are so much harder to wade through because reasons. Most enemies are fairly trivial to defeat and the only change in difficultly that I have found is exactly how long it takes to clear a room, not how challenging that room is to clear.
On top of the fairly lackadaisical approach to enemy design, the new characters, Team JNPR, that have been teased for quite some time, released as paid DLC for a game that has not even been able to provide more than a few hours of content for its "engaging storyline". I am not expecting this game to be completely DLC free in its full release, but I cannot accept paid DLC for a game that still has not lived up to its self-proclaimed greatness.
I really enjoyed the time that I have put into this game, but I cannot recommend it if the trend this game seems to be following continues. Random price changes and paid DLC for a seemingly incomplete game is not something I want to see to a franchise that I am a big fan of. Sorry Grimm Eclipse and goodbye, you were a good idea, but your execution was flawed at best.

I loved the first Trine. The game came out of nowhere and blew me away. My friend and I finished the game on co-op although I had to plow through the last agonizing and infuriating level by myself, but that's beside the point.
If anyone ever played and loved Lost Vikings on Sega, this game is definitely for you. This Nvidia phys X physics engine is still limited to a two dimensional game but I can see it expanding further. Although this time around the engine can pump out even pretties graphics and textures which I didn't think was possible.
The soundtrack is amazing, it calms down your nerves and makes you forget about all the worries in the world. The author was the one who made the soundtrack for the Angry Birds by the way. The narration is realistic and believable. The game once again feels like watching and playing a fantasy tale. At times, I simply wished to simply run forward and sink in the world of Trine without any enemies or obstacles. I just wanted to enjoy the foreground, the background, the physics, the tessellation particles, etc.
As with the first game, you collect vials and then use them for upgrades. 90% of the vials are more or less easy to obtain, much like in the first game; and there are several ways of obtaining almost every vial. You no longer retain your upgrades and abilities from the first game, so you have to reacquire the old ones as well as obtain only a couple of new ones.
Apparently the story takes place a few years after the first game. The awkward alleged womanizer wizard Amadeus is older now and is now a family man. Pontius is still the dumb and fearless fat knight and Zoya is still the same slender thief.
The trio is quickly reunited for a quest to save the kingdom, again.
The thief is still my personal favorite character to play. The acrobatics are still rewarding to conduct and you want to pat yourself on the back every time you manage to shoot the grappling hook as you fall to your death and suspend yourself in mid air. The thief will be the one to get most of the vials, artifacts and other miscellaneous collectibles (like drawings and poems) from hard-to-reach areas anyway. However, later on the wizard becomes extremely effective since you are then able to conjure several items and be able to float yourself and the entire party across impassable lands.The physics and the general precision is once again impeccable. The story now introduces orcs as opposed to the same old boring skeletons and other creatures. There are a handful of bosses still and they are fun to battle. The melee system is still as refined as in part 1. You can block, swing, shoot arrows and use the environment to your advantage (for instance dropping a rock onto an enemy while playing as a Wizard)
The game CAN get frustrating sometimes, especially when you attempt again and again to jump on that ledge or attempt to swing over and get that orb or vial. It's not the fault of the controls per se, it's the physics and the gravity that often prevent you from conducting flawless maneuvers.
The game apparently also has more replay value than the first one. There are more unlockables and extras this time. Once you finish the game, you can start a new game + and experience some new things, allegedly. PLUS, this time we get online co-op. Yes, thank you very much. Whereas the first game only featured a 2 player offline co-op, someone always had to be the brains and play as the two characters most of the time. Not this time. Now you can play as one of the three characters. You can use either text or voice chat to coordinate movement. I strongly recommend playing this game in co-op mode. It might get repetitive at times, but no puzzle is every the same so there is still enough variety, plus I don't think I saw a single piece of environment being recycled.
In general the game is quite easy. It does not call for a repeated frustration. There are plenty of checkpoints that will resurrect your dead companions and there are almost always more than one way of overcoming an obstacle.
The bottom line is that this game makes you regret that the world of Trine is only confined to a video game.
