This is overall a very good port of one of the very few mobile games I have ever found enjoyable to play. Visuals are improved with lightning effects that add a lot of atmosphere, the UI is much easier to manage with keyboard and mouse and installed on an SSD the loading times are more or less non-existant.
The game has also been entirely rebalanced for the PC release. In-app purchases of loot cards are gone and the requisition points you earn during missions to purchase the cards with have been greatly increased, so that you on average get the funds to buy a new card (with a new marine and two items) after every fifve missions, in addition to the free loot card you get for finishing every four-mission chapter of the campaign. Experince gain from the missions has also been doubled compared to the iOS version which makes for a much faster progression with little grinding required.
My only disappointment so far with the PC version is the extra content. Although advertised as three more Space Marine chapters the new chapters are not complete, and consists only of one each of assault/tactical/devastator marines and one veteran. By comparison the original three chapters had approx. 18 different marines each, including champion and hero tier marines that are entirely missing from the new chapters.
My take on this is that if you have played the iOS version to death and finished the campaigns there is little new content here to make it worthwhile to play the game all over again. But the improved visuals and UI combined with no micro transactions makes it a good choice if you haven't tried the game before or if you have just started out on the iOS version.

Now, I've played every Dynasty Warriors game starting from 2 all the way through this one. My repetoire includes all the various expansions as well. For better or for worse, it has been an enlightening experience that allowed to truly explore my preference in gaming and the unshakeable urge to follow a series, even one with a poor reputation. I love the Dynasty Warriors franchise, and it will always hold a place in my heart, This game is no different,
That being said, this may be the first in the series that I have actually felt bored with. At this point, the whole schtick of putting 300 men on screen at the expense of poorly rendered models has gotten to me. Furthermore, as a game purported to be a strategy spin-off of an otherwise linear beat-em-up, Dynasty Warriors 8 fails to deliver any truly intuitive gameplay decisions.
The biggest issue would probably be the extreme repetition. Empires offers more "options" for a player to take than any of the previous entries. Subjugation, secession, betrayal OUTSIDE of battle maps, etc. However, aside from the occasional kick I get out of being a massive clod and betraying my current empire, there's little here that actully feels like it actually varies the gameplay. Oncey ou've settled into a new empire (or started your own), the formula is as follows
1. Quest in order to make a friend or three
2. Invade
3. Marry [insert husbando or waifu here]
4. invade
5. defend (maybe??)
6. rank up to marshall or strategist
7. invade
8. rank up to leader
9. invade
10. repeat step 9 until you have a frothy mixture
The additional things you can, such as subjugate vagabond units or make alliances that barely matter, offer a chance to break the tedium a little bit, but they result is always the same.
Obviously, being a Dynasty Warriors fanboy, there are positives I could name. Interaction with fellow officers is always neat, something I love about these games. Creating your own self-insert is always entertaining. The visible sign of progress, displayed through the contiguous blob of a single color on the campaign map, is definitely keeps the player at least marginally interested in pushing its boundaries a little further. There are some others I could name, but in all honest they're just my own pandering towards the franchise.
Recently, KOEI released Nobunaga's Ambition: Sphere of Influence. It's a decent attempt at grand strategy, and I think KOEI would benefit from taking a few elements from it and incorporating it into this game. Were they to truly expand upon the actual strategic and light role-playing aspects of the Empires spin-offs, they would have a real winner. Find a way to break the battle tedium by having more scripted events, both in and out of the battlefield, and do away with the whole "capture bases until something good happens" streak.
I don't want to stray away from how I truly feel about this game. I enjoy it just as I have previous Dynasty Warriors games and I'm sure I will find continued motivation to come back to it and conquer the Han again. However, I think Empires offers me a good chance to be truly vocal about the actual state of these games. If KOEI were to expand upon the strategic points of the game while making battles actually feel worthwhile, it could be a serious winner. All they need to do is make a fresh start.
Also what's with the DLC prices? That♥♥♥♥♥♥s wack.
Post-Script: A few other things, mainly just specific little details that I hope KOEI looks into in the future.
x. Make officers more autonomous. Officers, particularly prefects and up, should be making more changes and doing more things on the campaign map. Limitations and the lack of many options on the map prevent this. However, having a force of 30 officers, but only about one or two of them doing something between each war council is a little annoying.
x. Expand the concept of strategems. Strategems could increase the diversity of battles significantly. New things like ambushes, setting fire to bases, and other "large-scale" motions would be a significant boon. Perhaps find a way to wrap this into the campaign map.
x. Expand upon the concepts of intrigue and subversion. It would be FANTATSIC to be a massive♥♥♥♥♥and plot your way to the demise of your enemies. Assassinations, bribes to switch allegiances and create discord, and fabrication of claims would greatly expand the depth.

Deathwatch - Enhanced Edition represents Rodeo Games first "in house" port from iOS to the Steam Platform. It's their first serious go at converting a paidmium title from IoS into a truly premium experience that doesn't necessitate further payments on the Steam platform, and in doing so they've rebalanced the economy, converted the graphics engine over to UE4, given the graphics a serious spitshine, as well as gone over the various UI systems to make them keyboard and mouse friendly.
In Deathwatch you control a team of five marines (Stop me when this starts sounding familiar), trudging down narrow corridors, setting up killzones and killing tyranids who charge into your firing range as they swarm towards you en masse, praying you mow them down quicker than they spawn towards you, and they will come in floods, so eventually you'll be overwhelmed. The trick is to finish whatever the mission is before you end up as Tyranid nom nom. All of this happens in a top down, turn based singleplayer environment where you spend AP's on each marine setting up overwatches and taking shots at opponents using probability to hit.
So. To recap. Small team of heavily armoured SPESS MAHREENS. Narrow corridors. Tyranid threat. Chance to hit. Turn based. Swarms of them. Few of you. Sounds like Space Hulk doesn't it?
That's because barring a few changes here and there, you'd be forgiven that you were playing a very polished version of Space Hulk, at times you're more or less doing exactly that, just with a mixed chapter of space marines and without a librarian or psyker to back you up (which sucks). The marines move pretty slowly and are clunky buggers, with overwatch limiting them to a ninety degree cone of fire. Setting up overlapping killzones is order of the day and making sure their backs are protected so tyrannids don't -eat them- is sortof vital.
Unlike the Space Hulks that are already on steam, the levelling system has a little more finesse, taking cues from Dark Souls, where here you won't permanently lose a marine if he's downed, but you WILL lose any unbanked XP, it's a clever system, ensuring that you're always balancing risk with reward, and as the later levels get tougher, you'll need to string together multiple wins in order to power that marine through the later stat boosts. Additionally you can further customise the Marines through their wargear choices and their weapons, the latter has a noticable visual effect which is a nice flourish.
Marines too, visually distinguish themselves from one another, with higher tier marines having more detail than their cannon fodder baseline cousins. The loot system is all held together by a "card" system which awards you cards for missions completed, and the chance to earn points which can be spent on card packs of three which can yield some very high end gear and marines for your deathsquad. All of this hangs together well, and gives both a sense of interest and progression, since there's always the chance of landing a high tier marine that could really help your squad or a really neat bit of loot that you can equip.
However, counter to this is that the game has a really perfunctory mission structure, with short,  mobile focussed missions that are very, very bitesized. I got through the better end of twelve missions in an hour, only to be stuck with a bug that locked me up for ages and had me sending mails to the developer whilst I waited for my save game to get sorted out. This is NOT a long game, and worse, there's no random mission generator as there has been in say, Rodeo's other games (Hunters 2 springs to mind), so the longevity of this title as is, is deeply suspect.
Then there's the so called enhanced content, which includes additional marines from the other chapters, except it doesn't really, because they've only included tier 1 versions and a tier 2 veteran along with tier 2 loot for one item. In short, for building a high end team, you won't be using the enhanced content for anything other than flavour, it's a stunted, unfinished tree that desperately needs fleshing out if it's to feel as complete and as enhanced as Rodeo claims on the advertising blurb.
This game is tricky. Part of me wants to like it, because there's the soul of a good Space Hulk game in here, but as it stands? It's not -good enough- to recommend to the public as is. Therefore I recommend with strings attatched. At the price point being asked, I would wait, because they're asking too much for what's on offer. With the enhanced content fully fleshed out, that would justify the pricing, but it's not, so right now this is strictly a "For the fans" game. Otherwise, hold fire, wait for the inevitable discount.

Skyfable! Fablerim! Fable: the Rim of The Sky! Skyrim: The Fablening!
Seriously though, this game is a wonderful cross between two games, and I'm sure you know which two by now. The story/plot aren't all that immersive, and at times it seems to take itself either way too seriously, or so not serious that it changes its Facebook relationship status and everything.
The combat is deceptively simple. It seems easy, until you get wolloped on by a boss and wonder why you don't seem powerful anymore. Turs out, you were that powerful, you just need to use your moves, combos, dodges, and spells more effectively.
The music is forgettable in most places, and nothing about 'big moment' swelling orchestral pomp really grabs your ear, but it does have a few memorable tracks lying around; sometimes in weird places.
The voice acting gets zero stars for not including Jennifer Hale, but since I'm not giving out stars anyway, just know that a lot of lines fall flat, and overacting was a problem in the sound booth, I'm sure. Not all bad though.
KoA:R gets points off for having yet another terrible crafting system that makes you run around for hours and hours, finding inane bullcrap so you can make something awesome, then find a better version of it in a shop twenty minutes later. F*ck crafting.
Overall, this game is really fun, has a lot of little easter eggs, and plays pretty smoothly. A nice romp through a fantasy world, killing baddies with big swords, magic, and whatever else you find. You loot dungeons, join guilds, go on quests, and all the other action RPG stuff you'd expect.

TL:DWTR;
This game is a combo of Bushido Blade or bb2, Total War, Skyrim, and kind of a turn based game strategy game. It's got some bugs, combat can be infuriatingly hard, and unnecessarily difficult in some respects on account of a little thing called reality, but that's not what we're here for, we all know that's a two way street. This game is amazing, I hadn't heard of it until I was searching through Steam and found it. I was skeptical but the reviews were crushingly positive and since this is the internet the sheer volume of positive reviews make it obvious this is a good game. It has a great deal of historical accuracy, and it is the first reference outside of my intentional personal studies that I have found by happenstance where they actually use the word "Vikingr" instead of "Viking". If Medieval Fantasy is your shtick but want a more realistic experience, you'll not need to look any further. Start as a slave, rise to King/Emperor- don't expect it to happen in week. This game is not for 'Casuals'.
Dat Body:
I was pretty skeptical about this game, but the overwhelmingly positive reviews made me take a leap of faith, and my name must be Altair or Ezio or w/e tf, because I landed in a hay bale without breaking my neck in the process. Although, if you start playing this game you're going to have a very intense first person experience getting skull-"loved" by an arrow or a sling stone. Or you'll be in the middle of some insane fight and literally be the only thing standing between victory and defeat, winning the battle through sheer focus and determination, and then that pansy @#! farmer you turned your back on because he wasn't a threat is going to pick up a random javelin you threw that missed a target (which occasionally happens in some pretty much impossible circumstances, so get used to that glitch) and make you another 1-0-8-7 in Agincourt. I'm not kidding. There are times when I aim at the body and the javelin goes over his shoulder by his neck repeatedly, then there are times when I am aiming my javelin at a dude's legs and seem to have unerring accuracy for throwing the javeling through his thigh gap. Once you see that happen three times in a row while zoomed in and then get your face cut open by an axe hit chain you don't know how to break, you're going to see how much patience you really have.
Or, when you're in a critical fight where you've been outnumbered and outgunned but used tactics and strategy to eke out an incredible (heroic by total war standards) victory, you may find that turning on "Bleeding damage" in order to get that extra flavor of reality just cost you an hour long fight that you have to re-do because your character fell unconscious from bloodloss, and that's only if you selected the option where you get to quit without saving. :)
Like Bushido Blade, some random basic could lob a javelin at you or run you up the back side with a pitchfork and smoke you even at 3/4 health and you'd be done. That's on Normal everything w/ max realism. It doesn't take much.
Like Total War, you can travel to towns and recruit units with your army and, as you acquire new towns through the royalty system/fiefdoms or w/e, you can develop those towns and raise a levy of soldiers from the town proper.
Like in TW and Turn Based Strategy Games, when you're not performing an action (on the World map only) the game doesn't continue unless you actively hold the spacebar to wait, or camp/rest somewhere.
Like in Skyrim, you are in first or third person viewing mode, and you can also use an aerial strategy view to fight from up and away, but I don't find that particularly convenient for dodging arrows. It's good to check quickly to see if your flank is getting crushed, but if you get too sucked into a particular fight you could lose sight of the bigger picture (that being that the infantry you had guarding the left flank of your spearwall got crushed because they didn't bother to turn around and fight the cavalry that charged in on them from behind until after two of them had died).
You can put yourself in charge of a division of soldiers and lead a unit and then put that unit in formations around you, like the unit blocks in Total War, but at a FP/TP perspective. Very intense. There are some other features that people will recognize as staples from a lot of FP/TP games, those being crouching and jumping. Crouching will make you crawl when moving forward or move slowly side to side/backwards while standing up. It's also good for stabilizing your character and improving your aim (not to mention nestling yourself in between four spearmen so you can hurl javelins at the oncoming enemy in safer conditions).
Jumping doesn't immediately seem to be useful as you have an infuriating delay when your character lands. It's not good for chasing people down (for instance jumping while running down hill would allow you to go further distance and catch up quicker), but the reality of it is that you land and your character has a 1 second delay, so it's actually worse to jump while running. I didn't think the Jump feature was useful for anything other can climbing minor obstacles until I decided to crank the game's combat AI up from "Normal" to "Good". I am a masochist, apparently.
So there I was getting wrecked by a footpad w/ an axe and a spearman when I'd been able to 1v3 those unites in normal combat AI, and starting to rage because I knew I had a faster weapon yet this footpad was hit chaining me to the point I couldn't do anything even while fighting and the few times I got to swing it was to block the damn spear. You get the drift.
So then I went to cry about it on the internet (See also: See if anyone else was butthurt about the combat) and anywhere I saw it, I saw people who were clearly legit gamers telling them to suck it up and put in effort. I should note, I didn't start Mount and Blade on Beginner Level in combat, I decided to learn at the normal level since that's how developers designed the average person to play it. That was probably a significant factor in my malaise, but I digress.
How to Break a Hit Chain and get some damage in:
+Use your Kick, if his block is still up when you go to swing, use a combination of side-stepping, kicking, and jumping while attacking.
+Use your weapon's reach to your advantage. If he has a spear, entice him to strike but dodge it (or try) and then get in close and crowd him out. If he has a weapon of slightly shorter reach, go in for the attack and back up at the last second so he opens himself up to strike only to get sliced by the tip of your Chipped Rich Briton Sword.
+Call your units to you/order them to charge, don't try to play Hero in Mount and Blade. Getting beaned in the back of the head with a slingstone can knock you unconscious, make you go blind, or make you start bleeding out.
This game WILL punish you for failure a *LOT*, for your own benefit, start learning without having to save every time you quit. :)

New Review 20 March 2014: I didn't think it was fair to keep my old review, nor fair to the players to read the old review if it was no longer relevant information. I will, however, keep it on here as a reminder of how far along Infested Planet has come.
Infested Planet is a top down RTS game that combines mobile tower defense with a king-of-the-hill aspect. The development team has come a long way in a short time (a few months) since my last post. They have been doing a lot of hard work to create a challenging and fair environment for the players.
The later missions are very difficult, putting your knowledge of the various units to the test. In order to complete them you will have to combine a number of different tech buildings and unit types in order to overcome the various enemies.
In-game unit details are not amazing, but they are informative. When you hover your cursor over a tech it will give you generalized information on what the unit does, including the hotkey it is assigned too. For instance, the officer unit tells you that after 'destroying a hive units gain %200 attack speed' but it does not tell you how long the buff lasts. You'll just have to become familiar with the units yourself, knowing their capabilities.

I bought the game during the Winter Sale. And I am not disappointed in the slightest. Infected Planet sports deceptively simple controls and mechanics. You shouldn't have a problem learning how the controls work if you're familiar with any kind of RTS. Seeing your squad march against seemingly endless hordes surely brought a smile to my face as they carved a path of Alien blood to their goal. And you're sure to get worked up as men fall one by one and you're forced to make a full retreat to your nearest bunker and hold the fort until reinforcements arrive.
You start off fairly simple, spawning into a Map with a Squad of five Riflemen in the opening level. Here you get a basic rundown of entry controls for commanding your unit and attacking. As well as how to complete objectives. Which mostly consist of taking all the control points on the map from alien hands. Other times you will have to protect several bases, or take the fight to them and kill as many of them as you can before time runs out. Capturing, or destroying a base (in the case of Raid missions) yields you BP which you use to switch up units in your squad, add members to it, create various turrets and defenses, or create structures that grant passive bonuses to help you out in the fight. The fun really begins when you start mixing and matching unit types, via upgrades you purchase in between missions with reward money you get. And you don't need to worry about not having enough money for them either. All the missions are infinitely replayable for farming or just to see how fast you can wipe out the enemy.
It isn't without a few flaws, however. At times you will lose track of your units, or be completely overwhelmed by a sudden increase in enemy difficulty via mutations. This may make some of the more casual players shy away, as you will have moments where a Tug-of-war situation suddenly falls into the enemy's favor after a long stalemate. Some minor improvements could include refining how you keep track of units. Maybe an at-a-glance color coded minimap could help if applied correctly. Overall, these minor gripes don't take away from the overall gameplay, and you can easily lose track of time as you watch your squad cut through endless amounts of aliens for hours on end.
The game is still in it's Beta Stage, but I'm already seeing tons of promise with the game's Skirmish mode, where you can play preset maps, or tweak several options and create your own unique mission. From the number of enemy hives on the map, to how long they spawn alien waves, right to the mutations and amount of funding you have at the start. This shows amazing potential for being a far deeper custom map generator using simple options. I've had my eye on Infected Planet for while, and I can say that if you're interested in trying it out, you should buy it and give it a try.

Do you like vampires?  Well there's two answers to this question:
- You do? Great!! Then you can help save them from sunlight, silver bullets and hired assassins by guiding them to their lairs.
- You don't? Great!! Then you can guide them into sunlight, silver bullets and hired assassins to your hearts content.
Whether you love or hate them, Vampires: guide them to safety is a fun and challenging puzzle game that's great to kill a few minutes or even spend an hour or two on. With increasingly difficult chapters which add new dangers and new tricks to use, it's certainly no walk in the park. More like a walk in a cemetary, at night, in the fog..... with odd sounds and a wolf howling.

This game is all about getting your vampires to safety before the sun rises.
It's quirky, its fun and full of charm. But, don't expect it to be an easy task, along the way you will come across puzzles, traps and all manner of nasty obsticels to try and stop you in your tracks. If you enjoy a challenge and a laugh then here's a game for you!

Vampires: Guide Them to Safety! is a game that I could recommend for two kinds of gamers: casual gamers as well as hardcore achievement hunters. To start with the latter, you will be challenged: Both mentally and in skill, it's genuinely demanding and only the finest will ever 100% this game.
Now casuals will have a blast, it's kind of cute despite its ghoulish theme and the game is easy to understand. It's perfect for a 'quick run', most levels don't take more than a minute to complete so you can just jump in and play for any period of time.
The game itself is hard to describe. I don't think I've ever played anything like it. There are some tower defense elements, a pinch of 'puppetmaster', a healthy dose of Lemmings and some influences from Orcs Must Die!. That may sound weird, it probably is weird, but it still makes for a very decent game.
Not knowing how/if the difficulty will ramp up, but there's plenty of gameplay for your money here. If I may give an estimate it'll keep you busy for at least 10 hours. And for 5$, that's a steal.

An old little gem from Apogee, this is a fun and challenging 2D platformer. When I was kid, I had the shareware version (back when shareware was still a thing), which included only the first chapter, and I had a lot of fun with it. Having the chance to finally complete it was great.
As far as story goes, like most games from its era, it doesn't have a lot. You play as a secret agent (hence the name) tasked to infiltrate a series of island controlled by an evil organization in order to recover the blueprints to a superweapon.
When it comes to gameplay, each chapter (there's three of them) consists of a large island filled with enemy bases you need to take down before gaining access to the island's fortress. Each level (or base) requires you to find an explosive to blow open the exit, although you might also have to find keys to unlock doors, or floppy disks to deactivate laser fields that may be in your way. There's also several enemies and different hazards on each level. As I mentioned above, it can be quite challenging, as some of the levels include sections that are basically trial and error, and you may end trapping yourself with no other option but to restart the level, which can be a bit frustrating. Even then, losing your three lives only forces you to restart the level, and all of them can be completed in a few minutes. Another good thing is that you can play the levels in any order you like, so if you find one too challenging, you can always go back to the island map and try another one, in case you're missing ammo, for example.
In conclusion, I recommend this game. Whether you lived through the 90s (or earlier), and have some nostalgia for the games of your childhood, or if you never experienced that era, and want to see some of the early days of gaming, you should give this game a shot.

I first got this game back in the late 90s on a 3.5inch floppy disk.  If you were not born in the 90s, or know what a 3.5inch floppy disk is.  Don't rate this review down.  I've seen a few 12 year old not get old games.  Don't be one of those.  I clocked this game back then, and I'm on my way to doing so again in 2015.
This game was and still is pretty sweet for a 2d platformer.   You have multiple gameplay elements to work with.  Its not just fight to get the key and open the door.  Sometimes you have to choose which key/door combination to unlock.  You may screw up requiring a reset of the level!  Add in the floppy disk/laser grid.  Dynamite to open the exit, satelite disk to find and destroy, and sometimes the invisible platforms to change the level layouts!  This gives a feeling of progress more than having to walk through a level again.
Oh and then there are the varied enemies you will fight.  The game only allowing you to fire one shot at a time slows things down some, but means this isn't about button bashing. Its more of a chess game about when to put yourself into harms way and attack.  Keep in mind you have a bonus if you survive the level with no damage.  There are quite a few enemies that have various strengths and weaknesses.  You can't just shoot and win.  Some you have to attack only at certain times, and in certain places.  Others will blow up and send shrapnel out towards you.  The blue ninja guy is one of my favourites.
Don't also forget the challenge of spelling S.P.Y.  It seems so simple but sometimes avoiding the letters you aren't ready to get can be fun/frustrating.
The graphics are nice and colourful, the sound is old school.
The only really bad thing is when you finish the levels and realise you are getting closer to the end.
10/10 would spell S.P.Y. again

Protips:
- Install the mods NRAAS Overwatch and MasterController (plus integration) to help reduce lag, crashes, and have workarounds for otherwise game-breaking bugs. NRAAS Register is also helpful to reduce lag via extended population controls. Overwatch is
to avoid any town eventually crawling to an unloadable halt, no matter how many different save files you make or how awesome your gaming machine is (this is due to a bug that spawns ridiculous numbers of cars in NPC Sim inventories).
- Disable memories immediately, and be sure to re-disable them when the game inevitably resets all its settings as if you've never played before (it likes to do that every once in a while). The memory scrapbook concept is a cute idea but very poorly implemented, as it will create huge save files and additional lag from all the memories being recorded by every Sim in the game.
- Get the fixed version of the Isla Paradiso world if you want to play in it at all (the fairly-unplayable version comes with the Island Paradise expansion). NRAAS Register becomes much more useful for this world specifically, because you can turn off immigration, wild animals, tourists, and other things that make even the fixed world laggy. Overwatch will also disable NPC Sims from adopting pets, which is a good idea because kittens and puppies lag the game out badly due to being unable to go up and down steps.
- Don't get a vacation home in the World Adventures expansion countries until you are absolutely sure you are done with opportunities related to that country. Buying a vacation home makes it almost impossible to get opportunities afterwards, especially in France.
- Either don't buy a home plot or alternate house in the To The Future expansion, or be prepared to randomly lose the lot and everything on if you change the future setting (which includes normal, distopia, and utopia settings). If you edit the future town to include buildings like a grocery store or school, these changes can also be randomly undone.
- Research expansions ahead of time for content and purpose, then add the ones you want to your wishlist and keep an eye out for Steam sales. Usually the big summer sale will at least chop off part of the obnoxious pricetags. - Make multiple save files for games you care about. I use 8 different saves sequentially numbered for every world that isn't just a random test of something, and I overwrite the oldest save with each new save. That way if one save becomes corrupted, I have 7 to fall back on, with varying degrees of playing time lost. Even with mods, some saves will corrupt, especially if the game crashed while saving.

Deathwatch is a turn based strategy game from Rodeo Games where you command a team of space marines from various chapters to defeat the Tyranid invasion.  You play through missions in a variety of locations and improve and customize your marines with new gear and abilities as they level up.  There is a wide variety of weapons and units from different chapters to mix and match to best suit your current objectives.  You open card packs to gain random new gear and units.
The story is okay and seems more like a loose framework for the battles rather than an in-depth narrative in the space marine universe.  There is a low variety of enemies, through the middle of the second act I have only encountered four-five types of enemies.  The strategy is not very deep but it still is enjoyable to play.
I would recommend this game to people who enjoy a light strategy experience over relatively short mission lengths with a single objective.  It is a good iOS port.

As someone who played through and enjoyed the mobile iOS game all the way through the first two difficulty levels and mostly through the last, I'm disappointed by this port.  It feels incomplete in some sense, and almost lazy.
For those not in the know, in the mobile version, kit/unit expansion was done through requisition purchases and in-app purchases (hereforth to be referred to as IAP), to buy cards packs.  These packs allow for you to get 3 cards, one marine and 2 items (with the chance for rare/epic cards).  This system made sense with IAP being a potential option for people who don't have the time to endlessly grind levels and get a chance at getting better marines or gear.
I agree with the exclusion of in-app purchases, let me say that right here.  But without them, the way forward is unfortunately set to be a grindfest, with a pack at the end of every chapter.  Let's be honest, systems like these - with randomized rewards in a boosterpack like purchase are designed to encourage people to spend real-world money over and over on cards/items they don't need for the chance of getting something they want.  That's how it works with trading card games, that's how it works in mobile apps.  This system does not make sense in a premium game with no IAP, and as such should have been replaced with something else more fitting.
Maybe non-randomised cards.  Gain more requisition per level like gold, buy a marine for X requisition, buy gear for X requisition.  Spend requisition on your existing gear to upgrade gear.  Meanwhile get exp on missions, level up and advance your marine.  And when your marine is capped, spend requisition to advance him to the next tier.  That's an example off the top of my head, and most likely would have been tweakable for a much better system than the one currently in place.  As it stands you get a small amount of req per level, can purchase tiny 3 card packs, and maybe trade in unused marines and items for small amounts of req, making obtaining better marines and gear a grindfest.  Not of the pleasurable kind.
Furthermore, the 3 Enhanced Edition chapters are not complete, and do not progress past tier 2, while the other 3 go to tier 4.  Also, the graphics aren't even visibly that much better and there is still no multiplayer.
TLDR: feels lazy, exp/buying marine system broken, incomplete bonus chapter rosters, still no multiplayer.  If you really liked the mobile one and want to grind your way through the game on PC go for it i guess...

I've been playing the Deus Ex series since the first one that came out 16 years ago in 2000. I've enjoyed the story depth that the series has had in the first Deus Ex and Human Revolution and the length and number of options that both games had.
Mankind Divided, is newest entry that I am currently still on the fence about. On one hand the visuals are amazing and the gameplay feels more fluid than its predecessors. Stealth in this game feels more challenging compared to other games I've played in the past. The weapon and augment options are just like all the prior Deus Ex games which is a nice thing to have. The two things that make it fall flat in my opinion is the length of the story, and the loading times.
In Human Revolution there were a few boss battles and what felt like a very long story game which made replaying the game to try and find all of the secrets fun and rewarding. Some people in the game did not like the boss battles but in original Deus Ex there were several battles once the story started to progress. Mankind Divided has pretty much only one boss battle at the end which is disappointing since it felt like the story for the game was just starting after finishing it. At least the visuals and what story was there was worthy of being part of the Deus Ex universe albeit short. Hopefully the DLCs they add will make it more worthwhile but with how DLC quality has been in games for the last few years I'm not holding my breath.
One major gripe I had of this game though is the loading times, especically when going between the two major parts of the city you play in. Sometimes it can take a minute or more just to load the next area. I hope next time Eidos takes a concept out of GTAs playbook and make the loading between areas feel seamless.
I do enjoy the game and the extra content like Breach and the extra side mission that should have been in the main storyline. Both modes are fun and challenging. With all the negatives the Mankind Divided has and how short the story feels, at least its not another Invisible War, that is one game in the series that should probably be retcon out of existance.
TL;DR:
Do I reccomend this game?
Yes, with reservations. Amazing eye candy and RP experience.
Should you get it right now?
No, wait for it to get cheaper because the story is way too short, or wait for a GotY/Directors Cut that has DLCs.

I'll likely come back and do a more in-depth review. But keeping it short: It is a great game, with a lot of good moments and enjoyable gameplay. Having currently played non-lethal I can see some issue with how I find that to make the game easier, especially later on - as a close-up takedown will work on everything, except robots.
That said, it keeps the feeling of sneaking and being the badass aug detective. It has all those extra things to discover and the knowledge that some things you fail, because you took your time and not because you never could save/do the action.
People have motives and things are interconnected. You feel part of the city (if you overlook the traders that just don't react to any changes in the city or actions you do, if they don't see it).
Are there flaws? Yea, a fair amount. I had about 7 crashes - mostly related to the shooting range you'll encounter. The rest felt more random. Mostly it was a stable and reliable game experience.
There is an overlooked area when it comes to the knowledge you can gather in the game, a problem the former game also suffered from. Meaning that while some information will lead to new interactions, at other times you can e.g know what someone will do or where they are, before you are told - as you had already hacked a computer or seen a note about it - but you apparently do not know it ingame as Adam. This breaks some immersion and while I was happy every time they did consider it.. it was a constant reminder so to speak, as how my searching and loot gathering had little purpose, except for directly story related ones.
If they fixed that up, it would make the whole game so much more engaging.. and oh removed the pointless shop, I would say a very high recommendation. As it stands, I guess it would be a 8,3/10 for now. I had a lot of fun and I am highly considering a replay with lethal means.

Oh boy. I bee seeing those negative reviews. Anyways, productive day? Yes, no? Well i'm glad you took your time to read this review. For one, gameplay and graphics arnt generally bad, their well designed out and rather spectacular. The music is great, my favorites being the Main theme and Soviet Theme. And when you first start out, you get a little boost of everything, which is nice. Maps and layouts, and even guns are nice too. And one of the best parts is that it's not a simple FPS, level up enough or buy the general class, and you unlock a RTS (Real time Startedgy) mode. Okay, those are some good things, now let's get into the bad things. For one, like any FPS (*Looks at CoD,CS,and Battlfield*) this one has a pretty nasty community aswell, thank god this game doesnt have voice chat though. But every single match chat is the same old cancer. Enraged people who not only get angry at eachother, but get mad the enemy team, to be honest, we've all had those moments. Next, whats with the United States and soviets being enemies in the game? I know this kinda takes a page from Operation Unthinkable, and it's to balance the game But who though of Operation Unthinkable? The British. And where are they? NO WHERE! Thats another thing, I know reto couldnt add every single faction that fought, but come on, not even the british or italian? I got heroes and generals looking for some historical gameplay, like I was in a real WWII battle. Now after all of that, every positive thing I said, besides music and maybe RTS, is obsoulete. All. Because. of Matchmaking. Oh boy. For me, I like heroes and generals, but I am not denying that it has some major flaws, i'm fine with going through the matchmaking hell, but some of you may not. So, as it pains me. A great company would work with the modders to eliminate the parts that conflicted with the online multiplayer and then patch the game accordingly so that the single player could still be modded and the multiplayer experience has fewer cheaters, all with the implied acceptance of the company.
A good company would crack down on the specific mods that allow people to cheat in multiplayer and let single player modding remain a grey area.
A bad company uses legal tactics to bully a dedicated team of loyal fans into killing a project they love because they think all mods are bent on destroying the
online section of the game.
If Take 2 is telling the truth, then they at least have a valid motive (even if what they are doing is wrong). The problem is that I don't think anyone believes that they are telling the truth. If Take 2 ever comes forward with a detailed explanation of how Open IV can help people cheat in multiplayer (or even better: video proof) then I will belive them. But even then, it will not fix the fact that their response to this was quite possibly the worst way to respond to something like this.
From a business standpoint, it makes sense for Take 2 to value GTA online above GTA single player. From their perspective, one makes them money, and the other
doesn't. That being said, one part of the game should never have to suffer for the other to prosper. You have a right to make something profitable, but you also have a duty to your customers and community to make sure they can use what they paid for.
For many people, Take 2 has intentionally failed that duty.
****UPDATE:
It appears that Take 2 has allowed RockStar to work with the team developing OpenIV to find some kind of solution. However, I still feel like Rockstar is the abused child of Take 2 in the sense that Rockstar has not been more forthcoming with information that any developer would love to give to their fans. I will not change my recommendation until Take 2 allows Rockstar to speak without threat of being whipped with a belt.

Truly a hidden gem, and definitely recommended, but with some flaws.
Pros:
+Really well designed environments, plenty of varied colours (think Fable or WoW).
+Enemies scale with your level
+Combat is fun, skill trees offer plenty of customization options, and are easily reset
+Some skills are very useful (blacksmithing and sagecraft, lockpicking, etc.), and it makes sense to level them up.
+Picking a 'fate' lets you obtain extra bonuses that are playstyle-specific
+Game is quite long, and there are plenty of quests to complete
Cons:
-There's very little depth compared to what you'd find, for instance, in WoW - not a lot of lore behind the quests, rather simplistic crafting system, few difficult questlines, not the best variety of enemies, poor interaction with NPCs.
-Upgrading certain skills is more or less pointless. For instance, increasing alchemy only helps you find ingredients more often, and to create potions with more ingredients. If you find the recipe for a potion online, you can make one by 'experimenting'. Having a skill dedicated solely to opening magical chests without taking damage is also irrelevant.
-The environment isn't really 'alive' - it's there so you can buy stuff and get/hand in quests but that's about it. There isn't much going on in cities.
-Difficulty is badly balanced. As you progress through the game (especially if you craft your own armour), even playing on hard is way too easy.
-DLCs don't increase the level cap.
If you love single-player, open worlds, this game is amazing. I probably have nearly 100 hours on Xbox, and I realized I wasn't even close to beating the game. A hidden gem, 10/10

I'm going to be fully honest. I downloaded this game about a month ago and left it sitting on my library until today. The reason I decided to play it after all this time was because I had just finished watching a video about Isolation and what it does to the human mind. I don't know what that video did to me but I went into a sort of odd state and was a bit more "depressed" than usual. I saw the game and was like why not. I started the game and clicked on extras to start. Saw the endings tab and noticed that there were 7 endings. I didn't think much of it at first so I decided to carry on with the game. The choices I made at first where to do what I thought was right and sadly I got the "Forgotten Adventure" ending. I guess you can thank the visual novel "Seduce me the Otome", because I got a similar ending on my first try of the game. (though i didnt feel like trying the other endings) Because the forgetting thing was getting on my nerves I decided to just go down all the paths. One by one I completed them all until I got "Ashley the end of the curse" (Which turned out to be my favorite at first). I was so content with myself that I actually finished all of the endings that I decided to check the endings tab to just admire my completion of the game, when suddenly, I saw that there was a new slot for another ending. I already did every possible route so I didn't know how to complete a new one. I turned to google (thank you for no spoilers) and found out how to complete it. I did as it asked and I just read the rest since there were no more choices. In all honestly I enjoyed everything about that route. Finally finding out things about Lillian and Ashley. It was sort of refreshing from the constant deaths of the other routes. When the credits came up I was happy with this ending....yet...there was something in my heart that was unfilled, like I wanted there to be something more to the end... I tried to not really think about it. But in all honesty, I was not happy with how the story ended, and I came to peace with it. I just turned to stare at my wall and wonder what if something was different... If they didn't need to die...Then all of a sudden...I see that I have more text pop up. I was confused, what else could the author add to such a ending... When I saw that ending.... That hole in my heart was instantly filled with joy. I kind of want a slice of life story of just them going through school and getting to know each other better it was SO GOOOOOOD. I could not be more happy with this Visual Novel. Creators, Thank you for making such a wonderful visual novel. I could of not enjoyed it anymore.

I think this game is better than Skyrim.
I liked Skyrim, don't get me wrong, but the games are so similar and contemporary I think it's impossible to talk about this game without mentioning Skyrim. They are both open-world fantasy RPGs that end with you killing a giant dragon. They both have HOURS of lore with multiple factions and sidequests. They both have numerous auxiliary systems outside of combat. And I think KoA is just better.
First of all, the open world is much more diverse and visually interesting than that of Skyrim. Skyrim is mostly snow, snowy mountain, snowy forest, and snowy plains. KoA has a desert, green plains, swamps, dark forests, deserted ruins, islands, and beaches. The Skyrim cities feel like three people and an IHOP, but the KoA cities seem so much bigger and complex. The Skyrim color palette is gray and then more gray, and sometimes brown, and sometimes bronze, while KoA hits pretty much every color in the spectrum with a thematic reason for each color.
Next, the combat in Skyrim has always felt very basic and vanilla, where you click, and then sometimes you super click, and sometimes you get a cutscene where you cut off their head. KoA is based on precise timing and has a lot more nuance to it. Each weapon handles noticeably differently than another, as opposed to somewhat faster for swords and somewhat slower for maces.
I'm not saying the KoA system is perfect, but it's definitely better. The problems come when you end up telegraphing your attacks for approximately thirty years while your opponents, which range in size from circus peanuts to beluga whales, thrash you for hours at a time before you can even blink, making blocking a useless joke for the most part. Unless, of course, you wear the worst armor and waste all your points on agility, which is just the worst skill set as opposed to sorcery and might.  However, once you level up and get the hang of it, the combat system is very satisfying. The only other complaint I'd have is that gigantic hammers/axes seemlingly have the same effect on your enemies as sneezing in their direction and so why are they even in the game then?
As for story, I just never got too interested in the Skyrim civil war and the "kill the giant world-ender" storyline is as generic as they come. Everything you needed to know about the story you learned in the very first scene. KoA, on the other hand, while still having an incredibly generic story, has a much more intriguing way of uncovering it, peeling back the layers bit by bit and leaving the player wondering. Skyrim tries this, and does unveil a couple secrets along the way, but from the get go you knew Alduin was a giant bad dragon, and you met the leaders of both sides of the civil war. Nothing you learned along the way really changed that.
KoA seems to have more enemy variety than Skyrim. Even if that turns out not to be true, it certainly feels like it. In Skyrim it seemed like you fought the same couple of enemies at a time will little variation. In KoA you could be fighting foot-soldiers, giants, dogs, fairies, and giant spiders, all simultaneously.
Both games have magic systems, and KoA is the clear winner. The most advanced spells in Skyrim felt like the second tier spells from Diablo 2 all the way back in 1999. They used a lot of mana and had relatively little effect without investing an inordinate amount of skill points into several relevant skill trees. Meanwhile in KoA, you start out with skills that provide situational advantages, like stunning, damage increase, slowing, and are leveled up to the point where you are consecutively calling down fire, lighting, and blizzards from the heavens with the wrath of God Almighty himself. Far and away the superior and more satisfying system.
In Skyrim your special magic ability is shouting, which you can't do at the same time as casting a spell or attacking for some reason, and each shout has such a long cool-down time that by the time you can shout again you forgot you can even shout. KoA has the tried and true "build up power bar then enter super-dude mode" but the cool part is that at this mode allows you to enter an optional quick-time event that potentially ramps up your XP significantly.
Both have auxiliary systems such as blacksmithing and potion making. Skyrim's systems seemed numerous and daunting at first, but soon proved to be simple and, well, boring. KoA's systems are a little bit better. Like Skyrim, the potion making system lets you experiment with ingredients, but KoA extends this same experimental system to it's other mechanics, like gem socketing, something Skyrim doesn't even have, which allows you to customize your player build in ways Skyrim could only ever dream of. Also, the speech mechanic in KoA is more frequently useful than that of Skyrim, which I rarely saw and used even less.
One way Skyrim has KoA beat is in the exploration system. KoA has the much more beautiful map and sweeping vistas, but, while still open world, limits your ability to explore them. You can't even jump without a situational prompt. You don't climb mountains you're not supposed to, unlike Skyrim, where you can theoretically reach anywhere with enough patience.
I guess what I'm saying is if you can only get either Skyrim or this game, get this game. If you liked Skyrim, you'll like this game. If you're a fan of open world Fantasy RPG's, this is a must have.

Torchlight 2 is a hack n slash game made by the original creators of diablo II.
The story is about a dark alchemist threatening the balance of the world by opening the nether portals for a cure of some sort.
There's a total of 4 classes, engineer, embermage, berserker and outlander, and you can add more with workshop mods, i'd recommend sinergy one but after you beat the main game due to the increased difficulty.
Once you create a character and select a faithful pet, you can even get the headcrab from half life 2 if you're into that O.o, you get prompt with a difficulty setting, nice mechanic, all the way from easy to elite and obviously the famous hardcore mechanic one death equals losing that character forever.
Each class got a nice set of skill trees and those skins are fun from level 1, unlike games like titanquest or diablo where the cooler spells require tons of hours in the game, plus you can learn additonal 4 spells for you and your pet, summoning creatures, haste, and more.
Your pet similar to the game Fate, can pick up items or take the items from your inventory to go to the town and sell it while you keep killing hordes of enemies, can also buy portals and potions if needed, there's also fishing spots you can catch unique fishes to transform your pet into monsters in order to make it more efficient in combat for the duration of the fish.
Game is a must have for hack n slash fans, and even if you're not one but enjoyed diablo II you should get it, even at full price is still a great deal.

This game heavily relies on knowing all the Deus Ex games that have been made. I have to say it's a beautiful game, walking through the streets of Prague for the first time, feels like the first time walking through Half Life 2's City 13. It looks real. You need a good Rig to play it on the PC, seems they have chosen to go with AMD instead of Nvidia which for me wasn't optimal but it ran well for my rig (Geforce 780Ti). It was also unfortunate that it was a port to PC which probably counts towards the crashes and mixed reviews.
The gameplay is good, there are always a few more ways of getting in or to a destination. The added augs change the pace depending if you like a softly softly approach or raining lead.
I like how they have given back-stories of well known characters that we have seen in the future and how they have influenced the past to get there.
They have also added an extra mode called Breach, where in the single player game you collect Breach software packets and use these in a sort of VR competitive hacking game with your friends. It's a different play style and it's nice to see something new apart from a single player game.
The end of the game feels as if it's a bit up in the air, however, this could be a way of linking the next bit of the story. As for Adam, he can appear disinterested and without emotion but the player's choices can create a better personality.
Pros
-Graphics are amazing (if you can run it)
-The new augs are fun to use
-Story links well with previous games
-Nice that you get thanked for doing good deeds
Cons
-Crashed a lot
-Long loading time between maps
-Had to change to windowed mode to get past some loading screens
To sum up, been waiting ages for the next part of the story, it was worth the wait and I'll probably do another playthrough again soon!

First off I want to make it clear that this review is targeted to people who have not generally played Dynasty Warriors in the past. If you are a returning fan of the series this review will mostly be irrelevant to you.
This game is simply not finished yet. It is a blatant console port with terrible pc controls and there is no tutorial that I can find. The game simply just dumps you into a campaign and you have to make heads or tails of the situation yourself from the beginning.
There doesn't seem to be a way to check or change keybinds in the middle of a battle, the mechanics of items and building are not explained at all, and supposedly if I equip the item for a horse I should start with a horse but that never happens.
The camera is god awful and there doesn't seem to be any way to make it simply follow over your shoulder. Instead I had to resort to manually adjusting it all the time which is a huge pain. I could be wrong and there might be a way to easily set the camera just like with a number of things I mention in this review but the total lack of a tutorial or help or support just makes it impossible to find.
This game also happens to be extremely glitchy, just not in the usual way. In battle it performs fairly well and while the graphics leave a lot to be desired it is at least fluid and decently responsive. However, this game has a lot of random fatal issues. It has crashed or froze and needed to be terminated three times in the few hours I've played it all in different situations.
Further I cannot seem to save in this game and I have no idea why. A quick online search shows a post in these forums asking the same question with no responses indicating a lack of customer support and/or forum help. The company in general seems to not have an English language department and communication is terrible.
Pros:
Battle sequences are decent if too easy.
Lots of characters.
Cons:
No tutorial/help.
Built for console, terribly ported.
Camera is inexcusably bad.
Graphics are pretty bad.
Tons of crashes and bugs.
English language side of things seems to be deserted.
All in all, if you're a fan of this series you probably have more general knowledge about it and could enjoy it. However for people just now getting into this series, it is a complete disaster. I wouldn't recommend it to you even if it was free.

The biggest issue here with a "sequel" game like Gunz 2, is it will obviously be compared to the first version.
It should not be mistaken as a sequel, but rather a whole different game. Maybe the fact that its called "GunZ 2" is confusing people (I for one think it should be changed). GunZ was it's own thing. The glitching found by users that increased the gameplay and skill level of GunZ 1 was the reason why it was popular (before IJJI ruined it).
As a very dedicated player of GunZ 1 (since international beta and the founding of the move "butterfly") The whole interface and getting to learn how to play GunZ 2 was very confusing. The first thing I did was enter a game and attempt to K-style, utterly failing. The fighting was very chaotic, seeing people stun locking each other and spamming... which made me feel overwhelmed. It wasn't my cup of tea, because I thought GunZ 2 would implement K-style, and make its actions just look more fluid and actually look like a real "fighting style" (which I still think would be amazing).
However, I can see where the developers are trying to go in their path. A type of third-person shooter gameplay where everyone can learn to play easily, while still trying to be as intense and strategic as a clan rank fight back in Gunz 1.  More like a very fast-paced, ninja, gun slinging, counter strike. Until they make the gameplay as I "think" the developers are trying to achieve (matrix + conker's bad fur day multiplayer + ninjas with guns) I'm going to opt out in playing this game.
TL;DR  After playing GunZ 2, I missed K-style and was too nostalgic of the old GunZ I dedicated myself to and uninstalled half an hour in.

A combination of hackers, pay-to-winner's, bland maps and poor team efforts makes this a pretty poor show for a game! The most redeeming quality this game has is that you don't have to buy it in order to be disappointed, you can get that for free!
Seriously though, the maps are basically the same as they were a year ago. There's some pretty poor physics in all areas of the game but a prime example is tanks getting stuck on rocks. There's such a massive grind to advance in any regard that it's so unsubtly pushing you to pay-to-win they might as well charge you to play the game and give up the pretence of there being no need to pay for anything - because there obviously is.
At heart this is basically a team game, and while harsh as all hell to blame the game for this, the reality is that the people playing, aren't really time players. There's the occaisional few that are playing "properly," but for the most part it's people spawning, jumping on a bicycle and riding off into the trenches.
Put in enough of a grind though, and the game is mildly enjoyable. As long as it's free, and you dont mind replaying the same maps over and over, I'd recommend trying it for yourself and seeing if you can put the time into it to progress.
Ultimately though, it's a no from me.

Portal 2: The Final Hours offers insight into the history of Portal 2 and offers a glimpse at some of the things that go on behind the scenes in the true leader of gaming...Valve. Since 1998, Valve has continuously been the bleeding-edge body of gaming technology--not EA, not Activision, not Ubisoft, but Valve.
This interactive e-book offers a hands-on multimedia experience into what really happens during game development. Being an engineer myself, I know that Murphy's Law prevails--anything that can go wrong, will go wrong. Even the leader of gaming technology cannot break this law. Yet the ability to start from scratch after stepping back and saying "this product sucks" is such a rarity to see in this day and age. This story offers a rare glimpse at the talent, the culture, and the decisions behind a multi-award winning product.

I would reccomend this game.  However, I do NOT like the fact that it is a fighting game that has a character rotation like League of Legends.  It's a fighting game, should I buy all the characters just to play them?!  I don't think so.  Unlocking them, I can understand, but I don't like it when games force you to buy characters with money forcing you to play the game more.  For example, me and my friends found characters we liked, played them a lot, and then the week ended, forcing us to buy them if we wanted to play them more.  On the topic of characters, none of them are really unique.  Brawlhalla has a weapon based system of fighting.  Weapons will spawn on the battlefield, and you pick them up and beat each other with them.  Each character has 2 weapons, but none of the characters really stand out.  Sure, they have different stats, but you never feel the difference, and they all have the same attacks, except for heavy attacks.  The controls feel strange to me, because while on the ground, holding up and attacking does the same thing as holding nothing and attacking, but to attack up, you must hold DOWN and attack, unless you are in the air.  Speaking of the air, the air combat feels really floaty, which causes 2 problems for me:  It's hard to combo, and it's too easy to recover to the stage.  When your objective is to prevent them from getting to the stage, why is it that it is easy to get back to it, and why is it hard to hit someone in the air?
It's a great game with friends, but all these little things add up to be dissapointing
TL;DR:  LoL character rotation system, too floaty, and characters don't feel unique

Trine 2, the game developed and published by Frozenbyte, has yet again out done themselves with the side scrolling puzzle games. The game its self has had a few new tricks rolled up their sleeves for traps and monsters. The characters remain the same three (what would you expect) as they did in the first one and the game had what feels like a complete graphics overhaul that made an already beautiful game absolutely gorgeous. Taking from the first one the game play is almost exactly the same albeit a few differences such as the skill trees and the wizard no longer confined to a mana bar. Probably the best improvement was the multiplayer. The original Trine had it as well but isolated to just that one computer and it required you to hook up another keyboard and mouse or game pad to play. Now they have reached the 21st century and added standard Internet and LAN games. They even added a 3rd player to compliment all three classes.
I will go ahead and disclaim this information. I absolutely LOVE the graphics in this “interactive photo shoot” of a game. Trine 2 embodies everything that visuals can illustrate in a video game. Very few games ever show the amount of detail this game does and still maintain a solid game play experience. From dark dank dungeons and forests to the awe inspiring beach and frost covered ice lands this game does not skip on the little things. Even though the little things seem trivial the game continues to impress you with those features. I found myself looking forward to the next background scenery and taking screen shots of them like I was some sort of tourist on a “once in a lifetime” cruise or expeditions.
In short this game though on the shorter side (in my opinion, not the same as what’s becoming an industry standard) of actual game play is roughly 8 hours, it is still worth it to play with friends. Their expansion Goblin Menace, will add about half of the 8 hours the first part ran you with but at its heart it this game is easily accessible to any range of gamer and will provide at least a few evenings of entertainment if not one solid night of hardcore gaming. I highly recommend this game for its multiplayer, puzzle solving techniques and retina enthralling visuals.

I rarely change my reviews, but guess this is the case. Because I finally finished it.
THE GOOD
The visuals and the soundtrack are gorgeous. The game gets a lot more coherent near the end. The gameplay elements were used to reflect the outcome of the story (which I won't spoil for you, because you want to get there yourselves) and it was impressive. In the end, it all turned into a simple, but pretty decent fable.
THE BAD
A bad PC port. Not challenging, but tedious and repetitve puzzles. Too much melodrama in the beginning. A corpse dismemberment segment not going with the overall tone of the game. Frustrating controls. A certain bridge sequence (before the Inventor's House) was bugged, so I had to restart the checkpoint several times. Motion sickness-inducing camera. Long "press and hold one button" sequences. Overall, almost non-existent challenge. Badly written introduction. Bad "invented language", almost like Simlish (whereas Simlish added comedic value to The Sims, this game certainly is no comedy).
THE VERDICT
The game, considering its low price tag and short duration, is certainly worth playing. It will be frustration to some players, especially to those playing on keyboard (the game is designed to be played with a twin analog stick controller, so if you don't have one, it's twice the frustration). Don't overlook the motion sickness part - with the almost constantly rotating isometric camera, could be a problem for people with easily disturbed vestibular systems. If you're in it for the journey, and not the challenge, you'll likely enjoy it.

Trine 2 is a beautifully crafted side scroller for the PC. The developers absolutely nailed the "fantasy story book" feel for the game. The puzzles are fun and theres replay value for completionists as there are blue baubles you collect throughout the game and some of them are very difficult to get to.
Gameplay wise, its nearly exactly like Trine 1 so there wont be many surprises there (except for multiplayer but ill come back to that) Combat is nothing special and frankily pretty easy most of the time, especially with the rogue and her frozen arrows. Bosses and mini bosses will give you the most challenge in terms of combat, many behaving like Legend of Zelda bosses, a la "dodge, wait, hit the weak spot". This isnt a negative in my opinion though as it goes well with the platform jumping and puzzle solving that makes up most of the game.
Where Trine 2 really improved upon Trine 1 was multiplayer. Trine 2 is a good game in single player, but with multiplayer player it makes it a whole new game and a lot more fun. There are settings you can adjust for multiplayer like everyone being able to switch to any character (allowing you to brute force some puzzles if you wish) or have each player control only one class at once if you want a challenge. You would think having multiple people would make most puzzles trivial but surprisingly the the puzzle difficulty still slowly curves upward and most puzzles difficulty dont rely on how many players you have in the game. Mutliple players makes easy combat even easier though, most enemies will serve as minor roadbumps and you and your friends plow through them.
If you're looking for a combat oriented game, this isnt the game you're looking for. If you're looking for a puzzle platformer with funny characters and stunning visuals that you can adventure through with your friends, Trine 2 is the game for you. Overall a short but fun experience, especially with multiple people and in my opinion definitely worth the 20$.

I did not intended a long review for such a short "game" (it's literally like max 30 minutes if you go straight through it) , but I want to say something so the creators of this "game" can improove in the future. It turned out waaaaaay longer and more like a personal letter or rambling to the creators in the end rather than a review , but its your choice to read it or not.
First of, I find the description and thumbnail misleading a little bit. Whats up with that second girl on the picture? She is not even in the story? I got the best ending I suppose from the first try (the cheesy one) and after that I went through all the choices (witch are 3 only by the way) and possible endings quickly to see what happens and I didnt find that second girl anywhere! I went through achievements and theres 2 girls supposed to be in this, but I m sure I went through everything in the story and nothing is there. In the "extras" I found the endings and there are those locked ones with no way to unlock them. Theres nothing else in the story except those 3 choices and as I counted, 4 possible endings. Whats up with thoses locked ones? Where did the second female character go? A bug or what? Anyway I didnt had her and dont know if its supposed to be this way, so to me, the thumbnail is misleading. Also the ''game'' didnt gave me the achievement I should have gotten. The Ashley ending.
Description states that it will test our istincts by making choices. Okay, its accurate by the fact, but I dont know either  my instincts are lvl 999 on steroids + on drugs + on coffee + I'm crazy + meow or those are really just obvious and flat, easy choice options? I waited for a twist or something, no, nothing.  Its like going right or left, good or bad, there is no tricky misleading or something that would make it harder to decide and more interesting to go through.  And as that, it gets boring . You know where you heading. A good interactive story should mess with your mind and make you confused to keep you thrilled and interested. Also as I mentioned, theres 3 choices in total only.
The story is written very poorly, specialy for something that is placed on Steam in my opinion. The word choices feel cheap, theres a lot of typoos and its generally a mess. I dont know who made this, but it feels like it was written by a 14 years old die hard anime fan, who tries to write something like this for the first time ever. There are even parts that make no absolute sense with the rest of the story. The ending with the cabin was so rushed,its like 3 sentences, but the cheesy one I got (the kiss and promise and yada yada yada) was endless. It was obviously pushed towards as a passive romance story either way or another. As I said, its just screams "I was written by a young , unexperienced teen". Maybe ir was the real goal in it, but I just hate cheesy teen romance in general, so it annoyed me. I hoped for something more interesting and unusual. Why 90% interactive stories are pushed towards useless romance? Not everything has to include romance, even teens who write should understand it. But okay, the choice to push on romance is not the real case...
What else can I say? I dont inted to be an♥♥♥♥♥*** and I dont know how Indie games get here (dont get me wrong, I LOVE indie games and more than that i LOVE to support indie developers,even tho this is not a game really, but first, I always need to judge it the way I think is realistic) , but I think this is too weak to be on Steam for now. If the story would have been better written I would totally give the green light, but I just cant, because with writing skills like that, everyone can get their interactive stories on here. Go to beon or something, theres thousands of teens who write like this and some are actually real good. This should be a browser game for now. All I want to say is that this is not  enough to put your material out there, read plenty of other stories like this around, take notes and improove the story. You will be surprised how you can improove it over time. I know. I'we been there. I have material I have written for many years and not posting it anywhere because I felt I havent squeezed out the whole potential yet. This could have a better future aswell, it just needs a lot of work still. And yeah, I know, its for free, but just because its for free doesent mean it can be poorly made and everyone should close eyes on it. Seriously, you can go and read tons of those on the internet and noone puts it on Steam. Why this then? Why it was more special than others to get here with all the defects?
I know the creators of this probably wont read the reviews and mine can be harsh, but I m serious  and straight forward on this, its better to point out the flaws, so you can make it better and work with it rather than nothing at all. Who knows, maybe if you continue to improove, you will earn some money with it in the future.
Right now a solid No from me, even tho I would be curious to see if they actually try to make it better. Best of luck to creators anyway!
