Torchlight II's story follows the events of the first game, although those who come into the game without playing the original will not be missing much. Players create their own hero from one of four new classes, and are tasked with preventing one of the original heroes, who has been corrupted, from bringing ruin to the world. The story serves its purpose of giving players a reason to head off for the next quest goal but for the most part is pretty negligible, with the exception of a few rare quests of interest.
The options for character creation are expanded from the original; there are now four classes and each class has options for its gender, hair, and face. Pets also make a return, with a number of new creatures added. The pets are welcome companions, assisting the player by participating in combat, learning spells, being able to summon minions of their own, and even travelling back to town to sell loot and buy potions so the player doesn't have to.
Basic gameplay follows the template used by other isometric and top-down action RPGs. Players move using the left mouse buttons and click on enemies to attack. There are a wide number of skills and spells available, with numerous ways to activate them through various hotkeys and on-screen icons. The game allows for a lot of variety in builds and play styles, with each level up providing points to add to attributes and to upgrade and learn skills. Also provided is a lot of variety in equipment with no class restrictions, with the exception of some unique loot, although a number of skills require a certain weapon type. Loot in the game is plentiful, but fortunately the game makes it very easy to compare picked up loot with that currently equipped and to switch it into the pet's inventory so it can be quickly sold. There will always be the occasional pause midway through a dungeon to conduct some inventory management, however, outside of these pauses the pacing is quick and keeps the action going at an engaging level.
The dungeons are randomly generated in terms of overall layout, but specific areas like boss arenas are preset. This means that when playing multiplayer or a new game plus, it isn't a matter of simply retreading old routes, and the highly enjoyable exploration experience that the dungeons provide is always there. There is always a danger of such generated dungeons becoming generic and repetitive but it is pleasing to report that the danger has been negated as well as could be hoped for. A number of tougher enemies and special challenge zones litter Torchlight II's areas, providing fairly regular breaks from the usual fodder (who can still pack a punch if players aren't paying attention) and making sure things don't get too repetitive. The player character can become briefly stuck in a crowd that's difficult to maneuver out of, but these situations are rare and typically caused by charging in too wildly rather than through any fault of the game.
With the exception of Hardcore mode, where death is permanent, players can respawn without too much consequence. A percentage of gold can be paid in order for the deceased character to reappear either where they died or at the map entrance. Alternatively they can respawn back in town for free. There are four difficulty options to choose from plus a toggle for the aforementioned Hardcore mode. The Normal difficulty is a decent, but not especially challenging, level for newcomers, so experienced Torchlight players will likely want to jump immediately into Veteran.
Difficulty in multiplayer is handled well, with monsters increasing in toughness depending on the number of players. While it's certainly not necessarily to enjoy what Torchlight II has to offer, there can be no denying the enjoyment of playing the game with others and it adds a more than welcome dimension to the game. Those afraid of having their loot taken by comrades need not fear, as players get their own sets of loot visible only to them. There is plenty of postgame content for players to sink their teeth into after completing the twenty hour or so main campaign, either by tackling one of the main postgame dungeons or by starting a new game plus, which keeps the player's progress but levels up all the opponents to match. New game plus might disappoint some, as it isn't possible to notch up the difficulty, so those hoping for a greater challenge in the main story will need to start a new character. The game has also been created with the modding community in mind, so even if Runic's postgame options run out there will likely be plenty of fan-made offerings.
Visually the game looks great, even on less powerful computers, and for the most part runs very smoothly. The art style is great, the environments are all nicely varied, and the UI is clear and easy to use. Even when hidden behind terrain, it's easy to see where the character is and to click on enemies thanks to a coloured outline that appears for any combatant potentially obscured. Spells and skills are all beautifully animated, and it's incredibly satisfying to see enemies explode upon being finished off with a critical hit. Voice acting is generally rare, but it doesn't feel like the game is missing much without it. The key quest givers and few animated cutscenes are voiced, and it's functional for getting the next task across, but there's not enough of it to have any major effect and can be easily ignored without anything being missed.
For me Torchlight II was an immensely enjoyable experience from start to finish. The game is more than welcoming for both fans of the original and newcomers to the series and is high amongst the better gaming experiences I've had this year. It might not bring anything particularly new to the genre, but those who choose to pick it up will be provided with superb value for their money.

This is actually quite good. Its basically a more laid back version of Insane Fishing. This is not a game you will play for hours at a time or anything but its a good game for a 15 minute break or if you want to take a breather from something a bit more in depth. Give it a shot.

A FANTASTIC little mod that blew me away. I've been an absolutely massive HL fangirl for the majority of my life and have spent over a decade immersing myself in its universe. This little game gave me an opportunity to dive back into it once again, for free at that!
The game itself is very short but throughout it you're put face to face with dozens of puzzles that bring us right back to what we all loved in Half LIfe / HL2. You follow in the footsteps of a small group of rebels and if you're observant, can see encoded messages on walls or in the form of tucked away notes that were left behind.
All in all, I loved it -- All of it. With no price tag, you have absolutely nothing to lose by playing it!

So, I never played the first GunZ and I keep seeing reviews on how its worse than the first. While I usually say "You cant judge a game based on its predecessors" I have a huge beef with this game.
For one, when I first played this game, Wayne, the Cowboy, was the newest character. There was no Campaign (I think). Coming back now as my friends have started playing it, I find not much changed. 3 New characters, maybe 2 more maps.
Theres still a lot of Character imbalance. Where they tried to balance characters, they ended up ruining them. Not only that, but there seems to be no ranking seperation; meaning if you enter matchmaking you are likely going to be playing against a bunch of high leveled or veteran players with a bunch of noobs on your team. You can't even surrender and leave until 3 minutes into the game and your *** is grass by the 2 minute mark. Not to mention it takes like 5 minutes to find a match, if you are lucky, so you feel even more angry having your ** handed to you.
I originally started with Rena, the ninja-girl. She has a fast melee, fast close range and fast medium range. You'd think shes balanced because she lacks a true long range weapon, but no. By the time you actually see her, she'll be within melee range in 3 seconds. By that time, you are doomed, because most of her attacks knock you down, at which point she pulls out a gun to finish them off.
Theres a Sniper, also unbalanced. Hes got a massively OP melee ability that insta-gibs, and hes basically the only sniping class around. I havent played him but I constantly hear he's tough for noobs to play.
I JUST bought Wayne, the cowboy. It looks like they tried to bridge the gap between the Sniper and something more close range, and then the offspring was a mutant monster wearing thousands of belts. His ability allows him to mark enemies in a channeled attack, which he shoots at for an Insta-gib. OP, but only if you are high level, because you can only mark one enemy at early levels. His melee is pathetic. No-knockdowns (At least that I have figured out), slow, and weak.
I wont even go into the other classes, because those are the three classes you will see most often.
Next up, is the mechanics. Running on walls, dashing and dodging. Makes you feel like a ninja. For that I give a thumbs up. If you can master these mechanics, good on you. I find myself an Okay gamer in most shooter environments, but the controls are a bit clunky for me.
There are two shops. A regular one, where you spend gold to buy stuff. I think the only way to get gold is from achievements and buying it. These items are semi-permanent. The items can break, then disappear. At which point you have to buy again. You can, however, repair these items. Another shop gives you temporary versions of the items, and you get the crystals and ores to buy from this "Random Roulette" shop by doing achievements, and winning matches.
All in all, it's a pay-2-win model where all you have to pay is your time and sanity (Or if you dont want to pay that, actual money). I don't recommend playing it unless you are an achievement ***** looking for stuff to add to your achievement list, a 3PS fanatic, or are being held at gunpoint. I am currently only playing because my friends somehow like the game.

I will not discuss the story or reveal any plots however I will simply critque what is good and what is bad about it.
The first major glaring issue anyone will point out is that the story is a complete mess. The writing seems more ameture compared to its predecessor. By this I mean the characters seem more generic and exaggerated to have one stagnent personality, causing them to feel like characters then being real people. An example is all of the main antagonists because they talk about a plan that never really goes anywhere or has any major effect on the story. The characters never evolve but stay stagnent as the rich evil bad guys.
While DXHR did suffer some what in this regard many of the characters had proper motivations and feelings. While no game can top the first Deus Ex, DXMD feels like a giant step backwards from DXHR. While the story is not completly bad it is unfinished and unresolved. This mostly is the nail in the coffin for DXMD because when the game does start ramping up it just ends. To sum up the story its like all foreplay without the sex. It gives a average start to building the games later stages but then it stops.
This is speculation but I believe that Square Enix most likely told them to cut the later stages of the game to be sold in there season pass. Thus due to the lack luster ending the story takes a major hit.
This is so far the best part of this game. With the new introduction of the experimental augs it allows you to have more freedom on how you want to build your character. Unlike DXHR, DXMD does not punish your for playing loud or stealth. Infact with the new augs it gives a nice balance to both playstyles. In addition to the playstyles the map design has significantly improved. DXMD has many different paths that get you to one location to another.
A neat addition is the different varienty of ammos that can be used as it adds another layer to the combat system. With the new ammo it helps flesh out the variety in combat.
Also weapon customization has improved alot more as well as you are able to change your attachments during combat, similarly to crysis. The shooting has also improved as using guns does not feel as clunky as it did in DXHR. If you liked the gameplay in DXHR you will love it in DXMD.
While the soundtrack is not as memerable as the first Deus Ex the ambient synth tracks are nice and keep a good atmospheric tone throughout the game. I would not personally listen to these outside of the game however they are nice to listen to while exploring the hub world.
The VO work done here is very good. While the characters are generic the voice actors for them aren't. The main lead Adam Jensen is a decent voice actor and suits Jensens character, however I believe nothing will beat JC Dentons voice actor.

This is the more contriversioal part of the game, atleast for the pc port. So far I can say the frame rate is shoddy even when turning down alot of options. With my gtx 980 in some places in the Hub world I stutter alot to the point where I get motion sickness. The visuals are a giant step up from the first game since your screen isn't covered in♥♥♥♥♥♥ While I am not the biggest fan of the art style, I do not think its bad and it looks decent.
Another negitive with this game is the long loading times, even with the game on an SSD it will take upwards of 2 minutes to load parts of the hub world. In theory I am not against this but the problem is your constantly moving from one place to another causing you to wait for long periods of times before you can do anything.
While there are a decent amount of negetives, I must say the amount of options given to customize the graphics and interface is a positive. I have never seen alot of Triple A games give customization of the hud and the fact that its in the game is a plus.
The story suffers from ending right when it starts and even then the story they set up is mediocre at best.
The gameplay is the best part of this game and if you liked DXHR you will love this.
The sound and audio is good and the soundtrack is nice to listen to while in game.
The technical side suffers from a few optimization problems however the graphics and customization of settings is great.
The game has great gameplay but no story to keep it intriguing at all, while the sidequests are the only decent part of the story I do not see myself replaying this game alot since I have no personal investment or care in what happens. I reccomend getting this game on a sale however and trying it out for yourself.

FULL REVIEW:

All I have to say is I'm having no issues with this game, and so far it's amazing which is what I expected it to be. The only huge dookie stain smearing this game is the unbelievably detestable single=use single-save consumable items obtained through pre-order/DLC, AND the third-party influenced in-game store which you can blame Square-Enix for. You don't have to use it all. I don't even know it's there. Other than that, which btw they don't detract from the game one bit, everything is fantastic.

I had relatively high hopes for this game. I wanted to enjoy it, and I really believed it would deliver right up to the end.
I had no performance issues. The stealth mechanics and level designs are great, the RPG elements work well, and the environments and city-spaces are beautiful. Some of the side quests are pretty good. All improved on from Human Revolution.
Quite honestly, it's some of the best stealth gameplay I've ever encountered with level design absolutely unmatched. The developers deserve a LOT of credit for it.
So, what then, is the problem here? Primarily, the writing and story pacing is abysmal. I don't think this is readily obvious at first. Contrary to what others say, I think the beginning bits of the game all work out quite nicely in terms of plot and conflict setup.
That being said, I'll warn that spoilers follow, as I want to explain just what exactly is wrong here.
The problem with the game isn't setting up meaningful conflicts and story threads, the problem is a failure to deliver on these potential conflicts and threads in any meaningful way. In some sense, the story's total failure to deliver on numerous tensions and threads in the story makes me feel like I just played the 1st half of a 2-part game. It's astonishing, really.
Nearly all the characters seem like they are going to go through some sort of arc, development or evolution but do not. There seem to be tensions between characters that are being built up for some sort of development later, but nothing is ever delivered. What happened to this game? I honestly want to know.
Jensen feels remorse for trying to make the world a better place but seeing the results of his decision in HR. So, naturally, one would assume that this idea would play into the story, what he does, what he thinks, and ultimately he would evolve his thinking about his actions. Instead, there is nothing. Just setup for something that the game doesn't deliver. Completely disappointing.
David Sarif never meets you in person, but is in contact with you for most of the game in relation to a sidequest about Jensen's 'mystery augments' that are *actually* very mysterious. What happened to Jensen after he was pulled out of the ocean? Who put the augments into him? Why do people involved in his augments turn up dead? What is going on here? I was totally shocked when the quest, and I'm not kidding here, ends with Sarif simply saying, paraphrasing here, 'Huh, doesn't make sense, pretty weird man' AND THAT WAS IT! I mean, what? There is NO way to justify this.
(I also miss Sarif's old voice actor, I liked him better)
They build up all this tension about whether or not Jensen can trust his superiors in the 'TF29' anti-terror group and deliver nothing. Jensen and his hacker buddy spend all this time suspecting the director, Miller, of being allied with the illuminati or whatever. The story reveals later that they were just wasting their time and there was nothing.
Now, see, during one of these missions, we're shown a whole sequence between these two illuminati characters 'Joseph Manderley' and 'Rob Page' that seems to imply they are really pulling the strings and Miller is innocent. Our hero and his ally, Vega, simply ignore this and press on.
I figured the game was setting us up for a reveal about these antagonists and their plans later, but, no, nothing happens. They are never seen again. Manderley and Page talk about their secret plans vaguely but we don't hear or see more of them after this, and the player does not confront or engage with them at all. Why? All of this feels like a script with literally half of the pages torn out.
In the middle of the game, the player tours Golem City, a segregated living space where the augs are kept separate from most of society and regularly abused. The game sets up an MLK-like figure in 'Talos Rucker' who seems to be sympathetic. He asks that the augs protest peacefully and respond to violence with love and compassion. I had figured, silly me, that the game wanted to aim for some commentary over the course of the story about social change and the different ways to accomplish it -- why violence doesn't work. They do set up a counterpart character to him, one who will use violence to achieve his ends, but there isn't really much delivery or reflection on their differences or why those differences are important.
The game plays around with all these broad, very human themes but doesn't go beyond surface level with any of them. Racism and fear stand out among them. The game makes a great show of the augs vs. naturals conflict and segregation. Mistreatment. Injustice. Etc. However, it doesn't actually talk about or reflect on these things in any meaningful way. It seems to think that they can just show brutality and bigotry and expect it to be meaningful on its own, without any further commentary or nuance. Its a shortcut the writers are using, and an obvious one. I am not impressed and, trust me, I waited patiently for the game to make it more meaningful, but it didn't.
Jensen, in particular, has a lot of opportunity to observe and reflect on these themes, being both subject to mistreatment as an aug and also exempt from it by having friends in high places -- somewhat of a 'Geralt-like' position in that respect. No delivery, though, like everything in this game.
Numerous other characters, themes and threads I'm not mentioning here had great potential but ultimately turned out to be nothing. What a waste.
There are around 12 side quests, a few of them with better arcs and writing than anything else in the game. 12 though, really?
By the time the game ends I felt like I had only started the game or was just finishing the prologue to the real game.
For a game with such solid stealth mechanics and level design, for a game that presents great choice in playstyle and approach, what a tragedy that it is such a mess in its pacing, writing and character development.
Make no mistake, this could have been a really great game, but it isn't. I'd advise picking it up when it's on sale for $20 or less.

As an introduction:
The last Dynasty Warriors game that I played was 6 and the last Empires I played was 5 on my actual Playstation 2. So when this was optimized for the PC and up for grabs, I didn't hesitate to test it in a sale, as one of my friends seemed to like it fair enough. Further, I did like them for the stories in 5 and the general challenge on higher difficulties. So when I compare this, I will mostly compare it to 6 or 5 Empires. Keep that in mind!
Review:
The series has come a long way since DW 2 - one being a Beat 'em Up and thereby doesn't count - and had some reinterpretations. The most notable was DW 6 which revamped famous characters like Lu Bu. Let me just make one thing clear, I am glad they switched back to the old character designs for Lu Bu. They didn't do this for all of them until DW 8 Empires, but he was such a huge departure! The black armored and highly painted drag queen look didn't fit him at all. Now he looks graceful and deadly again. He still has his new weapon with his daughter owning his old hellebarde.
This minor point aside, how does DW 8 Empires compare to 5? As I previously mentioned I haven't played 6 or 7 Empires, so if any change was made prior, I can't judge it.
The gameplay has expanded with the Free Officer mode, so even losing your country does not end the game. You don't even have to start with one. Now you only lose upon death, which in this iteration is far harder to achieve then in 5. In 5 though you switched rulers then, here you are bound to your character. Something one might find less grand in the overall picture as the idea of the battling generations of the three empires falls flat with this feature.
The huge amount of events that DW 5 Empires boasted was significantly reduced in favor of clear and less events, with less forced or even complex triggers. That means some things nearly never happen. Also the amount of historic scenarios has been greatly reduced. This does streamline gameplay, but lost a lot of the story-telling focus of DW 5 Empires I enjoyed.
While the own officer area has expanded too with more visual features and the ability to let Steam share them on the internet with others, most of them will be named weird as not many immerse themselves in the Chinese history or naming convention. And some just look plain weird. Thus I tended to execute them whenever I got one with a bad name. Nothing personal, but foreigners have nothing to do there. So while this feature is a nice gimmick, it didn't find support with me. One can turn it off though. Following this, one can also build their own custom scenarios for the map and share them online.
If you achieve certain goals in order in the game, including the new but VERY repetitive quest system, you can get new titles that change your officers special abilities. If you unlocked one, you can set it to custom rulers by default. This is a nice goal for the long term, but will be a grind for certain special titles that tend to get overwritten by higher ones before aquiring them. So expect a lot of planing here.
The greatest change to the game was to the campaign and developements mechanics. So if you played DW 5 Empires, depart from that, and fast. Provinces still have local resources that must be unlocked with production buildings, but those count for the whole empire and not locally and some need a huge empire to begin with as they need up to 4 or 5 or 6 of them. And each province only has 2 bulding slots! This also includes schools to learn new battle tactics. This has also changed from DW 5, as you decided upon those tactics after you acquired them prior to the month and how to use it. Your advisors were thereby extremely important in DW 5 empires. Here, while the mechanic with bribes and special abilities has become more intriguing - especially the abilities, they do little that is important. Waiting for the Moloch strategem was important in DW 5 or others on high difficulty. Here you just call ONE. They are not such great game changer and affect the whole turn. Depending on the advisors ROUGH character, they might build something or do some politics, though. Yet, you can steers those anyway and force them to comply.
The system is only for the player to become an advisor. As a ruler they matter not, sadly. Further the intimidate ability is so broken, I won a extreme difficulty campaign in 5 years with its help. I only had to fight 5 chaos battles - all awfully hard with low starting equipment, mind you - overall unless I abused the province damage mechanic upon attacks. Something that makes the game a lot easier too. If you have money, you don't need to defend, you get a general with mass repair and just fix the provinces back up. This makes the game once again far too easy. This includes UNLIMITED savestates on Chaos difficulty.
The aforementioned battle mechanics that gave boons prior after being purchased in DW 5 Empires with the help of your advisors are permanently learned here and can be used in any battle. The only positive change here is the interactive element of tactics that beat each other or the fact of preparing and faulting an enemies grand ploy. For a general mechanic the old version was more immersive, reflected the permanent costs and more challenging in a long campaign.
The one thing I missed the most were the many cutscenes and collectible end movies from the past... and the story. But since I had departed from the repetitive gameplay for years, it felt REALLY refreshing for the first moment in a long time.
After all this, what is my judgement of DW 8 Empires?
Pro:
- Free Officer Mode with Quests to get your own empire and equipment going before taking on the land
- Potential to become advisor or ruler
- Better personal battle mechanics since DW 5
- Forgiving gameplay (Unlimited Savestates on Chaos, rare conquest through neglicience)
- More Character Design Options
- Character and Scenario Sharing
- Titles and internal goals to "collect"
Contra:
- As a ruler, your officers regardless of post don't matter, only their abilities.
- Advisors have limited impact on the game, your directive does.
- The new strategic campaign mode has been reduced in difficulty and streamlined, feeling less important
- Abilities are always available, losing their unique and game changing touch
- General difficulty reduced overall (westernized gameplay)
- Less historic scenarios and events
- Less cutscenes and beautiful music
- Unless you know how, you have to deactivate the custom officers in general to prevent XXRoxor45 to appear
Conclusion:
If you like the DW series, 8 Empires will change some things up from 5 and deliver a new and fresh way to play this spin-off series for once. So if you always wanted to focus on one character, are new to this spin-off franchise overall or have a less masochistic side to yourself, this game will keep you entertained for hours. My rating would be Finish it or if you enjoy such games, Complete it and see all of its facettes.
For the die hard DW fans who still own an old PS-System and DW 5 Empires and don't believe in a future remake, play this, enjoy it, then go back to your old friend and see the marvel that was DW5 Empires once more. The graphics will never compare, but enjoy the music, the detail to stories and events, the scenarios, the strategic map and importance of advisors, and rule China once again like a true master on Hard or Chaos. DW 5 was a game made on the pinnacle of the DW series story drive and focus. That focus hurt the gameplay of DW 5 itself with its character focus instead of the game campaing, but it was a marvelous uptake for the Empire game that only had appeared with DW 4 Empires. And I actually enjoyed the stories of DW 5, gameplay aside.

Dynasty Warriors has always been one of my favourite game series. DW6:Empires is probably the game I've logged more hours on than any other I've ever played. I love everything from the format to the hilarious pronunciations of Chinese names in the early games. Zhou Tai is as always my prefered character (even in DW6 when they replaced his iconic sword with a generic, spikey blade) and I love turning the reclusive, rough voiced pirate into a feared warlord in a comical, over the top Three Kingdoms period. That is why the Empires series is such a good concept for DW and always has been since 4. Alas, once again Koei insists on ruining it with a dumbed down, blatant cash grabbing scheme. The PC ports of both this title and XL are pathetic, direct PS3 versions of the game. I had believed that Koei had intended to bring in new fans from the West and to revitalise western interest in the series and allow them to take the risk of expensive voice acting and an improved vigour in developing future titles. Instead, it is clear to me that porting the game to the PC was just a way of pulling in more revenue without a single regard for old fans or those trying for the first time. The presence of over £135 of DLC is a plain insult to customers (£15 for some costumes, sod off Koei) and the original asking price was far exceeding even those of AAA games on release. I am chosing to no longer buy Koei games for the foreseeable future.
As for the gameplay, there are some brilliant new features this time around. The customisation that, lets face it, we've all wanted since the beginning is finally available. Extensive and fun character creation as well as the ablity to design your own troops, warhorses and flags is a blast despite lacking in content and overall features. No more purple clad soldiers fighting rag-tag amalgamations of Wu, Wei, Shu, Jin, Yuan and Lu Bu troops! Alongside these features, the scenario creator finally allows us to create the kingdoms we want and play out interesting new historical scenarios. The ability to have children has also finally been introduced, however the resulting offspring often never looks like their parents and is always attired in a really silly collection of edit pieces and look quite ridiculous. This is though, where the good ends. The campaign is only interesting for a few hours with very few events and boring cutscenes colouring your playthough. The system introduced in 7 to allow your character to develop a personality has been watered down and is fairly pointless. The ruler system featues also only consist of a select few options such as getting on good terms with officers and levying taxes or being philanthropic. It has lost its flair and the 'throne room' sequences get very boring, very fast. The implimentation of 'stealth' missions also betrays Koei's blatant disregard for fun and essentially boil down to avoiding a watchman with a torch and murdering an officer (permadeath is always a good thing and I'm glad it has finally been properly implimented in an Empires game but the system is only part of 'stealth' missions and no of big battles), repeat the same mission over and over again until you assassinate the ruler.
I could go on and on should I like to, but I shan't. To conclude, I am very disappointed and frankly insulted by Koei from this game and I would only recommend it to fellow diehard fans of DW and to buy it on PS4 (if you have one). I see this game as the arbiter to the downfall of a once great developer and beloved video game series. I hope in the future it can be revived, but for now the seires has died.  What a shame.

This is actually a 5-year old game that has recently seen a re-release with slightly updated graphics, some new game modes and 2 new achievements. As with many such examples the "vanilla" version is not available anymore, however, those (like myself) who had the original version will be happy to see the EX version immediately become available in their Steam library.
This is a horizontal shoot-em up with some pretty challenging and fast-paced gameplay. The design has a lot of steam punk elements and, for some reason, the Hungarian voiceover was replaced by an English one as default. As already mentioned, the game is quite challenging as it is not forgiving: while we can endure several hits they make us lose our weapon upgrades that makes battles significantly more difficult. Time is also a key factor and by getting hit it can get reduced to a point where completing the level will not be possible.
The story is quite interesting and there are a lot of cutscenes within each stage. As the game is difficult on the normal setting already it is highly recommended that you start playing it prepared - do not expect that Sine Mora is for casual players. Other than the often unfair difficulty this is a great purchase given the amount of games available in this rather obsolete genre.

Old-ish (2001) THQ game, but the first of a series, and a great FPS. I recall Red Faction 2 being awful.. Guerilla had its moments as far as 3PS' go. This game, however, has a nice plot, fair graphics (and hardly needs a top GPU), decent voice acting, non-stop action, and strange yet not totally distasteful music. Takes about 7-10 hours to complete, and for the low price, is worth it. Tip: manually save often, because when you die, there are no set restart points, it goes right back to the start of the game regardless of how far in you were. Saving gives a "Load last save" option and makes life easier. There are plenty of guns, no melee, vehicles, and set to Hard or Impossible should make a fair and enjoyable challenge for veteran gamers. Been a long time since I played this.. but have enjoyed the replay; a very nostalgic game!

I was sceptical about how people portrait this game at first and considered that even if playerbase problem is here, it will be fine as long as gameplay is fun.
Unfortunately, after playing it for a bit I found that it is not worth playing even from gameplay perspective.
There is one main thing you need to do in game about flying dragons that fight other flying dragons - it is flying and combat mechanics. This game dissapointed me in both of those things.
To start of, completely terrible tutorial that does not really teach you anything aside from basic "press this to do that", which can be covered just by looking at controls. Tutorial did not explain how aiming works, when you will hit enemy or not hit him, how to aim at moving target etc. You will be fighting other dragons in game itself, but tutorial does nothing to give you practice of doing exactly that. So when you will get in your first game you will be completely clueless and farmed by more experienced players, which is terrible first hour experience.
At the start you can only play one dragon and other dragons are locked. After you do your first battle (in which you are likely to be massacred due to not knowing of how to do air to air combat in dynamic situaion) you are likely to get at least some DNA and try to unlock new dragon thinking that with more agile dragon you will have better chances, but that will most likely do you no good either, because even most agile dragons feel like flying potatoes due to terrible flying physics.
Talking about flying physics, which should be one of 2 main components of the game, it is utterly bad. Dragons act like some sort of mix between helicopter and baloon.
Second part of the core - actual combat, is no better either. It was neither fun non engaging, and lot of it was completely unintuitive and terrible. For example very first thing I trying to do after getting in my first combat was to land on the rock so I could aim better. But guess what, dragon that slowly descends to smooth flat surface will get damage instead of landing on it, because there is no landing mechanic, but there is "collision damage" mechanic, where you take damage just for touching things... Aiming your main weapon, turrets, is done in direction you are facing only, and you can only shoot directly to the front. That is actually fine mechanic that is not new, but way it is done makes it almost completely unplayable to people who played air combat games in the past, mainly because of terrible user interface and bad flying physics. You can't ram into another dragon and use your claws for melee combat either. In other words, any elements that would actually be relevant for DRAGONS air combat are not there. You can replace dragons with "flying gun that faces in direction it is flying" and nothing will change. You can't even rotate around your body axis! It is pretty much "WASD" in almost same way as it would be on the ground instead of air, with addition of buttons to go up and down, this is how it feels. Games about aircrafts have aircrafts behave more natural then dragons in this game, which is completely dissapointing, because you would think that actual alive creature would perform better.
Finally, user interface. It is terrible. At the very start game trew at me message with contents of something like "You can play tutorial to learn things. You can skip it and play it later." No question asked. But under that message there are "Yes" and "No" buttons, on which you will stare with confusion not understanding which one is to play tutorial and which one is skip it, because there was no clear question asked, but it asks you to answer yes or no. After you get in main menu, you will see lot of things and stuff that is not explained anywhere and is scattered all over screen, with game forcing you to figure out what is up by yourself instead of giving simple explanation about it.
When you will actually get to gameplay, you will find that your crosshair will be facing only direction your turret shoots (which is direction your dragon is facing), but dragon will try to face into direction you face your camera on. There is no any indicator on where your actual camera is facing. There is no option to control dragon while having camera to only face direction you will be shooting, so this is very bad design.
After you get new dragon, you can't even test it anywhere. If you press "tutorial" after buying new dragon, it will just use defaut first dragon. This is something so simple, yet even that is not here.
And lastly, actual matchmaking. For my first game I queued into team deathmatch  and it placed me on empty map with no one aside from me. After waiting for a bit, someone actually joined it on enemy side, and guess what, it was player with level 20+ and non basic dragon. I had no means to defeat him because my basic dragon had worse agility and I just could not turn around faster than he would fly around me. If I would stop to do that, I would just be killed as easy target, if I would try to dog fight him while moving, I would get killed because he is more agile. Add to that fact that it is my first game and he is experienced in it, and you get the idea. To add to that, other people started joining game, and it is not uncommon to have completely unbalanced games with 3 against 1 and such. No balance whatsoever.
My verdict: bad experience in general from first minutes, and even if you will force yourself to putup with all that, because basics of the game are not done well either (combat and flying physics) you will likely endup not enjoing it even if you ignore everything else.

A good piece of material for those who want to know background stories of Portal, even other Valve series.
An interesting read. There are so many stories about the development of the game, and from the people who made it.

An interactive, digital, audio filled, book. Such a lovely treat to take a small trip into Valve to see just how they ended up where they are now. Of course, as the title says, taking a look at Portal 2 itself. You can't go wrong with this.

Gameplay Video:
Starting as cat with a basic rod the controls are simple, you can play this with one hand. Fishing up the smaller species initially and selling them will reward you with money, which is used for purchase of better rods or upgrades to current equipment. The game then introduces you to it's quest system, completing these tasks rewards larger sums of money. While questing the fish catalog becomes useful as it will display all species in the game.
Sometimes fishing in the depths you may discover rare hats, which not only look cute on cat but give large bonuses to both your fishing abilities and values of catches. More tongue in cheek one-use items available later include rockets and bombs but everything has it uses. In these cases scaring away packs of fish or making your cast go much further with cheaper rods. Boat travel is also included, but I have not progressed that far yet.
Content wise, If you check the store page the developer mentions and I quote.
"Regular updates will bring new fish, boats, hats, and entirely new mechanics to the game, extending your experience and offering new ways to master the game. "
Addictive and enjoyable for all ages. Easily recommended.

I like this game, even though I'm not a fan of this type of games in general.
I'll start with a summary:
Game-wise, the options are limited, but the game remains fun.
Technically, I have yet to encounter a bug that would impede the gameplay. The devs also keep the lower end in mind, but there is room for improvement there. Respect the specs.
Visually, the game loosely follows the source material, incorporates more realistic shading and uses original character models. This was a subject to a little controversy during EA, but despite rooting for the other camp I think the game ultimately came out on top.
All in all I'd give it a 7.8/10 "Will have a fun time playing coop with friends on occasion"
And now for a small wall of text:
I veer more towards FPS titles and more openworld rpg games, often times bordering on sandbox. This game is third person, linear with invisible walls everywhere and a severly limited system for customisation of gameplay. So why do I like it? All of abovementioned contribute to it being exceedingly simple and compact. And as far as design goes, simple and compact is a good way to go.
I have been following the game since early access and had my fair share of doubts about some of the dev's decisions, some of which made me post salty comments, but when faced with where their journey took me, I can't help but see it all made sense.
-The combat system saw many iterations and cutting off excess fat and clunk was benefitial in the long run. Now I'm not saying the game is perfect as it is now, but it has gone trough a lot of improvement. I am looking forward to what comes next.
-The progression started off almost simplistic, with progress being reset every play. As it is today, you can beef up your character and hit harder and stay that way, or you can CHOOSE to reset and git gut urself to compensate. You'll also get a number for this that you can increase and show off and brag about it. If you want to, of course. No shame in not being a ranked hunter. No shame at all.
-The visuals became more and more realistically shaded, for the better or for worse. It turned out ok in the end, but I still remember the update with experimental shaders and WIP models back in early access that made me see what I can't unsee. As it is now I think it will nicely go along with the more realistic shading of the upcoming RWBY vol 4.
As time becomes more of an issue and timesinks cease being comfortable to get away with you realize the point in middle sized games. There is no 40x40km map, but at the same time it is not a small platformer. It's in between. There is no need to allocate time for a 6 hour session when a fun game with friends can be had in 30 minutes.
As for the DLC, I put my money where my mouth is. I bought it. And I bought it for a friend. It is additional content well worth the 5€. Nora best artilery.
The game could have a tutorial, but with the simple combos it has you really don't need it. It is entirely possible to figure it out in a very short time with some button mashing.
Hardcore fans of the genre may not find it challenging.
Hardcore fans of the show may not find it containing Zwei.
Hardcore fans of fun may find it short but fun.
And I think that's what matters in the end.

I had relatively high hopes for this game. I wanted to enjoy it, and I really believed it would deliver right up to the end.
I had no performance issues. The stealth mechanics and level designs are great, the RPG elements work well, and the environments and city-spaces are beautiful. Some of the side quests are pretty good. All improved on from Human Revolution.
Quite honestly, it's some of the best stealth gameplay I've ever encountered with level design absolutely unmatched. The developers deserve a LOT of credit for it.
So, what then, is the problem here? Primarily, the writing and story pacing is abysmal. I don't think this is readily obvious at first. Contrary to what others say, I think the beginning bits of the game all work out quite nicely in terms of plot and conflict setup.
That being said, I'll warn that spoilers follow, as I want to explain just what exactly is wrong here.
The problem with the game isn't setting up meaningful conflicts and story threads, the problem is a failure to deliver on these potential conflicts and threads in any meaningful way. In some sense, the story's total failure to deliver on numerous tensions and threads in the story makes me feel like I just played the 1st half of a 2-part game. It's astonishing, really.
Nearly all the characters seem like they are going to go through some sort of arc, development or evolution but do not. There seem to be tensions between characters that are being built up for some sort of development later, but nothing is ever delivered. What happened to this game? I honestly want to know.
Jensen feels remorse for trying to make the world a better place but seeing the results of his decision in HR. So, naturally, one would assume that this idea would play into the story, what he does, what he thinks, and ultimately he would evolve his thinking about his actions. Instead, there is nothing. Just setup for something that the game doesn't deliver. Completely disappointing.
David Sarif never meets you in person, but is in contact with you for most of the game in relation to a sidequest about Jensen's 'mystery augments' that are *actually* very mysterious. What happened to Jensen after he was pulled out of the ocean? Who put the augments into him? Why do people involved in his augments turn up dead? What is going on here? I was totally shocked when the quest, and I'm not kidding here, ends with Sarif simply saying, paraphrasing here, 'Huh, doesn't make sense, pretty weird man' AND THAT WAS IT! I mean, what? There is NO way to justify this.
(I also miss Sarif's old voice actor, I liked him better)
They build up all this tension about whether or not Jensen can trust his superiors in the 'TF29' anti-terror group and deliver nothing. Jensen and his hacker buddy spend all this time suspecting the director, Miller, of being allied with the illuminati or whatever. The story reveals later that they were just wasting their time and there was nothing.
Now, see, during one of these missions, we're shown a whole sequence between these two illuminati characters 'Joseph Manderley' and 'Rob Page' that seems to imply they are really pulling the strings and Miller is innocent. Our hero and his ally, Vega, simply ignore this and press on.
I figured the game was setting us up for a reveal about these antagonists and their plans later, but, no, nothing happens. They are never seen again. Manderley and Page talk about their secret plans vaguely but we don't hear or see more of them after this, and the player does not confront or engage with them at all. Why? All of this feels like a script with literally half of the pages torn out.
In the middle of the game, the player tours Golem City, a segregated living space where the augs are kept separate from most of society and regularly abused. The game sets up an MLK-like figure in 'Talos Rucker' who seems to be sympathetic. He asks that the augs protest peacefully and respond to violence with love and compassion. I had figured, silly me, that the game wanted to aim for some commentary over the course of the story about social change and the different ways to accomplish it -- why violence doesn't work. They do set up a counterpart character to him, one who will use violence to achieve his ends, but there isn't really much delivery or reflection on their differences or why those differences are important.
The game plays around with all these broad, very human themes but doesn't go beyond surface level with any of them. Racism and fear stand out among them. The game makes a great show of the augs vs. naturals conflict and segregation. Mistreatment. Injustice. Etc. However, it doesn't actually talk about or reflect on these things in any meaningful way. It seems to think that they can just show brutality and bigotry and expect it to be meaningful on its own, without any further commentary or nuance. Its a shortcut the writers are using, and an obvious one. I am not impressed and, trust me, I waited patiently for the game to make it more meaningful, but it didn't.
Jensen, in particular, has a lot of opportunity to observe and reflect on these themes, being both subject to mistreatment as an aug and also exempt from it by having friends in high places -- somewhat of a 'Geralt-like' position in that respect. No delivery, though, like everything in this game.
Numerous other characters, themes and threads I'm not mentioning here had great potential but ultimately turned out to be nothing. What a waste.
There are around 12 side quests, a few of them with better arcs and writing than anything else in the game. 12 though, really?
By the time the game ends I felt like I had only started the game or was just finishing the prologue to the real game.
For a game with such solid stealth mechanics and level design, for a game that presents great choice in playstyle and approach, what a tragedy that it is such a mess in its pacing, writing and character development.
Make no mistake, this could have been a really great game, but it isn't. I'd advise picking it up when it's on sale for $20 or less.

Deus Ex MD is a disapointing entry in the Deus Ex series. It has a minimalistic, bare-bones story that feels like it ended half-way through. In a setting rich in conspiracy, the only question Mankind Divided leaves you with is : where is the rest of the game?
Despite being graphically stunning, Mankind Divided is a terrible Deus Ex game (but fairly fun as a game in itself.)
There are effectively four missions in the game and one of those is a tutorial. Sure, there is a lot to do in exploring Prague (which is a wonderful setting and Mankind Divided does an excellent job as realising the city as a near future city on the edge.) However, exploring Prague never feels like a substantial part of the experience and is a poor substitution for scripted content.
Mankind Divided's virtues are superficial and its flaws are deep. Tacked on micro-transaction heavy breach mode is the most obvious of its failings, and it doesn't take very long for the busywork to start feeling like a game by UbiSoft.
I don't feel robbed for my time, but I also don't regret putting the game down for nearly a week after my first day with it to play games that embody more of what Deus Ex was about than this. If you wanted a smart, branching narrative, then you will be moderately disapointed as well. This has a dumb, forked narrative. (e.g. the big mid-game reveal is that Bob Page, the villain from the first game and one of the Illuminati, who the game heavy-handedly tells you are the badguys, is the villain.)
I wouldn't buy this at full price. I'd wait until the "I didn't ask for this" edition comes out and goes on sale.

I've only played this game for a few hours altogether so far, but I feel like I should already leave a comment at least, if not a "review."
I saw the name and I saw the footage, and of course it's a Super Smash Bros.-style 2D platform-fighter.  I felt like it was going to be an artless ripoff, but the reviews were already positive and it's free, so I liberally applied the ♥♥♥♥-it adjustment.  Color me impressed.
I was worried about it being F2P initially, of course, but that's definitely not an issue with this game.  Legends can only be permanently purchased with gold, it seems, which is only unlocked during gameplay by completing matches and missions.  Missions can only be completed in matchmaking via online FFA or ranked 1s and 2s.  However, completing custom online matches still rewards Legend XP and match gold!  I was pleasantly surprised to discover this when I invited a friend of mine to play a custom online match on a team with me versus medium-difficulty bots.  I think this makes grinding much more approachable to people like me who frankly suck at PvP...
As far as spending money goes, you can purchase Mammoth Coins that are used for unlocking Legend skins, weapon skins, taunts, and sidekicks.  Five bucks nets you 100 MC, and everything ranges from 40 to 200 MC on the... "Mallhalla" store (cute).  Only one item actually seems to be 200 MC right now, with the next expensive tier being 140.  That's like seven bucks, which seems pretty reasonable as far as I'm concerned.  They definitely aren't trying to strongarm me into buying anything, I can't even buy Legends with MC.
The gameplay is very fluid.  Connection isn't perfect yet, but I can forgive that for now, especially since I don't have to pay for the privilege of lagging to death.  The game itself is very gentle on any PC, I can't imagine many people have problems with performance if I don't.
The weapon system is really cool too, in my opinion.  Each Legend can fabricate one of two weapons alternately by picking up weapon spawns on the map, and the weapon combination that each Legend has available to it are displayed by their stats on the Legend Select screen.  Each character has a slight twist on how they use each weapon, but you can be sure more or less that they have nearly the same feel -- using the spear on Ada and using the spear on Orion feel similar even though they have some different moves.  The same can be said about using the lance on Orion and using the lance on Sir Roland.  They're not copy/pasted movesets but they're not wildly different either, so it's easy to move from Legend to Legend without being terribly uncomfortable.
It's a 2D platform-fighter, as mentioned above, and it plays nearly identical to Super Smash Bros. in basic terms.  Two to eight Legends fight each other on arenas of floating platforms.  You try to build damage on the enemy Legends so that you can smash them off the side of the arena and screen, killing them the same way you would in Super Smash Bros.
If you enjoy playing the Super Smash Bros. series for more than just the familiar faces, Brawlhalla is definitely worth trying a round or two in singleplayer for free just to see for yourself.  The download is small, the game is easy for computers to run, and it's free to play and easy to learn.

Kingdoms of Amalur is an interesting game. The world is grand, larger than many other games, yet almost intimidatingly so. The graphics are nice, not quite great compared to today's games, but much better than those in the time it was released. The music fits quite well with the areas.
The combat mechanics are easy enough to follow and learn, and the custimization is quite fun. The weapons are fantastically fantasy-based, often being impractical for anything but a game. It has the feel of an MMORPG, but sadly lacking the Massively Multiplayer part.
Traveling between locations is a challenge as monsters are everywhere, and side quest dot the cities and countrysides. Monsters move around sections of the map, and can join each other in combat if you aren't quick at killing them off. Stocking up on healing items is a safe bet for travelling, especially early in the game.
As a whole it's a good game, but it's a shame that the developers put so many details into it as a foundation for something much larger. In it's origins, this was going to be a base for an MMORPG, which is shown with the map size and UI choices. If you want to try this, I'd recommend buying it on sale.

A first person shooter where you are the only one who can save the miners of Mars from oppression and effective slavery.  The exploitative and heavy-handed mining operation on Mars advertises itself as something very different to their workbase, and the corporation in charge seems happy to live up to the 'bad guy' template.  Spearhead the independence of the Red Planet!
Enjoyable gameplay, though as of today (2015), it's a bit dated.  The AI is simple, but not unintelligent - giving yourself away means guards will track you down.  The plot is simple, but gives a good pace and leaves little doubt to who is deserving of the 'hero' title.
The weapons have a decent variety to them, and let you choose your preferences for taking opponents out, with their own feel and method of play.  You also get the feel of the main character being a miner, not a professional soldier, with the way that accuracy is handled - even with the reticle dead on, your shots may spread.  It's easy to visualise that as being drift from an inexperienced shot.
The sound quality was a bit average, even for the time, with some noticeably cheap voice acting and special effects more akin to an arcade game than a first person shooter.  It's not bad enough to be cringeworthy, but it does break immersion pretty badly at times.
As said, the game's dated now, with graphics having been left well behind*.  The AI is a little predictable, running to you, shooting/hitting at you, and then running away if they get hurt, before returning to repeat the cycle.

Honestly, I'm beyond disappointed.
Prior to the Mortal Kombat X launch, I was genuinely excited for the game. I had some good memories ofplaying the older games as a kid, and I some fun with MK9, but was a bit disappointed with the balance of the game.
So, I preorder this game. It looked well polished, great graphics and sound, smooth looking gameplay, tons of content, it had it all right? The launch was shaky at best. NRS tried a "streaming download" system with this game, where you downloaded the game in parts, and could play it as soon as it downloaded the parts necessary for gameplay. It's imilar to Blizzard's  system in that respect, except it didn't work. I'm going to largely ignore the launch issues here, because they were fixed pretty soon, even if they left a bad taste in my mouth.
So, game finishes installing finally, and I hope online after a bit of practicing combos. I'm greeted with the most unplayably laggy online fighting game experience of my entire life. I am talking a solid 2 seconds of delay here. After a few more matches, all ending the same way, I decide to play some story mode. To be fair, the story is pretty fun, and well done for a fighting game.
I decided to wait until the port was fixed, with the lag issues and a nasty memory leak being present. I kind of forgot about the game for a while until I saw some cool Jason and Predator DLC matches on youtube. I figured "Hey, the port has been out a while, they probably fixed the problems right?", no they didn't.
Not only was the game still a mess, but NRS decided that they would completely abandon development of the PC version of the game, and it would no longer recieve any patches or DLC. This for me was the last straw. I'm personally never supporting NRS or WB games on PC  again until they can prove to me that they deserve respect as a developer on the platform.
Do yourself a favour, save yourself a headache, and buy a game that actually works like Guilty Gear or Street Fighter.

Full disclosure,  I played Diablo 2 for years.  When ever I had to upgrade to a new computer, I would buy a new copy of Diablo 2 and the expansion and install it.  I have played hundreds of hours on both Diablo 2 and Torchlight 2, except I don't play Diablo 2 anymore.   Even the vanilla version of torchlight 2 has deep custimization of character classes with different gameplay for all.  For me it is like the developers of Diablo 2 heard all the complaints I had about it and then fixed them for torchlight 2.   Just the shared stash by itself is such an implovment.  The modding is not as deep as Skyrim, but it does allow for things like new classes.  Some people are put off by the graphics, but I for one  am happy that  it is not another drab, tired fantasy, midevil, D&D, tolkienesque clone.  Instead, we are given a colorful, exotic, steampunk, H.P. Lovecraft  setting.
The only cons I can think of are cons that all ARPGS seem to have.  The  story is generic and it is on rails.  You are the chosen one out to  stop the great evil before the end of the world, bla, bla bla.  Unlike a sandbox RPG like an Elder Scrolls  game or even Dragon Age,  your only choice is to do side quests or ignore them with no real consequences.  That does not detract from how much fun this game  is.  Bottom line, this game is well worth more than full price and is I think the best ARPG out now.

Very nice, informative and interactive background story of the development of Portal 2.

It was interesting to read some of the design ideas and game mechanics during the early stages of Portal 2 (it didn't even have portals!). This interactive digital book contains a ton of pages, took me about 2 hours to complete. I also got a sense of what it takes to produce a game at Valve, how many ideas are experimented with and how many ideas are cut. This may not be new to veteran Valve fans, but the executive Valve team has a very good eye for fresh new ideas and talent, this book goes through the series on how people found their way into working at Valve. The last few months before the Portal 2 release had some nail-biting events.
If you are a veteran game enthusiast like me, this is worth the buy and read.
This is a great story, lots of interesting stuff about Valve, combined with a lot of behind the scenes stuff.

Its a really great smash-like game that's more focused on reaction and counters rather than action and attack. I absolutly LOVE this game, but here are the characters that are ridiculously overused and how they normally play based on my experience in competitive and, to some extent, normal online.
1-Hattori: The sweatiest tryhard who will do 1000 attacks/second, throw every weapon off the stage so that you won't get it, will leave the second the match is over and will never treat it like a game.
2-Bodvar: Is generally fun to fight, but you just see a lot of Bodvars and 1 in 10 act like most people who play Hattori.
3-Ada: The character that will spam the same moves with guns and can be fun to fight when she has a spear.
4-Orion: The character that spams his side heavy and hardly does anything else.
5-Lucien: You don't see Lucien as much anymore. I don't have a lot of problems with him other than the amount of easy combos this guy can do and his seemingly high damage with very fast speed.
I really love this game, but somethings need to change so that more characters get the spotlight, specially with how easily it is to combo with guns and how spamable the laces are. Still, this game is absolutely amazing, but a lot of the things I've mentioned are brainless and not fun to fight against.
Two of the things I think the game needs:
1-1v1 matchmaking that doesn't affect the person's ranking. (Think the normal online mode, but just 1v1)
2-A weaponless mode. It is really fun fighting without a weapon, but there's no real way to casually practice against other players like practicing in the 4 person ffa online mode.

Deus Ex: Mankind Divided is a fantastic game in a lot of ways. The level design is superb as to be expected with the Deus Ex franchise. The one hub in the game, Prague, is huge and incredibly detailed. The game looks amazing, and it plays well too. A lot of things like the cover system have been significantly improved.
The side quests in this game were wonderful and took up a lot more time than they did in the other Deus Ex games. Unfortunately, that is all I can praise. The story itself is dissapointing to say the least. It feels very short, ends abrubtly, and leaves a lot of plot threads for either another game or the 2 story DLC's that are going to come out. The setting is also frankly boring. While it sounds neat that the Augmented are being segregated when in usual sci-fi it would be the normal humans, nothing is done with it besides the obvious "racism is bad" metaphor. There isnt a 2 sided debate that has good points on both sides like in the previous game, Human Revolution. It also feels very bizzare how the only hub in the entire game is Prague. I was very impressed by how intricate the Prague hub was, but i would have gladly taken a smaller Prague if it meant we got to travel somewhere else. For gods sake, this is a Deus Ex game and you dont even go to Asia! You technically do go to other places in the world, but these are only in the main levels and you dont get to explore the area outside those levels in other countries at all. But, I can overlook all of that because Gameplay is King and this game has had the best gameplay in 2016 besides the new DOOM. What i cannot overlook is the greed in Square Enix. PRE-ORDER BONUSES BOUND TO A SINGLE SAVE SLOT AND MICROTRANSACTIONS IN A SINGLE PLAYER GAME ARE AWFUL. THIS IS A $60 GAME WITH NO MULTIPLAYER ELEMENTS ASIDE FROM THAT STUPID BREACH MODE THAT NO ONE CARES ABOUT (Deus Ex GO, a mobile puzzle game feels more like a console game than Breach which is saying a lot), AND YET YOU CAN JUST BUY PROGRESSION IN THE GAME. AND I STILL HAVENT FORGOTTEN THE 'AUGMENT YOUR PRE-ORDER' THING. Absolutely cannot reccomend buying the game given these greedy developers. The main Story Mode here is a series of short fights strung together by long cutscenes and story dialogs voiced by the various characters involved. The cutscenes and story content seem to last longer than the actual gameplay much of the time but don't worry, when you replay you can hold LB to fast-forward the cutscenes. They are totally awesome though. The sharp, detailed artwork pans around in 3D as the characters talk to you about the mission, then the scene seamlessly blends into 2D, your plane settles in its firing position and off you go.
You control various designs of WW2 style propellor planes but your enemies are highly advanced mechanical aliens with fabulous tentacles and so forth. As you shoot to the right and try to dodge incoming bullets, colourful powerup beads drift past and you have to try and catch them before they disappear off to the left. When you get blasted or hit an obstacle, instead of losing health your powerup beads are released and your firepower diminishes to a trickle until you frantically pick up your lost beads - they bounce off the edges a couple of times before they disappear so you usually have time to recover most of them.
There's a sort of points system where you're awarded 'coins' for completing stages. When you die(I think that happens when you run out of firepower but I'm not sure) you can use these coins to respawn and try again. When you finally run out of coins it's Game Over and you have your final score. In this case you don't necessarily have to start again from the beginning, you can start at the beginning of any of the 7 chapters you've completed.
They've certainly squeezed every last drop of replay value out of the available content: Arcade Mode lets you choose any type of plane in any colour to suit your mood; Score Attack invites you to repeat each story chapter and try to improve your scores on each one; Boss Training lists each of the game's bosses for you to beat up over and over again; Challenge sets you a series of standalone tasks that are not present in the main story mode, such as dodging mines; Versus is a multiplayer mode where you get to shoot each other.
Most of the negative criticism of this game centres around the poor hitboxes and sluggish responsiveness. These people make fair points, but they are clearly young, 'serious' players of modern shooter games with high expectations and the reflexes of a housefly.
I used to play this type of game in my youth, on the big arcade machines, and this is exactly what they were like. It brings back all the nostalgia and schoolboy excitement but with modern glitzy graphics and sounds. I'm definitely what you would describe as a 'casual' player here, and I love having all the graphics and story with small doses of shooting in between. I'm not on the edge of my chair yelling at the screen in frustration, just enjoying the experience with all the colourful symmetric bullet patterns flying all over the place.
The voice acting is great but, be warned, the characters use very strong language, I'm talking drunken-sailor level swearing and references to♥♥♥♥♥♥ Is this really necessary, I ask myself. This is just the type of game that would appeal to kids with all the colourful stuff flying around the screen, but unfortunately you can't even disable the sound for the kids because the effing and blinding is still there, in all its glory, on the subtitle boxes.
I've only played story mode on easy setting so far, and even then I started to struggle on chapter 3 (of 7). There's hard mode and I can't even imagine what that must be like! So yea, I suppose I'm contradicting myself having said it's for casual players. I don't know. I'm confused. Suffice to say that I keep dying but I don't care.
12 achievements which seem to be extremely hard to get judging by the global stats, and are represented very nicely in-game. I have zero and not expecting to improve that count any time soon. Trading Cards, Cloud and Leaderboards all supported but sadly no Linux.
From my perspective I'd say it's well worth full price, for the production value and generally slick presentation. I'm no shooter expert though, so I don't know how it holds up gameplay-wise against the many other titles in this genre. You'll have to work that out for yourself.
This game has its haters but I love it. It's not something I'll be spending long sessions with, but it's perfect for dipping in and out of when I'm in the mood for a bit of fun and eye candy.
It's fair to say that there are some inconsistencies and annoyances, for example walls camouflaged against the background so you crash into them accidentally, so if you're a purist shooter expert this may not be for you.

With the caveat that I'm not a big shmup guy, I thoroughly enjoyed Sine Mora and the improvements brought with the EX version. Lovely art, an engaging minimalist story and a slow-down mechanic for the reaction-time challenged, what more could you ask for? I've seen some people lamenting the difficulty, but honestly playing on normal mode I haven't had much trouble, and while there's a definite element of pattern recognition at play I've managed to beat most levels on the 2nd or 3rd try at most. Plus, once you beat a level it's unlocked as a starting point, so no need to run through previously completed ones if you're not chasing scores. I can't really say where it falls in the pantheon of shmups, but if you're the kind of person who likes to occasionally dip a toe into the genre this was a uniquely entertaining entry in the genre.

Its a really great smash-like game that's more focused on reaction and counters rather than action and attack. I absolutly LOVE this game, but here are the characters that are ridiculously overused and how they normally play based on my experience in competitive and, to some extent, normal online.
1-Hattori: The sweatiest tryhard who will do 1000 attacks/second, throw every weapon off the stage so that you won't get it, will leave the second the match is over and will never treat it like a game.
2-Bodvar: Is generally fun to fight, but you just see a lot of Bodvars and 1 in 10 act like most people who play Hattori.
3-Ada: The character that will spam the same moves with guns and can be fun to fight when she has a spear.
4-Orion: The character that spams his side heavy and hardly does anything else.
5-Lucien: You don't see Lucien as much anymore. I don't have a lot of problems with him other than the amount of easy combos this guy can do and his seemingly high damage with very fast speed.
I really love this game, but somethings need to change so that more characters get the spotlight, specially with how easily it is to combo with guns and how spamable the laces are. Still, this game is absolutely amazing, but a lot of the things I've mentioned are brainless and not fun to fight against.
Two of the things I think the game needs:
1-1v1 matchmaking that doesn't affect the person's ranking. (Think the normal online mode, but just 1v1)
2-A weaponless mode. It is really fun fighting without a weapon, but there's no real way to casually practice against other players like practicing in the 4 person ffa online mode.

I started my jouney in Swadia with nothing to my name. I, Griffith, made my name as a commander of a mercenary group: The Band of the Hawk, until I gained enought renown that and swore my Vassalage to King Harlus of the kingdom of Swadia. I fought with him for several months. I won many battle, lost a few less, and lost countless men. But throught this I began to make my way in the world.
It wasn't long before the Kingdom of Swadia began to lose ground after all of the wars it had been involved in. I knew the country would not last much longer in this world. With this in mind I asked King Harlus to release me of my Vassalage. Because I was now such a respectable man and a renowned fighter, he released me respectfully and held nothing against me.
Soon after I met a fallen lord who claimed to be the rightful ruler of the Khanate. I swore my sword to him and set out on a quest to help him restore his lost kingdom. Now, with a sizable force, we seiged castle after castle and town after town until we crushed the Khanate and restored my lord to the throne. After our victory, he released me from his service and I was now alone again with my mercenary band. I spent the next few months fighting other lords wars in the deserts.
I began to notice weakness in the nation that I had just helped to rebuild. The lords bickered with eachother and trust was non-existant. I decided to use this weakness to seek a throne of my own. I began my attack by seiging a castle as an offical declaration of war and a signal of my betrayal. The country was weak and I stomped my enemies under the flag of my new nation: "Falconia." The already weak nation was quick to fall. In one final battle, and the fall of their last city, I captured and executed the king I betrayed as a show of strenth and as a call to the world that Falconia is real and to be taken seriously. Now the Band of The Hawk was not only respected... but feared.
After that a few lords from around the world came to swear fealty to me and my nation began to grow. We toppled entire kingdoms and conquered to region in only a few short months. I, Griffith, was now high emperor of Caldaria.
Thats how this game goes. It's the best non-linear game out there. This was my story, but everybody else' will be different. 99/10. A true open-ended RPG fan can't find a better game than this.

Short (6 hours), yet recommened piece of work. Reading the other reviews you get the picture: beautiful art work, pleasant music, touching story. While the puzzles never get very difficult, they didn't get repetitive or utterly boring either. I really liked the gameplay concept (one gamepad, two characters), which kept me challenged, and the relationship between the two lovable, likeable brothers.
Wanna sit down, relax and get into a very enjoyable journey? This is it.

I picked this game up in the Christmas sales for €1.49, I said "Sure it's cheap, why not". Then WatchModjo put up a "Top 10 Best Indie Video Game Stories" video (which you should watch for some very good recommendations) and I said sure ♥♥♥♥ it, I may as well play it. I highly recommend you play with a controller, although you will get mixed up at times, it happens.
The story is about two brothers on a quest to the Tree of Life, for a cure to their fathers life threatening ailment. The overall story covers so so much, like grief, loss, adventure, companionship, love, friendship, fear, strength and humor. The achievements come from a few little sidequests and actions, which should be explored on your playthrough, some will make you laugh, go awww or even gasp.
From first glance, I thought the game would be all happiness, with an upbeat tone throughout, this is not the case in some parts, you will come across grim scenarios, moments where I felt like I had disrespected something or someone. If you see this game on sale or as part of a daily deal for €1.49, I would highly recommend picking it up. It's a game that's 4 hours long at max, something you could play and finish in a night and tells such a good story. It goes to show such a cheap and simple game can even out do a €60+ game. Of course, it does have a few glitches here and there, I had it crash once and stutter on cutscenes but nothing to write home about.
An idea I would pitch is a two player option, I could see this being a lot of fun with two people, although as frustrating as Portal 2 co-op. Still, you could go halves with the controller or alternate methods of controls.
Pros +
- Great Story
- Interesting NPCs and Characters
- Good puzzles
- Nicely paced
- A rainy day game
Cons -
- Controller required
- Couple glitches, nothing major at all
