The other reviewers aren't exaggerating when they say it's a clumsy port with terrible controls. I bought it anyway, because there are always those comments on DW ports- but this one is much worse than usual. So be aware that it will take a fair while to get used to the terribly rigid and awkward controls! For example, using a controller you have to move the camera to strafe or go off in any direction other than NESW. If you can get past the controls and movement, it's not so bad. The weirdly rigid controls were terrible until I got used to it, but after the first few days it hasn't had much affect on my enjoyment of the game (as you can see from my time played!)
Other than that it's standard DW fare, with some extra gameplay elements added.
- There's the addition of a 'strategy system'- you choose up to 6 abilities to use in battle.
- There's an actual change in strategy compared to all other DW games, in that you are required to use strategy even on normal or lesser difficulty. You can no longer make a beeline to the enemy main base, you have to have control of an unbroken line of bases leading from your main camp to the enemies' main camp. The enemy is also stronger in their area of control- where you are further from your bases, troops, and supply lines. You can't go lone commando as much as you can in other DW games- not saying it's a bad change though!
- You can influence your leaders policies, slander other officers to get them fired, tax areas under your control, raid an area to weaken it before invading, get married and have kids who follow in your footsteps and in general look like their parents.
As always in Empires, you can make your own character. They've gone farther this time, and you can mix and match some pretty nifty characters. You can have your custom officers (and those of others) enter the game at random. They seem to have more customization than in previous Empires, and the faces certainly look better than they have previously.
All in all, there are some really interesting changes to the gameplay in this version of DW but I would recommend it only IF you can get past the truly horrible control scheme.

Mankind Divided does everything that human revolution and to an extend the original do, except it does it better and adds a lot more depth to the gameplay in a very dynamic and fluid manner. The controls are instantly recognizable by every pc player, mouse and keyboard worked perfectly and i hardly had to change any control-settings to instantly jump in.
All the great mechanics of human revolution are back and slightly enhanced, for instance you're no longer forced to hack every terminal, computer or securuity system even if you have the code for it to get the most xp out of it - you still can, but you don't have to since you'll get the same amout of xp as you would if you were hacking. The level design is absolutely amazing - you have atleast 3-5 different options to get through every area of the game and there is no sense of "damn i investet in the wrong abilities" - every possibility is covered - always.
The new augmentations added to the game are also a very welcom change of pase and add another layer of envoirement interaction. The remote hacking tool let's you remotely disable cameras, laser grids, robots, drones and interact with many other different envoremental items like ladders, blinders to obscure the A.I.s view into a room and a couple of other things. You can use it to enable or disable radios or tvs to create distractions. Simply put one out of the many new augmentations that not add only a singular purpose but give you multiple options on how you want to use them and approach any situation within the game.
Jump higher and use the new Icarus Dash? no problem you're able to explore different parts of the map now. Combine it with the remote hacking tool and you'll be able to traverse the map in a completely different manner than before. You can reach new places and use the envoirement to your advantage.

Not gonna say much except this: Makind Divided won't answer every question you have after human revolution, in fact it will open a ton more but also gives you new ideas to play with. It feels like an intro to a bigger game, or atleast as part 1 of 3 of a new trilogy. The endgame is further away than it ever was. If Human Revolutions scope of story introduced you to this world - this adds a TON more background information, reintroduces some of the franchises most enigmatic characters and delves deeper into what is really going on withoug giving you any answers.
Some of the most interesting story bits of the game you'll find by exploring. By picking up items that give you the possibility to then, if you keep exploring access certain places where you'll find computer terminals and ebooks. Those "hidden treasures" contain some of the most interesting bits of story this game has to offer and you'll feel rewarded to finding them in the first place.
So is the story good even if it feels cut short? Yes! The story is very much on par with some of the best out there, even if the scope isn't that big. It feels like the first book in a series of more awesome books that guide you through amazingly craftet twists left and right without feeling to be overplayed. You'll be pleasently surprised by the high quality dialogue and voice acting aswell as the exceptionally good cast behind almost every side character.

Again i can only praise the overall sound design, as mentioned earlier, the background themes and well placed envoiremental sounds only enhance the exceptionally good voice work here. And to those who like to explore every bit of story there is - the voice acting of certain characters actually play a big part in some of the possible twists. You'll understand when you play the game.

Okay i'd like to say this first:♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Microtransactions. No matter where and when and how, if you're paying a premium price up front, there is no excuse for ANY developer to include microtransactions. And even though i do love the game and think it is probably the best in the series so far, this can not be overlooked and i hope games media in general will start banning games from awards and other events if there is a 60$ price tag added ontop of microtransactions. They work for free to play games but not for a supposed triple a title period.
Now to the topic at hand, i don't know why there are microtransactions included at all. You will NEVER ever need them in the single player since you'll be getting praxis left and right and still have enough credits to buy pretty much anyhting you want. There is no need to ever spend a cent on any of this.
The same goes with the "one time use pre-order dlc" they might as well not be there at all. The skins are nice to have but just that, skins. Everyhting else is kind of pointless. The game clearly was not deisgned to give the player any incentive of ever buying anything from thier shop which is a commendable but still sad thing. Why are they there? because the publisher said so - food for thought.
The optional breach mode is in my opinion a very welcome change of pace. Alot of people don't like it, others condemn it because of the mictrotransactions, but again - those "pay to win" elements are not necessary to be there in the first place. You can beat EVERY mission in this mode without ever droping a cent. Everything that you can buy with real money can also be earned relatively quickly by using the credits you earn for completing missions.
You do feel however, a huge spike in difficulty once you reach the "tier 3 server" which is kind of the reason most people feel they have to buy those premium weapons to get through that part of this mode. But first of all, at that point you already completed two thirds of the mode and with a bit of pre planning and preparation those missions can be done aswell. This is the part where you'll either learn from you experience so far, or just expect a pushover difficulty level which is at that point the players fault.
So after about 60 hours, i managed to beat the game on the "give me deus ex" difficulty, explore every corner of prague and do every available side quest and "points of interest" that i could find. In that time i also managed to "complete" the breach mode (all missions done aswell as most challenges completed). And after those 60 hours it still feels a bit short, because i wanted more of that quality, i wanted some more amazing envoirements to sneak through and more excellent story. The end of the game teases you of things coming in future games which might be it's biggest flaw.
Instead of giving you these amazing missions and exotic locations that are talked about you're playing the prologue to those experiences instead of actually getting to see the meat of it. So if i had to slap a rating onto the game it's an easy 9/10 in my book. DX:MD is by far one of the best in the franchise and tops human revolution in everyhing but size of story. You won't regret getting this game unless you rush through the main campaign without doing any side stuff. Trust me you'll be disappointed by the story if you do not find certain emails and other stuff that adds an even wider context to things happening the game.

TL:DR: Buy it when the GOTY-edition is on sale, skip it until then. Consider replaying 'Human Revolution' in the meantime.
PRO's:
Eyecandy: The game is gorgeously looking.
Leveldesign, absolute freedom on how to execute a mission choosing between a near infite array of possibilities. (Example: The Bank.)
"Side" content: Well written and composed, gives the feeling that even the unimportant NPC's are people too. Downside: Poor execution of this content. (A: You've really got to look for it, sometimes. B: The game would benefit more from a decent main plot than it would from the fact that "NPC X" lost her cat.)
Skill Tree: Full customization of the character to fit into any kind of playstyle. Although, on the downside, by the end of the game it's very well possible to nearly have all augmentations unlocked, which (if played "right") makes Jensen an unstopable killing machine, regardless of specialization.
CON's:
AI: It's perfectly possible (I played on the "give me a challenge" difficulty) to leave bodies in plain sight, have the enemies go ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, trigger alarms and wait for everything to cool down (possibly after hacking in to the alarmsystem), just to see the enemies return to business as usual as if nothing happened. This is worked in several missions as well as in the social hub.
Bad optimisation at first, no longer much of an issue due to patches.
Breach-Mode: I don't even ...
Bugs (even game-breaking), no longer much of an issue due to patches ; although seeing people disappear into the floor/wall/objects is a turn-off. As is people killing me with invisible guns and camera's seeing through walls.
Content DLC releasing a month after launch: Not okay. Either put this content in the game, or wait longer before releasing. This gives me the impression content was cut from the game in order to milk more money out of the consumers. (Combine this with some of my other gripes, and I'm sure you'll see I could be on to something.)
Microtransactions: Having people pay real life money for in game money/items or even XP is *NOT* okay.
Paywall: Certain content (abilities, weapons, ...) are hidden behind a €4.99 paywall.
Social Hub: There's just one. It's not that big. It gets boring real fast and, aside the vendors and sidequests doesn't really add much of a value as being a social hub. Especially compared to Detroit or Hong Kong of the previous game.
Story: Seems to be missing a lot of things which have been cut out. (Example: Game ending leaves several questions unanswered ; Side missions don't really have an ending, they *just end* ; Characters drawing conclusions in between mission based on information the player (could have) missed ; ...)
Voice-acting: Not Peter-Dinklage-In-Destiny bad, but bad. (Example: Sarif ; Czechian "accents" overall.)
I could go on and add more things, but I'm lacking the time. I'll edit the review to add stuff if I feel like it.

Let me start by saying that I've had this game since it was first released as an open beta, and have seen it improve by leaps and bounds. Therefore, this review may be a tad optimistic, but that's becasue I see where the game has come from, where it is going, and I'm satisfied with both.
So...
Start out by saying this is not a AAA title. It does not play like one, it does not run like one, and it is not priced like one. This feels more step-up-from-labor-of-love, borderline indie game.
Which it is.
The combat is fairly similar across characters, with a few differences. Some characters are definitely better than others.
The story is...ok. First time around, it's alright. The only time you'd really replay it is for either grinding or speedrunning.
Yeah, there's a lot of grinding in this game. And not necessarily the fun kind either.
So, what's good about it?
Well, although the combat system can be a bit spammy at times, the rewards for delving deeper and figuring out original stuff are certainly there. If it feels too simple, you can complicate it. If you feel overwhelmed (realistically you won't, but for the sake of argument) you can dumb it down.
Horde mode was just added recently, and although there's currently only three maps right now, I can see it being a lot of fun for quite a while. Much more difficult than the Story, and spamming will only get you so far. Good luck beating it with less than a full team.
Honestly, the game is hit or miss. If you like the combat, it'll probably keep you interested for a decent amount of time. If you don't, then stop, because it really doesn't get any better.
As for the DLC fiasco? Well, it's not great, but it's certainly not as horrendus as it seems. JNPR was going to be DLC from the beginning, and considering they're a package deal instead of $2.99 per character, it's better than I thought it would be. Of course, I'd have liked it if they were free, but that's cause I'm cheap.
That being said, they are well worth it, considering how much fun these characters are.
Except for Ren. Why the hell can't he attack out of air dash!?!
$25 for the whole package is on the more expensive end of being reasonable, but it's not too bad.

I'm not even really sure how to review this game.  I very much want to like it, but I just can't.  The combat system is primarily at fault for this.  It's some strange combination of dynasty warrior styled multiple opponent combat and arena fighting game.  Dynasty warriors works because of the large area of effect that attacks take up, but in this most attacks only target a single opponent, which is only chosen based on the direction your camera is facing and the direction button your pressing.  I'm not really even sure which combination of the two targets what opponent.   This makes using ranged attacks a chore, and melee unforgiving because it's too difficult to specify that "yes, I do want to attack that grimm that's attacking me before he gets his attack off" or "no I want to keep attacking this grim because my combo will move me out of the way anyway."
There is a counter system, but its use is not effective or fun.  When you're fighting multiple opponents that each can attack without regard to the others.  This means that you often wind up countering into an attack from a different opponent.  If it were more like Batman where enemies avoid each other in order to line up attacks then the counter system might work.
Many of the "boss" fights aren't difficult, they're merely tedious at best and frustrating at worst.  They don't take a lot of skill, just a lot of running a round spamming attacks.  The gameplay is irritating enough that I don't want to force my way through even for the story, and I want to know the story because until the show says otherwise; it's canon.
If they had split either direction and gone dynasty warriors against hordes of Grimm (like the show) it would have been good.  If they had gone for a more combo oriented arena style fighter it would have worked.  Instead they've managed to split the difference between the two just enough for the game to not work either way.  As much as I love the show and am following the manga, I can't recommend the game.

Sine Mora EX is a side-scrolling shoot'em up that provides a unique challenge, where time is the ultimate factor. Mixing classic shooter sensibilities with contemporary presentation, Sine Mora EX is a gorgeous shoot'em up offering both a Story Mode that weaves an over-the-top tale and an Arcade.
I'm torn. I like shooters, and Sine Mora EX is a very pretty shooter with all the important mechanisms, weapon upgrades, multistage bosses, great looking, etc. It has an interesting mechanics where you have given time for a level, each hit taken substracts from that time, each kill adds to that time. When the time ends, you die. There are several ships to fly with somewhat different main weapons and totally different bombs. And have I mentioned that it looks great? It does.
The problem is the game is sometimes overwhelmingly unfair. Take one of the bosses for instance, the boss enters from the left side, where you usually position yourself. If it touches you it's insta kill, and you have zero time to react. There's a level where you fly through a cave, touching a wall equals being hit and it's very easy to touch a wall because sometimes the barrier wall will look exactly like the background wall. Unavoidable insta-kill lasers? Yup, you can find them here. So basically while the game is very pretty to look at and quite fun to play, sometimes you just die, for some random reason that is so very unfair it ruins all the fun you had just a minute ago.
It's not a bad game, it just requires more patience than I can muster.
I liked:
* looks, it's a pretty game
* some boss fights are really cool
I disliked:
* the insta kills
* unfairness of some levels/enemies
Get this if:
* you like tough as nails sidescrolling shooters and are not easily discouraged
Don't get this if:
* you're bad at shooter games, there is no easy mode here and limited continues
* you're short on patience

Highly enjoyable game.
Dragon games are rare, for reasons I don't understand. They always seem to be from small studios. They always introduce new and interesting "flying monster" designs to pair against their classic dragons.
This one is no different. It follows the formula, but with a sci-fi twist.
It's a lot of fun, I have to admit. It's not perfect. The game's evasion mechanic needs work, for instance. Some beasts don't have quite as competitive abilities as others. So, don't get me wrong, it isn't flawless, but it IS fun.
Yes, you're basically playing a gunship dueling game, if your gunship also had a flame thrower.
Yes, that is a good thing.
---------------
HOWEVER
Absolute trash community.
I do mean complete garbage.
With the exception of maybe 2 or 3 people, the accusations you see are real. People will sit with healing dragons in groups in death match and heal each other, waiting for you to spawn. If you get them low on health they will sit there so their friend can get the kill, denying you any experience.
Team Death Match also has people who will shoot you in the back, although I honestly don't know why it's such an issue, maybe they know each other. Whatever the case is, they abuse the game in a way which kills it for other players.
As it is now, there is absolutely no reason to play this game, there is simply no way to make progress if you encounter any of the Russian players in groups. Individually, they're quite easy to shoot down usually. I've met only two players who put any actual effort in to trying to fly their dragon well, the rest were cannon fodder at best, but when in groups they will swarm you and help each other out.
Perhaps this would be less of an issue in other play modes, but as a new player you can ONLY do Death Match or Team Death Match, and it's a long grind to Level 10 to unlock the next play mode, and then you need even higher levels to get the ones after that. At level 9 I've essentially given up, needing tens of thousands of experience, but getting maybe 100-200 per game because kills are routinely stolen after being ganked by my own team mates.
I don't understand how it is fun for them, and the devs have made it clear that with their primary coder being away for the time being that there will be no continued development until they get a new coder. We shouldn't expect to see anything to improve player experience in the near future, or for features which are advertised as "soon to come" to arrive either.
The game itself is fun, but much like EvE Online and League of Legends, a toxic community destroys it. As it doesn't already have a large player base, I can see how this is a real theat to the continuation of the game in the future, and I hope they get a handle on it before they have to give this otherwise gem of a game up and shut down the servers.
For now, it sadly gets a thumbs down. It doesn't deserve it, but as the player community is a part of the game experience, and the game is not designed to support harrassed players, there's no way else my reccomendation can go.

Deus Ex: Mankind Divided is a great game. It has a well written story (for the most part - more on that in a minute), a very satisfying minute-to-minute gameplay loop, and incredibly well designed interesting and versatile levels.
It has a lot references to the prior games (including referencing characters, origins, and groups from the very first Deus Ex) but could easily be enjoyed as a standalone game.
If you enjoyed any of the other Deus Ex games, you will enjoy this game.
There's only two flaws in the game IMO. Firstly - it runs pretty awfully. It's clear it was made for consoles first, then ported to PC. The gameplay systems don't suffer, but the performance does. They have already improved it a LOT with two patches, but a lot more love is needed.
The second flaw is the ending of the game. I won't discuss specific spoilers...
The game's narrative ends in a very unsatisfying abrupt manner. Part of this is the game being a victim of it's own systems - you are faced with a choice. The choice is meant to be impactful and intense, but if you have played the game like most Deus Ex fans do - exploring everywhere, doing everything, etc., you will be likely able to do both options in the choice, even though the game suggests you cannot. This removes the stakes for the final conflict and means it feels very underwhelming. Up until this point, the narrative thread had been fine. It's just the final moments that let it down.
Overall, this is the second best game in the franchise (the best still being the original Deus Ex) and is a great game in it's own right.

However, the story is so sparsely fleshed out, the characters make it feel like the game is set within a Michael Bay buddy cop film. The poor and vague Eastern European accents are unconvincing and the art direction at Eidos have completely abandoned the gritty futuristic sheen of DE:HR and replaced it with some kind of badly developed social realist film. Along the way you will experience pointless ‘places of interest’ in order to begin side missions. They should be named places of disinterest. The side missions are so sterile and predetermined. The voice acting is just bad and completely off with the tone of the franchise, which to me was reminiscent of Mass Effect 2. At least that game had a lot of incredible side missions and like Human Revolution, had a bit of scope to it.
Ultimately though this game became more enjoyable on the second play through, I maxed out all my Augs and it made the game a hilarious sand box to ♥♥♥♥ about with, The Nano blades are a refined version of the crossbow from DE:HR which created the funniest takedowns being able to pin people against walls and crates. The new Tesla gun and P.E.P.S that can destroy a police drone in one charge are both amazing.
But unless they return to the art direction of the previous game they risk putting me off wanting to buy any future DLC or game. Not only is the campaign terrible but also the side missions are almost as pre-determined as the narrative campaign is. This whole game is an 'on the rails' interactive movie with a goofy physics sandbox to mess with along the way.
In summary, if you were to compare these games to their film counterparts you would have to say that DE:HR was Ridley Scott's Blade Runner, and DE:MD was Neill Blomkamp's District 9.
But it was definitely amusing and I love the gameplay mechanics of the franchise. I hope they make the game a whole lot less camp. It's a full reversal of the grit of the previous game, they had a real opportunity with their portrayal of Golem City but they just made that a short pit stop. That could have been a sprawling place to travel to for side missions but you can only go there once and it wasn’t shocking at all no matter how much the cut scenes, which I eventually gave up watching, liked to big it up.
It's a bit like Django Unchained.

2.	 Then delight in the most brutal depictions of enacting some Terminator extreme prejudice♥♥♥♥♥♥on your fellow man.

Okay, I have been proven wrong before when I have enjoyed a game in Beta, but I really hope this goes through into actual full release.
When people say it is like Smash they are right. When thy say it is a Smash clone, they couldn't be any more wrong.
The basic set up is very Smash-esque but the play is a style in its own right. You play on a 2D stage with minor elements of hazzard such as pit falls and smashing an opponent off the stage which is all very Smash like.
But where it comes into its own is its style of combat. You all start off bar fistedwhich all have the same move set of a straight knuckle, upper and sweep to knock an opponent off.
But each character has two sets of weapons which you obtain randomly from pick ups in on the stage, a good few seem they are cloned but most have their own unique combat style and flare, making no two the exact same to play as. You also play with low gravity and a lot of moves capable of keeping you air born, making for some cool air born fights and juggles. Even when it seems to be over when you are falling to your death, you can make an epic come back when you use the right moves from the edge of the stage.
The combat style is what I love the most though about the game. It is all fast, all go with no time to rest, yet it flows really nice and keeps you excited, even if you are losing you are still just enjoying the rush and pace.
To top off, each character has their own bio and are quite unique in the looks department and varied. There is quite a selection already and can't wait to see what other characters they release and what new weapons they include.
All in all if you like Smash, Get it! If you like a decent and developing fighting experience with quirky characters, Get it! If you just want a game to let off steam on or just enjoy PvP, Get it!

The game that started it all, , Red Faction is still a great game that started the idea of a destructible world and succeeded. It's a great FPS and an absolutely fantastic, classic experience. A strong first person shooter of a classic era, the destruction lets you do anything. Got a locked door in your way? As long as you have ammunition, you can blow a giant hole around it, or even under it.
Mars is to provide more resources and possibly become a new Earth. It is commanded by Ultron, a conglomerate familiar to fans of the Saints Row series, that commands slaves to do all the work of gathering resources for them. You begin as a miner, soon freed by the rebel group known as Red Faction, quickly finding no alternative, you ally yourself with the rebels. Quickly working your way above ground and destroying all the things important to Ultron, only to finish the game by cutting off the head of the snake, letting the body die. Who is the main character, you ask? Why Parker, of course, a character that has a section of the planet named after him in Red Faction: Guerrilla. If you like going back to classics or trying to understand the appeal of a classic game, or maybe want to know more about the history of the Red Faction series, then prepare to be excited because this game is fantastic.

If you liked Diablo 2, you'll love this game. While the story and composition are almost exactly identical to D2, there are a few changes that I absolutely loved. I found the skills very approachable, you can make your build as simple or as complex as you want, and most builds are effective. You can no longer upgrade gems the same way, so you don't need to feel compelled to collect and keep all the gems. They added a limited ability to respec your character, so you have a few levels to play around with skill choices, which I found useful. However, the most notable change (for me) is the independent treasure drops. There is no longer a mad scramble for the best loot if you play multiplayer. You can take all the loot you see, which made multiplayer infinitely more enjoyable for me.

Much like past Empires releases, 8's release throws in a handful of new things for you to mess around with. You can get married and have kids, and make decisions about being a freelancer or a servant, but ultimately everything you do is in service of unifying China, usually by force.
Right off the bat, you'll create your own hero to fight as, rather than the main entries' focus on fighting as a variety of different warriors. Pick their design, armor, and moveset from Dynasty Warriors 8 and set them off onto an adventure which will involve sticking with them long term, until they carve their own destiny out for themselves.
A big part of the strategy involved in Empires comes down to deciding how to best spend your time. There is a menu-based system in place which gives you a series of options, with each available action taking one month to complete. After a certain number of months, you'll attend or host a war council meeting where your long-term objectives are set. The challenge here is working out how to balance your time.
Initially, I sided with a much larger faction and piggybacked on their success. Every time a new objective was set, I had to decide how much of my time to dedicate to furthering the goals of my faction, and how much of the time to put toward working on my own personal goals. Every month I could avoid working on faction goals allowed me to grow slightly closer to independence.
There was also the balancing act of working out how long to spend with that faction before going solo. The longer I stayed with them, the more resources I had at my disposal for personal growth, but the larger my faction grew as a potential threat. Knowing one day I would split off, I didn't want to put too much of my effort into beefing up a future enemy.
Once you eventually break out solo, you have a lot more say over how to focus strategically. You can go fully diplomatic, violent, or a mixture of the two, but violence overall feels the most fulfilling route. You have to try and keep a mental handle on how thin it's safe to spread your forces, how fast it's safe to expand, how long you can stay put fortifying yourself, and how fast your enemies are expanding their influence. There were a number of things I constantly had to be aware of, but it never felt overwhelming or unfair. Combat is pretty much unchanged from Dynasty Warriors 8, which in my opinion is a good thing.
The dual weapon switching, combos, and special attacks remain unchanged, with the main differences being tactical elements of how you engage in fights on the battlefield. Empires features a far more detailed map, with a higher focus on overall strategy when overtaking bases. You'll find a series of strategic bases, which need to be overtaken one after another to work toward the capture of the main base. The more detailed map allows for more strategy, but it also caused me some stress while trying to make progress across the map.
Feeling like I had to always be aware of enemy movements and counters to my advance meant that where I would have powered forward in a main Dynasty Warriors game, here I often stopped and backtracked to keep the odd one or two people from slipping through my net.
Ultimately, I came away from Dynasty Warriors 8 Empires extremely satisfied. The tactical elements outside of battle were well balanced as to be challenging while fair, and the combat carries over the best elements from the main game. It's a bit of a specific niche it's catering to -- fans of Dynasty Warriors combat and long-term strategy elements -- but if those two things are your jam, then Empires should have you hooked.

How this game has a mixed rating at the time of this review I have no idea.  I'll tackle the main three issues people seem to be complaining about.
1.  Microtransactions.  I didn't even know they had them to be quite honest.  Beat the game and spent 24 hours on it, not once did I see anything mentioning microtransactions.  Not once did I feel the need for them.  In fact, if anything this game could stand to be a little bit more difficult.  I maxed out everything I wanted to about half way to 3/4 the way through the campaign.  I can't imagine what people would want to buy.  But hey, if some guy wants to throw more money at the game, let him.  This game is amazing and I want more of it.
2.  PC performance.  Now I have a 1070, so I may not represent everyone, but I ran through this entire game, everything on Ultra (no MSAA, Hard Contact Shadows ON) without ever dropping below 70fps.  This is not a bad port.  These guys gave us really high end graphics options, and it seems people cried because their 1080gtx couldn't max it at 4k.  That's silly.  Overreactions galore here.
3.  The rushed ending.  Well, I can see why people would say this.  But really, my main complaint here is that the game is so damn good I didn't want it to end.  It still gives you 20-25 hours of gameplay EASILY on ONE playthough.  You could rush it down to less time, but then if you are speedrunning why is game length a concern of yours.  There is a full game here no question.  And it's a very good game at that.
Now that that is out of the way.  This game is amazing, it rocks, go buy it.  Best stealth game I've played.

Despite minor issues I've gotten with the game (I've listed them below) and the publisher mandate for micro-transactions (and the poor handling consumable of items from DLCs), it's been a fun ride so far. It's also stressful, but I find most stealth-based games stressful anyway :)
I want to take a moment and touch on people's opinion of Jensen. Maybe it's pointless to state it, but how people perceive Jensen is biased on how they play the character in the first place. In games, the player characters are supposed to be our proxy, a way for us to interact with the game world. If we pick decisions that make Jensen seem bored, then that's how he'll come across. So far, I've picked decisions that make him appear passionate to me. Of course, I have the social enhancer augmentation installed, but I found the answers that got me the best results tend to be worded with compassion.
Other than that, the game's fairly solid (even on day 1). I like that there's usually more than one or two ways of getting around. The game will funnel you into a specific spot from time to time, but that shouldn't surprise anyone.
As for the issues I've mentioned (basic computer specs: i5, GTX 960 (2GB RAM), 8GB RAM, installed on an SSD):
This has been touched on by other reviews, but I like to put my two cents in. The micro-transaction isn't in your face at all. I think the only way I could access it is by going to the main menu. I don't remember seeing it or being pestered to buy something from their store while in game.
The only thing that bothers me is how they handled consumables provided by the pre-order/DLCs. When they say one use, apparently they meant it literally. You only get to use it once on one save. It's probably using the micro-transaction system to deliver this consumable. I'm not happy about that, but I also disabled the consumable DLC so I don't have to think about it. I'm not sure how the weapons are handled. I get the sense that they're also save-locked. I never took them out, saving it for the hardest difficulty instead.
Honestly, the game was designed well enough that you shouldn't need the extra consumables anyway.
Ultimately, this does have me concerned regarding how micro-transactions is seeping into single player games. I would understand if they had it for their Breach mode (which I haven't tried yet), but for a single player game? And to have them save-locked? It's absurd, but not so much that I think the game deserves a bad review.
---
In the end, I'm having a lot of fun with this game. I believe it's worth checking out.

After over 1300 hours invested in the game in both single and mostly multiplayer, it pains me to give a negative review to this game. Let me preface that this has been my favorite game of all time until this point. The mistakes made herein by R* are so damaging that the community cannot even function in remotely the same fashion as it has been for the last four years.
Starting with MP, the gameplay decisions made by R* regarding online in the last year have been greedy at
. The latest multiplayer update introduces so many balance-breaking features it's nearly impossible to play in any manner that isn't DayZ-like self defense. The latest update has enabled modders to break the game even further for defenseless players by incorporating blantantly overpowered vehicles and weaponry while increasing the cost of such items immensely. It has encouraged the purchase of SharkCards like no other update prior. Because without cash, you're as good as ashes with this update. Everything is so unforgivingly expensive that if you aren't modding, aren't buying SharkCards, or aren't already sitting on a wad of cash, you have one hell of a fight just to get your car across Los Santos.
And of course, let's not forget the elephant in the room. The cease and desist of OpenIV. It was the saving grace of GTA. It gave GTA V longevity that its developers couldn't replicate. Thousands upon thousands of modding videos on YouTube garnering
of combined views are now useless. One of the biggest gaming communities on the earth with thousands of contributors, millions of users and players are now at a loss without modding. Modding videos, funny moments videos (most of which have mods), and other mod-inspired GTA videos such as role-play, cinematics, etc are now a relic of a bygone era. R*'s easiest and largest source of free advertisement is now utterly useless. The income of several YouTubers has also been damaged due to the sudden, unprovoked, and unprecedented actions by R* and its publisher Take2. The amazing GTA V Redux mod and others like it are now trash. The hundreds and thousands of hours and passion developers have poured into mods for the game are now for nothing.
I have single-handedly convinced dozens of people to buy GTA. I have bought GTA V for several more. After this, I regret ever making that mistake. Still one of the best shmups out there, and easily one of the most beautiful creations in this genre. This is not essentially a bullet hell shmup, but much more of an R-type, G-Darius, or something similar with flying puzzles and gigantic boss fights. It's also very cinematic with a surprisingly mature and well-written storyline with cool anthropomorphic characters.
You can skip all the cutscenes with the press of a button. This makes replaying story mode a breeze. There is a time mechanic that heavily weighs on how you progress. Getting hit reduces your time, and doing other things make it increase until you get to a checkpoint. In story mode you play as various ships with different weapons and looks throughout the seven stages. It's all very well done, and the graphics are a high watermark for the genre.
The levels can get tough, so you will have to play through it a couple times to gain knowledge about the fights. Some of the later sections can be quite devious, and on the harder mode are extremely challenging. Even for me as an average shmup skill level I had a blast going through the EX version here. The improvements are all welcome, and the game seems  a bit more fair now. The 16:9 presentation is amazing, and at 4K Ultra this game is worth playing just to see all the art and thematic elements in the various stages.
There is a decent campaign here and other modes to play afterward. SIne Mora EX remains a quality product with great presentation and mechanics. Highly recommended.

Graphics:
The graphics in Sine Mora Ex are simply beautiful. A 2d game with 3d elements, the colors pop on the screen and the scenery draws you in to the game. From the clouds in the sky to the oceans below, each element in the game is highly detailed and a wonder to see.
Sound:
The sounds in Sine Mora Ex complement the graphics perfectly. With many different enemy ships, types of ammo and levels, each sound can be differentiated on the screen. This is impressive considering the fast pace of the game and amount of enemies that are attacking constantly. The music, composed by Akira Yamaoka, Sound Director of Silent Hill and Shadows of the Damned, is amazing and a blast to listen to. The voice acting is great and provides a movie like feel to the characters.
Cinematics:
Sine Mora Ex’s cinematics are top notch. Level intros have a neat conversion between 2d and 3d which is very smooth and eye catching. Boss intros have a great anime feel and are just as entertaining as fighting the boss itself.
Content:
Sine Mora Ex has great replay value by providing 5 game modes and 7 levels of gameplay.
Story Mode is more open to novice players or players who are new to the genre and the storyline is intriguing.
Arcade Mode steps up the difficulty and removes the story elements of the game. I found this mode is much faster paced and the enemies were much less forgiving.
Score Attack mode allows you to go back through completed stages to gain your best score. Again, in Score Attack mode the game ramps up the difficulty only allowing you to choose Hard or Insane difficulties…this mode doesn’t mess around.
In Challenge Mode, you play party game like events that are so difficult I couldn’t complete the first one…so be ready to die, again…and again.
The last mode, Versus, you can play against your friends locally on the same machine.  You can also team up with a friend to Co-Op the story mode part of the game.
Unfortunately there are no Online versus modes, which was disappointing.
Controls:
Sine Mora Ex is smooth as butter when it comes to the controls. Maneuvering the ship is very satisfying and responds perfectly to button presses. The controls are perfect for the fast pace of this game and you will only have yourself to blame for the many deaths that will occur. With the time slow down feature you will be doing your best matrix in a plane impression with ease. Another cool control feature is the cut scene fast forward button, allowing you to fast forward any cut scenes you have already seen or if you are just in a hurry to keep fighting.
Gameplay:
Sine Mora Ex gameplay ramps up the side scrolling shooter genre with cinematic boss battles and many power ups that enhance your weaponry. Featuring boss designs by Mahiro Maeda, one of the most prominent Japanese anime creators, Sine More Ex’s boss battles have the best animation of just about any game out there. With 2 boss battles per stage, the game brings a frequent challenge that won’t leave you disappointed and you won’t mind fighting again when you inevitably die.
Power ups appear frequently after killing enemies and collecting tokens will give you upgrades as you go along. The cool thing about the weapon upgrade system is that after collecting 10 weapon upgrade tokens the upgrade becomes permanent. However, before you get 10 tokens you need, enemy hits will cause the tokens to float out on to the screen but you can collect them again before they disappear, a very cool gameplay feature saving you a little frustration.
Instead of a health bar, Sine Mora Ex is all based on time. If your timer ever runs out, your ship explodes and it’s game over. To gain more time, each standard enemy kill adds 2 seconds to the clock. Killing weapons off of a boss provides up to 12 seconds to the timer. Timer upgrade tokens also appear after killing some enemies and will add 5 seconds to the timer. The downside is that each time your ship is hit you lose time, making your dodge skill very important to your survival. When you die, you get continues that lets you start from the last place you died. Each mode only gives you so many continues and each one used penalizes your final grade.
After completing each level, the game grades you based on score, hit ratio, penalties and continues used. After defeating a level, the game unlocks the boss fights to fight in a Boss Training mode and the level is unlocked to select at the beginning of story mode or score attack mode.
Summary:
Sine Mora Ex is a unique side scrolling shooter with 2d and 3d elements working in harmony. With beautiful graphics, many game modes and fun controls, Sine Mora Ex is a must play for any gamer looking for a challenge and fun gameplay. The only real complaint I have is the absence of an online mode but that doesn’t keep this game from being a blast to play. I score this game a 9.5 out of 10.

Trine 2 review
I recently picked up Trine 2 in the latest Humble Bundle (9), along with a few other games, however Trine really stood out to me, whether it was 3 player co-op puzzle solving, or it's beatutiful graphical fedelity, Trine 2 is really something not to be missed.
As a game, the narrative is told through picure based story books, and a in game commentary which includes hints, narrative and so on. In terms of voice acting the characters can be very cliche and average, however the main narrator is very good and a times rather humerous.
You start the game, and awaken as a bashful wizard named  "Amadeus the wizard" of whom is awakend by a bright flash of light and procceds to follow it, you then take control of Amadeus and go on a chase, of where the game introduces the main game elements and mechanics of which include sumoning boxing and moving objects to help you move through the extrodinarily dense world.

Eventually you come to the 'Trine' of which telleports you on a quest, one that is unknown at the beggining, you then come to meet Pontius the knight. Of whom is the main brawler character and does most of the core combat, whereas Amadeus does most of the puzzle work, this allows the player to switch through the 3 character at will without any "hand holding"
After the knights introduction, he comes to meet Amadues and the two are transported.
The screeen fades and you are met with the final character.
Zoya the thief, the 3 protagonists then meet and begin to conversate to go on an adventure together, of which the trine so abruptley interupets and wiscs them away to the probelm ro danger that the 'trine' has called them for.
Each mission has you switch between the three characters making use of there alilties for the puzzle solving, this consists of Levitating items, braking down walls and grappling to advantage points, however the game never tells you which approach is right, allowing you to discover which way to take, and this gives the game multiple ways to do things and adds to the replayability.
It's the puzzles themselves that really shine though - physics and the elements are the backbones of the game, so you'll find yourself doing stuff like hovering hollow logs under waterfalls to create jets of water that make a giant plant with bouncy leaves grow, or using portals to make fire cross the level and heat up a cauldron that then releases bubbles you can jump onto.
The game also features a multiplayer/ co-op section of which 3 players either local or through direct Invite can complete the missions together rather than switching between the character you work together to get the job done, this is how i played through most of the game, it made it far more enjoyable with friends and allowed for good team work.
Trine 2 was a delight simple puzzle solving with breath taking visuals allows for a great time, especially with friends!

Just finished this game minutes before writing this review. What a fantastic experience.
Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons is a game about two brothers who set off on a journey to find a cure for their father, who has fallen ill. Their journey will take them from the outskirts of their village, through massive caverns, across mountains, and beyond.
Let's talk about the gameplay. The game revolves entirely around a unique mechanic: You play two characters at once, the titular brothers. Each one is controlled by one of the control sticks, and one of the triggers/whatever button you have up there. They must work together in order to solve puzzles and progress through areas. Sometimes, a specific brother is needed to perform an action. The puzzles are not difficult at all, nor is the game, so if you're looking for challenge, that's not here. (Though to be fair, the amount of difficulty you have may differ depending on your ability to control two characters at the same time. Most sections of the game are rather slow paced and easy going, though, with plenty of time for each brother to do whatever they need to do to get through each obstacle, so you won't be twitch-reacting with both at once or anything like that.) The game is also quite linear, with very little side exploration, though occasionally you can perform optional tasks which will reward you with achievements (There are no achievements earned by just playing through the story). Though the game may be easy, the level design is very good, and the puzzles are still fun to solve. They don't feel like like actual "puzzles" which were installed into the areas to impede travellers (and players), rather they are simply obstacles which the brothers must use their own unique skills to bypass and move on with their journey, and are easily figured out with a bit of observation or logical thinking.
Visually, the game is an absolute masterpiece. Every single area of the game is stunningly beautiful in its own way, from the brothers' home village, to the lofty peaks, to the massive caves. You will often be able to see far off into the scenery, often spotting places you will eventually reach, and even those you have previously passed through. Scenes like this can often be viewed by sitting at benches located throughout the game, which causes the camera to pan upwards for an overview of the area, and what lies beyond. This is effective in making it truly feel like you are truly progressing through the journey, and playing the game is worth it just to see these beautiful sights; the journey is truly the reward in this game.
The game does not have any dialogue. The characters speak a few words in their native tongue now and then, but nearly everything is told through actions. The game has a nice soundtrack, with mostly calming tunes as you traverse the areas. Now and then, there'll be more adventerous and epic ones, and even a few creepy and unnerving ones as the brothers come across new scenarios and situations. The background sound effects are also very nice, and help build up the atmospere for the areas, which in turn helps immerse the player into the journey even more.
Final verdict? The game is a must-buy for fans of the adventure genre. The presentation is absolutely amazing, and the journey is its own reward. My only regret is that the game is very short, clocking in at somewhere between 3-4 hours in length. This is one game I truly wish there could have been more of, because it was just that good.

RWBY: Grimm Eclipse is essential playing for any fan of the series. The creators have gone to great pains to ensure that the game looks and feels like the show in every way, down to the textures, colours and animations. Each character of the four main - and now team JNPR as well - handles easily, with fluid controls, dynamic attacks and all of them differ from each other enough to make playing as the whole team worthwhile.
The campaign is divided into ten chapters (I like this touch, over calling them missions), all of which culminate in an endurance challenge where you must stay alive (and sometimes protect certain items) from increasingly difficult waves. Although the campaign might quickly become repetitive, it is fun to try playing as all of the different characters, and multiplayer is strongly encouraged, because, I'm going to be honest here, this game is brutally difficult. While it is of course possible by yourself - the developers have made up for this by allowing perma-levelling - it is strongly encouraged you play with someone else.
That said, multiplayer isn't always an advantage, because sharing experience is impossible, and with many little boosts scattered across each chapter, you'll constantly be competing for the next level. Besides this, enemies quickly scale in strength to become essentially insurmountable without help. The first chapter might just be manageable, but you'll quickly find you'll be reloading a lot just to get the next level up. As a side note, ranged attacks, especially once they've been levelled once, are extremely powerful, and a definite recommendation for keeping your distance.
All-in-all, Grimm Eclipse is a fantastic game for everyone who loves RWBY, and it's canon, too! The voice acting is impeccable as always; the chapters are beautiful, both in design and appearance; and now it works for Mac!

Deus Ex: Mankind Divided looks like it has everything going for it. The combat is enhanced from Human Revolution with more options available, it has new augmentations to experiment with, the graphics are improved, and areas are littered with small details to create a pretty convincing hub world of Prague. It all looks and plays nicely, but something is missing. This game fails to present an interesting story to drive you forward and main mission has no sense of urgency. The characters so far lack personality and the fact that you are hardly contacted by them through your infolink means that they just fade in your memory.
Adam Jensen, the main protagonist, is a huge problem for me. He just doesn't seem bothered or interested in anything and comes across as if he has been just woken up. I don't like listening to his half-arsed questions. Some of the other voice acting is pretty poor as well with no one really giving a stand out performance. Most of the dialogue had me zoning out and it is not helped that the lip-syncing is slightly off either.
Its a shame as the level design is generally very good with alternate paths and ways into buildings and rooms. There are lots of hidden areas and places that are locked down and require a higher hacking level to break in so require a revisit, however, this I feel is also detrimental to the game itself.
It starts in Dubai with a tutorial-esque mission to get you used to the controls and mechanics. You are part of a task force and dropped into an abandoned hotel to disrupt an arms deal. The level is fairly small but packed with routes and for a first mission it does well to introduce you to the games elements. After that mission you arrive in Prague and there is an incident which damages your body. Awakening in your apartment, you have to get your augs repaired and go to work to see the Director of the taskforce. That is okay as a first task but the hub of Prague is very large and scenic. I spent hours exploring the shops, apartments and sewers and totally lost the urgency to see my boss. It sounds like a strange complaint but when you are allowed to do various side-missions and basically mess about without any nagging to do the main story mission it sometimes lessens that mission. 10 hours later, I met my Director but wasn't scalded by him or interested in what he had to say. Adam Jensen's "broody teenager" act didn't help either. For me, I think they should have had you arrive at your workplace to solidify some main characters and interactions and then let you lose on Prague.
Maybe it is just down to my playstyle but I felt more like a cat burgular/intrusive customer/lost tourist than I did an investigative agent. Its seems strange that members of the public and impatient shop keepers will one moment tell you where to go, and then next moment they allow you to open the trunk of their car, hack into safes or just walk into their apartments whilst they sob over being evicted or casually chat on the phone. This freedom of exploration is usually is good in a game like Fallout, which is a sandbox world but Deus Ex has always had hubs with interesting side missions and characters. This Deus Ex game has had me just read through pretty dull e-mails, find a few drug dens, forge some identifications, and randomly find a cult (which is just a bit too bizarre for this game). Mostly dull stuff.
The premise of segregating the augmented people from the non-augmented people just seems a little too far fetched to have been introduced over a short period of time. Its trying so hard to create a believable world but then I can spring around and take what what I wish. I am not really invested in anything that is going on and its affecting my enjoyment.
Gameplay is fine with some interesting police AI. For example, you can trip an alarm but if they don't see you do it then they will pass you by and check the area. I also caused a drone to kill some crooks as I set of a car alarm which caused them to be hostile to me, but as I didn't shoot back the drone decided that they were in the wrong and slaughtered them for me. Little things like that are great but then you see people stuggle to navigate doors or strangely physically run from desk to desk in small circuits in your HQ. Placement of objects is weird as painkillers can be hidden away in some secret room, yet diaries, credit cards, and safes with guns are left open or casually sit on tables. Its a just mixed bag.
Overall I have not found much to make me want to push on with the main mission and I am just going through the motions. It has quickly become a chore that drags down the otherwise good work and make it hard for me to play.

I was headed towards a dungeon to complete a quest, ended up exploring the whole map, killed all the mobs, searched for the golden key to open the golden chest, went through a random portal which reserved me a side mission and finally started the dungeon.

Pros:

-Good combat system. In general, you can't simply spam click to clear mobs, the game pushes you to dodge abilities, manage your mana pool and react to different scenarios (use abilities to trap big guys, use your escape ability to..well escape,etc).
Cons:
-The story is bad, this is definietly not the game to play for its story. To be honest, I stopped caring about the story very early on.
-Can get a bit repetitive.
-Okay character custimization (character creation allows you to play very little with your character's features).
8/10, great game to pick up when it goes on sale.

This game feels like it has even less content than its predecessor, DW7E. If you are a DW fan you will probably like it, otherwise I wouldn't really recommend it. The graphics are subpar for this port, and gameplay is the formulatic DW appraoch, with the addition of extra strategical elements. You can build facilities to enhance your cities while recruiting officers into your army and drafting troops, and going on quests to earn additional items. Since there is 1 map for each city, things get repetitive very quickly as you can end up fighting over the same city with another faction for a while.
My biggest gripe with this game is the world completley revolves around your character. Don't want to join the invasion your army is about to do? Then they automatically lose! Go along and get KOed? Your entire army is routed, regardless of your remaining troop strength! Enemy officers will drop whatever they are doing to chase you across the map, which provides a challenge, but is overall stupid and reduces your own allies to simple distractions. In the end, the game boils down to lasting long enough for your officer to become so OP they can just kill everyone themselves without any fear of retaliation and then steamrolling the map, which kind of goes against the strategic angle this game is trying to push. Strategy elements feel more tacked on than anything and in the end its like any other DW game, where you feel like you're just a one man army who needs to occasionally babysit his more inept comrades.
Anyway, I did enjoy the game, but I was expecting better. Overall I would give it a 7/10.

I've been away from this series for a while and came back to it when I saw Empires had made its way onto PC.  (Hint that maybe bringing your future Empires games to PC, and with English translation, or, at the very least, strong enough mod support that people can translate it)  It's at least passable as a port.  It did require a bit of setup, I had to set the texture detail because the CAW parts were pixelated like a hentai crotch by default.  However, once I did that, the characters looked good, not out of thsi world, but good.  The controls had to be set up, which isn't a huge deal, I set mine to Xbox 360 style I'm used to, it works alright, aside from the back and select button being reversed due to how my combat controls are set.
Those are my only real issues with what I expect to be there.  I've got a whole list of things that I wish were there, but they're just suggestions for other parts to add in for DW9: Empires.  I'll include what I hope to see next time at the end.  The things that really have me loving this game so much are the CAW, the family aspect, and all the new move sets that I missed out on since briefly getting into DW6.
I love the character customization.  The detail has improved so dramatically since the last one I picked up.  It really isn't lacking for much, maybe include more skin color options (I would like an orcish snot-green skin, rather than a wicked witch green, but not that big of a deal), a few more body shape sliders, and some better facial hair, because, sorry, but some of that looks like♥♥♥♥♥♥ like they literally just caked some♥♥♥♥♥♥onto their face,  I would like to have the option to set characters to have relationships, like husband and wife, father/son/daughter, and friend or sworn brother, stuff like that to help in scenarios so that we don't have Cersie Lannister professing her undying love for Jeoffry, though that would fit the character, she likes to keep it in the family.
Speaking of family, but excluding incest-though it could happen with the characters, as far as I know-I thought the idea of being able to shag Lu LingQi was pretty sweet.  It really adds something to the playthrough, though, maybe in the next game, or with a patch, allow for more children, like once every few years, assuming the husband and wife are happy together.
So, since last I really payed attention to Dynasty Warriors, they got a whole new faction of characters that didn't exist.  These characters have flying swords, a jet spear, a gattling crossbow, and a weird combination of a tonfa cannon and whooping cough.  I would ask WTF, but these characters are so fun to play.  These are some really fun move sets, even if they would never have existed at that time.  I did have a bit of an issue figuring out what the EX moves were, until I realized it was just continuing to press the heavy attack at the end of certain combos.
This game is basically everything I thought would be great to include when I was playing DW4 Empires (speaking of which, that was some weak character creation at the time, possibly the worst of all games at the time, aside from Samurai Warriors 1, which wasn't even a character creator, just pick a character model and name it)  Really learning from the past in many areas.  I know this isn't the best port, and most people seem to think that these games don't really change between sequels, and they may be right, I did miss a chunk of the franchise for a few years, but compare this to Madden or Call of Duty, They basically toss in a few revamped textures and update a few rosters and call it a day.
Now, as for the things I'd love to see in the next one, but aren't a complaint or actual issue:
1: Mod support.  I know you're hoping to make some cash off of DLC, and you may still be able to, but mod support up to the capability of making entirely new move sets would  be awesome, and the sales from people interested in buying a moddable DW make up for the price of lost DLC sales (though I'm sure I'm not the only one waiting for those prices to drop dramatically becore I even think about buying them).
2: Online coop.  I can't do splitscreen anymore, online would be so awesome though.
3: Samurai Warriors 4: Empires with english translation, for PC.  Bring all future Empires games to PC.
4: Warriors Orochi Empires.  I have seen some things about Warriors Orochi and an Empires version would make it a game I'd want to buy.
5: More soldier options, would be fun to make the Amazons with an army of female warriors.
This is all I ever wanted from a Dynasty Warriors game but why is the dlc so pricey....oh well, I guess I well just find some mods for free.

After over 1300 hours invested in the game in both single and mostly multiplayer, it pains me to give a negative review to this game. Let me preface that this has been my favorite game of all time until this point. The mistakes made herein by R* are so damaging that the community cannot even function in remotely the same fashion as it has been for the last four years.
Starting with MP, the gameplay decisions made by R* regarding online in the last year have been greedy at
. The latest multiplayer update introduces so many balance-breaking features it's nearly impossible to play in any manner that isn't DayZ-like self defense. The latest update has enabled modders to break the game even further for defenseless players by incorporating blantantly overpowered vehicles and weaponry while increasing the cost of such items immensely. It has encouraged the purchase of SharkCards like no other update prior. Because without cash, you're as good as ashes with this update. Everything is so unforgivingly expensive that if you aren't modding, aren't buying SharkCards, or aren't already sitting on a wad of cash, you have one hell of a fight just to get your car across Los Santos.
And of course, let's not forget the elephant in the room. The cease and desist of OpenIV. It was the saving grace of GTA. It gave GTA V longevity that its developers couldn't replicate. Thousands upon thousands of modding videos on YouTube garnering
of combined views are now useless. One of the biggest gaming communities on the earth with thousands of contributors, millions of users and players are now at a loss without modding. Modding videos, funny moments videos (most of which have mods), and other mod-inspired GTA videos such as role-play, cinematics, etc are now a relic of a bygone era. R*'s easiest and largest source of free advertisement is now utterly useless. The income of several YouTubers has also been damaged due to the sudden, unprovoked, and unprecedented actions by R* and its publisher Take2. The amazing GTA V Redux mod and others like it are now trash. The hundreds and thousands of hours and passion developers have poured into mods for the game are now for nothing.
I have single-handedly convinced dozens of people to buy GTA. I have bought GTA V for several more. After this, I regret ever making that mistake. After everything the fans have done for R* to put GTA V where it's at now just feels like a stab in the back. I can only presume that RD2 will fall to the same fate... Perhaps R* will learn in time for then. Until now, any future release just reeks of distrust and greed.

It's ok.  It's also free.
When Gunz (1) came out I dropped a lot of time into that.  Compared to 1 I found 2 a bit lacking.  For the most part the maps are a lot smaller and that works out due to a lower team size (4v4 matchups).   While I agree that the maps should be small and tight for the low man teams it still felt claustrophobic at time, especially compared to the large (huge?) maps of 1.
What I don't care for is that the teams are so much smaller.  There are a lot less ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t type moments, like getting shot from behind and what not, but the difference in skill level really, really shows in 2.
2 also adjusted gear pretty heavily.  Please note that I didn't play around with the gear system so much.  To start, you're no longer an every-man: the type of gear you can equip is locked between different characters (classes).  These characters level individually, although you may unlock (purchase with in game currency) all of them with ease.
From what I recall (it's been a while and like I said I didn't do much with the equipment) gear degrades over time (matches).  There are also cool looking pieces that have slightly better stats but I'm not sure about the specifics.  I believe they fade over time (like 6 hours), though.
There are pay to win elements but they're fairly weak.
In addition to team deathmatch, elimination, gladiator (elimination: melee only) and objective (do the thing!) there's a story mode but I found it pretty unforgiving.  If you die in the story mode you need to use accrued, finite credits to revive.
The biggest complaint I have is that there are no longer servers.  Instead, a player/team uses matchmaking to find opponents.  One of the players in the game serves as the host.  This inevitably leads to whining about lag, which I think I've experienced in every single match I've been in.
The in game community has been, from my personal experience, fairly mean spirited.
The overall feel of 2 is very similar to 1 so that's good.
Either way, check it out, it's free.  I had fun with it for a little while and that's worth something.

While GTA V does have a very enjoyable singleplayer campaign with some great characters and memorable moments, it stuffers from many issues that plague both SP and especially MP that Rockstar doesn't seem to care to fix, instead of putting out free DLC (the free part is nice, and some of them are cool DLCs) but they are just designed to be increasingly expensive and to drive sales of overpriced and scummy Shark Cards.
This is in addition to Take Two's crack down on singleplayer modding, even though it does not harm MP at all and they have never done anything to actually stop cheaters anyway.
First of all, singleplayer's problems. There's absolutely nothing to do that makes it worth to keep playing singleplayer after you beat the story. There is no insurance for cars so once you lose them you have to rebuy and remod them, wtf!? I am not sure if there is any way to keep making more money either.
Plus there is no sign of any SP DLC or expansions, it seems that, despite earlier confirmation from voice actors and suggestions in game of SP DLC, they ahve ditched it just to focus on selling shark cards in MP.
Multiplayer... where do I even begin?
- Menus are laggy, like unreliable when clicked and slow. I have never experienced this in any other game.
- P2P servers and how you can easily switch straight to MP from SP mean they don't have any real way of stopping people from just using mods in multiplayer (which is utterly bizarre for an MP game from such a big company).
- Also does nothing to stop hackers, there are hackers everywhere.
- Driving is still just hold down W to go faster and faster! Kind of hard to maintain a reasonable speed. Plus the AI likes to randomly swerve into the wrong lane.
- Can only start a private MP session with friends FROM SINGLEPLAYER. If you're already in MP you have to leave and start SP and then switch back... this makes zero sense and is frustrating. Especially due to the long load screens.
- Many other smaller issues I don't recall because I stopped playing like a year.
- No support for steering wheel peripherals.
If you are looking for a knock off smash bros and want to have fun with friends its pretty cool.

As a holder of previous Sine Mora, I recommend to avoid this game.
1. Don't be fooled by the name of "Sub-Weapon". By using the traditional shooting game genre terms, the SW in this game is in fact a "Bomb". No seeker missiles. No spread shots. No charging shots. You're only allowed to shoot the enemies in front of you since there're no "Sub-weapons". Not much like a hero, eh?
2. You'll lose some of your powerups if you collide with your enemy or specific terrain. But if you have full powerups, one touch will make you lose them ALL. You don't have much chance to get them all back in a tight fight, so you must be pretty skillful to take the rest enemies down to make up the firepower loss. In other shooting games, there'll be some backup supplies (remember Striker 1945? Those little red ones?), but in the game, you get nothing. GLHF.
3. Some SWs don't even have invincible time which means you can't eliminate the upcoming threat by using your SW. If you really want to beat the boss fast, just make sure you don't lose any weapon powerups, then smash the shooting button like mad. It works best in that way.
4. Some bosses will shoot tiny missiles which will perfectly blend in with the background.
5. Terrain kills. And repeat. And repeat. And REPEAT.
I can play Gradius V for the whole day. But this game...better avoid it.

What a gorgeous game that I really really wanted to like. I played this game back before EX came out so I thought I'd give it a try again. Now I remember why I stopped before. The level design and time mechanics completely ruin the experience. The game uses a time slow down function to get you through parts of the game. However, you aren't always going to have it since it's a limited resource so you will end up banging your plane against a wall most of the time.

After over 1300 hours invested in the game in both single and mostly multiplayer, it pains me to give a negative review to this game. Let me preface that this has been my favorite game of all time until this point. The mistakes made herein by R* are so damaging that the community cannot even function in remotely the same fashion as it has been for the last four years.
Starting with MP, the gameplay decisions made by R* regarding online in the last year have been greedy at
. The latest multiplayer update introduces so many balance-breaking features it's nearly impossible to play in any manner that isn't DayZ-like self defense. The latest update has enabled modders to break the game even further for defenseless players by incorporating blantantly overpowered vehicles and weaponry while increasing the cost of such items immensely. It has encouraged the purchase of SharkCards like no other update prior. Because without cash, you're as good as ashes with this update. Everything is so unforgivingly expensive that if you aren't modding, aren't buying SharkCards, or aren't already sitting on a wad of cash, you have one hell of a fight just to get your car across Los Santos.
And of course, let's not forget the elephant in the room. The cease and desist of OpenIV. It was the saving grace of GTA. It gave GTA V longevity that its developers couldn't replicate. Thousands upon thousands of modding videos on YouTube garnering
of combined views are now useless. One of the biggest gaming communities on the earth with thousands of contributors, millions of users and players are now at a loss without modding. Modding videos, funny moments videos (most of which have mods), and other mod-inspired GTA videos such as role-play, cinematics, etc are now a relic of a bygone era. R*'s easiest and largest source of free advertisement is now utterly useless. The income of several YouTubers has also been damaged due to the sudden, unprovoked, and unprecedented actions by R* and its publisher Take2. The amazing GTA V Redux mod and others like it are now trash. The hundreds and thousands of hours and passion developers have poured into mods for the game are now for nothing.
I have single-handedly convinced dozens of people to buy GTA. I have bought GTA V for several more. After this, I regret ever making that mistake. After everything the fans have done for R* to put GTA V where it's at now just feels like a stab in the back. I can only presume that RD2 will fall to the same fate... Perhaps R* will learn in time for then. Until now, any future release just reeks of distrust and greed.

As someone who just returned to gaming about a year ago after not playing anything (PC or console) for like a decade, the constant lag and mountains of downloads and the myriad of other issues with online games has been a regular pain in the butt.
I just happened to see this game advertised as a free-to-play on Steam, saw its similarities to Super Smash Bros., saw the great ratings, and gave it a shot.
The incredibly small size of the game, along with its absolute smoothness, is amazing to me.
I've been confused time and again after buying what seems like a very small, non-intensive and non-demanding game, only to find that it drags my computer down to the ground ,barely runs, and introduces itself by necessitating a 2 hour download.
After the 2-3 minute download for Brawlhalla, I seriously imagined that (as with so many other games) I'd find that I'd just downloaded the client, and that I'd then need to create an account for some random company before downloading the 3 gigs of the actual game.
That was not at all the case here.  2-3 minute download, start up the game, and I'm instantly playing.
Just wanted to say thanks to the developers, and I hope everyone else is enjoying it as much as I am.  It's simple, but it's so smooth and fast, and it's great fun.  And the amount of options already - be it 4 v 4 free-for-alls or 1 v 1/2 v 2 ranked games - leaves a good amount to explore.
Great stuff, and I hope other Free-to-play game developers take note.
