TL;DR: An even mixture of RPG and Visual novel. Well done story and gameplay, nothing extraordinary, but worth a play.
Loren: The Amazon Princess is one of those rare birds of a Visual Novel that is equal parts RPG gameplay and story sections. Both are executed well, and complement each other very well. If I was to sum up the game it one word, it would in fact be competence. While that shouldn't be rare, the fact that this game executes everything well, with very few stumbling blocks, is worthwhile enough for me to give it my reccomendation. I did truly enjoy the game in my first play through, and the only frustrations I found were in acheivement-hunting for 100% completion, given it requires quite a few playthroughs in order to get all the romance acheivements.
The story is nothing outstanding. Your main character is a slave to the titular Loren, and the game plays out as you being the deutaragonist to her. You can pick your gender, which will affect romance options, though the game treats bisexuality as the norm, as most characters have romance options with both. When I say it is not outstanding, that doesn't mean it is bad. It is a good story, and I enjoyed it at first, but it doesn't push any boundaries, and stays fairly in line with common tropes of the fantasy RPG genre. If anything, the game could be closest compared story wise to Dragon Age: Origins. Big bad threat, have to convince various factions to follow you, recruit a diverse cast, talk to them over the campfire to get their stories and personal quests. If the game has any faults story wise it is that you really don't have much control over the story itself. Dialogue options tend to be selecting tone of your character (or increasing romance points), and you get very few major choices throughout the story. Your ending is basically determined by who you romanced, a final option at the end, and whether or not you did the DLC content.
Gameplay wise, combat plays out in a turn based style, with your characters arrayed on a 2x3 grid opposite your opponents similarly laid out grid. Turns are according to a characters speed and the 'delay' of their last attack. A lot of the combat is based on status effects. The entire rogue skill tree, and most fighter skills rely on the opponent either being staggered (which can occur through powerful hits), or having various other status effects applied through spells or other skills. The game seems to be intended that you would apply status effects with mages, and have the rogues/fighters take advantage of them to deal tremendous damage. In practice though, since most fights including bosses are against masses of enemies, I found it better to stack three mages with max level AoE spells, and blast them down, leaving fighters/rogue for cleanup. The game has a fairly simple level up system, where your characters get stat points every level, and a skill point every few levels. The skill points let you progress down (short) talent trees, usually getting rank 1, then 2, then 3 of an ability. For most, this is just more damage, though mages progress from single target, to row, to all. There is practically no reason to spread things out, and far better to get rank 3 in a few abilities to deal massive damage, and spread out later to other damage types. Each character has a primary and secondary skill tree. The primary tree is of the fighter/rogue/mage basic class, and the secondary is unique to that character. This allows every character in the varied class to have a unique feel, a definite bonus.
The game is intended to be played multiple times, hence the sheer amount of romance acheivements being practically more than the rest all combined. After you finish the game, the game does let you put it on story mode, which essentially disables combat, and lets you quickly skip through the game to the various endings.
The only major downside I found in this game was inventory management, and the lack of leaked experience. In essence,  if you want your characters to have great gear, you will need to buy it. The costs for said gear are extremely high. You can lower the costs by doing repeated fights in towns, but it only works for that town. This also serves to give you money and vendor trash, but in small amounts. Story fights give you only the occasional decent piece of gear, and character side quests will usually give you a major item, but I went through the game with most of my party missing a huge chunk of gear slots, and even my main characters were often missing rings and belts. In addition, experience is not leaked to non-party members, which means that in several sections of the game where you are forced to use certain characters (their sidequests, sections where you have to fight through hordes and have characters get worn down), if you have been focusing on a single party you will be punished severely. The only way to catch these characters up is the aforementioned grinding fights, which barely give decent experience.
Overall, Loren is a well done game. It will never sit on my 'Oh my god, you must play this!' list, but it is well executed, competent, and deserving of play if you enjoy these types of games.

Although I have dropped it before completing my first playthrough, I must recognize that "Loren, The Amazon Princess" is an amazing mix between a turn-based RPG and a Visual Novel with romance elements. If you enjoy any kind of tabletop RPG, especially the medieval fantasy ones, you'll love Loren's gameplot: there'll be a great variety of well-described Elves, Orcs, Amazons, Witches, Wizards, Necromancers, Slaves, Dwarves, Dryads and many other typical characters from classic RPG present in Loren.
The turn-based RPG mechanic of the game is simple and grants lots of fun. A full playthrough has about 10 hours if you aren't a slow reader or thorough RPG player. Sadly for me, as the game progressed, I feel a bit tired of the repetitiveness of the battles and decided to drop the game. Also, the romance mechanic feels a bit disconnected (it's more like optional) from the main plot and reinforced my repetitiveness feeling. That was only my personal experience, but I think the game is pretty good and worth your time anyway.

Unfortunately, while all the elements are here for an interesting game, the gameplay feels cobbled together, and the story is a little too cliche to keep my attention. A good effort, but alas one that doesn't appeal to me.

As someone who is a huge fan of otome games and games like Dragon Age, that feature combat as well as rich interactions with party members, I was sold on Loren the Amazon Princess from the start.
The plot isn't terrible. It's cliche, but these days, many high fantasy adventure games follow the same tropes. Though cliche, there was a certain charm about the story that led me to continue to play the game. Combat is decent, though monotonous after a while. I found myself powering through battles just to get to cutscenes and camp, just so I could interact with the characters some more. The characters, while nothing terribly original, were fun, likeable, and reason enough to keep me coming back to play some more. Pleasantly enough, the interactions seem to change slightly depending on your character's gender, which makes for a refreshing second or third playthrough. As I mentioned before, Loren isn't unlike Dragon Age as far as party relations go. You're free to romance your party members if you so choose (some are only open to MCs of certain genders), or you can just remain platonic with them. Either way, I enjoyed that this game features a way to get to know the party other than snippets of dialogue from cutscenes.
Loren the Amazon Princess is a game definitely worth picking up if you enjoy otomes and/or action adventure games with rich party interactions.

This is a early play review
Basically this game looks like a typical dogfighter, however, instead of jets or helicopters you control a dragon. just thinking that a flying manta ray could be classified as a monster, I'm not sure it fits into the "dragon" catagory.
Each dragon has a different characteristics and special abilities that are indicitive of that species. Blinding the enemy, breathing fire for close range combat, Poison, explosive blast, vampiric leaching of life, stunning, healing yourself and ally etc.
Limited purchasable items are available for the dragons. Items can be won or earned by logging into the game or after the match via the lottery. The items currently include skins or "DNA Points" for the dragons but not much else.
Weapons, dragons, abilities can't be upgraded using points as far as I have seen but I could be wrong.
The arenas are nicely constructed with beautiful detail and they range in size, but aren't very dynamic. ie No destructable content. (The plasma orb that can kill a dragon won't leave a burn mark on the landscape let alone make a pit in the ground or walls)
As for the gameplay, the controls aren't very difficult. Standard w,s,a,d movement with q and e as altitude control.
The shield (triggered by holding the right mouse button) isn't very good as you may try to use it and it doesn't respond right away, or sometimes at all.
It is fun, if you have the patience for a game based on repitition with little depth. I'll suggest a few ideas even though I doubt they will be taken up.
Adding a Campaign Mode would help players understand the backstory and reasons why anyone would strap weapons to a dragon and set it lose.
Adding a system to allow players to spend DNA points on the dragons base abilities such as speed, stamina, health etc would go a long way towards making this a great game.
Setting up the matches to be based on the players level would be a required so nobody can twink the dragon and troll people with lower levels and are just begining ie a level 10 harassing a level 3 just because they can and find it funny. IMO thats why most early players don't return to a game that could be great.

The bad:

I'm giving this a yes, but it's not a definitive yes.
The gameplay delivered is fun, it's the typicaly dynasty warriors slashing action combined with the pseudo strategy aspects of the continued Empires series. There are plenty of awesome weapons, characters, maps and strategies to give some of the Romance of the Three Kingdoms lovers something fun to play with. I've followed the series from DW4, and while I can say that it might be getting a little repetitive, Koei has put out another solid game. There are so many awesome custom creation options available, it's something they've nailed! There are custom warriors, armies, horses and even banners.
It's fun and finally on PC!
I won't go too in depth with the general aspects of the game, you should just give a few Youtube videos a try. I play through it
if you're interested on seeing how it plays.
However ... there are some major cons. I cannot give this game a complete thumbs-up, it really deserves a 'so-so' grade at this point. I went with thumbs-up because I've been a fan for years, and I get nerdy and giddy playing around with some cool ancient china figures.
Drawbacks:
- Awful optimization and poor port to the PC: The graphics are from the PS3 port, which is disappointing given the potential. On top of that, there are way too many visual bugs for this game to be a full release. It feels like they never beta tested it! At any point you are susceptible to brightness flares or a complete black out during combat. Oh by the way, don't Alt-Tab. You really won't have any idea what the duck happened once you tab back in.
- DLC Cash Grab: I hate yelling at companies for selling DLC, sometimes the extra content is just something you need to be willing to put extra cash out for. This, however, is awful. They have about 200$ worth of DLC available, but the game looks like it should still be in Alpha! I can't believe I paid full retail given it's state, and I have no idea how they expect me to forkout 22$ for about 80 decent character re-skins. They might be insane.
- New Stratagems Aren't Up to Par: The new gameplay offered is fun, but the strategy overhaul they tried their hand at is going poorly. The card game you play during battles feels like cheap power-up stuff you'd expect in some MMO's. The fun system of jumping into a base to surprise them with a fire attack is gone, now you just walk in and draw a card like you're Yugioh. I'm not going to say it's awful, it's just not as immersive as I hoped it would be. There are still awesome combos you can pull off, and the overall effect of the stratagems is still positive.
It's Easy: Lately the game seems to be taking a dive towards the easy side, and this installment isn't much different. The stratagem system can easily be overlooked and enemies can be obliterated by some very cheap moves of your own. The strategy aspect of the game, I.E the campaign map, is shallow as usual. I had so much fun with DW6E, which was even more shallow, but this game just doesn't have the same feeling. It's not as fun repeating the same moves, you get kinda tired of the rinse repeat with invading people. The bonus point system is kinda fudged, you can boost yourself 50 levels ahead of everyone else for almost no cost.
If you're new to the series, hold off until the price goes down. If you're a returning fan, give it a shot and tell us what you think!

Don't be put off by the large thumbs down at the beginning of this review, and don't get me wrong. I love Dynasty Warriors. I've been playing the series since DW2. HOWEVER, I cannot with a clear conscience recommend this game. Dynasty Warriors 8 Empires, while a good game, is a horribly unoptimized port of the console version. The default keymaps are awkward at best, and you're definitely playing Russian Roulette with the graphics in this game. Eyeballs come loose from custom characters and float around, an effect that is hilarious at first, but believe me. It gets old quickly. Additionally, weapons disappear, shields get misplaced, and entire towers hug your weapons, blocking 90% of the screen.
The graphical glitches don't occur for everyone, though, so if you're feeling lucky, feel free to buy the game. However, I do recommend getting DW8XL over DW8E unless you're like me and can largely ignore the textures jumping around. Seriously. That's the major reason I cannot recommend this game. The glitches are that distracting.

This is not really a review. It is more like a personal opinion than anything else. I'm a fan of the old school Mortal Kombat series and I must say, since the first Mortal Kombat in 3D I have lost faith in the series, and I must confess this is the first game in the series I've played more extensively than any other, besides the endless hours/days/months I spent playing the vanilla ones.
Anyway, I am playing on a laptop and even though I've got a good machine (I can play witcher 3 in medium/high settings for instance), the game kept running very poorly, and I couldn't understand why. I found out the game was forcing windows to use my on-board graphics board (intel), instead of my geforce. I was close to quitting because the game looked like it was made by a blind, sexless monkey, but as soon as I managed to find the solution on the web (for those with a geforce graphics card on a laptop, just go to nvidia settings and make sure you force its usage by default, and not the generic Intel card), the game ran almost flawlessly, regarding framerate (some screen tearing on cutscenes but nothing incapacitating).
The story mode is kind of cool, but stupidly superfluous. Still, it's probably the only way to make a story mode in a game like Mortal Kombat. I found it quite an interesting experience. It's quite easy but a bit challenging until you start evolving your fighting skills, but you'll reach the end in a couple of hours. I did it for the koins, for shinnok and all the other stuff.
The faction thingie in the game is, once again, very different from what I was used to, but an interesting game mechanic never the less. I haven't played online yet and I'm not planning on doing it. I prefer Mortal Kombat as a single player experience.
Now, after completing the story, the game is far from over. You got a lot of rewards to win, leveling up, items and even hidden fatalities, and alternate costumes for your fighters. You gain koins, you get inside the Krypt (kind of a marketplace for hidden stuff - beware of the monsters you find here. Monsters you fight using quick time events), and you start spending your hard earned koins on goodies.
What I like the most about Mortal Kombat X is the fighting itself. Challenging even on easy, you really feel you're playing a fighting game. It's absolutely horrendous when it comes to blood spilling and I must say, I love it. The fatalities are very well done and the graphics go alongside with the horror show. It's exactly the feeling I used to have when I was a kid, playing Mortal Kombat on my commodore amiga 600.
Awesome fighting game. I highly recommend it to someone who has a good PC, with a bit of patience to solve some unresolved technical issues so the game can shine in all its glory
Give Mortal Kombat X a chance. It's a good game and should be in every gamer's library who likes fighting games.
Go go Mortal Kombat.

This is an incredibly Tolkein-esque story, with scenery and creatures that seem to be right out of middle earth. The music is gorgeous, art style exquisite, and storyline heartbreaking.
Although I have heard complaints both about the game controls and the choice not to use English within the narrative, I personally love both of these components. While the controls do take some getting used to, and you have to work throughout the whole game to keep little brother on the right of the screen, it is a really incredible way to expand possibilities for a puzzle based game.
As for the language, I love that the whole story is in a made up language, as it lets you read into the characters more and possibly even connect with them more than you would with them speaking English. The game really makes you feel for the characters before springing an incredibly emotional ending on you, and it really is the perfect formula.

About 114 hours hours in at the time of this review.
And I haven't tired of the game yet. Somewhat addictive, lol!
First off- it is an "older" game, fairly typical of RPG's of that time. Runs great on my 5+ year old desktop toaster, running  Win7 Pro 64 bit. I have seen some reports of it not running well on new Win10 rigs, but can't confirm what the issues may be. Other than... Windows 10? (Nothing against Windows 10... it just has a ton of issues running older games.)
Graphics are good, clean, crisp, with good animations for the time. The animations are smooth, and look much better than some newer games. No lag, fps issues, stuttering or hitching in my game so far. (Though I will say the game was released just before my rig was built, so the system specs I have may just be "perfect" for what the game was made to run on.)
4 Races to choose from, great customization for character appearance (cosmetics only), Destinies (aka/Classes) are slightly limited, but you can choose to mix 1, 2 or all 3 Destinies together by applying Lvl Up points to the respective skill trees. Only 1 point per Lvl Up for specialities... think carefully before applying that single point. Specialities give buffs to certain abilities, some are rather unneccessary to level up IMO. (Mercantile... gold is a bit scarce at the beginning, but it won't be for long.) Your Destinies (or Fates) cards give buffs as well, and you can switch them around, but only when you Lvl Up.
Combat is really fun. Not too hard, but not too easy either. Enemy types range from monsters with different attacks and buffs and weapons, to humans. Some are easy to kill, some are a real B**ch. Some weapons seem OP- Chakrams were supposed to be too OP according to other reviewers and folks on the forums. I chose a Mage/Warrior mix, with Greatsword/Longsword and Staves/Scepters. I can use any weapon I choose, but the ones I chose to level up in the skill trees give me buffs, while the ones I did not give only simple dps. (Also keep in mind you can find a Fateweaver at certain loactions onn the maps, and pay gold to to respec your character's weapons skills, spells and such, change Destinies. So don't panic if your build seems bad, find a Fateweaver, smash destroyable props to collect more gold, or sell off excess inventory for gold o to pay the Fateweaver. The fee is quite reasonable, all things considered.)
You have to make choices. Some choices will haunt you. (Like stealing from the Vorms... and killing them and the NPC there that I had a side quest for... failed because I did not turn it in before killing them.) You can lose some valuable or not-so-valuable quest rewards based on choices you make. I would redo that one, lol. (I lost a merchant location by having to kill them... don't steal from merchant facilities, lol!)
The story is good, it has enough depth to make me want to keep going, to see where it leads. Some choices you make in dialogue exchanges seem to change the course of the story as well. The map is HUGE, even without the DLC's. (I have not even touched the DLC's yet...). Lots of nods to mythology and historical lore and well known fables or stories. Some are factual history that has been altered a bit to fit the game's story, but it all fits and worls well together.
Quests/sidequests... you will be smothered in quest objective markers on the mini-map. Up to you if you want to take every side quest offered. Some are very long and somewhat drawn out for the meager rewards you earn. Some are faster and reward you quite handsomely. Some, (Tasks) can be neverending and are simply a way to earn fast gold for your character. No clue if skipping some of the side quests affects the story and game progression. The Main Story quests seem to be the ones you MUST complete.
A definite buy, perhaps best on a deep discount, as the dev studio that made the game went under some time ago, so there will likely never be a sequel made. (Which is a crying shame... I can see so many branching paths that could make for good lead-ins to a sequel...). So your purchase is only going to support the publisher (whom many of us have mixed feelings about). Keep an eye out for sales here and on bundle sites. If you missed it in the Steam Halloween Sale, it will likely come up on deep discount again soon. And at 144 hours so far, seeing many more to come (only 2/3 of the base game maps explored, lol), it was worth it to me to get this game.
As far as replayability, IMHO, there is some, trying out new Races and Destinies, seeing if different choices in specialities, weapons and dialogue choices make a real difference, and completing different side quests and tasks that you skipped in a previous playthrough. I'll let you know about that when I start a second run, in a few hundred more game hours. (You can only have 1 character going, no ability to start a second game with a new characte, without manually copying and moving save files around.) You can save the game frequently (and you should), to go backwards and restart a quest or try to get all achievements in one game. Don't lose track of where you saved and why though... having dozens of self-made checkpoints is great, until you realize 6 of them are labeled with the same town or location, and you don't know which one to choose to go for that achievement.
I like it. I am saddened that the dev studio that made it is gone. And that the game never seemed to get the attention of gamers like I feel it should have. (Which is why I am first playing it almost 6 years after it's release... I never knew about it until I saw a friend's screenshots.). Great older RPG, more open-world than many, more choices you can make to create a more unique playthrough for yourself.

Before I go on, let me tell you this game despite being quite old still holds up and is still quite good.  I think a lot of the professions were kind of dumb and boring but whatever, all around good, buy it.
No I am here to discuss the repeatable quest, likely the laziest design element of this game and most useless.
I'm almost certain the repeatable quest was invented by Blizzard for World of Warcraft.  Blizzard was trying to push end game raiding and loot collection as their big draw.  Only problem was that it took too long to earn money which was needed to pay for ever growing item repairs, reagents and any special enchantments.  Now a good developer would think "how do I make this fun."  The easy solution is to make the experience revenue neutral where you can earn money by doing the thing you do.  You'll do easier content so you can afford more expensive content, easy solution... and I'm pretty sure eventually they did implement something like this.
But in the early parts of the game they asked this question instead "how do we make this game consume more time?"  The answer was repeatable quests.  People could spend all of their time burning through their daily quests in order to get the income they needed to afford all the things that are unaffordable.  So they made it so that people would have to spend 1-2 hours a day "earning money" in the game to afford things.
So Kingdoms of Amalur decided to add about 20 repeatable quests in the game.  They do not earn experience, only money.  By the end of the game you will have earned somewhere in the excess of $10M with a giant pile of money just sitting there.  There's rarely a point where you will buy anything of particular value.... especially if you level up alchemy.
It's a design element that is entirely pointless.  Absolutely no one is going to spam repeatable quests for cash.  In this case the developers of this game asked themselves, "What do all RPGs have?"  And they answered, repeatable quests.  They never once asked themselves if they added anything to the game or whether they are fun.  People like to feel like they have completed everything in an RPG before they move on.  These quests leave you sick to your stomach.

You are a slave in the Amazon queendom of Aravorn. One day, your queen Karen disappears without a trace. Her daughter, princess Loren, is determined to find Karen and chooses you as a companion on the journey, mainly because you know healing magic. Along the way a diverse group of able talents joins the search party, and a war breaks out threatening the lives of all inhabitants in Aravorn. And this is just the front face of an even greater threat.
Loren the Amazon Princess is mix of a role-playing game and a visual novel. The story is told through dialogues, where the player has some opportunities to add a bit of personality to the character he/she controls. This eventually leads to some romantic opportunities with other characters in the party of heroes. Some violence is of course needed once in a while with turn-based fights of classical type where some loot can be obtained. The loot can be equipped, or sold in shops where some other equipment can be purchased. Finally, the player and all companions level up once in a while so all standard elements in a role-playing game are included.
Apart from the tediousness of levelling up and equipping fifteen-ish characters and the annoyingly generic background music, the game is quite enjoyable. Loren the Amazon Princess is neither pretentious nor bland and I am surprised by the large number of hours I have already invested to finally see the end of the story.

Wow. A lot of fun to be had here. Mixes up the visual novel storytelling experience with oldschool style RPG battles (think "Legends of Grimrock" for another modern example of this type of battle strategizing), and this really helps keep interest and attention as you progress through the plot. As you work out the skilltrees in the first few hours, the game is already all but begging for a second playthrough in which you'll actually know how to pair the skills well. Normal difficulty sent a few curveballs at me, so I expect Hard will be quite a challenge. My wish for improvement is probably in the game's equipment offerings. The variety in shop inventories feels sparse considering the number of equip slots each character has and the wide-ranging party you're meant to outfit and maintain, and anyway the paltry amount of gold on hand without continuous grinding seems only enough to buy a couple items.

Really enjoyable RPG/VN, definitely a good buy if you can get it under $10~$15.
The story itself isn't entirely new, but playing it from the role of the "sidekick" adds a nice change of pace. Plenty of enjoyable story and good laughs to be had. Romance options are overwhelming and each plays to the strengths (and weaknesses) of how each character is written, so it all feels genuine and makes a good read. Very open to all types of romances. The romance aspect seems nicely woven into parts of the game beyond the romance itself, and has plenty of detail to it that caught me off guard. Playa' at your own risk.
The art style is nice, good detail. Nothing for graphic-junkies, but has a nice nostalgic feel to it. Combat system is easy to pick up and work with. My first completion was on Normal, and the difficulty was very well done. No super difficulty spikes, but boss fights always felt challenging (excluding once where I was decked out in elements the boss was weak to) and later battles often demanded attention. Music was pretty nice, always fit the mood of the game.
Choice system is nicely done. Nothing overly spectacular, but definitely well done. Some choices reached nearly to or fully to end game. Story has a good variety based on your choices and character.
Is it a good game? Abso-freakin-lutely. Is it worth $20? If you've got the money, yes. I'd highly recommend the Deluxe edition
. If you can get it for $15 or under, you're doing yourself a crime not getting it. Great props and kudos to Winter Wolves, Loren is very well made RPG/Visual Novel hybrid game that I would like to find and see more games like it. I'd also like a direct sequel, but beggars vs choosers.
(Update May 2016): Having done a few more playthroughs, I cannot put enough emphasis the level of detail that was put into the writing. Even triple-A titles rarely, if ever, have such attention and branching in their stories. Each playthrough always feels different, and even the romance/romances you pursue change and alter nearly every scene. Whether you're an achievement hunter or just love good romance stories, Loren The Amazon Princes is beyond worth it. Even full price, this is a purchase worth much more than what you're paying for. Treat yourself by buying this. You'll never regret it.

This game looked interesting to me, so I decided to check it out. The tutorial was fun for me, no glitches experienced. I enjoyed flying and diving into the water at that part. It gave me starry eyes. Then when I actually got into the game for battle for the first time, there was nobody else to fight, so I went to a different server. People were there, but I couldn't spawn in! My dragon was invisible, wouldn't load, and wouldn't move. I assumed it was a poorly made "Spectator mode." So, I joined another server. The round was getting ready to begin in 5 seconds. I waited patiently. As soon as the round began, my dragon was STILL invisible and couldn't move. That's when it hit me. "This isn't a Spectator Mode! It's a glitch!" Literally every time I tried to play, this "no-spawn" glitch occured. Making it very unenjoyable. Sometimes I would even get the "battle prize" at the end of the battle without even having gotten a chance to battle. How frustrating. Later on in the game, I got a crate full of 6 DNA, and decided to get a new dragon with it. Guess what? That new dragon actually worked and allowed me to spawn and play. Wow.
That's a bad sign when your DEFAULT dragon that you automatically get when you first begin the game doesn't work outside of the tutorial. Imagine if I had 0 DNA. I wouldn't have been able to experience anything.
Because of this game-stopping glitch, I can't really recommend this game. It's not even just the glitch though. It's also the fact that there are OTHER glitches, such as the match not ending correctly. It's also the fact that I don't like how the servers work, you can't choose which server you want to go on to. The game randomly picks one. Meaning you could spawn into a game with 0 players, or spawn into a game with 2 players, or a game with 8 players. It would be better if I could personally choose which server I want to spawn in, so I always spawn in a populated one. Also, the aiming. The aiming isn't too great. It's slow. (Dunno quite if that's because of the dragon I chose or because that's how the game is.) You can turn your dragon to face the target head on, but the targetting icon will still be trying to catch-up with your screen. So, because of that, you could be facing a target, but still shoot to your left or right, completely missing the target because the icon literally represents where your dragon will shoot, it's not just there for visual help.
I'll probably keep the game just for something to play when I get a little bored, since it has a nice concept and there are still aspects about it I like, but there are too many cons for me to suggest it to anyone else.

I have been a fan of the Dynasty Warriors series since the PS2 era. When they first introduced the Empires line to the series it was a breath of fresh air in what was quickly becoming a stale room. Four games and two generations later I can say that they seem to be taking more steps backwards then forwards. The game feels....empty. No where near as many cutscenes or special dialogue between characters. The concept of having characters get married and heve children mid game is interesting but that alone is not worth the entrance fee.
I can only hope that Dynasty Warriors 8: Empires was an experiment in new mechanics and not a standard they hope to shoot for in the future. Ever since they ended the Romance of the Three Kingdoms series, none of which ever released in english for the PC, they have had a massive gap in their line up. For a company known for their hack and slash series they actually made the best Freeform Tactical RPG ever in my opinion with ROTK X. Let us hope they look to their past to take steps forward instead of stumbling forward tossing things at the wall to see what the minimal they can make a profit on is.

I really wish I could recommend this game because it seemed to be right up my alley, but unfortunately it fell flat in some key areas that ultimately made it disappointing.
Like many shop keeper style games, this game does a pretty good job making money flow fun to manage, and inventory interesting for a while. The economic core is solid, and once you get a hang of the thief system, and then eventually the robot system your empire will run with satisfying smoothness.
The problem was, where to run it to? For a long time I thought I was running it to the Champion unlock, which was the most "expensive" unlock in the game (don't worry, no real-world microtransactions). Once I actually got that, though, I was disappointed to find out your Champion was just one more menu, and that you really didn't get to interact with the Champion at all beyond pointing him in the right direction and collecting his loot.
So then I thought I must have missed part of it, like these barbarians. Barbarians is an unlock at one point that actually doesn't make sense to take in-game. It causes your shop to be "30% more popular" but then causes near daily Barbarian attacks that often take up a third of the day, meaning it's ultimately a loss of money. But hey, some of them drop loot, and you can always use more dead bodies, so maybe it would be fun and worth it? Unfortunately, this is where the game REALLY let me down. This is the only real combat in the game (You get to zap theives, but they don't fight back), and it totally sucks. Barbarians die in 1 or 2 sword hits, or 1 zap. Their AI just tells them to run forward at you and attack, with basically no strategy, not that they could really strategize given that there's at most 6 of them, and they all have identical melee attacks. There are Barbarian bosses, giants who take 6 or 7 hits to down, but they're super slow, and very easy to out manouever, and that's really the only strategy you need.
There's no opportunity to use all those awesome items in your shop to battle the Barbarians, not that you would even need any extra power seeing as barbarians are so easy to defeat. You can't go on adventures with your champion, so even though you get to arm him, you don't really get to see the benefits or results of that. Basically every item in this game exists as interchangable crap, and that's a real shame.
Compare this to a game like Recettear, which was a shop keep game that I think handled some of these issues way better. Recettear let you go on adventures with your champions, and arm them in a way that you could really tell the effects of your weapons and armor, making them seem like things that actually mattered in a larger world. The combat wasn't super difficult, but it was at least a legitimate part of the game. It also had a story to drive you forward, and real secrets to unlock, while Shoppe Keep has a small list of accomplishments and statues for you to knock out of the way, and not a single character or plot line to follow.
So that's my story of warning, I really played the hell out of this game looking for the gem I thought was going to be there, but was really let down.

TL;DR, If you enjoy SSB, or ever have, this game is worth a try. Even if you don't, still worth a try. Most you'll waste is 10 minutes of your life.
This game is Free, and it is (currently) a very small file size. Download took me 1 minute. This alone should be motivation enough to try it.
I downloaded this game because of the small file size, and the few reviews saying that it was similar to SSB. Which it is. This is a pretty good SSB styled game. The characters are all interesting, and the online is rather easy to jump into. Did not experience any lag (this may differ for others).
The combat is a bit... Meh? I find it fun, however the variety is rather lackluster. A lot of the characters share weapons, with only a few move sets changed up to feel a bit different. Otherwise, the combat is similar to SSB (if not more fast pace). And don't get me wrong, the characters do have different move sets. But they share similar combat styles, so it is odd. The combat consists of fighting with your fists until weapons drop, and then picking the weapon up for a random(? I have no idea how this works, to be honest) weapon. Each character has 2 available weapons that they can pick up, offering different playstyles on the fly.
Alongside your account level, you can level up each character individually. This makes for some interesting... stuff? I just like the feeling that it offers, like every match won/loss is still a step towards something.
The microtransactions were to be expected. However, they follow the theme of most MOBAs. You can get all of the characters for free, just by playing the game (A LOT), or opt to spend money on them. It even offers an "All Legends" pack, similar to Smite's "All Gods" pack. This is where you purchase all the available characters, including any future releases. They also offer free legends on a rotation schedule, so you will never be without a character, and you'll be able to try them all out. They also offer skins for characters, as well as for weapons, and other stuff.

This game is obviously a labor of love for the devs, and it shows.
Describing the bare bones mechanics don't do this gem justice.  It's better than the sum of the parts, and this in spite of ommisions, flaws and some annoying issues that are understandable in an Early Access title.  The cavalry, as they say, is coming but not present.  The melee system is slated for an overhaul.  The almost constant blare of spam music makes muting the offending players a game within the game.  The naval battles lack the hurly burly chaos of the land engagements, and the oceans seems empty by comparison.
It is more Hollywood than history, thank goodness, but the historical flavor is deep, impressive and simply a pleasure to see and hear.  There are Shakos galore, gloriously ridiculous and colorful uniforms, playable drummers, fifers and fiddlers that give buffs to nearby soldiers and sailors, and sound damn good while doing it.
The eye pleasing maps  evoke the far flung battlefields of the era, and combat is variously exciting, hilarious, rewarding and maddeningly random.

Run to get it, on sale or not.

Brothers bills itself as an “epic fairy tale”, and while I’m generally hesitant to endorse that kind of hyperbole, two playthroughs left me with little doubt that it deserves that lofty description.
For one, Brothers unquestionably succeeds as a fairy tale, conjuring up a large dose of the whimsy, scope, and spectacle that one expects from the genre. In the space of a few hours, you’ll tiptoe past giants in cavernous mines, gaze upon the aurora borealis while crossing snow-capped peaks, beat back wolves in a menacing forest, swing through the ruins of an ancient castle, and hang glide through a forested valley. Brothers understands that fairy tales succeed in part because they appeal to the wild, unconstrained parts of our imagination, and it parlays this knowledge into a whirlwind journey that transports the player across a series of diverse Scandinavian landscapes. This Scandinavian character manifests itself in far more than just the game’s gorgeous setting, however. While Brothers is undoubtedly a fairy tale, it is a fairy tale in the image of Hans Christian Anderson and other masters of the genre, a story that eschews the simple platitudes of children’s narratives for a complex, emotional story that is not afraid to confront more mature themes of guilt, loss, and personal sacrifice. The game certainly has a number of light-hearted moments, and they are essential in the development of the story’s unique charm, but it also has distinctive moments of darkness, searing images that wrest us from our contentment and remind us of the risks and dangers inherent in such an epic undertaking.
On a more mechanical level, the control system, which allows you to manipulate both brothers simultaneously, can best be described as “stripped down”. Each brother’s actions are mapped to one side of the controller, with one button (the trigger) solely responsible for all potential actions. This streamlined control scheme saves you the trouble of having to simultaneously execute advanced button sequences, and substantially reduces the learning curve of what could otherwise have been an overly complex system. As it stands, the control scheme holds up well. It takes a little getting used to at first, and there are times when you might wish that you could toggle actions (some actions will require you to just hold down the trigger for extended periods of time), but within half an hour or so you’ll be zipping through the game’s gorgeous environments with relative ease. It isn’t wildly innovative, but it pushes the traditional boundaries of single-player gaming enough to make the game’s numerous puzzles seems fresh and exciting, even if they tend not to be overly difficult to solve.
While I loved the story and appreciated the simple elegance of the controls, I think my favorite part about Brothers is the frequent, subtle nods the game makes to the playfulness and insatiable curiosity of childhood. Our titular heroes may be on an epic journey of life and death importance, but they still have the realistic mannerisms of kids who are just soaking up the wonders around them. They laugh in amazement when a friendly giant helps them ascend a steep cliff. They playfully interact with strangers on their initial journey through their village. They gaze in awe at the stars, pointing upwards at the luminous constellations which light their journey. These small but frequent touches humanize our protagonists and connect them to the player. We might not be able to empathize with the precise struggles and concerns that the brothers face on their epic journey, but we can all relate to the sense of wonder we feel when we witness something heretofore unimagined, a sense that lies at the heart of what makes fairy tales, and this game, special.
It certainly isn’t the only thing that makes this game stand out. The music is as effectively stripped down as the control scheme, a subtle tour de force of haunting chanting and mournful viola and piano melody lines which mirrors the grim nature of the brothers’ task. The environments are lush, beautifully animated, and incredibly diverse. The graphics themselves aren’t particularly cutting edge (rather reminiscent of Fable, actually), but the level design is nothing short of breathtaking, with the traversable parts of it every bit as gorgeous as the wonders visible just off the beaten path. But in the end, I think this game succeeds most as a plaintive ode to the curiosity and wonderment of childhood, and as a reminder that there are moments of joy and laughter to be found even amongst the most dire of circumstances. You’ll be hard-pressed to find a better way to spend an evening.

If you like Picross, you'll like this game. It has plenty of puzzles for all skill levels, and then there are the user-submitted puzzles--like the Steam page says, you'll never run out.
Controls are simple: Left-click fills a square, right-click places an X. You can click and drag to fill multiple squares at once in either a column or row, but not both (so accidentally twitching or flailing won't totally mess up your work). You also can't overwrite a square with the opposite type; you have to--for example--left-click a filled square again before you can place an X. All in all, this makes it virtually idiot-proof and is a good thing when you're focused more on the numbers than the screen.
The original puzzles are well-designed; I've played other games that required guesswork, but although sometimes I get stuck looking for that one square-shaped lynchpin, I haven't yet come across a puzzle in this game that can't be solved by logic.

Let's start with Mount & Blade: Warband's very interesting take on singleplayer where you hire troops, complete missions, fight, trade, conquer and strive to rule the kingdom that I really enjoy. I've never really seen it done like this before, it's really a cross between an RPG and strategy game kind of meshed into one. I think there's plenty to do and ways to play in the singleplayer but if you do start to get bored, there's a million massive overhaul mods which add almost everything you could ever ask for.
Now to what I like most about the game, the multiplayer. This game has the best multiplayer competitive gameplay experience ever. Period. Well, I guess that's just my opinion, but I love this game. There's been other games after this like War of the Roses, Chivalry Online and Life is Feudal, just to name a few and in my opinion, they don't even come close to the perfection of combat that this game is. The combat basics are very simple, and anyone can fight using a shield (to varying degrees, obviously), but when you have to fight with blocking, it becomes a whole 'nother game. The combat is smooth, responsive, impactfut, strategic and intense. I know that's a lot of words, but really, the combat is a masterpiece. I have never seen it done better. Now, what makes the multiplayer even better than just the superb combat system is the class architype system. Yes, it's been used in many other games but honestly, they feel completely different and have their own high skill ceiling to master. The classes, Infantry, Cavalry and Archer/Crossbow all are extremely enjoyable to play and can have a huge impact on the game. The gamemodes are typical of any other game, sieges, one-life round based money system where you just kill your enemies, deathmatch etc. The money system is really awesome the way that the better you play, the more income you earn which lets you buy better weapons and armour. "But doesn't that mean one person could get gear up then wreck everyone?" you might say! But what makes it EVEN BETTER is that fact that since this is a 100% skill based game, a naked person with a club who is the better player can beat a fully armoured knight with a great sword. Anyway, where this multiplayer system REALLY shines is when you have clan wars. Having a group of players assigned to different roles and fighting in medieval combat against other clans with an insane amount of skill involved where one good player could literally defeat 10 people on his own, is immensly enjoyable and satisfying. That being said, it can also be extremely frustrating if you make a mistake, die early, or get focused. The skill ceiling in this game is one of the highest I have ever seen, in any game, ever. One good player can make the biggest difference in a match, and a fight between two good players is a sight to behold, let alone two clans full of amazing players fighting it off - there's nothing more intense.
Now to the negatives I can think of. The graphics are quite dated now even though it's a decent looking game. The factions are quite imbalanced which sucks. The community, atleast in Australia, is tiny now and the competitive scene is long gone. It's basically just a group of trolls who play now which is no fun.

Let me say something before you read this wall of text: I'm a HUGE fan of RWBY, and I DO like this game. But there are a lot of problems that curse this game right now, that's why I'm posting a negative review. If you're a fan of RWBY like me, consider reading this before buying ---
Devs are listening to the community, updates are coming out, and DLC's are being released. But it still doesn't feel like a RWBY game for me. There's no interaction between the characters, just some voice acting and text. It feels empty.
Even some cutscenes would be awesome, then it'd actually feel like we're part of the show, for now it's just "do this, go there, protect this, kill this boss". Furthermore, the new "villain" has never been mentioned in the show, it's like we're fighting in a completely different universe. No background, no context, poorly written story. This is what ruined this game for me.
Combat is awesome though. We could use some more skills (only 3 per character for a total of 4 characters [8 with the JNPR DLC] right now), but many of the combos can also be seen in the show (which is a big + in my eyes), even though ultimates don't feel unique enough: AoE damage and that's it. Something like Yang temporarily activating her semblance, or Weiss using her sword's dust powers, would be more fitting than a plain "kill everything around you with a button" attack. Blasting my RWBY soundtrack while fighting off some Grimm is awesome though, it makes up 80% of this game, but sadly it is also the only aspect of the game that I like.
Challenges are pretty fun but insanely repetitive. I'm still sitting at Rank 2 and I'm planning to reach Rank 10 as soon as possible. But then I won't really know what to do anymore. Maybe Horde mode will change something.
TL;DR Incomplete game, it doesn't feel like RWBY at all, but more of a random hack'n'slash game with RWBY characters and enemies. So much more could be achieved with this game, but hopefully it will be improved.

Before I go on, let me tell you this game despite being quite old still holds up and is still quite good.  I think a lot of the professions were kind of dumb and boring but whatever, all around good, buy it.
No I am here to discuss the repeatable quest, likely the laziest design element of this game and most useless.
I'm almost certain the repeatable quest was invented by Blizzard for World of Warcraft.  Blizzard was trying to push end game raiding and loot collection as their big draw.  Only problem was that it took too long to earn money which was needed to pay for ever growing item repairs, reagents and any special enchantments.  Now a good developer would think "how do I make this fun."  The easy solution is to make the experience revenue neutral where you can earn money by doing the thing you do.  You'll do easier content so you can afford more expensive content, easy solution... and I'm pretty sure eventually they did implement something like this.
But in the early parts of the game they asked this question instead "how do we make this game consume more time?"  The answer was repeatable quests.  People could spend all of their time burning through their daily quests in order to get the income they needed to afford all the things that are unaffordable.  So they made it so that people would have to spend 1-2 hours a day "earning money" in the game to afford things.
So Kingdoms of Amalur decided to add about 20 repeatable quests in the game.  They do not earn experience, only money.  By the end of the game you will have earned somewhere in the excess of $10M with a giant pile of money just sitting there.  There's rarely a point where you will buy anything of particular value.... especially if you level up alchemy.
It's a design element that is entirely pointless.  Absolutely no one is going to spam repeatable quests for cash.  In this case the developers of this game asked themselves, "What do all RPGs have?"  And they answered, repeatable quests.  They never once asked themselves if they added anything to the game or whether they are fun.  People like to feel like they have completed everything in an RPG before they move on.  These quests leave you sick to your stomach.

Kingdoms of Amalur is a wonderful Action RPG.
I'm actually replaying the game right now and am aiming to complete all quests on all maps. While I'm still far from finished, I've already played it through (without the DLC) previously outside of the Steam ecosystem.
Let's start with the bad stuff which PC players will quickly notice:
- The game is definitely built for consoles. The Keyboard/Mouse controls work but are inferior to the controller.
- The graphics weren't very detailed back when it was released and certainly haven't become any better.
- Quests tend to be very repetitive go there, kill X enemies or gather X resources. The voice acting is however pretty good and the dialog isn't bad either.
- Difficulty drops off after a while on all deficutly settings. This is especially true if you're aiming for full completion because you'll be over-leveled.
Now let's end this review with the good things:
+ Attacking enemies with the combos is *fun*. Especially if you're using a controller. The way you knock your enemies around as a warrior, crouch behind unsuspecting victims as a rogue or blast them into oblivion as a mage is just so enjoyable.
+ There are *a lot* of quests and the map is really big.
+ Incredibly unique side characters. I'm not talking about the main companions that accompany you on your main quest. They're pretty bland, to be honest. No, its the little NPCs on the side which give you a single quest or interaction which really pull you in.
+ While the graphics aren't very advanced, they're nonetheless beautiful. It's really enjoyable to run through a cavern with mana flowers which starts to bloom as you walk by.
+ Regions really differ from each other. There are forests, deserts, highlands, mountain ranges, waterfalls... just running through the map is enjoyable!

Time of Dragons is a really fun roguelike game about rebels (the Punks) fighting against an authoritarian government. Gameplay consists of attacking bunkers (FPS sections) to acquire gear, credits and tech, then going back to base and using the collected credits to buy new rooms & room upgrades, which will then grant your characters bonuses. When a character dies, he/she gives a permanent bonus to other characters, and when all characters die, it's game over and you're taken to the marketplace, where you can use your collected tech to buy new Punks, gear, weapons, rooms, room upgrades, room slots and character slots.
As the game is currently (July 29th, 2016), version 0.2.1, the game is still lacking in content, as it'd be expected of such an early version. But even then, I still had some good hours of fun with this - 9 hours registered right now, which were needed to unlock everything currently available. If at this current, early development state I was already able to have so much fun, I can only wonder how many hours I'd put into this once the full version is out.
As it'd be expected of an early version of the game, there are a few issues, but only one is worth mentioning right now, which is an issue with enemy hitbox sizes. Sometimes, the aim reticle can be right on top of an enemy, but it still shows up as white (meaning the shot will miss).
However, the dev is active and listening to player feedback, taking note of all issues reported and fixing them ASAP.
Definitely a game worth supporting and recommending. Even as an early access title, I still recommend it at full price.

REVIEW BASED ON WINDOWS TABLET PLAYTHROUGH
I purchased this game while looking for something to play on my Windows tablet.  While I was able to play on my tablet, I would stop short of calling this game completely “touch-friendly.” It does use certain mechanics, such as “hover” to see info about items and spells, that are not native to a touch device.  While the information is still accessible, without “hover” the process is cumbersome and often frustrating.  Luckily, installing a virtual mouse/touchpad took care of this problem and I could access everything in the game with ease, as though I was using a real mouse.
Loren the Amazon Princess is, in large part, a virtual novel and the strongest selling point is easily the story.  In fact, I feel it is on par with several AAA franchises, such as Dragon Age and the Elder Scrolls.  The characters possess a lot of personality and I feel I really got to know them through the game's dialog and narrative.  While the game takes place in a modest open world and there are a few side quests, it is never so overwhelming that you lose track of the main story and your ultimate goal.  By the final chapter, I felt my decisions had weight and the lives of my party depended on me making the correct decisions.
This game isn't all story, however, and the combat is well done.  It is turn based and conducted on a static grid, with opposing parties each having up to three characters in the front row and three in the back.  While the setup is simple, there are enough skills, spells and items to keep the combat dynamic.  I played on “Normal” difficulty and I found most battles challenging enough that I couldn't just tap-tap-tap through to be victorious.  Strategic planning, resource management and a proper roster were key to coming out on top.
All in all, I was pleased to find the game had many pros and almost no cons.  It is worth a play if this is a game type you either already enjoy or desire to try out.

My favorite thing about this game is the fact that you can play as a male or a female character AND that the majority of the game's cast members are bisexual. Meaning, if you wanted to romance Loren (the Amazon princess), you don't have to play as the male protagonist to do so. (There are two characters of the romance-able cast that are strictly heterosexual and two characters that are strictly homosexual, however, which makes it impossible to gain every possible ending with only one of the playable characters. But hey, more replay value, I guess.) I especially like that a character being bisexual isn't treated as a huge deal. Just a general "oh, hey, you're into both genders". I wish more games (and real life) were as accepting.
*A heads up to people who buy this game though: The game is a pretty solid mix between RPG and dating sim, though it is significantly easier to avoid the romance side of it than say, the Persona games. Vice versa, if you are more interested in the romance elements than the actual RPG gameplay, once you complete one playthrough, you unlock Cheat Mode, which lets you skip battles- should you want to get to a different ending faster.
TL;DR, here's a pro/con list:
Pros:
+The art (whoa, equal opportunity fanservice, what a concept!) More available if you download the Uncensored version...
+Male/Female protag options
+Lots of romance options, because of predominantly bisexual cast
+RPG elements pretty solid: lots of customization, skill trees, a decent amount of armor and weapons to choose from
+You can save pretty much anywhere in the game if you press Esc.
+Lots of save files
Cons:
-There's a pretty big spike in difficulty towards the end of the game *coughfinalbattlecough*
-No CGs or animations
-Romancing people is pretty...easy. There's literally an option that says "Romance". Though, I will admit, some of the funniest parts of the game are romancing characters that *aren't* people you can end the game with.
-When your character interacts with someone, you have to choose between "Joking", "Friendly" or "Forceful" instead of picking the actual thing you wanna say. Often times, Forceful makes you sound like an insensitive ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and Joking an insufferable♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ leaving me with Friendly as the only viable option 9 times out of 10.
I'm not saying anything about the price of the game. It may be a little pricey, but the game isn't *that* short, especially if you play on Hard. I also like supporting independent developers. If it's on sale though, and you're teetering on the fence, just go for it.

I still think you should play this one somehow if you like fighting games, but avoid it on PC unless it's your only option.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

So… Dynasty Warriors 8 Empires (DW8E).
For this review, I will often refer to Dynasty Warriors 8 Xtreme Legends (DW8XL), since I feel like comparing them is a good idea. You will find a TL;DR at the end of this review.
The Dynasty Warriors is known for its good soundtracks. This one is on exception. Sadly, there are not many different BGM since you can only have those from DW8E and DW8.
I don't have much to complay about this game's graphics. They are pretty much the same as for DW8XL. Yeah. The same. Which means that it is a PS3 port with awful pixelated textures. If you can overlook this fact, the game is visually pleasant.
Basically, the gameplay is the same as for DW8XL. Very dynamic, you will probably have a good time with it. There are two major additions:
The reason why I only gave a 7 to the gameplay is because of the game balancing. Forget about other difficulties than Hard and Chaos. Even hard is not really… hard. In chaos mode, if you choose to begin with the item you already unlocked, you will find the game desperately easy. And if you choose not to do this, once you get them via normal gameplay, the result will be the same. Basically, either you will like slashing through enemies mobs like butter, either you will blame the game easyness. Choose your side!
Sadly, the strategy mode is the major point where DW8E fails. It lacks a lot of dynamism; the AI will most of the time act quite passively toward you, which means nothing really exciting will happen. Aside from that, you will be able to unlock different commands (strategies) to use during strategy phase but most  of them will be largely unused except for the sake of unlocking some titles. In other words, the strategy aspect is quite bland and can quickly become boring, solely as a transition between battles.
The Edit Mode! The most interesting feature of this DW8E. Thanks to this, you will be able to create your very own characters. You will get to choose their aspect, their voice, their moveset and even their musous and rages. The editor is quite complete (even if a bit more functions for the face edit would not have been too much) and you will probably spend some hours creating characters. There are a gound amount of gears, but you may find yourself quite limited after some time. Having the Famous Officers outfits to choose from would have been a good idea, but you can't, except for Guo Jia and Guan Yinping.
Note that in some way, the Edit Mode has replaced the possibility to customize weapons we had in DW8XL. It may make your gameplay heavily weapon reliant so that you may avoid some weapons that have bad enhancements.
It's Dynasty Warriors! If you liked the previous ones, you can only enjoy this one too! However, you may find some battle-heavy playthrough boring after a while. (Those that requieres the Defensive Ace title for instance.) Hopefully, these playthrough are not so common.
The porting of this game is awful. Of course, it runs smoothly at 60 FPS but that is not the point. As I said earlier, it's a PS3 port that is already more expensive than the PS3 version, but it's not all. As far as the keybinding goes, it is a bad porting. The commands appears only as keyboard input so if you are playing with a controler, you may have a hard time figuring what button correponds to what action. (And let me give you a quick advice: if you decide to buy this game, do not activate the V-sync. It seems to cause some problems too.)
Oh. And Alt-tabbing will freeze your game if you do it out of battle.
It's a game on which you will most likely spend a good amount of time. There are a few cons, it's true, but overall it's a game you can enjoy. Chances are you will find that it's fifty well spent bucks.

I love Dynasty Warriors, espically those in the 'Empires' side-series. That's why it feels very disheartening to say that I actually
recommend this title to everyone. A lot of what's been added I really do enjoy. The new strategy options and quests are a lot of fun, the 'Way of Life' title system is really cool, and the ability to create custom units, banners, and scenarios/campaigns is something I've been insanely excited for! Not to mention that no matter how repeative the combat is, I still get a kick out of the endless slaughter!
That all being said however, there is a lot about this game that does not sit right with me. There are a lot of cool things you can do during the strategy phase... when the game allows you to do them. If you're trying to progress through the ranks of a kingdom, expect to not have very much freedom to do outside of what the ruler tells you to do. As a Lieutenant/Commander, you're essentially bound to the will of the ruler until you get a promotion (which if your playstyle is more evil, will never actually happen). Even then, once you're promoted to a Prefect, Marshal, or Strategist you lose the ability to do things such as quests, where some of the more unique scenarios and interesting cutscenes are. It's almost better to just stay a Free Officer/Vagabound Unit or just become a ruler yourself.
Another issue is that the game just feels cheaply made, both in it's inital form and its translation. Enemy and ally AI and pathing is abysmal. During some of the stealth quests (which I actually find a lot of fun, espically assassination quests), I've seen the patrol units stuck running in circles or stuck in place because they accidently collided into something and it threw off thier programmed path. It makes it hard to progress when you have 5 mins. and you can't move because the patrol got stuck in a wall and will sound the alarm the moment you step too close.
Presentation is also rather off-putting and a tad glitchy at rare moments. It's funny how the game doesn't even resemble a lot of what the promo screenshots from a couple of months ago looke like. One of my favorite stupid moments was when I was launched fifty feet in the air using the Sword & Hook air launch combo.
The english translation is trash. You can tell they didn't care enough to double check the sentence structure so you don't get things like 'Promoted to Liu Bei by Marshal'. Disappointingly, the English dub cast does not appear in the game, which means that all dialogue and cutscenes are in Japanese. This would not be an issue usually, but in certain cutscenes they don't even bother to put subtitles in. Some of the coolest cutscenes are ruined by the fact that I can't actually see what the characters are saying. This game was made cheap, and it clearly shows.
I WANT to be able to recommend this game to everyone, but these issues are so frustrating and distaseful that even I can't take a sort of humorous pleasure in them. If you like Dynasty Warriors as a series, enjoy a good slaughter, or can get really into character customization I can recommend this game. However, if you're bothered by poor AI, a lack of free choice, and incredibly cheap translations, don't bother or at least wait until it goes on sale. If you hate Dynasty Warriors...well, No. Despite all of this I still enjoy this game for what it is.

EDIT: After going back and re-reading my review I noticed that it was more of a DLC rant than review of the Sims 3. I will now attempt to rectify that. For more on the game, go to the paragraph that starts with "Gameplay:".
Let's establish the difference between "Expansion Packs" and "DLC"
Expansion Packs are like mini sequals to games. They add new features and expand upon the old ones. An example of a Sims 3 Expansion Pack would be World Adventures or Island Paradice. These two added signifigant ammounts of content to the game, as well as add new features like treasure hunting, and exploring, as well as adding new areas and features to base game items, such as the training dummy, and board splitter.
DLC is usually much smaller than an expansion pack in that the ammount of content added is neglegable to the overall experience of the game. This can be seen in things like texture packs, or more specifically to the Sims 3, "Stuff Packs". Or the cutting of features such as the ability to make your own towns, and replacing that with the ability to buy more (non customizable) Pre-made towns.
*Just making the quick note that while you can still create custom towns for the Sims 3, it has been made a far more tiedious process, requireing you to download a seperate program with a less user friendly interface, as opposed to the town creation system used by the Simes 2.
In short, Expansion Packs are reasonably priced additions that improve the overall quality of the game, while DLC is a form of nickel and dimeing justified by the additions of insignifigant content, and should never be the same price as an expansion pack, or full game.
Gameplay: The Sims 3 does not make any great bounds in inovation from the Sims 2 (The sims are a bit smarter, they won't drown if you take the ladder out of a pool now). It's still the same Point & Click style "God Simulator" where you can create your own sims (less customization options for vanilla, more added with each expansion pack), create your own house or customize a pre-made one. (While there is decent variety in furnishings etc. the developers still push the microtransactions with an in-game "Sim Points" store, and DLC page).
You can still do (more or less) all the same things you could do with your sims from previous games, go to school, take several different carear/job paths (more interesting options with DLC), go to university (DLC), get married and start a family (streamlined without DLC), or even more outlandish things like go to the future (DLC), go live on an island with mermaids (DLC) Become a fantasy creature, things from fairies, werewolves, etc (DLC). Become a preformer (Limited options without DLC).
You can also controll the longevity of your sims. Change the lifespan of a sim from 30 days to 1000, your choice.
The game is owned by EA. EA has it's own gaming platform (Origin), since EA has it's own platform, it doesn't bother to optimize or patch any of it's steam variants (See Sims Medieval). So if you wan't to play this you're going to have to use Origin (same with any game made by EA really.)

This is one of those games that had clearly bought many moons ago and has lay dormant in my library, until I decided to have a go at it last week.
Where to start.
It is a short, linear, simple, non-challenging game, with not that much going on...
BUT, it has been a long time since I enjoyed a game this much
- It has one of the best stories I have played in a while: In a relatively short amount of time, Brothers manages to deliver a story which is very relatable, has you symapthising with the characters almost immediately and is a joy to play. There are only a few 'story' games that I have really enjoyed (specifically Portal 2 and South Park: Stick of Truth), but this is definitely up there
- It has great settings, with a variety of location, all which look amazing and really make you feel as if you are in the game, with help from the fact...
- It has an amazing soundtrack, which was so good that I actually listened through the credits, rather than skipping them. It manages to convey the different situations in the game brilliantly. And finally...
- The characters are fantastic. Without a recognisable language and names for most of the characters, it would seem hard to see how this game would work, but it does. It just does.
Overally, I would hugely recommend this game - I have a notoriously short attention span and ended up playing the whole game through within a few nights. It will stick in my mind for a long time and I will definitely be back on it soon, to get all of the achievements and just to play through it again. At full price, yes it might seem a little much for quite a short playtime, but it is worth it. 9/10
