OMG still in shock with the release of empires on PC. I have long heard of it, but haven't been able to play the "Empires" of a Dynasty Warriors game since it usually goes out on PS3 or XBox. And here it is, right on my doorstep, on steam. What better way than to test it out.
This review should be unbiased (Sort of), as I have been a dynasty warriors player of Dynasty Warriors 3, 4, 6 (5 skipped due to not being on PC), 7, and 8. I have experienced all the 1 vs 10000 army battles, while slaying down all that stands in my path (including gathering the courage to stand against the mighty Lu Bu, though mostly getting my blade handed back to me 10 times fold).
And this dynasty warriors has been a blast. You get to keep your 1 vs 10000 action, slaying ten thousands of soldiers and officers on the battlefield (Though I play this as an Assassin's Creed game, always targetting the officers first). The new addition is the Empires side of it, where you get to choose to be a ruler, where you can command you kingdom, and take over the vast land of China, while slowly threatening all the kingdoms around you to just give up and hand over their land to you, or you can join as a free soldier, joining any kingdom you want (I remember the time I joined Cao Cao's kingdom as Ma Chao, then ran away when he started to lose his battles over to Sun Jian's place. Then after that, the same again to Liu Bei, and yeah. You get the idea. Betrayal is the way to live here, like Lu Bu :P).
Anyway, the point is that you can always run around, making friends with officers, even becoming BFFs with them using the "Swear siblings option" (My siblings on my first playthrough were Liu Bei and Sun Shang Xiang (Yes, kind of ironic, judging by the historical site, but oh well), and they helped out a lot (kind of)), though you can only pick two siblings (Which, many people complained about, though many people reasoned with Liu Bei only having two, and if there are more, the "Sworn Siblings" wouldn't feel special anymore). You can also get a spouse in Empires which can provide you with a child to fight for the next Generation (Dynasty Warriors 9!).
The "Create new officers" option was also a blast. I spent basically half of all my Empires time creating new officers and sending them on mock battles. Each of them all had different abilities. I enjoyed ordering them around and having them do formations that made them confused. Anyway, you can also create you own scenerios.
Priceless moments of kingdomship and leadership include the ordering of the final battle. What I tried was putting timid people like Xiao Qiao as the leader. Suddenly Xiao Qiao became very "Leadery" (Yes, the word doesn't exist, but oh well), and started ordering people around. The ironic part was that she was ordering around the Wei Forces (A setting that was accidently set by default, haha).
Another moment is putting Liu Bei and Sun Jian as my subordinates under Cao Cao (The three kingdoms united!). And basically, random officers started taking every kingdom's places. But basically, the empires options are a lot like Romance of the Three Kingdoms in the Ipad or Iphone, if you have played it, also by Techmo Koei. There are a lot of priceless moments I have encountered in this game, that have made me gone WTF in scenerios or have laughed until I cried due to knowing the historical reference and just watching the what-if scenes drives me crazy.
One thing I would have Techmo Koei improve is the price of the costumes. I mean, I like all those costumes, they are very creative as DLCS, but serioesly? $12.99 dollars just for buying a couple of captain falcon and power ranger suits for my characters? I mean okay, it is limited edition, but seriously. Another feature I would have Techmo Koei add is online battles, as they would really make this a very memorable game. But I don't really care anymore. The important thing is that I have experienced Empires myself and have experienced all the cries and joys and laughs of the game.
8/10 is the fairest score I can give for the game, considering all the pros and cons. To sum it all up, this game was truly one of the best so far that Koei had ever released. I really like all the features that have been offered. Two thumbs up, even four with my foot thumbs, for Koei to be creating such a game that has been able to get me hooked for so long.

It's Dynasty Warriors.
You've probably already made up your mind on if you'll enjoy it or not. But, I'll go into it none the less.
Dynasty Warriors 8: Empires is a stand alone expansion / spin off of the latest game in the series. The game sees you create a character and aim to unify ancient China. Forge bonds with historical figures, wheel and deal with leaders, find a spouse and raise a child. As long as it helps you control the country, you better believe that you should do it.
The game is split distinctly into two halves. The first being the action game. This is your standard Warriors afair. Capture bases, commit genocide, do not pursue Lu Bu. As this game is based off of Dynasty Warriors 8: Xtreme Legends, you get two weapons of various abilities and affinities to swap between, air cancels, parrys and much more.
The second half is unique to the Empires series. And that's the politics mode. In between each action sequence you are placed at your home base. From here you make desicions based on how you want to complete you goals. Do you want to protect a caravan that is about to be attacked in hope of gaining some resources and good karma? Do you want to invade a region that is attempting to usurp you? Or maybe you want to coerce folk into joining your cause? It's all here.
Now onto the technical aspects. This is a port of the PS3 version. It does run smoother however, my game never dipped below the 60FPS it was locked at. But in a way, it doesn't excuse the blurry texture or the muddy detail on the armours. One interesting thing of note however: some faces look better in this version then the otherwise supioer PS4 version. It's more of a personal preference of course, but this of course doesn't make up for the lackluster port.
Over all, if you like the Warriors games, pick this up. It's one of the better ones. If you're new to the series however, you might want to look into picking up Dynasty Warriors 8: Xtreme Legends, as that is a bit more beginner friendly.
Also, if you have a PS4 you may want to pick it up over there.

I originally wanted to play this on my smartphone, but couldn't get the app to work right. Thus, I was glad to see the game appear on Steam. There is so much to say about it, but I'll do my best to keep my thoughts organized.
Despite the title of the game, my first playthrough was only 6 hours or so. However, the story has many paths to take, so there's plenty motivation to replay it several times. There are six romance options to aim for, each with special CGs to unlock. There is technically a seventh character to romance, but this comes up at the end of the game, perhaps for someone who didn't romance anyone throughout the game.
While this story takes place in the United States, it's obvious that it wasn't written by an American. Definitely not a complaint, just an observation. I suspect it was written by Canadians, due to Canadian websites being listed at the end of the bonus chapter. There are also subtle writing differences. The British U, such as "Favourite" versus "Favorite." Common phrasing of school grades, such as "Grade 8" versus "8th grade." Also, some of the story involves the jr. high schoolers having to choose which high school to go to. That's definitely not a common American practice in the educational system. In most places, students have to go to whichever public high school is in their district or pay tuition to a private school. However, I'm not an expert on the entirety of the United States, so perhaps some states do things differently.
The best aspect of this visual novel is the representation of marginalized groups of people. The beginning of the game allows the choice of pronoun and whether to look more feminine or masculine. I admit that an androgynous option would've been nice too. Among the characters, there is plenty of queer representation. That was to be expected. Luckily, there is also a lot of racial diversity as well. I believe the protagonist is racially ambiguous on purpose, so most people can insert themselves in his/her/their place. There are actually more people of color to romance than white people. That's probably a first among all the otome VNs I've played. I was really pleased to see an Arab character! He was even developed enough so that the player can learn a bit more about his culture, including when he takes a trip to Dubai.
The bonus chapter is political. I refer to it as the Anti-Trump chapter. The chapter touches on many topics that many Americans are concerned about. Women's Rights. LGBTQ+ rights. Immigration policies. The Muslim registry. The increase in hate crimes. Knowing that many Americans feel helpless during Trump's presidency, the chapter was added to help marginalized groups of people feel less alone. It also gives American and Canadian resources for ways to resist oppression and become more active in grassroot social movements.
Admittedly, the game can use some work. As stated earlier, this game was first on smartphones, and didn't port well for PCs. There is no skip option for already read text, which means lots of rapid clicking after the first playthrough. There's no way to scroll back to change choices. Sometimes a glitch occurs when saving, in which it resets the chapter. While not necessary, a gallery to view CGs later would be appreciated too. There are also a few typos throughout the game.
Regardless of its flaws, I highly recommend the game. The story is slice-of-life, but still very interesting, with decently developed characters and a variety of romance options.

OK, I'm honestly not sure how I feel about LongStory, altough I did enjoy its opening chapters enough to recomend.
However, the longer it went on the more it seemed as if the plot was just being made up as it went along with no direction. Drama for the sake of drama, rather than character development.  I played once through as a female character trying to date Abby, so perhaps it seems more conherent if you are dating someone else.
Game starts off like most romance visual novels, having your character meeting a small group of people that includes your potential love interests (2 males, 2 females).  The only annoying thing really is that the player character, Sasse, having just moved to a new school becomes weirdly obsessed with Em, the person who had Sasse's locker before her and why Em left the school.  Problem is, I was never invested in the Em mystery, I wanted to focus on Abby and Colin, the friends I was trying to make here; but no matter the dialogue options you pick, Sasse remains obssessed with Em, despite the fact nobody else wants to discuss it (Norra says it best at one point, "I. DON'T. CARE. ABOUT. EM.").  The game wanted the player character to want to know why Em left school, and so much of the dialogue was driven by that - but I as a player was never invested.
Then chapter 4 hits, and it introduces a new character,
, the game's non-binary love interest... who royally messed up my dating sim.
Given the number of times the dialogue options kept appearing to get me to date this new character, I could be wrong, but I got the impression this was the writers intended love interest, and despite rejecting them over and over again my intended relationship with Abby was speared as it didn't fit the game's intended story (she didn't even appear in the Epilogue as a speaking character).  Although strangely the very last sentence gave the the option of an entirely new lesbian love interest,
who had not expressed any interest in me previously... so at least Sasse didn't end the game single, even though it came out of nowhere and its not who I wanted her to end up with.
Perhaps other characters have better endings to their relationships.
.  I have considered if the game is just trying to be close to real life, and often people don't end up together at the end.  Even so, given most dating sims end with you being with your romance option (and the game advertises itself as a romance game of your dreams) I feel there should have been a way to end up with the romance option you wanted (if there was I couldn't find it).
I also find it really strange that the epilogue devotes itself to Sasse worrying about her friendship with Marcel.  Again, this could be different if he was your love interest, but my Sasse spent very little time with Marcel, he was the introvert of the group who she had the weakest relationship with  (I had a better relationship with the unseen character dressed as the school's turkeyhawk mascot).  It just seems the epilogue could have instead been an opportunity to engage with your intended love interest and get back in a relationship with them, ending the game on some closure to THAT relationship, rather than spending it on a side character I didn't really engage with (I was only half heartedly reading the dialogue, that's how little I cared about Marcel's arc).
So, as a dating sim I found Longstory really lacking, and there are much better options.  It was certainly not the "the queer positive romance game of your dreams", although I will give credit where credits due, I don't think I've seen a visual novel with a non-binary love interest before.
As a slice of life game however, it was enjoyable.  Takes about 5 hours to complete, and the art style is interesting, the characters are ok (some have better development than others), and before the story started falling apart in later episodes I was enjoying it.  The story also deals with a lot of relevent issues, particularly transgender issues which don't get enough focus in most media.
In all I enjoyed the 5 hours I played, although would have liked the tighter plot.  I enjoyed my time with the characters, just wish I could have had happy ending. Will I play it again? Yes.  And if the publisher makes another visual novel I'd check it out.

The way this game broaches sensitive subjects, like learning disabilities and journey to self-identity, is really well done. Some of these things can be scary for teens to confront on their own so it's really important that more and more of it shows up in the media. Games are a terrific way to do that seeing as how they're interactive and feel more personal. I also think this is the first time I found Shakespeare to be romantic and heartracing—something that never happened when I read it in high school (was more into his comedies). The dialogue is a bit glitchy, especially on the cellphone. Sometimes, text would show up as the protagonist saying it when it should be the other character speaking. If you click too fast, dialogue won't show up on the phone either. There is also no way to scroll back up to see text you might have missed.
The art is simple yet serviceable. It's a bit unsettling that the character's facial expressions and body is completely mannequin-like while their face is emoting in the corner with each new dialogue. A character would be upset and I wouldn't know it if I only looked at their model because their character model would be grinning from ear to ear while their bust shot at the bottom left corner looks like they're about to cry. It breaks immersion at times but it's not enough to make me stop playing.
My main gripe with LongStory is that it needs an auto-read/skip feature so that I wouldn't have to manually click through dialogue. Or at least the ability to go through dialogue using the keyboard instead of the mouse. The romance routes don't branch off very far from the main story so it's a waste of time clicking through text that's already been read. If I wanna play a different romance, I shouldn't have to read through dialogue again. It gets tedious after a while and clicking that much hurts my hand. It also took me a while to realize that you can load other saves with the Play (triangle) button so the game menu doesn't utilize conventional visual novel options.
Growing up in the world we live in today can be daunting but it's gems like this that give me hope that things will be okay. I can see this game as a great teaching tool for a high school Humanities class or something. I hope someone is able to add it to their curriculum! This is a terrific visual novel overall, especially for teens and tweens who are trying to find themselves or who just want to occupy themselves for a few hours.

I'll start by saying this: I know I only have three hours played total on steam, but if xbox live kept track of hours played, you'd see how much i loved this game when i played it years ago. This game has a nice, gorgeous open world full of places to discover, little shrines to find and from which to recieve blessings, decently designed enemies (aside from some of their move sets, I'll talk more about that below) and some world bosses you'll run into here and there, obviously dungeons and whatnot, and some seriously nice gear. Like, World of Warcraft mythic raid kind of gear, and thankfully, you don't have to wait until you're a stupid high level or are nearing the endgame to get some badass armor and weapons, but you dont get them too early on to the point that there's no real reason to explore the world in search of good gear, which I think is a big plus. It has a really good crafting/upgrading system that lets you fuse two of the same weapons together to make the strongest of the two even stronger, and allows you to not only place gems or runes (forgot which one) into sockets, but also lets you physically or magically enhance your weapon, like enchanting or tempering the weapon so it can either do more "penatration" damage, "cold" damage, or..BOTH! Or more, basically if you have, say, ten crystal shards and the right blacksmithing level/skill, you can enchant or enhance your weapon for ten, or if you have twenty, then for twenty, and I'm pretty sure there isn't a limit to how many times you can do that, if I remember correctly. The game has a good amount of side quests, which admittedly sometimes seem a bit generic, but most are fun to play through and complete. Now, the story, I can't say for sure whether or not it had a good ending or whatever because when i played it on the 360 years ago, I would mainly just do side quests, farm for materials to upgrade my gear, and plunder dungeons and sheeit lol so I didn't actually finish the main quest, but I did get like halfway through, maybe a little farther, and i personally like it. For me, it was gripping, interesting, and just overall fun to follow and actually pay attention to, instead of just skipping all the dialog cutscenes like i do for a lot of rpgs, especially mmo rpg's. The only two problems I have with this game are that A. Some of the enemies, like wolves and sprites, do nothing but spam a charge attack just about constantly and it's really annoying to try to fight them because their charge attack is guaranteed to make you stumble for a second, and they give you just enought time to recover from it before they immediatley do it again, and B. There's no way to zoom the camera in or out or just adjust the field of view in general without a program, and that program doesnt even work very well in doing what it was specifically made to do, but that's not really that big of a deal to me. Aside from those two problems, this game is honestly one of the best single player rpg games I've ever played, and I don't normally play single player games unless it's and elder scrolls title, because the elder scrolls is the best. lol Get this game if it's on sale, or pay the full twenty for it, either way just buy it lol Honestly I'd pay more than twenty for it.

Graze Counter is a charming Bullhell from upstart developers Bikkuri Software, and they did a damn good job for their first title on steam. The visuals are clean and crisp, controls are tight and it offers a new take on the old mechanic of “grazing.” It isn't as hard as say most things made by CAVE or the like; so if you're just starting off enjoying Danmanku give it an extra point. Not to say it's easy, there's the great “Unlimited” mode which should give most a run for their money. Also a mission mode, which I did fine a little disappointing, but it teaches the core mechanics very well (Also, beating it unlocks a personal favorite of mine, the boss rush).
The basics are: Get as close as you can to om coming fire, fill your counter meter, hit cancel and have fun. Collect yellow starts to fill your break meter, which you can use as another form of bullet cancel along with added firepower. Beat some bosses, unlock new ships (eight total) and work your way up to beating the very hard but very entertaining Extra stage.
I have a few gripes with the game; the music isn't very memorable, and it lack some basic features. There's no real pause menu, so if you want to restart or quit to the menu you have to hold down a set of keys (explained when you first start the game). There's no online leader boards. The game only saves replays if the option “Skip Dialogue” is off in the menu, and to even see those replays you need to press (default “Y”) on the main menu, NOT select “Score Board.” Finally there's no steam cloud saving, which cost me nearly five hours of lost play time.
Even after all that, I had a blast. Must of, or I wouldn't have unlocked everything twice.
Is it worth the asking price? Yup. But pass on the soundtrack until you play the through the game, maybe you'll like it more than I did.
Major points to Bikkuri Software for giving out a demo to try and their support staff listening to and fixing problems that come up. They made a fan and I'm waiting for their next game.
Final note: As of the time of writing 8/18/17. Use the open beta found in Steam's game options. It fixes the controller problem I had with using SCPTools and the game not starting if more than two game pads are plugged in at the same time.
It makes you sweaty, like mom's spaghetti.But no seriously, it is really fun.

Edit: Devs commented on my review with ways to fix the problems I've listed instead of blaming it on something else. That's actually really impressive to me, and I'll reccomend the game just for that fact that the devs sincerly want to make a good game.
tl;dr: Buy it on sale if you can deal with the lag and general beta nature of the game, otherwise wait until it's out of beta

This game is fun. It also does what it sets out to do well and with a high degree of polish. The people that didn't like it probably should have looked closer at what they were buying before dropping their cash, or just played the game differently.
* The high fantasy setting is incredibly well developed. If you hate high fantasy, don't buy it.
* The lore is extensive, coherent, and superbly written. If you don't like having to listen to tons of dialog...don't listen to it. It's optional.
* The combat is arcade-y, solidly implemented, and generally easy to excel at. If you want Dark Souls, go play Dark Souls. That's an awesome game too.
* Todd McFarlane was the art director, so of course it looks like World of Warcraft. WoW has been copying his art style for years.
* All of the dialog - tens of thousands of unique and meaningful lines - is fully voiced and NONE of it sucks. That's unheard of. If you don't like good voice acting, there is something wrong with you, and If you don't want that much...remember, it's optional and SKIPPABLE.
* The story is well written, and some of the side stories are fantastic. It's not the Witcher, but if that is your minimum threshold, you will probably never like a game ever again. I think what annoys people is that there are no massive twists or big reveals, but that isn't a requirement for good storytelling. If you want that, go play Bioshock again (or System Shock if you are old enough).
* Bugs aren't actually all that common. In hundreds of hours of play, I've only had a couple crashes. Some quests can get bugged, but give me a break. There are hundreds of them - go do a different one.
* There is a TON of content. This is a good thing, but it was my biggest complaint when I first played it, and is proof that I am just as much of an idiot as everyone else here. I got bored on my first playthrough, because I felt compelled to 100% the game. That's my fault, not the game's. If you don't have OCD, you should be fine.
There you have it, the only real problem with the game is that it is too big, with too much to do. What a stinker.
Seriously. The game is good and plays well. If you don't like it, you're probably playing it wrong. Highly recommended.

Put simply, I enjoy this game. I have some gripes, but the game is fun enough to play, and the competition isn't too difficult because the game isn't too hard to master.
As far as my irritations go, they mostly boil down to two things.
1. The dodge mechanic feels absolutely useless. I'm not sure if I'm not using it right or what, but half of the time it won't even trigger. It is perhaps true that I'm far too used to dodging from Smash, but the dodge here only seems to activate if I'm in the air. On the ground, its pointless, as the attacks are faster than the dodge and it gets punished.
2. Jumping is just so damn floaty. If an opponent throws you off the stage, even with no damage, they can simply juggle you downwards. The time you spend trying to get back up or jumping off the wall is enough for them to continue to just push you down. Until they get the kill. Its a bit frustrating and most of the time it seems like there's more point in just letting yourself die, and that's not how it should be.
On a positive note, the game plays wonderfully. Its like a mix between Super Smash Bros and League of Legends, with a bit more slow, deliberate combat. The characters have fantastically funny backstories, and each one is uniquely designed. Sadly, some of them borrow their weaponry and attacks from each other, but maybe its something they'll fix in the futue.

As someone that played the original Deus Ex as a pre-pubescent teenager, I am confidently saying, "Deus Ex is back and better than it has ever been." Human Revolution was just the start and with Mankind Divided this team has reached a whole other plane. From the art and graphical tech, to the level design and the gameplay, Ubi Montreal really nailed it. Secret buttons and vents and conspiracy nuts and security systems and a massive, painstaking detailed hub and levels. It makes me wonder what gaming would look like if every team took four years to make their sequels.
: I didn't even notice the microtransactions until I saw reviews mentioning it. They are NOT pushed inside the game - it's just a pause menu option that says "Store". If you want to buy Praxis kits or Credits for a stupid price, then you can -
.
I would go as far as to say that anyone complaining about the option to buy praxis kits and credits in a single player game should be summarily ignored. This game does not deserve a "Mixed" review score on Steam.

If Steam had the option to rate with the thumb in the middle, this game would get it.
But in the end, there was a hint too much that made me cringe to validate a recommendation.
First this Item-shop-scam they pulled on pre-orderers: Shortly before launch the bonus changed names and the consumable-items in it switched to be one-time-use only, so you can only use the consumables for one playthrough. Costumer-appreciation at it's best...
Controls
While there are worse console-ports around, you'll notice it very clearly at some points.
The controls in general are more wonky and sloppy than in the first game. Sometimes the cover-system glitches and you can't go into the same cover you just used. An edge you used a hundred times to pull yourself up suddenly won't trigger and jumps that a toddler could make don't work because there is no point to pull yourself up.
Sometimes you can't even jump through open windows, Jensen is just hopping in front of it like some kid standing at an ice-cream truck.
Story:
If you enjoyed the two-faced characters and sudden twists in the story of Human Revolution: Be prepared to be disappointed.
In my experience characters who are knowingly involved with the illuminati are so obvious that they might as well wear a "Yay! Illuminati!"-shirt with a blinking pyramid on it.
Same goes for everyone with a secret.
The side-missions are interesting, but also suffer from besaid points.
There is a post-credit-scene again, but while the first game gave you a subtle hint, this time you're almost slapped into the face with what's to come in the DLC/next game. Almost like the "To be continued" at the ending of Matrix 2.
You'll encounter some points in the game where the story has pretty blank spaces, kinda reeking of DLC.
The world:
Prague is pretty, large and detailed. Lots of exploring and a lot of objects to interact with. Better than Detroit or Shanghai. However, Prague is pretty much the only real city. Golem City is named a city, but it's more like you combined the capsule-hotel in Human Revolutions Shanghai and the Blacksite from the HR-DLC. Other than that you'll just have the usual all-hostile missions.
The racism is pretty much the only topic in the streets. There is no one just living his life, everyone is babbling about the racism.
Gameplay:
The new augmentations all have their use and are mostly fun. Especially remote hacking and the tesla-system.
I'm a bit disappointed that the Titan-aug pretty much is a god-mode if you got enough items to refill your energy.
There are no real combos for the augmentations. First off your energy-bar is pretty limited so you can't really combine them yourself.
Some game-supported combos would have been nice. For example dashing through your enemies with your blades extended, multi-dashs through the air...some things that showed how Jensen is adapting to using his augs in combat.
Overall, if you liked Human Revolution, I think you'll like Mankind Divided, but I'd suggest to wait until there is a version with all DLC's on sale.

I personally recieved this game from a friend who had a closed beta code before you could recieve them from their website. He attended an event and recieved the codes from the Devs table.
I was initially excited about this game as I was an avid smash bros. player who really wanted something similar on PC.
Which Brawlhala tries to deliver.
It's understandable that a game in "early access" is not going to be perfect, which is why I held off on my initial reaction for a solid few months, maybe even longer.
I can clearly say now that even through patch after patch, this game just doesn't lead up to the expectations.
Brawlhala desperately tries to fill the niche role of a 'brawler' on steam at a whopping cost of $20. This is utterly ridiculous, a game that looks and feels like a simple newgrounds flash game should not and WOULD not be sold at such an unreasonable price, this is an immediate turn off (as I have stated prior I understand that the game is 'free' from their website but if this game ever comes out of early access, their starting price is absurd).
Regardless of the price, if the game is good... price should be a none issue right? Well yes, however that is not the case.
Brawlhalas controls feel unpolished and floaty, character inputs and actual in-game actions don't represent each other. A game that is targeted toward a competitve audience really doesn't fit the bill if the game has no consequences for your actions. Like other Brawlers you can spike opponents and send them downward with relative certainty that you recieved a kill. However, in Brawlhala, characters have the ability to triple jump and wall jump to contiue their ascention back onto a platform, not only that but certain moves also allow travel in air at ridiculous distances.
On the note of competative play, the game feels extremely casual and floaty for the player, ESPECIALLY with its unique weapons system that allows a player to go from melee hand to hand combat to melee weapon, mid-ranged and ranged combat in the middle of the match. It's interesting to see players utilize items on the field to their advantage by juggling weapons and using them to spike. However it also adds uncertainty to the match. Items that fly in horizontally from side to side of the stage can actually harm you as well as give your opponent a competitive edge. Such as giving them a bomb or a trip mine, in a competitive enviornment if the player is uncertain of the flow of a match based on items drops... Then theres an issue. Especially with a ranked system in place, this is just unacceptable. It almost feels like Mario Kart, except instead of gradually gaining better items as you decline in places, you can simply acquire a star in first place.
My biggest complaint other than the lack of on screen action and input correlation, would definitely have to be the character balancing and damage indicators. I've been pretty composed this entire review but I'm going to have to break my composier to ask why the ♥♥♥♥... did the Devs find it to be a smart idea to use COLOR... as a damage indicator as oppose to possible Numbers? Or Health? Something more concrete than a contrast of colors. Orange could mean death...? or not...? Being red is bad but what shade of orange-red will allow me to UNDERSTAND when it's an optimal opportunity to knock out my opponent.
With that out of the way, let's go ont to character inputs and balancing. I understand that as an early access game, there will be patches and hot fixes very often, however there is no way to understand or learn an enemy character(s) strengths and weaknesses with with a wide array of weapons to use along with the character typing. It seems almost as if every character is literally the same in style except for the weapon utilization that they have. Nothing is unique and it almost feels one sided to fight gun users as a spear user. There's no counterplay and it's just plain unclear to players what they have to look out for. Most of the game is hitting your opponent with enough light attacks until you can use a strong attack, however there is no actual rewarding system to a GOOD player when they land a certain attack. It's genuinely a beat em' up in the likes of castle crashers where you hit the attack button until the enemy dies...
Or of course you can get hit by a bomb and die as well very abruptly.
I think if the Devs were to fix the game in any way. I'd have to say the biggest changes would have to be the core gameplay along with its physics (I'm looking at you triple moon jump) and character inputs relative to their actions.
I really wish I could like this game but honestly it feels very unpolished and dare I say Hyped for literally no reason at all. It's mediocre at best.
On that, all I can say is that you should buy and play Rivals of Aether as oppose to this game unless they can get their act straight.

I had never played a visual novel type game before, so this was something slightly new to me. I can say that it won't be my last though, due to this game. Not exactly long, though full of replay value, you play as one of two possible characters on an adventure filled with light but fun RPG elements. Add in some really well developed characters, and a surprisingly decent score, and you have a game that I found myself playing through three times with a few days of buying it.
Though in terms of things that I did not like, I would have to say the conversation options. Specifically, how you usually only have three choices: joking, friendly, forceful. Just those three options may not always cover how I would have responded. Also, the game simply lists those three options, and not the actual response that your character gives; so at times I found myself thinking "that is not exactly friendly", or "I would not have said that". It is a small complaint, but still.
Luckily, the game usually allows you to backtrack a bit, and with plenty of options in terms of difficulty level and play style, you can play the game through how you want to.
The art is pleasant, though some times repeats (in terms of backgrounds for different settings being the same). It would have been nice to have seen perhaps more variety with the characters and the stances they holding during conversations, but this is again a small complaint.
One last "bad thing" before one last "good thing". The game comes "censored", meaning if you want the version where the characters dress a little bit more liberally, you have to download the demo, open up you regular save file in it, and set the preferences to uncensored, save, and then open up the save file in the actual game. It is all a little bit silly, but worth it. ;)
I was pleasantly surprised by the romance system, and the variety of potential choices it offers you. Whether you play as a male or female character, the game offers you some specific potential romances for each, and they a few that overlap between both. So you have you choice, and I found myself being drawn to and becoming invested in the growth of these relationships.
All things considered, despite the few small grievances I mentioned, the amount of fun, and how much I became invested in this game in such a short time, leads me to highly recommending this game.

Browsing through Steam. Bored out of my mind, wanting a good game to pass the weekend. Find this hidden gem randomly. See a few good reviews. Buy it around noon.
Twelve hours later -- straight mind you, no interruptions since install point -- and it's 1:15 AM. I'm asking where my Saturday went. The game took me for a ride and held time hostage, and I didn't even try to negotiate its relase.
The story is very enthralling. The characters have true flesh and blood to them. I enjoy the interactions I experience. I'm not even aware of my own perspective regarding the decisions and reactions from my party, I'm so wrapped up in the mentality of the PC and the persona that I've become augmented with. I'm having to force myself to step away for a break, lest I end up impacting my health from refusing to put down this novel of an RPG.
To call this game a visual novel mixed with an RPG doesn't do it justice. That's to imply that, in my opinion, a visual novel is expected to have high quality writing and a caliber of a story that's beyond an RPG. To me, this game is the very definition of what a -role- playing game should be as. Your emotions are stimulated time and time again. It pains me to find the lack of words to properly describe how I feel about my experience with this game, for I'm not a great enough writer to convey it.
The gameplay its self, surprised me. It's simple to understand, easy to walk into. This could be your first RPG ever, and you'll feel very comfortable with how fights play out just after a few encounters. You find what works best for your tastes easily, but you're not forced to stay in this comfort zone. Branching out and trying new methods and testing out new ideas is easy. The game permits you to play safely, while at the same time presenting you with a challenge each step of the way. You can see what best affects your enemy, and what your general damage will be. You will never enter a fight you can't win, and at times you will find minor fights off on the side that your party will merely laugh at as they effortlessly dispatch them. That is because you are rewarded for finding an effective style of fighting, while you'll still find the fights progressed by the main story constantly challenging you. There will never be one set perfect way to end a fight. Being versatile and adaptive will ensure constant victory without defeat, but you will be testing yourself as much as your own heroes throughout the game.
You might notice I didn't talk too much about the mechanics -- that's intended. The fights play out like some of the "classics" of the RPG series that Final Fantasy inspired. You have your statuses, your weaknesses, your damage types, your weapon types, so on and so forth. The options to pick from range as wide as you'd want. There's ways to farm up gold from fights if you desire to gear your party to the teeth for each encounter, but you have to explore and test and discover what's the best way for you to earn your gear and gold. I won't spoil that for you.
To conclude, this game is a work of art. Whatever doubts I had of this game were washed away within moments of playing this game. If you desire a game driven by a story that permits you to influence both the outcome of the events, and the progression of the characters through the actions of your PC and the decisions they make, all while staying organic and natural, to be topped off with a solid combat experience that feels rewarding and challenging every step of the way, this game is a perfect pick for you.
I must highligh, you get to make several decisions in the game. Majority of the time, for your character. A few instances, for others. In my opinion, each instance had a natural progression to each stage you encounter. The outcomes felt "real". They don't feel forced, or awkward. In part due to the quality of each character's personality and behavior, in part to the amazing effort put into writing every line of dialogue. I have yet to find a single issue I could mention of this game. If I had to pick a "perfect video game", this would be at the top of my list.

GunZ 2...it's pretty much another eastern 3rd person shooter clone...and a very bad one at that.
GunZ 2 features 2 main modes...a PVP mode, and a PVE mode, and I honestly have trouble determining which one is worse. On one hand, the PVE mode is pretty bad. It's brutally diffucult. You pretty much die after taking 5 hits, so the learning curve is pretty high to start. But even the most experienced player will find it's impossible to clear the PVE mode because of the shockingly limited ammo supply characters have. With little to no way to restore ammo, you find yourself, one way or another, out of ammo, and forced to use your melee weapon...in a gunfight. Death usually follows shortly after that...and then the game will try to pressure you into buying revival tokens. Clearly, the PVE mode was crassly put together to force players to buy revival tokens. It will take close to 30 tokens to clear your average level, so unless you enjoy paying close to 60 dollars just to clear a level, I suggest you steer clear...
Despite how awful the PVE mode is, the PVP mode is worse. Basically, it's entirely pay to win.
Once you're dropped into a PVP round, which will most likely lag and stutter to a strong degree, you'll notice the only way to really get kills is to use a melee class, or a sniper rifle.
But not just any melee or sniper rifle, oh no! You need the special premium gear, which can only be obtained by using this game's abomination of a cash shop, the "telsa shop." Basically, while other games charge you big bucks for game winning items, THIS game charges you big bucks for a CHANCE at game winning items.
The kicker? Even if you spend hundreds of dollars (which is, by the way, a low estimate of how much it will cost)
and get lucky, there's no guaruntee that your class will even be able to use the item you get.
Basically, this game is a very expensive coin op. Pay for extra lives, or you can't have fun in PVE.
Pay for the best gear in the game, or you can't have fun in PVP.
Best to stay far away from this game, unless you happen to enjoy flushing money down the toilet.

Despite being completely free, this is one of the most gripping visual novels I've read on Steam!
It is quite a short story; someone who reads fast might find themself done with it after about an hour, but there are multiple paths to take and several different endings. I found myself so engrossed in the story after reading it the first time that I went back and tried a different route in order to discover more about the characters and the world in which they lived. What I found exceeded my expectations. I ended up reading the novel five or six times, each time learning new things and seeing a new side to the story. In the end I had read all there was to read and experienced each ending, including the true ending which you can only get after completing the two different majors routes. I felt this ending really ended up tying everything together in a nice fashion and left me fullfilled.
The writing is both straight forward and poetic, it has a lot of work put into getting through things like emotions and enviromental details to the reader. It was not a particular difficult read, so it should be a good choice for anyone interested in drama and thriller novels. I say thriller in a sense that I felt the story had a horror setting and some elements of horror, yet I personally did not find it scary. It was however able to get feelings of sadness, happiness and chilling vibes. The story does involve concepts such as murder, and it does involve a few scenes that may be unsettling to some, so it might not be suitable for children or anyone who finds these sorts of things unappealing in a novel. I personally felt it was kept to a pretty mild level however, and the story put the most emphasis on building up two diverse characters and letting the player choose how to deal with being trapped in a dark mysterious forest.
Apart from a few spelling mistakes and minor errors in terms of grammar, I felt that the writing was of high quality and at no point did I struggle to understand what the author was trying to get across. The novel is also available in a few different languages, so it should be quite accessible regardless of your english skills if you understand one of the other languages better. I do not however, and as such as I have only read the english version and can not judge the other translations. I do believe they should be of high quality as well however.
The writing is accompanied by music and visuals; including characters, backgrounds and some effects. I felt that these all did their jobs well, although of course preference in terms of art style is something that is also highly subjective. The art is cute, and the characters have a few different poses and face expressions to further emphasise emotions. The game's soundtrack may not be too vast, but the songs are pleasing to listen to and range from eerie atmospheric tracks to dramatic choires and finally to melodic piano compositions. There are a few effects as well, and although they aren't too noticable, they do help with the atmosphere and give the world further depth.
I very much enjoyed this novel! I recommend it as a dramatic halloween story for anyone who doesn't mind a bit of fantasy violence and would like a rather short but gripping tale that takes you for an emotional rollercoaster and finally warms your heart. If this was for sale rather than free, I sure wouldn't mind paying a couple of euros for it as I valued it far more than some other novels with pretty hefty price tags.
I can't wait for your next project, Eternal Night studios! Thanks for a pleasant read and I hope I can support you in the future. Trick and Treat gets a heartly recommendation from me!

LongStory has some decent ideas when it comes to, well, story. The bullying aspect of high school definitely rang true, and the online relationship with Nora was very similar to the internet relationship I'm actually having. Unfortunately everything built around the story is lacking in a way that means I can't recommend a purchase in its current state.
LongStory was initially designed for a mobile platform, and it definitely shows. No sound effects, no text skip, and an extremely clunky 'episode' system that means one wrong choice can force you to give up half an hour of progress. Some of the decisions I had to make were two options I never wanted to select (blabbing about the secrets of someone who's sworn you to privacy, where there's no third option to keep quiet). A lack of transitions and repetitive music make the pacing very uncomfortable at times, and a complete lack of internal dialogue/narration causes the text to feel clunky (especially whenever it's describing what the TurkeyHawk does).
If it was a more competent port better designed for PC, I might've been willing to stick with this game for longer. As it is though, I don't think I have the patience for it.

I have played many visual novels at this price point, and can easily say that for your money, LongStory is the best bet.
The art is super high quality, the writing is incredible, and the overall experience perfectly weaves the nostalgia of high school with plenty of humor and sadness.
You can tell, from the jump, that the queer experience is important to the developers. But I think the thing that makes this game stand out over most others in that particular sphere is that it tells a story that anyone can relate to, and it puts you in charge of exactly how to tell that story.
It has some of the most genuinely engaging choices in a game like this. In TellTale games, most choices are a binary between two routes, but in LongStory, choices genuinely feel organically linked to the kinds of slice-of-life high school drama that don't shake out easily. Sure, you can tell this girl you like her, but what if she says no? You can ask for a guy's phone number, but what if he gets freaked out? These things sound mundane on paper in comparison to Zombie Attacks or Intergalactic Space Conflicts, but the game's writing is so immersive that I found myself caring much more about whether to hit on one of my friends than I ever would about shooting an army of space aliens.
I've played enough visual novels at this point to be able to easily recognize flags that will dramatically shift the story in one direction or another, but in LongStory, no single choice feels like it is going to set you down an A or B path. Instead, the game feels like it is genuinely evolving in step with your choices as you make them, telling you a story that is actually tailored to each one of those choices, rather than throwing five or six smaller choices at you until you reach a larger, more divergent decision.
There are a few very minor technical hiccups here or there, but considering we're in a time when every Triple A game has them, I can confidently say that the few quirks I've run into so far don't really detract from my overall enjoyment of this stellar narrative at all.
It probably comes off like I'm writing a love letter to this game because it speaks to my experience, so for those of you who get annoyed by "issue games," I want to make it perfectly clear that half of me expected to be bored stiff by this game. I don't particularly identify as queer or trans, and it's only through the writing and storytelling of this game that I found myself relating to its subject matter. Every conversation plays out like a hilarious and awkward back and forth between the main character and a cast of colorfully defined romance options and side characters, and it feels like a genuine picture of High School romance and intrigue.
I can see where that might not be for everyone, but I think this game has a much wider audience than people on the fence might think after a first glance. The themes are universal, and the game gives you true ownership over your identity as the player, giving you boys, girls, and even a giant, gesticulating Turkey to fall in love with.
If you're a fan of the genre, Life Is Strange, or are just looking for a totally different kind of video game narrative, you won't go wrong with LongStory. I'm going to be thinking about it all year. It's the kind of game that reminds me just how powerful a medium games are for telling stories.

Now with that out the way, this is not a bad port now that Dynasty Warriors fans can finally play an Empires game on the PC. is a 'good enough, I guess' PC port despite the biggest downfall once again being... no online multiplayer! But there are still online functions available such as the ability download and upload custom created officers. The graphical quality is great, more so on the character models themselves than the environments, but could still have been improved vastly if the PC version was given some more care. (Maybe a future HD texture pack, Koei?)
There isn't much of a story to be had in this iteration of Dynasty Warriors 8, but instead you more or less craft your own in the Empire mode. You'll be making many choices that have various beneficial or disadvantageous outcomes and that will also lead your character down the path of good or evil themselves. (Think Liu Bei or Lu Bu) You don't however need to be the leader of an empire, you can instead serve under another and get promoted in rank (thus make more choices each turn) as time goes by. The choice is still there to betray or secede your current ruler though.
If you're a big fan of the Dynasty Warriors series, then you can expect hours upon hours of content to get through. The maximum amount of turns allowed per new Empires session is 600 - giving you plenty of time to unite China under one rule. The addition of 'stratagems' and the marriage/children system also gives more purpose to the game than from previous titles - as everything from the past Empires iterations has been improved upon here, including the custom character creation which provides a huge amount of customisation options.
My biggest gripe was in fact the price of the game, at least in my region. £40 translates to paying more for the PC version (which has no online multiplayer) than the console versions which basically includes more content because of this. However, I decided to buy Empires regardless because I knew I could personally still get many hours of value from it. Though, being the owner of a past Dynasty Warriors 8 title on Steam, I was expecting at least some form of a discount due to the high base price for this title.
Highly recommended to past Dynasty Warriors fans as DW8 itself was one of the best titles in the series yet. As for people new to the series - I would recommend you go back a step and play the original DW8 title first. Empires expands upon this version and takes it almost in an entirely new direction, as have done all the past Empires versions.

I guess I can't really do a full review yet for now, since I've only played through the game once and romanced one of the characters (Colin), but I'll write my thoughts based on my experience and update this review in the future when I've explored more options.
So I was really excited about this game because I was always really itching to play more LGBT+ romance games, and I'd say that I enjoyed this one despite its flaws. I liked the characters and the charming art style, and it was overall a pretty immersive game. Well, for the most part. I liked that there was so much drama, although if teen drama isn't really your thing then that might be a drawback for you. Personally, I'm a messy b*tch who lives for drama, so I was totally eating it up.
There are a few things I disliked about this game though that I hope the developer could fix. My biggest issue was that a lot of the time I felt like choice was taken away from me, and my character acted in ways that I NEVER would've acted and I couldn't help that. They can be extremely nosy and intrusive, and a particular spoiler-y instance was when

Also I just wasn't really satisfied with the final two chapters. Chapter 8, the second to last one, I think should have been the last one and also should've been optional, because it's a standalone chapter that has no relevance to the story or decisions you made in the previous ones, so I felt like the game shouldn't have made that chapter mandatory, or at least saved it for the end. And also with the last chapter, I thought it focused WAY too much on one single character, and said character wasn't even the one I romanced, so I wasn't really quite satisfied with how everything ended. I'm planning on doing another playthrough romancing that character I mentioned, since the last chapter is so focused on him and it would probably more meaningful if he had been a love interest.
A few small smaller gripes I have is that there's not really an options menu to speak of, just an option to mute or unmute, and also there's no "skip" feature that's really handy in VNs if you wanna breeze through dialogue you've already seen. I'm really hoping the developer adds this because as it stands, starting another playthrough is very time consuming.
With all the criticisms aside, I do think this game is worth a try, especially with this current sale. I just hope that the developer will tend to some of the fixable technical issues with the game. I will update this review once I've played through more scenarios.

There are plenty of pros and cons to this games. Especially if you're a fan of the show already.
PROS:
The graphics while nothing ground breaking looks like the show. The animation is certainly fluid.
If you're familiar to the source material you'll notice things. Such as certain songs from the show, locations, and some of the comedy (especially from Professor Port)
Each character feels different. Yang for exanple is slower yet hits harder, Blake is speedy but takes more damage, Weiss has a variety of attacks the others don't, and Ruby is fast and has a wide reach.
Even the enemies feel different. Each Grimm acts in a different way, has different attacks and signals, etc.
CONS:
The game is a traditional hack and slash. Fighting hordes of enemies to progress, Grimm popping out of every corner. Its not bad but it can be repetitive.
The characters say the same things when they do things. Such as if you fail a mission the exact same dialogue will play from the professor. When you pick up an item you'll hear the same dialogue. Things of that nature.
The leveling system doesn't feel that essential. They do give some perks but nothing really unique. Faster health recovery, more powerful attacks, things of that nature.
All in all I'd have to say if you're a fan of the show and wanting to play as the characters you're going to enjoy it. At least a bit. If you're just wanting a 3D hack and slash there are a lot worse. However if you're expecting a huge game, you may not find it here.

I haven't sunk anywhere near as much time into this game as I had the last DW game on here, however, I think it's time to give it a review anyway.
This game does still suffer from many of the issues I listed in my previous review of DW8XLCE, small number of resolution options, no mouse functionality, obscene keyboard defaults, low amount of graphics options, a lack of multiplayer online, and it being over-priced.
As with DW8XL on steam, this is a port of the PS3 version of Empires rather than a specific PC version and this is clearly reflected in the visuals. It must be said, however, that this game is a lot more functional at Launch than Xtreme Legends was at it's launch. Indeed it would seem that this is the most functional version of the game on day one in the EU & States, as the console versions are apparently choked with bugs, one of the most common being character voices being switched in immersion breaking but amusing ways (Ma Chao speaking with Diaochan's voice for example). This is absent in the PC version, along with a series of other bugs.
It seems that the PC version comes with much of the pre-order DLC avalible for other versions of the game free in the base game, another plus. Another rather large plus, though not one that has been openly talked about by Koei itself or even by the community at large, is that the costume DLCs (the most expensive DLCs for both Empires and XLCE) are transfereable from one game to the other so as long as you own the costumes in XL already, there is no need to buy them again for Empires, and if you buy costume DLC you didn't have later in Empires, they'll unlock in XL. This is a small but nice touch and one that I am pleased to have found in the game. One last major positive is that this game (I'm uncertain of if this is true for the other versions of the game) has every armor, hair, and accesory peice of CAW from Dynasty Warriors 7 Empires avaliable at the start, including the DLC ones. Once the inevtiable DLC packs for CAW begin to come out, I think I may lose contact with everyone and everything I know and love due to sheer obsessive focus on creating new custom officers!
A big problem I have, however, is that (at least in the UK) the PC version, despite having the graphics of the PS3 version and a lack of online co-op, is the most expensive version of the game avaliable that I've seen. Amazon sells the boxed copy of Empires 8 for 29.99, I beleive the PS3 digital version is slightly cheaper, and yet here we have less content than both of those versions are are paying a full £40 upon release. This was also the case with XLCE (though with a higher price-point there) and is something I honestly don't understand. Why are we to be made to pay more when we are granted LESS features? How is that fair?
Regardless of the issues that I have raised, I will still be playing this game to death. I adore the Dynasty Warriors series, the Empires spin-offs especially, and this one seems to be the most well featured of all of them as of yet.  Despite this, it is over priced, not as well featured as the other versions of the game, and despite being on certainly the most potentially powerful platform, we recive the less graphically impressive version of the game. Having said this, Koei does seem to be slowly learning that it actually HAS an audience on steam, as more and more of their games are slated for release on steam in future (if I have the cash I will CERTIANLY be buying Bladestorm Nightmare when it comes out next month) and it seems that with each release they are slowly improving their PC releases over-all. It's a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ situation for us to be in, having bad ports now and having to wait for them to get better, but for fans of Koei games (such as myself) surely it's better than what we had before. I've been playing this game for awhile and I personally enjoy it. Most of the bugs are UI/lobby related and the core game-play works well enough for a free game. Sure, the recent update added micro-transactions, but it's VERY far from a pay to win game. After having it be 100% free for awhile, I didn't mind pitching in $8 for a new dragon to support the devs.
My advice: Play this game with minimum expectations and just play it for awhile. Sure you'll die a lot at first, but it becomes enjoyable once you eventually learn how to move and shoot. Overall I give this a
. It's a fun game, just that the bugs need to be worked out before I'd give it an 8-9/10.
- Dragons with FRICKIN' LAZURRS strapped to their back!
- Decently balanced game-play. Each dragon class is the same for everyone, each weapon type damage the same as everyone. Doesn't matter what level you are. If you screw up, you die just as easily as everyone else. Although that's not to say there isn't room for improvement.
- "Paid dragons" are obtainable with normal game-play, and don't give an large, unfair, advantage. I bought one of the dragons and it's stats barely differ from it's default counterpart. Mostly cosmetic changes with a new ability, but still relies mainly on player skill. Advantage is marginal at best.
- Game-play is quick, fun, and straight-forward for the most part. This is the kind of game you play if you want a break and want to shoot down some dragons.
- Graphics are okay, but sub-par. Sound design is rather simple. There's definitely room for improvement.
- Learning curve ranges from moderate to hard. This is in-part due to being in the same room as experienced players. You will die a lot before you get a feel for how to move and shoot in this game. Then again, that's the same for most games.
- Bugs. Bugs everywhere. Ranges from spawning outside the insta-death fence, to crashing when trying to load certain maps, to errors when unlocking dragons. The UI feels really clunky. Features like room/lobby info are missing, there's no chat history, and dragon selection in-game sometimes glitches. Just to name a few.
- No option to chose a room. Can't even know how many people are in a specific game mode without entering it to check. It's just "choose a game mode and hope for the best."
- No team auto-balance. It just places people in each team in order of when they first joined the room. This sometimes leads to all the high-level players being on one team, and low-levels on the other.
- Not a whole bunch of people play. Depending on what time you're on, all the game modes can be empty. Granted, people do still play and there are occasionally have full rooms.

This is an incredibly charming doujin shmup that takes Psyvariar's 'grazing' mechanic and pairs it with a meter-building system: indirect contact with bullets (i.e. using your sprite but not your hitbox) causes you to build up the meter of a 'Counter' laser, which rips through bullets and enemies to produce lots of yellow stars, which in turn build a 'Break' gauge. Entering Break Mode allows you to deal significantly more damage to enemies, who will now drop lots of
stars, which are subject to various score multipliers at the end of each stage.
There's a really gratifying flow of tension and release to this dynamic, as you try to avoid expending your Break too early on minor enemies, in spite of the onslaught of their bullets, and save it for more lucrative targets such as big tanks and bosses. Stages are short and tightly designed, every placement of every enemy screaming for you to squeeze more and more scoring potential out of it.
The game's absolutely chock full of stuff to unlock, too. There are eight playable ships in total, each one (beyond the first two) unlocked by clearing the game with a different character. Apart from two which are souped-up versions of the starting ships, they all present vastly different ways of playing the game. One, for example, has no Break gauge but two 'options' which deal vicious damage when you're grazing, while another can only fire at short range but comes equipped with the lethal laser-sword from the developer's earlier Kirisame Blade series. There are so many play styles covered that you're bound to find something that gels with you.
Aside from the main game and its three difficulty settings (Novice, Arcade and Expert), there's a robust Practice Mode which allows you to set not just your stage but all sorts of starting parameters (gauge percentage, score multiplier, rank, etc), and a Mission Mode which presents you with various tasks to complete, each one teaching you something about how to play the game well. (This is so useful that I'd recommend playing through at least half of them before really getting stuck into the core game.) In addition to these, there are three Omake modes, two of which are unlockable by clearing the main game once and one by clearing Mission Mode. These are Boss Rush, Unlimited Mode and Extra Stage. From what little of it I have seen, Unlimited Mode appears to be simply the main game played at Expert difficulty and set to the highest rank from the beginning ('rank' in the context of shoot-'em-ups is a clumsy term for adjustments to difficulty made on-the-fly according to performance). Extra Stage is a unique and extremely difficult level which also begins at max rank.
The main game isn't forbiddingly hard, though. In fact, it's an easy one to recommend to newcomers to the genre, since it's a reasonably easy single-credit clear on Arcade difficulty (my last run was a single-life clear and I finished with nine lives in stock, because it hands them out like sweeties), and strongly encourages the habit of playing to maximise your score.
It's also full of nifty references to other shmups, though it doesn't lean on any of them for inspiration. The two ships playable from the start recall the Vic Viper and Lord British from Gradius. Stage two is named Crystal Labylinth (sic) after one of arcade Gradius III's most notorious levels, and features the same projectile ice blocks (though with much more predictable behaviour). This stage also features in its background a grid pattern laid over what appears to be a city bathed in blue light, which is very redolent of Image Fight's aesthetic (the first half of Image Fight taking place in a training simulation). Many bosses have a Raiden-style red jewel at their centre, and the 'Counter' laser itself is modelled on Donpachi's trademark infinite streams of energy. There are loads more.
Graze Counter's a lot of fun and I think you'd have a blast with it. The core mechanics are so satisfying to use that the game manages to feel thrilling even throughout Novice mode (where there's no harm in starting), and its tightness and brevity make it a manageable one to learn and go a long way to ensuring you'll want to return to it repeatedly to tidy up aspects of your run. It appeals to newcomers and old hands by being both easily accessible and hugely rewarding of efforts to dig deeper into its systems.
Graze Counter is a rewarding bullet hell experience in which you graze bullets and counter them.

A fun little indie shooter with a 16bit aesthetic.
The basic concept of the game is that you build up a meter by grazing (being near) enemy bullets. When the meter is high enough, you can activate a laser counter attack that destroys enemy bullets. The ability to frequently cancel enemy bullets combined with fairly generous slow down makes this game more relaxed than most shooters. I was able to clear expert mode with Type-1 after about 2 hours using no continues and with 2 deaths. If you want a bigger challenge, you have the option to turn off the slowdown which does make the game significantly harder.
There are a good amount of options available. You can select from 3 difficulties, and pick 1 of 3 different bonuses for your ship. You can also choose an alternate mode that disables your main shot in exchange for making your counter laser much stronger. For the ships, you have 8 to choose from, though 2 of the ships are just overpowered versions of the first 2 ships.
A mission mode containing 20 missions serves as the tutorial. Each mission is very short, and teaches you about different mechanics in the game. They're generally pretty easy and you should do them first to get a feel for the controls.
There is an unlockable boss rush mode, bonus stage and extra difficulty setting. Slowdown is absent in the latter two modes, and the bullet speed is turned up on top of that. Unfortunately, you can't save replays in the extra difficulty.
Of course, like all games, there are some flaws as well. The english translation isn't great (which is kinda weird considering there are 6 people listed under 'proofreading' in the credits), though the cutscenes can be disabled so it doesn't really matter after your first time through.
The stage design is fine for the most part, though there are some problem spots. In one section in stage 3, a swarm of enemies comes up from the bottom left side of the screen without warning, which will probably kill you the first time you see it. Another issue is that a couple enemies fire from further down on the screen than they're normally allowed to, which can kill you if you weren't expecting it. A similar problem exists in expert mode where the enemies can shoot suicide bullets. If you kill enemies that are offscreen, they still spawn suicide bullets, which sometimes leads to bullets coming out of nowhere from the side of the screen.
The last main issue is the lackluster scoreboard. It's unclear it even exists; if you select the scoreboard option on the main menu, it takes you to a mini scoreboard that only shows the top score for each mode. The real scoreboard and replay system is accessed by pressing the 'slow movement' button on the main menu (note that for replays to be saved you must have cutscenes disabled) Additionally, the different ships are not balanced in terms of scoring, or seperated on the leaderboard, so all your scores with the weaker ships will get overwritten when you play the stronger ones.
To summarize:
-The counter laser is a satisfying mechanic
-Full keybinding support
-Practice mode
-Good range of difficulty and options (though generally on the easy side unless you turn off the slowdown)
-The translation is pretty rough
-Obtuse scoreboard
-A few areas where enemies/bullets can come from places they shouldn't

As disappointing as it's promising, Kingdom Of Amalur: Reckoning has good combat and character progression systems, which unfortunately cannot compensate for its flurry of bad technical/design decisions. A great concept, with a bland execution.
Several other reviews mention the general boredom emanating from the game. After reading, I wondered "How bad can that be?"
Not recommended.
+ Depending on the player's taste, the art style is a hit or miss but still got old very gracefully
+ The combat system is great
+ The levelling system is interesting
+ Lots of content
± OST is uneven, sometimes great, sometimes forgettable
± Fights could leverage the combat system way better
± Character design is generally unoriginal
- Generic story
- Bland, mute, expresionless main character
- Generic level/world design
- Drop system is antiquated (if enemies visibly drop weapons, LET ME PICK THEM UP!)
- A giant heap of bad game design that constantly break both immersion and motivation
- Not challenging enough to justify its length, not innovative enough to justify the lack of challenge.
Kingdom Of Amalur: Reckoning is a wRPG which has everything needed to become a force to be reckoned with: you're spawned, resurrected into a vast world divided by an ancient war between Fae people and Humans, and it is up to you to learn more about your own destiny through a huge amount of quests and lore.
Clever skill tree and destiny system support a great combat gameplay. Combat is a cornerstone of this game, and doesn't feel like it has aged even if the game was released in 2012. The art style, if not too out of the ordinary, has also aged very gracefully.
Unfortunately, though, one can only flee the curse of aging for so long until it catches up. KoA:R skin might still be silky smooth, but its values are from another time.
In 2017, after the advent of Skyrim, Dragon Dogma, The Witcher 3 and Zelda: Breath of the Wild as new standard setters, the game feels like it's been collecting all the typical RPG design mistakes to combine them into one stack of fun-killing can't-have-good-thingness.
Where we could have had a truly open world experience, testing our mettle in beautifully choreographed combats and transporting us into an epic, emotion laden story, we get RNG in all the wrong places (wolves dropping iron swords and theft spotted in empty rooms), a mute hero meddling with underwhelming characters (yes, we get it, you were a drunk, could you please stop mentioning it until your next Fateweaver Anonymous meeting?), useless dialog choices (the obvious answer VS the blurt on crack cocaine), and a level design so dull the whole game couldn't be less linear if it were a never ending corridor.
This, probably comes from a design perspective where players have to go through the game 'as intended by the developers', instead of delivering a universe to explore on their own, along with the mechanics to do so in a creative and enjoyable way. Maybe it still worked in 2012?
On the top of these already immersion-breaking problems, come several technical issues, and man how do they pile up. The camera seems to never quite catch the right angle, the HUD is humongous (about 20% of the screen space) and can't be customised, the main character pulls equipment out of nowhere (I know, I know, but really, every time a non-magical shield seems to unfold from the palm of its user out of the somehow dimension, a baby dragon dies), loading a save from an empty dungeon spawns enemies at you as soon as the game is loaded... and there's more, but I think you get the gist by now.
The cherry on the sugar free, carb free, gluten free cake: in normal difficulty, fights can be summed up by spamming a couple of technique again and again, without any real strategy (disclaimer: I'm not even a fan of hard games), so much that even the city guards aren't much of a challenge. The lack of a tactical dimension defeats the whole purpose of the combat system, and adds some boredom to the mix.
Some titles do have their flaws, I am thinking of Sleeping Dogs, another 'Good concept but wew is this thing finished?' kind of game, which is full of good ideas but whose design flaws make it permanently walk the line between enjoyable and mediocre. Sleeping Dogs, though, tries. There is a story, there is some sparkle to the work, some vibrance here and there that helps players stick with the story and make the whole work worth more than the sum of its parts.
KoA:R though, is the opposite, and lets the sum of its parts overpower its general concept, leaving the player languishing for a potential that never really manifests... kind of the feeling you would get if you were expecting to drink Sprite and ended up gulping down soda water (no offence meant, soda water).
In conclusion, I can't recommend this game, even at a discount price, except if you're using it to study bad design decisions (then it's a huge bang for your bucks).
